articles.title: Nuevo GTA 6 hace que Xbox cree una consola en forma de cocodrilo: se llama Xbox Series X-BITE y se va a sortear
articles.text:
La Xbox Series X-BITE es la respuesta de Microsoft a la expectativa generada por Grand Theft Auto VI. La compañía presentó una edición especial que esconde una consola Series X funcional dentro de la figura de un caimán de tamaño real, inspirada en la fauna de Florida.
El anuncio llega semanas antes del lanzamiento del videojuego de Rockstar Games, previsto para el 19 de noviembre de 2026. Aunque no hay un referencia textual al juego, debido al acuerdo de marketing entre PlayStation con Rockstar y Take-Two Interactive, en la presentación hay varios detalles que dejan claro el motivo de esta edición especial, que no estará a la venta.
Cómo es la consola de Xbox con forma de cocodrilo
La Series X-BITE representa a un caimán que parece haber tragado una videoconsola. La pieza supera los 1,50 metros de largo desde el hocico hasta la cola.
El reptil tiene ojos de color verde cuya pupila está inspirada en el logo de Xbox. En su cuerpo se puede ver iluminado el logo de Xbox Nexus, y entre las fauces del animal reposa un control inalámbrico personalizado con marcas que simulan mordeduras.
Para fabricar la pieza, Xbox trabajó junto a John Nolan Studio, un estudio especializado en animatrónica y diseño de criaturas que participó en producciones como The Witcher y Jurassic World: Dominion. El equipo combinó modelado 3D y escultura para reproducir la textura de la piel del animal e integrar los componentes de la consola en su interior.
Existe una única unidad de la Series X-BITE y no estará a la venta. Xbox aclaró que se trata de una fabricación personalizada y que ningún animal real fue utilizado durante su elaboración.
Cómo participar en el sorteo para tener la Xbox en forma de cocodrilo
La dinámica para ganar la consola se desarrolla a través de las redes sociales de Xbox. El período de inscripción comenzó el 3 de noviembre a las 9.00 hora del Pacífico y se extiende hasta las 23.59 del 10 de noviembre de 2026, también hora del Pacífico.
Existen tres formas de participar: a través de X, Instagram o TikTok. En cualquiera de las tres plataformas, el mecanismo es el mismo: seguir la cuenta oficial @XBOX, compartir una de las publicaciones designadas para el sorteo y escribir manualmente el hashtag #XbiteSweepstakes en el repost.
El hashtag debe tecleado a mano: las publicaciones que no lo incluyan de esa forma quedan automáticamente descalificadas. Además, la cuenta utilizada para participar debe tener su configuración en modo público mientras dure el concurso.
Cada persona puede sumar hasta tres entradas en total, con un límite de una por cada red social. El uso de dispositivos automatizados para participar está prohibido.
Cómo se va a elegir al ganador
El concurso está abierto a residentes legales de los 50 estados de Estados Unidos, Washington D. C. y Puerto Rico, mayores de 18 años al momento de inscribirse. No se requiere ninguna compra para entrar ni para aumentar las posibilidades de ganar.
El sorteo aleatorio se realizará alrededor del 11 de noviembre de 2026, a cargo de GMR Marketing, entre todas las entradas elegibles recibidas durante el período habilitado. El ganador será notificado por mensaje directo en la red social utilizada para participar y tendrá 48 horas para responder con su nombre completo, teléfono y correo electrónico.
Luego de ese primer contacto, deberá confirmar su elegibilidad y proporcionar una dirección de envío dentro de las 24 horas siguientes. Si no cumple con los plazos, pierde el premio y Xbox intentará notificar a un suplente, con un máximo de cinco intentos antes de declarar el premio vacante.

articles.title: Oracle Database pitches one engine to tame enterprise AI data - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Same model, better answer: Enterprise data is what turns generic AI into a business tool
Generic AI models can write SQL, but they don’t know a company’s orders, customers or revenue definitions. Now, Oracle Database aims to give AI agents the context to move a stalled order forward.
But that shift raises questions about complexity, lock-in and security as AI agents start acting on live transactions. Oracle Corp.’s answer is a converged platform that keeps vectors, graphs, documents and transactions in one engine, according to Hasan Rizvi (pictured), executive vice president of product and research, database engineering, at Oracle.
“If you ask a generic AI assistant, you get a generic answer,” Rizvi said. “If you ask an AI assistant that knows your business, you get a much better answer. Where is the stock? How can I fix the transaction? How can I expedite the delivery?”
Rizvi spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed database convergence and the safeguards needed for AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)
Convergence over specialized databases
AI lets teams spin up applications and data stores very quickly, making data sprawl everybody’s problem. Skeptics favor specialized databases for each workload, but new data types built inside Oracle’s engine inherit proven availability, security and scale, according to Rizvi.
“We’ve been working on this engine for 40 years, which is highly available, highly secure, highly scalable, highly performant,” Rizvi said. “If you build a new data type or a new workload in the same engine, you get all that benefit, multiple decades’ worth of investment.”
Choice is the other half of the pitch. The database runs on-premises, through Oracle Cloud@Customer and across multiple public clouds, and Oracle used the event to expand Iceberg support in its Autonomous AI Lakehouse, Rizvi noted. But security is where AI raises the stakes most, with Oracle’s Deep Data Security defining access policies in the database itself, so a user’s identity travels with every request from an agent or AI-generated app.
“Before, it took a lot of time and effort to find vulnerabilities to exploit them,” he said. “Now, with AI, it’s made it very easy to reverse engineer fixes for attackers to attack.”

articles.title: La mission Artemis II a percé un trou dans la haute atmosphère, de quoi perturber les signaux GPS
articles.text:
Voici une conséquence que l’on n’avait pas forcément vue venir. Les moteurs de la fusée Space Launch System (SLS) d’Artemis II ont laissé une cicatrice de plusieurs milliers de kilomètres dans le ciel américain. Et les chercheurs y voient un nouveau risque pour les systèmes de navigation.
Le 1er avril dernier, la fusée SLS de la NASA s’est élancée depuis le Kennedy Space Center en Floride avec la capsule Orion et quatre astronautes à son bord : Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch et le Canadien Jeremy Hansen.
Cinq jours plus tard, l’équipage a contourné la face cachée de la Lune, offrant à l’humanité des images époustouflantes et inédites. L’amerrissage du 10 avril a marqué la fin du premier vol habité vers la Lune depuis plus de cinquante ans. Et si l’agence spatiale américaine a déjà les yeux rivés sur Artemis III, des scientifiques de l’université Cheng Kung à Taïwan et du centre Goddard de la NASA se sont intéressés aux répercussions du vol de la surpuissante fusée dans l’atmosphère.
Trois perturbations en moins de deux jours
Leur étude s’intéresse particulièrement à l’ionosphère, une couche de l’atmosphère gorgée de particules chargées appelées électrons libres, qui commence à environ 50 kilomètres d’altitude. Pour la sonder, l’équipe a exploité les données de plus de 3 500 stations au sol réparties sur le continent américain pendant le vol, puis mesuré le temps que mettent les signaux des satellites de navigation à les atteindre.
Les chercheurs ont conclu que l’ionosphère a été secouée à trois reprises. D’abord lors du décollage, puis environ 1h48 plus tard, lorsque l’étage supérieur du SLS a rallumé son moteur pendant 18 minutes afin de hisser Orion sur une orbite plus haute. De quoi ouvrir une sorte de « trou » dans la couche, c’est-à-dire une zone où la densité d’électrons est bouleversée. Celle-ci s’étire d’est en ouest sur plus de 5 000 kilomètres au-dessus de l’Amérique du Nord, et se déplace à environ 8 kilomètres par seconde, soit la vitesse du vaisseau.
Puis, un peu plus d’un jour après le décollage, l’allumage du moteur d’Orion pour quitter l’orbite terrestre en a provoqué une troisième, de même forme mais plus faible. C’est une première : jamais une même mission n’avait perturbé trois fois la même région.
Quand le signal change de rythme
Ce phénomène tient à l’altitude à laquelle les allumeurs se sont allumés, à environ 185 kilomètres et donc, en pleine ionosphère. Leurs gaz d’échappement y ont été injectés directement, un peu comme le sillage d’un bateau. « Les lancements de fusées produisent ce genre d’effet, mais nous n’avions jamais vu ce type de manœuvre orbitale lors d’une mission interplanétaire », explique à Space.com Charles Lin, l’un des auteurs de l’étude.
Toutefois, il faut savoir que les satellites GPS évoluent à plus de 20 000 kilomètres d’altitude, bien au-dessus de l’ionosphère, et que leurs signaux doivent la traverser pour atteindre nos téléphones et nos voitures : la position se calcule à partir du temps qu’ils mettent à arriver. Quand la densité d’électrons change, ils arrivent plus tôt ou plus tard que prévu, et le calcul se fausse.
Les conséquences pourraient être concrètes. « Une erreur de positionnement de quelques mètres suffit à faire changer de voie une voiture autonome », estime Charles Lin, qui évoque aussi un impact possible sur les drones. Si ce phénomène n’est pas alarmant en soi, une tempête solaire pouvant brouiller le signal pendant des jours, les chercheurs estiment qu’il est crucial de mieux surveiller ce phénomène. « À l’avenir, avec de plus en plus de missions vers la Lune et Mars, ces effets de météo spatiale deviendront bien plus importants », prévient l’expert.
L’ionosphère est une couche de l’atmosphère (environ 50 à plus de 1 000 km d’altitude) où le rayonnement solaire ionise les gaz et produit des électrons libres. Les signaux GNSS (GPS, Galileo, etc.) qui vont des satellites jusqu’aux récepteurs au sol traversent cette zone, et leur vitesse de propagation dépend du contenu électronique le long du trajet. Quand la densité d’électrons varie, le signal subit un retard (ou un avance apparente) qui se traduit en erreur de distance, donc en erreur de position. C’est un des principaux facteurs d’erreur côté “atmosphère”, surtout pour les services de navigation grand public. Les systèmes de correction (SBAS, RTK) et les modèles ionosphériques existent précisément pour limiter cet impact, mais ils ne gomment pas toutes les perturbations rapides et localisées.
Un « trou » ionosphérique désigne une zone où la densité d’électrons est fortement modifiée sur une région étendue, ce qui perturbe la propagation radio. Lorsqu’un moteur-fusée s’allume à l’intérieur de l’ionosphère, ses gaz d’échappement peuvent déclencher des réactions chimiques et des recombinaisons qui raréfient localement les électrons, un peu comme une “trace” dans le plasma. À la différence d’une tempête solaire, qui agit de manière globale et peut durer des heures ou des jours, l’effet d’un allumage est plus localisé, lié à une trajectoire et à une fenêtre temporelle courte. Les deux phénomènes peuvent toutefois produire le même type de conséquence pour la navigation : un biais sur le temps de propagation des signaux. L’enjeu, côté GNSS, est surtout la prévisibilité et la capacité à détecter ces anomalies en temps quasi réel.
Les stations GNSS au sol enregistrent en continu les signaux de plusieurs satellites et peuvent estimer des variations de retard ionosphérique en exploitant notamment les mesures multi-fréquences. En comparant le temps de trajet apparent des signaux (et ses variations) entre différentes stations, on reconstruit des cartes de contenu électronique total (TEC) et on repère les zones anormales. Un événement comme un allumage en haute altitude laisse une signature spatio-temporelle : elle se déplace et s’étire selon la trajectoire, ce qui permet de la distinguer d’un bruit de fond. Plus le réseau de stations est dense, meilleure est la résolution pour détecter des structures fines et rapides. Ces données servent aussi à améliorer les modèles de correction utilisés par la navigation de précision et les services de surveillance de l’intégrité (aviation, applications critiques).

articles.title: La France teste un robot maçon capable de construire 60 m² de mur en une journée : il pourrait arriver sur les chantiers en 2027
articles.text:
La France teste un robot maçon capable de construire 60 m² de mur en une journée : il pourrait arriver sur les chantiers en 2027
Fin octobre, près de Paris, Bouygues Construction a mis au travail le WLTR, un robot qui monte des murs de briques sans échafaudage. La machine a déjà tourné sur une centaine de chantiers en Europe et doit arriver sur ses premiers projets français début 2027. Elle soulagera les équipes, sans régler à elle seule le manque de maçons.
Sur une base mobile verte, un bras articulé saisit un bloc de terre cuite, l'enduit de deux cordons de colle et le pose au millimètre près, avant de repartir chercher le suivant. Du 26 au 30 octobre 2026, la scène s'est répétée à Chilly-Mazarin (Essonne) sur Scale One. Bouygues Construction a inauguré le 6 octobre cette plateforme d'essais de 2500 m², où le géant du BTP teste en conditions réelles robots, matériaux et procédés avant de les envoyer sur ses chantiers. Le maçon robotisé y partage l'espace avec un humanoïde, un chien-robot de surveillance et une imprimante 3D à béton. Drôle de voisinage…
A robot bricklayer named WLTR could soon be the solution to the UK's bricklayer shortage. It matches the output of five bricklayers and one laborer per hour, and is operated by just one person pic.twitter.com/wsrl3KPRds
— Reuters Tech News (@ReutersTech) May 19, 2026
Robot WLTR : une cadence théorique de 60 m² par jour
Le WLTR, surnommé Walter, pèse 2,5 t et vient de République tchèque. Le briquetier Wienerberger a conçu les blocs, KM Robotics et GreenBuild se sont chargés de la machine. L'opérateur charge les plans sur une tablette et un laser à lignes croisées donne l'alignement, puis le robot monte la paroi jusqu'à 3,50 m sans échafaudage. Les briques Porotherm “Robot-Ready” ont des encoches latérales où vient se loger la pince, et on les assemble à la mousse adhésive Dryfix ou au mortier-colle à joint mince.
Côté cadence, la fiche technique annonce 7,5 m² par heure en moyenne, avec des pointes à 10 m². Les 60 m² par jour qui circulent sortent de là : un chiffre théorique, calculé sur 8 h parce que les droits syndicaux des robots, pourquoi pas ? Selon Wienerberger, une douzaine de machines tournent déjà et ont monté plus de 55 000 m² de murs sur plus de 100 projets, de la Tchéquie au Royaume-Uni. Chez Bouygues Bâtiment Industrie, Philippe Robinaud a annoncé un premier déploiement sur des projets pilotes au premier trimestre 2027.
BTP : la robotique face à une profession qui ne trouve plus de relève
Les maçons manquent partout en Europe. En France, le métier revient chaque année parmi les plus difficiles à recruter dans l'enquête Besoins en main-d’œuvre de France Travail, et il vieillit sans que les jeunes s'y pressent, rebutés par les charges lourdes et les mêmes gestes répétés dehors, quel que soit le temps.
	
La machine créerait même des postes qualifiés, puisqu'il faut toujours des opérateurs pour la superviser
Au Royaume-Uni, où le robot a bâti en 2025 un lotissement de 27 maisons à Durham, le promoteur Jan Telensky ne tourne pas autour du pot : “Il n'entre tout simplement pas assez de maçons dans le métier.” D'après lui, la machine créerait même des postes qualifiés, puisqu'il faut toujours des opérateurs pour la superviser. Elle prend surtout en charge le plus pénible. Elle soulève des blocs jusqu'à 90 kg, et avec l'échafaudage disparaissent les risques de chute. Le maçon devient dès lors pilote. Deux personnes suffisent : un opérateur, plus un assistant qui alimente les palettes.
Productivité du robot maçon : des promesses à relativiser
Combien de maçons remplace-t-il ? Cela dépend beaucoup de qui répond. Auprès de Reuters, Jan Telensky parlait de cinq maçons et un aide. Le fabricant GreenBuild évoquait jusqu'à 200 m² par jour. Le groupe autrichien PORR, lui, a constaté sur un chantier tchèque une productivité parfois comparable à celle d'un seul maçon expérimenté. Les chantiers publiés tournent plutôt entre 5 et 7 m² par heure. On est donc loin des 200 m².
Le WLTR est à son aise sur les murs longs et droits, percés de peu d'ouvertures. Attention, il ne pose pas le premier rang ; cette assise de départ, les maçons la règlent à la main, au mortier hydrofugé et au laser, car la machine ne rattrape pas les défauts de la dalle. Il lui faut aussi ses briques dédiées, et les colles ont leurs exigences, puisque les avis techniques imposent de poser à 5 °C minimum, sans pluie ni gel. Des travaux visent à adapter sa pince au béton cellulaire et aux blocs de béton, ce qui lui ouvrirait bien plus de chantiers.
D'ici là, Walter reste un équipier de plus sur les bâtiments qui s'y prêtent, pas un remplaçant. Encore faut-il former ceux qui le pilotent.

articles.title: PlayStation 5 enfim volta a entrar em promoção em até 12x sem juros • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
PlayStation 5 enfim volta a entrar em promoção em até 12x sem juros
PS5 Slim Edição Digital possui SSD veloz interno e controle DualSense; oferta do Magalu no AliExpress oferece console da Sony com desconto de 18% no prazo com cupom
O PlayStation 5 Slim Digital está saindo por R$ 3.750 com cupom AFFNOV09 em até 12x sem juros na loja do Magalu no AliExpress. O console da Sony, com SSD veloz e que traz um controle DualSense, recebe desconto de 18% sobre o preço base de R$ 4.599, reajustado recentemente.
Esta é uma rara chance de adquirir o modelo base do atual sistema da Sony com desconto no Black November 2026, já que ele não tem aparecido em promoções no varejo nos últimos meses.
O PS5 Slim é o modelo revisto do console lançado em 2020, com design compacto, mas a mesma performance. Seu SSD interno de 825 GB e os 16 GB de RAM garantem o carregamento quase instantâneo dos jogos, enquanto é possível expandir o espaço interno com um SSD externo e/ou um M.2.
Seu controle sem fio DualSense possui feedback háptico avançado, que oferece tensão e resistência nos gatilhos conforme a interação, enquanto respostas táteis e de áudio via alto-falantes embutidos fazem o jogador se sentir na pele do personagem no game.
O sistema reproduz gráficos em 4K a uma taxa de até 120 fps em TVs compatíveis. A tecnologia de ray-tracing entrega renderização de reflexos e sombras mais realistas, tornando a jogatina mais imersiva.
O PS5 Slim roda todos os jogos do PS4, mas não possui um leitor de mídia física. O acessório, também compatível com o PS5 Pro, precisa ser comprado à parte.
Este console suporta Wi-Fi 6 e Ethernet para acesso à PlayStation Store, que oferece jogos digitais e acesso a apps de streaming, como Apple TV e Spotify.
O PlayStation 5 Slim Digital (R$ 3.750 com cupom AFFNOV09 em até 12x sem juros) traz duas portas USB-C e duas USB-A, e inclui um cabo USB-C duplo para carregar o DualSense.

articles.title: CPUID Readies CPU-Z for Intel Razor Lake, Two Generations Out
articles.text:
Thursday, November 5th 2026
CPUID Readies CPU-Z for Intel Razor Lake, Two Generations Out
CPUID has released CPU-Z 3.02, and the first line of its changelog simply reads "Intel Razor Lake support." Razor Lake is the processor family expected to follow Nova Lake, and Intel has yet to officially announce it. The changelog doesn't say which Razor Lake variants are covered or how deep that support goes, so this could be anything from basic detection to early groundwork. The November 4 update also adds the AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700, along with fixes for an SPD reading issue on Intel Broadwell-E and a validation problem on Windows XP.
Of course, system tools tend to pick up new chips well before they reach store shelves. HWiNFO added early Nova Lake support back in August 2025, and the first Nova Lake-S desktop chips still aren't expected until Q1 2027. HWiNFO also added preliminary support for Razor Lake-AX in August this year, the rumored large APU that could pack up to 32 Xe3 GPU cores alongside on-package memory.Leaks so far point to a Razor Lake family made up of desktop Razor Lake-S chips, mobile H and HX parts, and the AX APU. A leaked partner slide indicated that Intel plans to keep the LGA-1954 socket around for multiple generations, so Razor Lake-S may well drop into the same boards as Nova Lake-S. Leaker Jaykihn has also claimed that Intel will turn to TSMC's N2X node for some Razor Lake production. Leaked roadmaps place Razor Lake around late 2027 or later, so retail chips are still quite far off.

articles.title: I've spent a week testing the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display — and it confirms my suspicions that Apple put the touchscreen on the wrong Mac
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
While all the talk is about the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display being the first MacBook with a touchscreen, the touchscreen is arguably not its most interesting feature; it works fine, but macOS is still an operating system built for traditional laptop inputs. Instead, it’s the gorgeous tandem OLED screen and industry-leading battery life that should get you excited here. Apple hasn't unveiled an M6 Pro or M6 Max chip yet; your choice is still between the M5 Pro or Max, so while performance is hugely impressive, it’s nothing we haven’t seen before. That said, if you’re a creative professional who needs an incredibly powerful laptop with one of the best screens on the market, this MacBook Pro is an excellent investment. The high-end components will be overkill for most people, though, and the price too steep; if you don’t need the power, there are much more affordable MacBooks (and other laptops) out there.
Reasons to buy
- + Gorgeous display
- + Incredibly long battery life
- + Excellent performance
Reasons to avoid
- - Touchscreen features feel a bit undercooked
- - Very expensive
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
At a glance: Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max)
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is Apple’s latest and greatest workstation laptop aimed at professionals. It doesn’t come with the newest M6 chip architecture, and instead sticks with the previous, yet very powerful, M5 Pro and M5 Max generation. The big change this time around, however, is the PROLED XDR Display. Apple has dropped mini LED technology for tandem OLED, and the screen is gorgeously vibrant — and it’s the first time Apple has included a touchscreen on a MacBook.
The Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display comes in two sizes: 14-inch and 16-inch. The 14-inch model starts at $2,899 / £2,899 / AU$4,599 and the 16-inch model starts at $3,399 / £3,399 / AU$5,499. These versions come with 24GB of unified memory and 1TB storage, and are powered by the M5 Pro chip (the 16-inch model’s M5 Pro chip features a more powerful 20-core GPU, compared to the 14-inches’ 18-core GPU). You can configure both models with the more powerful M5 Max chip up to 128GB memory and 16TB of storage, but things get very expensive, very fast.
The launch of the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display comes at a time when there’s a lot of competition in the prosumer laptop market, thanks to the launch of a range of laptops powered by Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip. These laptops, such as the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark and Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, have powerful chips, unified memory and touchscreens (many of them are OLED as well), which pits them squarely against the new MacBook Pro.
Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display scorecard
How the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display scored in our review

Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max): Value for money
Starting at $2,899 / £2,899 / AU$4,599 for the 14-inch version, and $3,399 / £3,399 / AU$5,499 for the 16-inch model, and going all the way up to an astonishing $14,549 / £14,549 / AU$22,424 for the fully specced-out model, the question of value isn’t so much about price, but about what this laptop can enable you to do.
Put simply, if you just want a MacBook that will excel at day-to-day tasks you’d be much better off buying a MacBook Air (M5), and even for more ambitious workloads, the recently-announced MacBook Pro (M6), which starts at $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$3,199, will likely more than suffice. Neither of those, of course, feature a touchscreen, but I wouldn’t suggest buying any model of the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display for the touchscreen alone.
Thankfully, this version of the MacBook Pro has other features that help to justify the higher price tag, including tandem OLED screen technology, a lighter design, and more powerful components. Despite being older than the M6 chip, both the M5 Pro and M5 Max outperform it, so if you need a seriously powerful laptop, and image quality is of the utmost importance, the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display could be a worthy investment, especially if its raw performance means you can complete projects faster, allowing you to take on more work, for example.
If you don’t need that kind of horsepower, then there are much more affordable options you should consider, tempting as the touchscreen functionality or OLED display might be.
Compared to rival RTX Spark laptops, the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is much more competitive. The Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark starts at $4,399.99 / £3,899.99 / AU$7,999, though it comes with a lot more memory, packing 64GB.
Meanwhile, the Surface Laptop Ultra starts at $2,599.99 / £2,599 / AU$4,399 for the same amount of memory (24GB), but only half the storage space (512GB). So, while the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is an extremely expensive laptop, when you consider what it offers, who it’s aimed at, and how much the competition costs, the price tag makes more sense, even if that doesn’t make it any easier to afford.
Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max): Design
- PROLED XDR screen is a clear highlight
- Slightly lighter than previous models
- iPhone-like Dynamic Island replaces the controversial ‘notch’ around the webcam
Given that the MacBook Pro design hasn’t changed in years, the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display in both size variants comes with some major tweaks in this department. This isn’t, though, the kind of overhaul we saw when Apple introduced the 16-inch and 14-inch MacBook Pros that replaced the 15-inch and 13-inch models, respectively, around five years ago; instead, this is a more subtle refinement of the design, and pretty much all of the tweaks are a result of the new display, so let’s start there.
Apple calls the new PROLED XDR screen "the best display on a laptop" and, to be fair, it has a good reason to be boastful. Previous screens on the MacBook Pro were already pretty darn good, and now Apple has swapped the mini-LED tech for tandem OLED. This essentially uses two layers of organic light-emitting diodes (OLED) on top of each other, rather than just a single layer, so peak brightness can go even higher, while the display can remain power-efficient. The PROLED XDR screen can achieve 2,000 nits of peak brightness, whereas the mini-LED screen of previous MacBook Pros had a peak brightness of 1,600.

Touch ID button
This button powers on the MacBook Pro, and can scan your fingerprint to log in
Combine that with the usual benefits we’ve come to expect from OLED displays, namely the higher contrast ratios and lack of halo effects (where there’s noticeable bloom surrounding light colors that bleeds into pixels that should be showing darker, or completely black, colors) that come thanks to each OLED pixel being independently controlled (including being able to be turned off completely), rather than relying on an LED backlight, which offers less precise control over the pixels in the display.
The contrast ratio of the PROLED XDR screen is an incredible 10,000,000:1, a pretty huge bump over the 1,000,000:1 contrast ratio of the previous model with a Liquid Retina XDR display. Contrast ratio is a way of comparing the brightest white to the darkest black of a display, and the greater the difference, the more vibrant the image quality, so you can forget about washed-out colors and blacks that look more gray, and enjoy rich, deep colors that really pop compared to darker tones, and even the total blackness that OLED technology enables.
While MacBook displays have supported the P3 color gamut, which is particularly important for people working with video who require accurate colors, the PROLED XDR screen also supports the Adobe RGB gamut, which offers wider coverage for green and cyan colors, and is popular with photographers and designers.
The addition of touch functionality has also had implications for the design. The hinges of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display have been tweaked to reduce movement and flex when you touch the screen. I’d have loved it if Apple had taken this opportunity to increase the amount by which the screen can be pushed back, ideally introducing hinges to allow the touchscreen to lie flat on a desk, or even flip behind the keyboard to turn the laptop into an iPad-like device.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
This would have made the redesign of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display even more ambitious, and would have likely meant much more work for Apple to ensure the macOS operating system works with a 2-in-1 laptop form factor, but it would have made the whole idea of a touchscreen much more viable. Instead, we’re still stuck with a traditional clamshell laptop design, so touchscreen gestures require you hovering your arm over the keyboard as you jab horizontally at the screen — it's not the most natural-feeling way to interact with a device, and this was one of Steve Jobs’ biggest criticisms of touchscreen laptops when, as CEO, he dismissed the idea of Apple making one all those years ago.
The PROLED XDR screen also allows for thinner bezels around it, and the once-controversial notch that surrounded the webcam has been replaced by Apple's Dynamic Island, as seen on the iPhone, which gives you quick touch access to controls such as media playback, AirDrop sharing and accessing Spotlight. It’s one of the best examples of Apple tweaking macOS to better make use of the touchscreen, and I can confidently predict that the Dynamic Island will be less hated than the notch, which was just dead space that intruded on the desktop.
The more compact Dynamic Island and thinner bezels mean the screen of this 16-inch Pro is slightly larger than on previous models at 16.3 inches vs 16.2 inches, with a higher resolution of 3472 x 2266 pixels vs 3456 x 2234 pixels.
The OLED screen technology (and new thermal system that’s used to keep the laptop’s components cool) has also helped Apple reduce the weight of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max) by half a pound — that's 15% lighter — and make it around 1mm thinner.
The MacBook Pro was always a great showcase that proved powerful workstation laptops don’t need to be big and bulky, so it's impressive that Apple has been able to make this new model both lighter and thinner.
The final design change is a relatively minor one, but one that will likely prove to be very popular. Apple has returned to having an illuminated Apple logo on the back of the lid — it's a nod to the past, while also helping the latest MacBook Pro stand out more compared to the previous models.
Apart from those changes, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max)’s design is essentially the same as the previous few generations of MacBook — but that’s no bad thing, as it remains a great-looking laptop with plenty of ports (three USB-C Thunderbolt 5 ports, SDXC card slot, HDMI, 3.5mm audio and the MagSafe 3 port) for pros.
Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026): Specs

Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max): Performance
- No M6 version with PROLED XDR Display
- Touchscreen is responsive, but not an essential addition
- Very fast SSD
I’m going to be honest: I think Apple has got itself into a little bit of a pickle with its M-series naming convention and release cadence. For a company that was often lauded for offering an elegant simplicity here, compared to the complexity of some competitors, it’s made a bit of a confusing mess.
Want the very latest M-series architecture, the M6, which is the company’s first-ever 2nm compute chip? Well, if so, you can forget about the PROLED XDR Display, as Apple is only offering it in the 14-inch MacBook Pro with Mini-LED screen. If you want the M6 and don’t care about a touchscreen or OLED, but prefer the larger 16-inch screen size, then you’re out of luck.
If you want the most powerful chips in a MacBook, then you’re left with the previous-generation M5 Pro and Max chips. But, getting an M5 Max-powered MacBook Pro doesn’t guarantee it’s the most powerful chip, as the default M5 Max chip that comes with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch features an 18-core CPU and 32-core GPU, but you can upgrade (for $300 / £300 extra) to a more powerful M5 Max with a 40-core GPU. To be honest, unless you’re working with extremely graphically-intensive projects, the standard M5 Max chip will be more than enough, and even the M5 Pro will handle pretty much anything you throw at it.
As I mentioned, if you want the M6 generation and the improvements it brings, namely with a smaller 2nm process, which should lead to better power efficiency, and a dual 16-core Neural Engine for improved on-device AI performance, then you’ll need to forego both the PROLED XDR Display and 16-inch screen size.
Benchmarks

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display model Apple sent to me for review comes with the M5 Max chip with 18-core CPU and 40-core GPU, 128GB of unified memory, and 2TB of storage. That’s a hefty list of specs, and would set you back a similarly hefty $7,399 / £7,399 / AU$11,699.
I’ve previously tested the M5 and M5 Pro in the 14-inch MacBook Pros launched earlier this year and late last year, and as expected, the M5 Max in my 16-inch Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is incredibly powerful, with macOS and its built-in apps all launching quickly and feeling fast and snappy.
When it comes to the touchscreen, macOS again feels fast and responsive, and using a finger to quickly browse up and down a website, selecting options in a dialog box or menu, and moving windows around the screen all feels natural, especially if you’ve ever used an iPhone or an iPad.
Unlike people who have only used Macs and MacBooks from the once touchscreen-phobic Apple, I’ve had extensive experience using Windows laptops and Chromebooks with touchscreens, so using one on the MacBook Pro isn’t as big of a culture shock as it might be to some. While it worked well, and there are some nice touches (forgive the pun), such as pressing down your finger on certain tools in Final Cut Pro to open up a radial menu for more precise touch control, I have to say that Windows 11, Chrome OS, and Google’s new Googlebook OS are better suited to touch controls.
This might come as little surprise, as this is Apple’s first MacBook to have a touchscreen, while Windows laptops and Chromebooks have had them for decades, and in the case of Chrome OS and Googlebook OS, Google has used its experience working on Android to develop the operating system. And, for as much grief as a lot of us (myself included) gave Windows 8 when it launched back in 2012, it inspired Microsoft to make a touchscreen-friendly interface, elements of which are still found in Windows 11, primarily with larger, easier to tap, buttons and menus.
Currently, macOS Tahoe still looks and feels like an operating system that’s best used with a traditional mouse and keyboard, because that’s what it is. But that also means some elements of the user interface, such as menus, feel a bit fiddly to control via touch.
Hopefully this will change if more MacBooks come out with touchscreens. But, because Apple has decided to put its first laptop touchscreen on its most powerful (and expensive) MacBooks, there’s a danger that the company will end up thinking that because the numbers of touchscreen MacBook users is so small, it’s not worth making big changes to the interface.
Another issue I have with Apple’s decision to put a touchscreen on its highest-end MacBook Pros, rather than a more mainstream MacBook Air or Neo — something I’ve written about — is that touchscreen gestures and controls often aren’t the best way to control a laptop when you're performing complex tasks where precision is key. Sure, you can pull up a virtual piano in Garage Band and tap on the keys on screen, but while this is handy for quick ideas, you don’t want to play or write an entire song using it.
Most professionals will have peripherals, such as physical MIDI keyboards, for precise control. It’s the same with photographers and digital artists — using your fingers to pinch and zoom an image feels fast and natural, as does scribbling some notes or doodles, but for long-term use, many professionals will use a drawing tablet. If the MacBook’s PROLED XDR Display was compatible with the Apple Pencil stylus, that would make it a more useful tool for professionals, but it's not, which is a rather odd omission.
One touchscreen-friendly change Apple has made to macOS, and which I’m a big fan of, is adding an iPhone-like Dynamic Island where the notch around the webcam used to be. Tapping this gives you quick context-relevant tools, such as media controls when watching a video. Spotlight search and Siri AI are now located here as well. This is a great addition that adds value to the MacBook Pro’s touchscreen, and I’d like to see it expanded, and more touch-friendly UI elements to make the touchscreen a must-have, rather than nice-to-have-but-far-from-essential, which is what it feels like at the moment.
The tandem OLED tech powering the PROLED XDR Display is a much bigger deal, and likely the reason why most people will consider the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display over the standard model. The previous Mini-LED screen was already one of the best displays you’d find on a laptop, and thanks to tandem OLED, this new screen is even better. Straight out of the box without needing any calibration, the colors are bright and vibrant — so much so that I was surprised to see that the screen was only at 50% brightness.
Placing my 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M5 chip and Mini-LED screen next to the 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch really highlighted just how much better the PROLED XDR screen is. The Mini-LED looked dimmer, despite it being at 100% brightness, even with the PROLED XDR screen remaining at 50%. Now, as I said, the Mini-LED display of the (slightly) older MacBook Pro is no slouch, so to see such a stark difference in image quality is a big deal, especially for people who want a laptop for working with photos, videos and digital art. The new support for Adobe RGB color gamut is another big plus here, though as usual for Mac devices you’ll want to turn off the True Tone feature — it tweaks the colors of the screen depending on the ambient light you’re working in, which can make what’s on the screen look better to you in that moment, but could lead to color inaccuracies in a production workflow.
I won’t delve too deep into the performance of the M5 Max, as it’s been in other Apple devices for a while now, but this is the first time I’ve used a MacBook running it (I have tested both the previous M5 and M5 Pro MacBook Pro models).
According to Apple’s benchmarks, the M5 Max is around nine times faster than the M4 Max when it comes to ‘first token performance’, while AI image generation is apparently around six times faster. If those are the kind of stats that excite you, then enjoy!
In our benchmark tests, compared to the M5 MacBook Pro with a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max) with an 18-core CPU and 40-core GPU unsurprisingly outperformed the older MacBook Pro when it came to graphic-intensive tests. In the 3D Mark Wild Life Extreme graphics test, for example, the M5 MacBook Pro scored 73.6fps compared to the M5 Max’s 214.1fps.
With gaming, the M5 MacBook Pro hit 11fps at 1920 x 1200 with Ray Tracing set to Ultra, while the M5 Max model managed a much more playable 38.75fps. This is a good example of the graphical performance gap, but if you want a laptop to game on you’re still better off buying a dedicated gaming laptop, which is a bit of a shame, as the PROLED XDR Display makes games look fantastic.
The SSD inside the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max) offers up to 14.5GB/s speeds, with Apple claiming it’s twice as fast as the SSD in the previous generation, and in our tests it scored a very good 13,334.7MB/s and 12,782.7MB/s write and read speeds, respectively. A fast SSD like this is important if you’re working on large files and complex projects.
The SSD in the Surface Laptop Ultra with RTX Spark N1X chip scored a rather paltry 1,921MB/s write speeds in comparison. Check out our benchmark result charts for more comparisons.
The rest of the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max) works as well as expected. The spatial speakers are loud and clear, and the Center Stage webcam offers excellent clarity, alongside some nice software-powered features that improve the image quality further. A nice additional feature added is that macOS will virtually stabilize the webcam’s footage if you’re using the touchscreen at the same time, to stop it wobbling while you’re on calls. It’s a handy feature, and shows the attention to detail we’ve come to expect from Apple.
Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max) review: Battery Life
Battery life results
How long does the battery last?
| Versus Comparison Data |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Attribute | Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max) | Apple MacBook Pro 16-inch (2024, M4 Pro) | Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Battery life video test | 24.35 | 21.5 | 11.383333333333333 | 
Apple has claimed the new 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display lasts up to 24 hours on battery when streaming videos, and up to 17 hours when browsing the web, and I found those claims to be pretty much spot on, with the device lasting an incredible 24 hours and 21 minutes in our battery test, which involves playing a looped 1080p video at 50% brightness.
It blows past the MacBook Pro 16-inch (M4 Pro, 2024), which managed 21 hours and 32 minutes in the same test, and over double the 11 hours and 23 minutes the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark hit. The MacBook Pro is able to sustain its performance when on battery life, rather than throttling it to conserve energy, so you’ll be able to go multiple work days on a single charge while still being productive, though of course the battery will drain more quickly if you’re using it for more intensive tasks.
The battery life is seriously impressive for a large workstation laptop with such powerful components and a bright and vibrant display, and laptop makers (as well as Nvidia itself) producing RTX Spark rivals will need to seriously up their game, given that they're only managing around half of what the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max) can achieve.
Should I buy the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max)?
✅ You want a powerful yet portable workstation laptop for creative work
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display performs brilliantly when tasked with almost any creative project, but the M5 Max chip really comes into its own when handling complex graphical workloads. Battery life is also phenomenal, allowing you to work on this laptop pretty much anywhere.
✅ Your work requires accurate image quality
The tandem OLED tech behind the PROLED XDR Display really is impressive, and thanks to support for the P3 and Adobe RGB color gamuts you get very accurate images without the need for deep calibration — making this MacBook a great choice for photographers and videographers.
✅ You develop apps for iPhones and iPads
One of the best use cases I’ve seen for the touchscreen aspect of the PROLED XDR Display is for app developers who can run emulated versions of their apps on the MacBook, and use the screen to see how touchscreen elements will work.
❌ You don’t care about the touchscreen
If you still agree with Steve Jobs’ touchscreen-on-MacBook skepticism, you can save a lot of money by going for one of Apple's many other MacBooks. You will miss out on the gorgeous tandem OLED display, however. 
❌ You only care about the touchscreen
Conversely, if you want a laptop primarily for a touchscreen, I’d recommend a 2-in-1 Windows 11 laptop or Chromebook, which are currently much better suited to touchscreen controls. Paying so much extra just for a touchscreen on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is a waste.
❌ You don’t need the power or image quality
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch is a very expensive laptop in all its configurations, and even the base model will be overkill for most users.

I tested numerous apps including Photoshop, and played Cyberpunk 2077 on it to see how it performs, and to see how good the PROLED XDR Display looks. I also viewed and edited some very high-quality photos by photographer Paul Reiffer, and supplied by Apple.
Throughout my time with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max), I used both the standard keyboard and touchpad, and the touchscreen.

Entre premières déconvenues et concurrence bien installée, la firme de Cupertino pourrait bien avoir offert à Samsung une occasion en or de renforcer sa position sur le marché.
Le marché des smartphones pliants est plus que jamais scruté par les professionnels et les technophiles. Alors qu'Apple comptait faire de l'ombre à Samsung avec son très attendu iPhone Duo, lancé le 23 octobre dernier, le scénario semble prendre une autre direction. Entre premières critiques, problèmes techniques et facture salée, le nouveau venu laisse une partie des fans perplexes. Un retournement de situation qui tombe plutôt bien pour Samsung.

Le lancement d’Apple fait-il les affaires de Samsung ?
En Corée du Sud, les ventes du Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 ont bondi de plus de 20 % du 23 au 29 octobre, selon les médias locaux. En septembre, l’annonce du Duo avait déjà coïncidé avec une hausse de 10 %. Mais aucun chiffre mondial ni preuve d’un transfert d’acheteurs vers Samsung : Apple a peut-être simplement réveillé l’intérêt pour le format pliant.
Son démarrage reste cependant agité. Des usagers ont signalé des fissures sur l’écran interne dès les premières heures. Apple reconnaît un problème touchant, assure-t-il, peu d’appareils et propose des remplacements. Ce "CrackGate" alimente aussi des soupçons non confirmés de contrôles qualité allégés. Les tests révèlent une pliure qui peut se marquer davantage, sans démontrer une faiblesse générale de la charnière.
Les livraisons se compliquent également. John Ternus, nouveau patron d’Apple, ne sait pas quand l’approvisionnement se stabilisera. Entre fabrication complexe et flambée du prix des composants, la situation est délicate. Samsung en profite d'ailleurs pour chambrer son rival dans une série de publicités.
Le confort et le prix font pencher la balance
Même format passeport, même écran intérieur de 7,6 pouces, la ressemblance s’arrête vite. L’iPhone Duo, plus lourd de 53 g, impressionne par ses finitions en titane et sa pliure bien dissimulée sous une dalle mate. Mais en plein jour, ses couleurs paraissent moins éclatantes que sur l’Amoled, certe brillant, du Z Fold 8.
Les coins arrondis et asymétriques de l’écran externe d’Apple gênent parfois la lecture vidéo. Samsung préfère une façade rectangulaire, proche du 16/9. Sur le Duo, la caméra selfie placée dans un coin reste discrète, mais celle cachée sous l’écran intérieur crée un cercle réfléchissant. Ajoutez des apps mal adaptées, quelques bugs et une barre d’outils encombrante, et l’interface de Samsung sous Android paraît plus aboutie.
Dernier argument, et pas des moindres : le tarif. L’iPhone Duo démarre à 2339 € en France et frôle les 3850 € pour 2 To de stockage. Le Galaxy Z Fold 8 bénéficie de promotions, parfois autour de 1500 €, et de solides offres de la part des opérateurs. Apple marque donc des points sur le luxe et le design, mais pour un usage quotidien, les années d’expérience de Samsung semblent continuer de payer.

articles.title: Container orchestration for AI: Latest trends at KubeCon - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
What to expect during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA: Join theCUBE Nov. 10-12
Kubernetes has emerged as the default container orchestration standard, a foundational platform layer across the enterprise. Will Kubernetes also play a central role in positioning the next generation of AI workloads for production?
This is the question on the minds of the cloud-native community as it gathers this month for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA in Salt Lake City. With the rise of AI agents that have progressed from answering user questions to executing code and running business systems, customers are increasingly interested in controlling what autonomous agents are allowed to do.
“That brings us to OpenShell, an open-source secure agent runtime that Red Hat is helping develop alongside Nvidia and, of, course, the broader community,” said theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante, during a pre-event interview. “The approach puts enforcement into the environment where the agent operates, setting boundaries around what it can access and execute rather than relying on a model alone to follow the rules. We think this is a central question for the next chapter of cloud native: how do enterprises give agents enough freedom to be useful without giving up control?”
During KubeCon + CloudNativeCon, Nov. 10-12, theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio, will feature on-site reporting and exclusive interviews with executives from Red Hat Inc. and Nvidia Corp., among others. TheCUBE will examine the latest innovations in GPU orchestration, agentic workloads and platform engineering as inference and autonomous agents move into production. (* Disclosure below.)
Container orchestration for AI
OpenShell, while still an early-stage project, is actively being developed for Kubernetes environments. The activity reflects growing customer interest in using containerized environments for applications, according to theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty.
“Fifty-one percent of organizations report that 51–75% of their applications now run in containers, representing a sharp rise from just a few years ago,” Nashawaty said. “Organizations now run the majority of their applications in containers which is a sharp rise that reflects the accelerating cloud-native transformation central to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon.”
OpenShell was accepted into the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a sandbox project in September. One component of OpenShell allows agents to run in isolated sandboxes with limits on the files they can reach, an approach actively supported by the cloud-native community within the Kubernetes ecosystem.
“It builds on top of some core Kubernetes special interest groups,” said Pete Cheslock, principal AI community architect at Red Hat, during an interview with theCUBE. “The Agent Sandbox is one of them so that you can deploy these agents in a secure way using Kubernetes APIs.”
Kubernetes-native security
Cheslock’s point about security highlights the growing concerns and recent publicity surrounding AI agents and their ability to break out of isolated environments and compromise systems. Rapid enterprise adoption and integration of AI are increasing the risk profiles for organizations, a topic that will be on the agenda for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon.
“Our research data reveals that 41.3% of organizations cite increased vulnerability risk as the top security challenge, introduced by faster CI/CD cycles and a tension that cloud-native teams are increasingly turning to Kubernetes-native tooling to resolve,” Nashawaty said.
Enterprise reliance on cloud-native tools and open-source software requires confidence that these technologies are safe to use inside enterprise infrastructure. In May, Red Hat and IBM Corp. unveiled Project Lightwell, a $5 billion commitment to help enterprises secure open-source software.
“For the last year, especially since the Mythos moment, [security] has been the first thing that we’ve talked about in every customer conversation I’ve had,” said Stu Miniman, senior director of market insights for hybrid platforms at Red Hat, in conversation with theCUBE. “We’re trying to make sure that customers can feel secure and understand and use these tools. There’s even more effort being put on security than ever, which has always been a focus of Red Hat. If we don’t make sure that layer is as locked down and reliable and trusted as possible, everything else becomes secondary.”
Tools for multicloud
At this month’s KubeCon gathering, theCUBE will explore how various practitioners are using Kubernetes to ensure workload portability across multicloud environments. Companies such as Vultr and ScaleOps are building Kubernetes-based tools that can support a range of platforms, reflecting enterprise computing trends.
“With our AppDev research finding that 94% of organizations now operate across two or more cloud providers, the demand for consistent, developer-friendly Kubernetes-based platforms has never been more pressing,” Nashawaty explained.
KubeCon also offers an opportunity to assess the progress of key technology projects under the CNCF umbrella. One of the major contributors in this arena has been Google LLC, which contributed the open-source service mesh Istio, serverless building blocks via Knative and Kubernetes itself. KubeCon is an annual reminder of how large the CNCF ecosystems has become, according to Red Hat’s Miniman.
“They’ve got a big ecosystem. I can give example after example of who created these technologies,” Miniman told theCUBE. “Oh yeah, the GitOps stuff came out of Intuit, and the platform engineering stuff came out of Spotify. Just find your focus and go in there, because there is no way you can cover all of it.”
TheCUBE event livestream
Don’t miss theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA from Nov. 10-12. Plus, you can access theCUBE’s exclusive content on demand after the event.
How to watch theCUBE interviews
We offer various ways for you to watch theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, including theCUBE’s dedicated website and YouTube channel. You can also get all the coverage from this year’s events on SiliconANGLE.
TheCUBE podcasts
SiliconANGLE’s “theCUBE Pod” is available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube, which you can enjoy while on the go. During each podcast, SiliconANGLE’s John Furrier and Dave Vellante discuss the biggest trends in enterprise tech, including AI, cloud, cybersecurity and infrastructure, with context and analysis.
SiliconANGLE also produces our weekly “Breaking Analysis” program, where Vellante examines major developments in enterprise tech, combining insights from theCUBE with spending data from Enterprise Technology Research, available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube.
Guests
At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, theCUBE will speak with Red Hat leaders and other industry executives about the latest innovations in GPU orchestration, agentic workloads and platform engineering as inference and autonomous agents move into production.

articles.title: Cette nouvelle fonctionnalité de WhatsApp est très pratique, mais controversée
articles.text:
WhatsApp propose une nouvelle fonctionnalité vous permettant de partager rapidement des photos récentes. Mais cette fonctionnalité, si elle peut s'avérer intrusive, peut également faire partir des photos que vous auriez préféré garder pour vous.
Partager une photo sur WhatsApp ne demande que quelques manipulations. Le processus se complique un peu lorsqu'on vient de faire une capture d'écran et qu'on veut l'envoyer aussitôt : il faut ouvrir la galerie, puis retrouver le fichier. Mais WhatsApp veut vous faciliter les choses, à quel prix ?
Un accès direct aux derniers médias
Après avoir lancé de nouvelles fonctionnalités sur iOS et Android, WhatsApp prépare la suite. Baptisée « Suggestions de médias récents », cette fonction intègre à l'interface de discussion les dernières photos et vidéos de l'utilisateur, qui peut ainsi les partager sans devoir passer par la galerie. Selon WABetaInfo, elle est en cours de déploiement progressif sur Android et iOS, dans les dernières versions de l'application.
Elle se présente sous deux formes, selon les utilisateurs :
- Une petite fenêtre qui apparaît au-dessus de la barre de message à l'ouverture d'une conversation, avec la miniature du dernier média enregistré dans la galerie
- Une miniature de ce même média qui remplace temporairement l'icône de l'appareil photo dans la barre de discussion
Dans les deux cas, un appui sur la suggestion ouvre l'éditeur multimédia de WhatsApp. L'utilisateur peut y vérifier le fichier, ajouter une légende ou des autocollants, puis décider de l'envoyer ou non.
Tous types de médias confondus
WhatsApp ne fait pas de distinction entre les types de fichiers. L'application peut donc proposer une photo qui vient d'être prise, une capture d'écran, une image téléchargée sur internet ou une vidéo enregistrée depuis une autre application.
Cela peut être pratique pour envoyer rapidement un contenu récent. Mais comme la fonction se contente de sélectionner le dernier fichier enregistré, elle peut aussi permettre de partager rapidement un fichier qui n'avait pas vocation à l'être. Et là, c'est la boulette ! Pour pallier à cela, WhatsApp affirme qu'un appui sur la suggestion n'envoie rien automatiquement. Il faut confirmer l'action, et la suggestion peut être écartée si elle ne convient pas à l'utilisateur.
Comment désactiver la suggestion de médias récents ?
La fonctionnalité est activée automatiquement pour les utilisateurs éligibles, qui peuvent donc la voir apparaître sans avoir rien configuré. Pour la désactiver, il faut aller dans Paramètres > Discussions > Suggestion de média récent et désactiver l'option.
Le déploiement étant progressif, il peut s'écouler quelques semaines avant que la fonction n'apparaisse sur un appareil donné. WhatsApp n'a pas communiqué de date de disponibilité globale pour tous les appareils.
Source : DigitalTrends

articles.title: Bitcoin: cómo se ha movido en el mercado este jueves
articles.text:
El bitcoin fue la primera criptomoneda que salió al mercado. Ideada por Satoshi Nakamoto en 2008, esta divisa digital promovía un ideal libertario y buscaba poner en jaque a las instituciones monetarias y financieras tradicionales luego de la crisis financiera mundial que se vivió ese año.
La victoria electoral de Donald Trump significó un movimiento positivo para las principales criptomonedas del mercado. A finales de 2024, bitcoin registró un nuevo máximo histórico que logró superar los 107.000 dólares por unidad, después de que el presidente estadounidense reiteró su idea de crear una reserva estratégica de la criptodivisa en Estados Unidos.
Las divisas digitales serán un foco de atención durante este año, las iniciativas del presidente de Estados Unidos y el desarrollo de nuevos modelos de inteligencia artificial fungirán un papel importante en la cotización de estos activos. Después del lanzamiento del nuevo modelo de IA chino DeepSeek, BTC y otras criptos cayeron en la mayoría de los mercados de valores.
Cotización de la criptomoneda Bitcoin
El precio de la criptomoneda bitcoin para este día a las 14:00 horas (UTC) es de 79590.55 dólares. Esto quiere decir que la moneda digital presentó un cambio de 1.92% en el último día, así como un movimiento de 0.0% en la última hora.
Por su nivel de capitalización, esta moneda digital ocupa la posición #1 entre las más populares.
Bitcoin alcanzó su máximo histórico
En marzo del año pasado el bitcoin ha logrado un nuevo máximo histórico, superando los valores anteriores y reafirmándose como la criptomoneda más importante en el mercado, acercándose a los 73 mil dólares. Este récord se obtuvo en medio de un flujo sin precedentes de inversiones hacia las criptomonedas, un acontecimiento notable para el sector financiero digital.
El aumento en el valor de bitcoin ocurre en un contexto donde hay un entrante masivo de capital hacia las criptomonedas, lo que indica un creciente interés y confianza de los inversores en estos activos. La subida del precio beneficia no solo a bitcoin sino que también tiene un impacto positivo en el mercado de las criptomonedas en general, favoreciendo una mayor estabilidad y visibilidad, de acuerdo a un análisis de Bloomberg.
Expertos financiaron este aumento a diferentes factores, como la adopción institucional de las criptomonedas, la búsqueda de alternativas de inversión debido a la incertidumbre económica mundial y la innovación continua en la tecnología blockchain que respalda a bitcoin y otras divisas digitales. Esta combinación de factores ha creado un entorno propicio para el crecimiento continuo en el valor de Bitcoin.
Cómo adquirir criptomonedas
Para comprarlas e intercambiarlas se utilizan portales especializados. Su valor varía en función de la oferta, de la demanda y del compromiso de los usuarios, por lo que puede cambiar más rápido que el dinero tradicional, pero mientras más gente esté interesada y quiera comprar determinada divisa, mayor será su valor.
No obstante, quien invierte en este tipo de monedas digitales debe tener muy claro que esta forma trae consigo un elevado riesgo al capital, pues, así como puede haber un incremento, también puede tener inesperadamente un desplome y acabar con los ahorros de sus usuarios.
Para almacenarlas, los usuarios deben contar con un monedero digital o wallet, que en realidad es un software a través del cual es posible guardar, enviar y hacer transacciones de las criptomonedas. En realidad, este tipo de monederos sólo guarda las claves que marcan la propiedad y el derecho de una persona sobre cierta criptomoneda, por lo que estos códigos son los que en realidad se deben proteger.

articles.title: Akasa Launches Smart Black SC12 High-Airflow 120 mm PWM Fan
articles.text:
Thursday, November 5th 2026
Akasa Launches Smart Black SC12 High-Airflow 120 mm PWM Fan
Akasa, a leading provider of thermal solutions, has launched the Smart Black SC12, a 120 x 120 x 25 mm PWM fan with a strong cost-performance ratio for system integrators and PC builders. Rated for up to 88 CFM, it is the highest-airflow HD bearing fan in the Akasa range. It is suitable for case intake and exhaust positions, CPU cooler heatsinks and radiators.
The Smart Black SC12 moves to a nine-blade sickle design with an improved blade curvature, delivering high-airflow of up to 88 CFM and strong aerodynamic efficiency. Together with a static pressure of up to 3.2 mm-H₂O, it helps keep component temperatures stable in dense chassis with restricted airflow.The hydrodynamic (HD) bearing uses an internal lubrication seal to limit oil loss over time, keeping friction and vibration low for smooth, stable rotation. The fan is rated for up to 40,000 hours of operation (around 4.5 years of continuous use), backed by a 2-year warranty.
The Smart Black SC12's 500 to 2,000 RPM PWM range lets a single model cover both low-noise and high-load positions in a build. It is rated at 10 dB(A) at minimum speed, rising to 31 dB(A) at full speed for maximum airflow. A rated current of 0.23 A at 12 V DC allows several fans to run from one motherboard header through a splitter or hub, within the header's rated limit, which simplifies cabling in multi-fan systems.
Pricing and Availability
- The Smart Black SC12 starts at £9.00 / €9.50 (prices may vary by reseller).
- The Smart Black SC12 is available to order throughout the UK, Europe, North America and Asia.

articles.title: TikTok Shop ganha aplicativo próprio para compras • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
TikTok Shop ganha aplicativo próprio para compras
App reúne vídeos, lives, cupons e rastreamento de pedidos. Não há previsão de lançamento no Brasil.
O TikTok segue tentando se consolidar como um marketplace e, para isso, está lançando um aplicativo próprio para a sua plataforma de compras. O app do TikTok Shop, antes apenas uma seção na rede social, mantém recursos como vídeos de produtos e transmissões ao vivo de vendas.
Por enquanto, o aplicativo está disponível apenas em Singapura, Malásia, Tailândia e Filipinas, segundo o The Verge. O Brasil ficou de fora dessa primeira fase, assim como os Estados Unidos e o Reino Unido. Com o app dedicado, a empresa parece buscar espaço diretamente entre concorrentes chinesas, como Temu e Shopee.
Ainda não está claro se o lançamento faz parte de um teste ou se o TikTok pretende levar o aplicativo a outros mercados, incluindo o brasileiro. No entanto, a listagem na App Store menciona a língua portuguesa entre os idiomas disponíveis.
Por enquanto, o TikTok Shop continua integrado à rede social no Brasil. Mas vale lembrar que, no início do ano, a empresa solicitou autorização do Banco Central para operar no país como uma fintech de pagamentos e crédito.
O novo aplicativo preserva parte da experiência de compras que já existe dentro da rede de vídeos curtos, mas oferece uma navegação mais próxima da encontrada nos marketplaces tradicionais. Nela, produtos podem ser descobertos por uma interface comum, com diferentes categorias e a seção de pesquisa.
No entanto, o app não abandona totalmente a razão de existir da rede social, apresentando a aba “Explorar”, que apresenta vídeos curtos sobre produtos disponíveis na loja, publicados na rede social, e permite assistir a transmissões ao vivo de vendedores.
O app deve manter benefícios para incentivar a instalação do novo app, bônus de primeira compra e promoções de frete grátis. Assim como na versão da rede social (e como é comum nos aplicativos de compra orientais), espera-se que o app traga opções de roleta para ganhar bônus e outras formas de reter compradores.
Ainda não se sabe se o TikTok pretende substituir a área de compras da rede social pelo novo aplicativo ou manter as duas opções.
Como observa o TechCrunch, a criação de um app separado também aproxima ainda mais o TikTok de empresas tradicionais de comércio eletrônico, mas vai na direção oposta de gigantes como a Amazon. A gigante estadunidense tentou reproduzir a experiência integrada da mídia chinesa com um feed vertical de vídeos curtos, o Inspire, na plataforma.
A novidade também acompanha outras tentativas da plataforma de expandir sua atuação para além dos vídeos curtos. O TikTok já incorporou ou testou recursos relacionados a jogos, restaurantes, esportes, reservas de hotéis e microdramas.
O TikTok Shop chegou oficialmente ao país em abril do ano passado, permitindo comprar produtos exibidos em vídeos e usar links adicionados por criadores participantes do programa de afiliados.

articles.title: The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 isn't Apple's flashiest new laptop, but it might be its best-value one
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Like its predecessors, the new 14-inch MacBook Pro delivers excellent performance for most tasks, long battery life, and better connectivity, all in a familiar build. If you already own a recent M-series MacBook Pro, it's not an essential upgrade; but if you're coming from an older Intel MacBook, or even an older M-series MacBook Air, and you need a powerful, well-rounded laptop that doesn't skimp on features or performance, it's an easy recommendation. Even with a new model sitting above it that offers a touchscreen PROLED display, Apple's most powerful chips, and a lighter build, there's still no arguing with the value proposition of the 14-inch MacBook Pro.
Reasons to buy
- + Excellent M6 performance
- + Strong battery life
- + Vibrant 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display
- + A familiar build with plenty of ports
Reasons to avoid
- - No changes to the design or colors
- - Still has the display notch
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
At a glance: Apple 14-inch MacBook Pro (M6) Review
Apple's latest update to the 14-inch MacBook Pro doesn't change much, but it keeps the line ticking over with the new M6 chip for improved overall performance and better connectivity, all in the same familiar build.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starts at $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$3,199, with 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. You can configure it with up to 32GB of RAM and 4TB of storage, add a Nano-Texture display, or step up to the more powerful M5 Pro or M5 Max chips.
If you need more power or a bigger screen, there's the 16-inch MacBook Pro with M6, or the 14-inch and 16-inch models with M5 Pro or M5 Max. The 13-inch and 15-inch M5 MacBook Air are better picks if you want a more portable build and can live with slightly less performance. If you want an OLED touchscreen and a thinner, lighter design, you'll need to look at the more expensive PROLED 14-inch or 16-inch models with the M5 Pro or M5 Max.
Apple MacBook Pro 14-inch (2026, M6) scorecard
How the Apple MacBook Pro 14-inch (2026, M6) scored in our review
| Group 1 Data |  |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Product | Value () | Design () | Performance () | Battery life () | Overall () | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apple MacBook Pro 14-inch (2026, M6) | 4 | 4 | 4.5 | 4.5 | 4 | 
Apple 14-inch MacBook Pro (M6) Review: Value for money
No, this isn't the headline-grabbing new MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen and a thinner, lighter build. Alongside introducing those new models, Apple is sticking with a trend I'm a big fan of: yearly updates that ensure the entry-level MacBook Pro remains a solid proposition, with Apple's latest silicon and other top-end specs under the hood.
Apple hasn't changed much with the 2026 14-inch MacBook Pro, but it didn't need to. As the entry-level Pro, and a step up from the MacBook Air in terms of specs, it offers more ports in a familiar design that's slightly bulkier than the Air, but still plenty portable. You also get a very capable 14-inch Liquid Retina XDR mini-LED display with a notch at the top, a clicky-clacky keyboard with nice travel, a larger trackpad, and great sound with Spatial Audio and Dolby Atmos support.
The big change is the M6 chip under the hood, with this model joining the still-available M5 Pro and M5 Max models. Those chips, while older, are more powerful, but don't let the M6 Pro's entry-level positioning fool you: Apple's latest silicon is no slouch, delivering excellent everyday performance with plenty of power for more intensive tasks, including photo and video editing, coding, and AI work.
I've been using the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 for the best part of a week, and it's been smooth sailing. It's handled my daily mix of productivity and creative work in apps like Slack, Safari, Google Chrome, Notes, Pages, Pixelmator Pro, and Final Cut Pro, running alongside Messages and FaceTime, effortlessly, without me needing to quit or close anything. The configuration I'm testing pairs the M6's 12-core CPU — split between two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores — with a 12-core GPU and Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and the base 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage.
Just like the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5, the new-for-2026 model with M6 starts at $1,999 / 1,999 / AU$3,199. Yes, that M5 model got a price hike earlier this year, but it’s good to see that Apple didn’t push this further, and with this price tag getting you the M6 chip, 16GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage, it's excellent value.
Apple 14-inch MacBook Pro (M6) Review: Design
- Same design as M5 Pro, with plenty of ports
- Excellent 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display with ProMotion
- Comfortable keyboard, oversized trackpad, and 12MP Center Stage camera
The M6 14-inch MacBook Pro sticks with the well-loved and well-tested design of recent Pro models. It's a little bulkier than the Air on account of its plentiful connectivity options, which include three Thunderbolt 4/USB-C ports, an HDMI port, an SD card slot, a headphone jack, and a MagSafe 3 port.
It's the same sleek design as the M5, M4, and even M3 versions that came before it. It's a design I know well, and one I use daily myself, and I appreciate that it doesn't feel too light or flimsy, but also not too heavy at just 3.4 pounds.
It keeps the same overall dimensions as last year's 14-inch Pro at 12.31 x 8.71 x 0.61 inches. You also get the same two color choices, Space Black or Silver; my review model is Silver, and it contrasts quite nicely with the darker, mirrored Apple logo on the rear — unlike the logo on the newly redesigned touchscreen MacBook Pro, though, this one doesn't light up.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The M6 Pro also doesn't pack Apple's fancy new tandem OLED display, which is a stunner, with especially impressive contrast and the added benefit of not having the notch. The 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display here is no slouch, though, and even with that higher-end model's arrival, this remains one of the best laptop screens on the market.
It supports refresh rates up to 120Hz thanks to ProMotion, and delivers a 3024 x 1964 resolution with vibrant colors and excellent contrast, including wonderfully inky blacks. I've found it great for photo editing in Photos or Pixelmator Pro, video editing in iMovie, CapCut, or Final Cut Pro, streaming videos, FaceTime calls, and even the more straightforward task of writing this review. I always appreciate those inky blacks as I type away.
I've become used to the rectangular cutout notch centered at the top of the display, and I'm still confident that if you've never experienced it before, any initial annoyance at its presence will quickly fade. I am eyeing the pill-shaped Dynamic Island on the more expensive MacBook Pro, but it's really not a necessity.
Here, the menu bar wraps around the notch, which houses a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera that keeps you in the frame and looking sharp during video calls. It also supports Portrait mode to blur your background, and you can use the edges of the screen as a ring light in low lighting conditions.
The keyboard still offers excellent travel, and a decidedly satisfying typing experience. I've written a few articles on this machine, including this review, and I still appreciate the Touch ID sensor baked into the top-right key. It's handy for unlocking your Mac, authenticating, and Apple Pay transactions. Equally, the oversized trackpad makes navigation easy, whether you're using classic point-and-click controls or gestures.
