articles.title: Russische Hacker sollen Website von Luxushotel ins Visier genommen haben: Was steckt dahinter?
articles.text:
Ein Websitebesuch reichte: So nutzten Hacker eine Schwachstelle in iOS und Android aus
Hacker:innen sollen Schwachstellen in den Betriebssystemen iOS und Android ausgenutzt haben, um Besucher:innen verschiedener Websites zu hacken. Das geht aus einem Bericht der Cybersecurity-Firma Sekoia hervor. Bei ihren Analysen identifizierten die Forscher:innen eine groß angelegte „Watering-Hole“-Kampagne, die verschiedene Infektionsvektoren nutzte.
Aufgrund technischer Überschneidungen, operativer Muster, der Opferprofilanalyse und der Infrastruktur schreibt Sekoia die Kampagne mit „mittlerer bis hoher Wahrscheinlichkeit“ der russischen Hackergruppe APT29 zu, die dem russischen Auslandsgeheimdienst zugeordnet wird. Die Sicherheitslücken konnten inzwischen geschlossen werden.
Hacker:innen nahmen Websites ins Visier
Den Sicherheitsforscher:innen zufolge hatten viele der betroffenen Internetseiten einen Bezug zum andauernden Krieg zwischen Russland und der Ukraine. Sekoia schätzt, dass die Angreifer:innen es dabei auf diplomatische Ziele abgesehen haben könnten. Die Angriffe begannen, sobald iPhone- oder Android-Nutzer:innen eine der Websites besuchten. Das Gerät wurde in diesem Moment durch ein in den Datenverkehr eingeschleustes Javascript erfasst.
Die endgültigen Payloads waren auf die jeweilige Plattform zugeschnitten und versuchten laut den Forscher:innen, Browser-Cookies, in einigen Fällen WLAN-Passwörter und sogar die gesamten Daten des Mobilgeräts zu stehlen. Einer der Angriffe habe auf die Website eines Luxushotels in der Nähe einiger britischer Regierungsinstitutionen abgezielt. Auch der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj soll dort schon übernachtet haben.
Auch america250.org zählt zu den betroffenen Internetseiten. Sie befasst sich mit dem 250. Jahrestag der amerikanischen Unabhängigkeit. Betreiber der Seite ist eine überparteiliche Gruppe aus Gesetzgeber:innen, Führungskräften der Wirtschaft und mindestens einem ehemaligen Mitglied der Trump-Regierung. Die Angreifer:innen registrierten eine ähnlich klingende Website und nutzten diese Domain als Reverse-Proxy. Die gefälschte Website lieferte Inhalte der echten Seite aus, denen bösartiges Javascript hinzugefügt wurde.
„Wir gehen davon aus, dass die Angreifer:innen diese Website aufgrund ihrer Verbindung zu einem vielbeachteten nationalen Fest bewusst ausgewählt haben, um das Ereignis möglicherweise als Vorwand für Spear-Phishing-Kampagnen unter dem Deckmantel von Einladungen zu nutzen”, so die Forscher:innen.
So gingen die Angreifer bei ihrer Angriffskampagne vor
Die Hacker:innen nutzten drei Infektionsvektoren. Dazu zählten die direkte Javascript-Injektion in den Datenverkehr legitimer Websites, Proxy-Domains sowie die Kompromittierung der Lieferkette eines ukrainischen Webanalyse-Dienstes. In der ersten Phase erstellte das injizierte Javascript ein Profil des Browsers und des Geräts der Besucher:innen.
Anschließend lösten die Angreifer:innen anhand dieser Informationen eine von drei Zero-Click-Exploit-Ketten aus, die ohne Interaktion der Opfer funktionieren. Laut Sekoia beruht die Zuordnung zum russischen Auslandsgeheimdienst auf den Profilen der Ziele und Ähnlichkeiten mit einem früheren Angriff, der ebenfalls APT29 zugeschrieben wurde.

articles.title: US government warns of 'ongoing cyber threat' amid mass hacks of industrial retail and military freezers | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The U.S. government is warning of an “ongoing cyber threat” facing industrial refrigeration units, after reports of cyberattacks targeting freezers and fridges in supermarkets around the world, U.S. military bases, and at least one blood bank.
U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA, the FBI, and several other federal government departments warned in a joint statement on Thursday that hackers are targeting and compromising internet-connected refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. The statement said that the hacks are hitting critical infrastructure, such as the food, agriculture, transportation, and medicine-shipping industries.
“If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system,” the agencies warn.
The warning comes after several waves of cyberattacks targeting industrial refrigeration units across the United Kingdom and Europe in recent weeks. Two separate waves of attacks allowed hackers to crank up the temperature on freezers and chilling units in at least a dozen countries, spoiling defrosted food and destroying produce. Some of the affected systems included remote-controlled refrigeration units made by Danish company Danfoss, which had stopped providing security updates to its customers’ freezers.
Hackers also targeted a blood bank in France, causing its refrigerated units to boost temperatures in its cold units containing donated blood supplies — but were stopped before the attack could compromise blood stores. The U.S. Department of Defense is investigating a spate of hacks targeting freezers run by the military, according to Reuters. The hacks were first reported by Signal and Silence.
The U.S. has not attributed the hacks to a particular group or government, but security researchers have broadly attributed the attacks to Iran; U.S. officials also reportedly suspect Iran is the likely culprit.
CISA, the FBI, and the Departments of Agriculture, Health and Human Services, and Transportation urged affected industries to remove remote control systems from the internet, change and strengthen passwords, apply patches where possible, and retire equipment that’s no longer supported by the vendor.
In a separate fact sheet, the departments said that hackers may attempt to “force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.”
“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” said CISA’s acting cybersecurity chief Chris Butera.

articles.title: Peligran los juegos físicos de Nintendo: su principal fabricante de memorias se pasa a los centros de datos
articles.text:
Macronix, uno de los principales proveedores de memorias ROM para los cartuchos de Nintendo, reducirá de forma gradual esa producción para concentrarse en memorias NOR flash destinadas a centros de datos de inteligencia artificial (IA).
El cambio puede limitar la oferta de juegos físicos para Nintendo Switch, aunque la empresa japonesa cuenta con otros fabricantes de este componente.
Los ingresos de Macronix por memorias ROM cayeron 39% en el tercer trimestre de 2026 frente al mismo período de 2025. La empresa registró, en contraste, un alza de 158% en las ventas de memorias NOR y de 768% en las de memorias NAND.
La decisión responde a la demanda de componentes para infraestructura informática. Miin Wu, director ejecutivo de Macronix, afirmó durante una conferencia de resultados que el mercado de memorias NOR para centros de datos “es muy robusto”, según Taipei Times.
De qué depende la continuidad de los juegos físicos de Nintendo
La compañía utiliza memorias ROM de Macronix para fabricar parte de los cartuchos de Nintendo Switch. La reducción paulatina de esa línea de negocio podría disminuir la disponibilidad de juegos físicos, pero no implica la desaparición inmediata del formato porque la compañía dispone de otros proveedores.
La empresa japonesa ya había manifestado que no planea abandonar los juegos en formato físico en sus consolas. Esa posición contrasta con la de Sony, que anunció durante el verano que PlayStation dejará de utilizar ese formato en 2028.
Los cartuchos de Nintendo Switch 2 usan memoria flash NAND, un componente cuya fabricación continuará dentro de la nueva estrategia de Macronix. Por esa razón, el cambio afecta sobre todo a los soportes que dependen de memorias ROM.
Por qué la inteligencia artificial está transformando la industria de memorias
La reorientación de Macronix se suma a otras decisiones de la industria de memorias. Micron anunció en diciembre de 2025 el fin de los negocios de su marca de consumo Crucial, dedicada a las memorias RAM y al almacenamiento SSD para PC, para priorizar la demanda de centros de datos.
El sector tecnológico atraviesa una escasez de componentes de memoria vinculada a la alta demanda generada por la inteligencia artificial. Las compañías están priorizando la fabricación y el suministro de memorias de alto rendimiento para centros de datos en lugar de dispositivos de consumo.
Asimismo, la presión sobre el abastecimiento alcanza al sector de los videojuegos, con efectos sobre empresas como Xbox y Valve.
Qué otras novedades hay sobre Nintendo
Nintendo lanzó Zelda: Ocarina of Time para Nintendo Switch 2 este jueves 5 de noviembre de 2026, casi tres décadas después de su estreno original, con gráficos renovados, música orquestal, doblaje en español y cambios de jugabilidad que transforman la aventura de Nintendo 64 en una nueva edición.
La versión digital tiene un precio de 59,99 dólares y ocupará unos 27 GB de almacenamiento. La edición física costará 69,99 dólares, según Nintendo.
El estreno está acompañado por una ocarina electrónica inspirada en el instrumento que aparece en la historia del videojuego. El accesorio permite interpretar las melodías del juego y se venderá por 49,99 dólares.
Los adelantos de esta edición mostraron gráficos ultradetallados e hiperrealistas. Nintendo integró nuevas texturas, secuencias cinematográficas ampliadas y personajes con actuación de voz.
La renovación alcanza a los controles de Link, el protagonista: puede saltar y correr libremente, tiene una cámara mejorada y nuevos movimientos para apuntar con armas. Estas modificaciones se suman a los cambios visuales y sonoros de la aventura.
El juego fue lanzado originalmente en 1998 para Nintendo 64 y se convirtió en el primer título de la saga con gráficos en tres dimensiones. Desde ese instante, se mantuvo entre las entregas más recordadas de la franquicia.

articles.title: Amazon agora oferece AppleCare na compra de iPhones no Brasil • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Amazon agora oferece AppleCare na compra de iPhones no Brasil
Garantia estendida da Maçã fica disponível automaticamente para celulares da marca vendidos no e-commerce.
A Amazon anunciou que vai oferecer o serviço AppleCare de forma automática na compra de iPhones na plataforma. A novidade foi anunciada junto à chegada dos iPhone 18 Pro e iPhone 18 Pro Max ao e-commerce. Apresentados em setembro, os aparelhos chegaram ao Brasil com preços a partir de R$ 11.999.
A novidade vale para qualquer modelo de iPhone vendido e entregue pela Amazon, garantindo 24 meses de cobertura global. O suporte permite acesso a substituições e peças originais da Maçã, além de especialistas da própria empresa nas Apple Store e lojas autorizadas.
A varejista é o primeiro e-commerce a disponibilizar o AppleCare, em parceria com a Assurant. O serviço já era oferecido para iPhones no país por meio da operadora Vivo e do banco Itaú. No site da Apple, também é possível contratar a garantia estendida, mas a opção está restrita a Mac, iPad e Apple TV.
Com a proteção estendida, os clientes podem acessar o suporte oficial da Maçã 24 horas por dia, além de contar com especialistas próprios da Apple em lojas oficiais e credenciadas. A ativação é automática e via IMEI, com reparos feitos por profissionais autorizados, garantia de peças originais e mais benefícios.
Apesar de chegar na Amazon, o AppleCare ainda tem algumas restrições por aqui. Antes da novidade, o serviço só ficava disponível para iPhones por meio de seguros feitos junto à Vivo ou ao Itaú. Agora, serviços como atendimento especializado direto pelo aplicativo e facilidade no acesso ao conserto do dispositivo não exigem pagamento de uma assinatura, por exemplo.
De acordo com a diretora de telefonia e serviços da Amazon Brasil, Gabriela Giannico, a ideia é “oferecer aos consumidores brasileiros confiança e segurança em cada etapa: compra, entrega e proteção a longo prazo”.
O AppleCare da Amazon funciona em parceria com a Assurant, que também está por trás do serviço oferecido pelo Itaú, disponível desde 2022 para clientes do programa iPhone para Sempre.
Segundo a Amazon, além do AppleCare em si, clientes também podem parcelar a compra do iPhone em até 12x sem juros no site ou app.

articles.title: Agility Robotics' Nasdaq debut invites scrutiny of humanoid robot market
articles.text:
Humanoid robots remain unproven at scale and have not yet achieved widespread commercialization, compared with industrial robots that have decades of proven track records in warehouses and factories. That frank acknowledgment is among the risks outlined in a securities filing by Agility Robotics—the first dedicated developer of humanoid robots to become a publicly traded company in the United States.
The robotics company, headquartered in Salem, Oregon, previously became the first to achieve full-time commercial deployment of humanoid robots at a customer warehouse in 2024. Now, Agility’s public listing on the Nasdaq stock exchange as of November 5 has come with financial disclosures detailing how the company plans to build a business around renting out or selling humanoid robots to perform manual labor.
“When we are doing robots as a service, it is much lower risk for customers to use it because they are getting a return on investment on day one,” Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics, told Ars. “Because they’re paying a rate that is comparable to the human labor rate, and that makes the economics pretty straightforward.”
Agility is one of many startups attempting to commercialize humanoid robots. But the company has stood out from the competition through its lead in deploying and operating Digit humanoid robots with multiple customers, including the warehouses of logistics company GXO, the South Carolina factory of German automotive manufacturer Schaeffler, and the automotive production lines of Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada. As Agility’s very first customer, GXO announced it would expand deployments of Digit robots beyond a warehouse in Georgia to additional facilities in North Carolina and Tennessee.
The filings accompanying Agility’s journey toward becoming a publicly traded company—based on a merger with a special purpose acquisition company—also provide a rare look at the business prospects and potential unit economics of humanoid robots. Most of its startup competitors remain privately held companies that have not been nearly as forthcoming.
Another exception has been China’s humanoid robotics company Unitree, which opened its books when it went public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange STAR Market in August 2026.
Robot rental or ownership
Agility described the “illustrative unit economics” for both its “robots-as-a-service” subscription business and an “ownership model,” which would involve corporate clients purchasing robots outright, in an S-4 registration statement filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on September 4.
With the subscription model, customers would pay a one-time cost of about $25,000 per robot for delivery and deployment to a work site, along with a recurring monthly fee of $8,500 for software and maintenance.
Customers can also purchase the robot’s hardware outright for a one-time payment of $200,000, along with another one-time cost of $20,000 for delivery and deployment. But that still comes with an annual subscription fee of $36,000 for software and maintenance, or about $3,000 per month.
In exchange for renting or purchasing the robots, customers would get access to the latest Agility robot, known as Digit 5, starting in 2027. The bipedal robot has swappable end-effector “hands,” can lift up to 50-pound loads, and can perform more than 20 hours of work in a 24-hour period with the help of a fast-charging battery system.
The fast-charging battery technology provided by the UK-based company Nyobolt requires just nine minutes to deliver 90 minutes of robot runtime. “We worked with them for well over a year to design the pack that goes in our robot,” Hurst told Ars. “So the battery pack is fully custom and is ours, and we have the exclusive agreement with Nyobolt around using their [battery] chemistry in humanoid robots.”
The Digit 5 also comes with an onboard safety system that enables it to detect humans moving nearby and take appropriate actions, like standing still or squatting to minimize the risk of harm. That could unlock more opportunities to deploy Digit 5 beyond the confines of isolated work cells within warehouses and factories, said Pras Velagapudi, chief technology officer at Agility, in a previous conversation with Ars.
During a presentation for analysts and investors on October 6, Agility’s chief financial officer, Michael Beer, described the Digit subscription model as allowing customers to replace $200,000 in annual labor costs with $100,000 in annual robot costs, while buying a Digit robot outright could replace $1.1 million in labor costs with about $400,000 in robot costs over five years.
Agility’s business costs and revenue
Meanwhile, Agility described its own annual operating costs per robot as being $15,000 to provide the necessary software and maintenance, along with a one-time cost of $15,000 for Agility to initially deploy each robot.
The robotics company also estimated each Digit v5 humanoid robot as initially costing Agility $150,000 based on the bill of materials. Each robot is estimated to have a useful operational lifespan of about five years.
But Agility anticipates that bill of materials cost falling to $75,000 per robot once it ramps up to annual production of 1,000 robots, and eventually $30,000 per robot if the company can produce 10,000 robots per year. The company plans to gradually ramp up production at its RoboFab manufacturing facility in Oregon.
When balancing such business costs versus revenue, Agility anticipates that it could earn about $500,000 per robot on an annual basis through the subscription model, and about $400,000 per robot each year if a customer purchases the Digit robots outright while paying ongoing software and maintenance fees.
The subscription revenue calculations disclosed in Agility’s S-4 filing were based on an unidentified customer’s $300 million order covering 1,000 Digit 5 robots over a three-year subscription contract.
However, such a customer order does not mean Agility is guaranteed to earn $300 million, because the contract requires the robotics company to deliver on certain “contractual milestones, product features and specifications.”
The robotics company’s financial disclosures also bluntly state that “Agility has incurred net losses since inception and expects to continue to incur operating and net losses for the foreseeable future.” In 2025, the company earned just $1.8 million in revenue against $140 million in operating loss, which shows it’s still in the early stages of building a sustainable business.
Future risks and prospects
Agility said it continues to devote “substantially all of its resources to research, development, and commercialization of its humanoid robot,” while continuing to expand the RoboFab manufacturing facility. On October 21, Agility also announced plans to build a new facility in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, for supporting Digit robot deployments and further developing the robot’s software and AI.
Beyond the challenges of building its own business, Agility’s financial disclosures also cautioned that “competition in the humanoid and robotics market is intensifying rapidly, with well-funded entrants including Boston Dynamics, Tesla, Apptronik, Figure AI, 1X Technologies, Sanctuary AI, Hexagon, and NEURA Robotics, among others, actively developing competing humanoid systems.”
Many of those companies have advantages, such as “significantly greater brand recognition, customer relationships, and financial, technical, manufacturing, and other resources,” Agility’s S-4 filing acknowledged. It also listed business risks involving uncertain AI-driven robotic performance in the real world, safety issues in sharing workspaces with human workers, changing regulations, and cybersecurity threats.
Still, Agility co-founder Hurst described a large potential market with “millions of unfilled roles” involving manual tasks that would typically require higher-cost but relatively low-skilled human labor. Within the next year, Hurst expects multiple Agility customers to be sharing videos of the Digit robots “just very boringly doing their work” to the point where “all of the excitement and hype and novelty of humanoids has worn off.”
“It’ll look a bit like the dawn of the automotive market, and different companies will have different niches—some companies will build the Ford F-150 and some companies will build a Mazda Miata,” Hurst told Ars. “There’s going to be a bunch of different niches for multi-purpose human-centric machines like these.”
Although Hurst sees Agility’s path eventually leading to a general-purpose autonomous robot in the future, he has consistently dismissed the idea of any company immediately deploying humanoid robots to riskier and less structured environments, like people’s homes. “Digit 5 is not going to walk into your living room and do dishes and stuff like that,” he said. “Nobody is.”
Whatever happens with Agility’s journey in the coming years, it will be instructive for anyone interested in the broader trajectory of the humanoid robot industry.
Jeremy Hsu is a reporter exploring a wide range of topics across deep tech and AI. He has previously written for New Scientist, Scientific American, IEEE Spectrum, Wired, Undark Magazine and MIT Tech Review, among many other publications, about topics such as deepfakes, data centers, drones, battery tech, robotics, and GPS jamming. He also has a Master of Arts in Journalism from NYU, and a bachelor's degree from University of Pennsylvania in History and Sociology of Science, with a minor in English.

articles.title: When bad data looks right: The hidden risk of automated reporting
articles.text:
When bad data looks right: The hidden risk of automated reporting
Why automated reporting needs better data validation
The biggest risk with automated reporting isn’t an obviously wrong number. It’s a wrong number that looks completely right.
As businesses automate more of how they collect, process and report information, errors can increasingly pass through systems without attracting attention. By the time questionable data reaches a dashboard or board report, it may have been categorized, calculated and aggregated several times over, giving the final figure a level of credibility the original input never deserved.
Co-Founder and Chief Product & Strategy Officer at Thrive.
The answer is to scrutinise the data much earlier in the process. Rather than relying on checks once a final figure has been produced, technology can help businesses interrogate the quality of data as it enters the reporting process, before an initial mistake has the chance to become an authoritative-looking result.
Building quality into the process
The move away from manual reporting has solved plenty of problems. Information that once had to be pulled together from spreadsheets, emails and different teams can now be collected, calculated and reported far more efficiently. That is hardly surprising, but the quality of the underlying data remains a major stumbling block. Automation does not resolve inconsistent interpretation; it can often scale it.
In fact, 77% of UK companies say data is their biggest challenge to using AI effectively. As automation and AI play a greater role in how businesses handle and interpret information, getting those foundations right becomes even more important.
A person manually compiling a report may spot something that looks unusual and question it. Automation without validation can remove some of those natural moments of scrutiny, processing information exactly as instructed without necessarily recognizing that something is missing, inconsistent or simply implausible.
An incorrect input can become even more inaccurate as it moves through subsequent calculations. If the wrong quantity is entered, then mapped to the wrong metric or valuation, the resulting impact figure can be materially overstated. Catching the error at the point of entry prevents it from compounding further down the line.

Why social value proves the point
Social value measurement provides a useful example. As organizations face growing pressure to prove the impact they create, the quality of the data behind those claims matters. Yet while 95% of senior sustainability professionals consider high-quality data important, only 27% say they currently have it.
Reporting has historically been less mature than the delivery itself. Social value activity can happen across different parts of an organization, with practitioners understandably focused on creating impact first and capturing the information behind it afterwards. The result is that organizations can be doing genuinely valuable work while still struggling to demonstrate it accurately. Poor evidence of impact is not necessarily evidence of poor impact, but externally, the distinction can be difficult to make.
The challenge is turning that activity into reliable, consistent data. Information may have been captured differently across teams, recorded against the wrong measure, or lack the evidence needed to substantiate it. That could mean an FTE job figure being claimed incorrectly, missing evidence, outdated definitions, or someone selecting the wrong metric because its name looks superficially similar to the right one.
For smaller businesses, navigating social value requirements can already be challenging, with 73% of SMEs reporting difficulties formulating social value commitments for government tenders. Making reporting more robust therefore cannot simply mean adding more complexity. Technology needs to make it easier to capture the right information in the first place.
This matters increasingly as social value data carries greater weight. Figures can inform bids and contract performance, and organizations are increasingly expected to substantiate the impact they claim to create. Getting the data right is therefore becoming a question of organizational credibility, not simply reporting accuracy. If leaders cannot trust the evidence behind a figure, they cannot confidently use it to evaluate performance, allocate investment or substantiate claims externally.
From automated reporting to intelligent validation
So, what does better automation look like? Impact data must be structured, validated and understood from the start, rather than just relying on audit or manual checking at the end to uncover problems. That means using technology to test information as it is captured, before errors become embedded in the reporting process.
Questionable inputs are far easier to resolve at the point of entry, while the person entering them still understands the context, rather than months later when teams are trying to reconstruct what happened. Technology can help by flagging information that looks incomplete, inconsistent or implausible before it becomes embedded in a wider calculation.
Consistency across teams matters too. Building clear definitions and requirements into the reporting process can reduce that room for interpretation and help ensure information is being captured in the same way across an organization.
Businesses also need to think about what happens to the evidence behind a number as it moves through the system. A final figure should still be traceable back to its source, so teams can understand where it came from, how it was calculated, and what supports it if challenged later. Maintaining that traceability becomes increasingly important as more stages of the reporting process are automated.
None of this means removing human judgement. The aim is to use automation to focus that judgement where it adds most value, rather than asking people to manually check everything or clean up problems at the end.
Automation has already made reporting faster and more efficient. The next challenge is ensuring it also makes reporting more reliable. The quality of the checks built into the process will become just as important as the speed at which information can be processed. Confidence in the final number should come from knowing the data behind it can stand up to scrutiny.

articles.title: Micron's $4.5 billion Taoyuan plant construction halted amidst labor dispute — company and union still haven’t reached agreement as latter asks for clearer profit-sharing terms
articles.text:
Micron's $4.5 billion Taoyuan plant construction halted amidst labor dispute — company and union still haven’t reached agreement as latter asks for clearer profit-sharing terms
Is this a thinly veiled threat?
Micron has paused construction on its Fab 11E site at Taoyuan as the company and its Taoyuan labor union have failed to reach an agreement regarding clearer profit-sharing terms. Bloomberg reports that activity on the site has all but halted, except for minor safety work, with some sources saying that executives are concerned about uncertainties regarding negotiations with its workers. The company hasn’t released a statement about the move but has already informed local officials about the suspension.
“Taiwan plays an important role in Micron’s global footprint, and our operations today continue as normal,” Micron said. “We are confident in maintaining business continuity for our customers.” The company has recently announced a bonus that could give as much as five times the annual salary of some eligible workers, and has also wrapped up a deal with the bigger Taichung union, although some members say they were dissatisfied with the outcome. On the other hand, the Taoyuan union is still holding out for better terms, with the two parties set to meet again on November 6. It even launched a one-day strike last month to show the chipmaker its resolve and how its operations could be disrupted if it does not meet their demands.
Workers from the big three memory chip manufacturers — Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix — have been protesting recently and demanding a bigger slice of the massive profits that these companies are currently making from the AI memory chip boom. SK hynix has recently agreed to pay staff $50,00 apiece, with each employee set to receive $477,000 in bonuses this year and up to $900,000 next year. Samsung Foundry workers also fought for a $340,000 average bonus, which received approval at the last minute and averted a massive strike that would have disrupted the company’s operations. Employees from these South Korean companies expect to nab performance bonuses of up to $400,000 and are rejecting coveted overseas training programs in favor of cold, hard cash.
While the company hasn’t made a statement regarding the suspension of work on its Taoyuan site, it’s hard to believe that the move happening so close to its next meeting with the Taoyuan union is a coincidence. It should be noted that Micron is also developing other sites across the world, with plans for an HBM fab in Japan, a $24-billion development on the way in Singapore, plus facilities across the U.S. Nevertheless, the company says it is looking forward to reaching an agreement with the workers, with the Taiwan government hoping for a win-win outcome for both parties.

articles.title: Ninja teamed up with Jonathan Adler to redesign its hit espresso machine, and the delightfully garish result will divide coffee lovers forever
articles.text:
Ninja has turned to designer Jonathan Adler to give its top espresso maker a 'glamorous' makeover, but is it high fashion or an eyesore?
It's... um... striking
- Ninja is bringing glamor to the humble espresso machine
- The new-look Luxe Café Pro was made in collaboration with designer and potter Jonathan Adler
- It's priced at $899 (likely £879 / AU$999)
If you've ever looked at your coffee machine and thought 'it's nice and all, but what I really want is a coffee maker so garish that I'll have to make espresso with my eyes closed?' then today is your lucky day.
Ninja has upgraded its excellent Ninja Luxe Café Pro Espresso Machine by getting renowned designer and potter Jonathan Adler to give it a makeover, and the results are, um, well... look at the picture and see for yourself.
The Ninja Luxe Café Pro Espresso Machine by Jonathan Adler is "the most glamorous espresso machine I've ever seen," Adler says. It's certainly very different from the usual look of even the most expensive and best coffee makers. And you've got to admire Ninja's bravery, because this is likely to be the Marmite of luxe coffee makers. For everyone that sees it and falls in love with its loudness there will be others like me who run away screaming.
I'm ribbing Ninja here, but I'm doing it affectionately: my kitchen contains multiple Ninja appliances, and while I happen to like their black and chrome looks I'm very much in favor of more interesting color and design choices — it's why the same kitchen also includes a brightly colored Smeg kettle, toaster and juicer. And this coffee maker is part of a new design direction for the brand, which means some really great-looking products such as the new Ninja MultiPot XL, which I think looks great in its multiple colors, and the gold detailing of the Ninja Luxe Café Pro Limited Edition by David Beckham, which launched in early 2026.
The loudness of the new version is entirely deliberate, I think: it's a halo product that'll raise awareness of Ninja's new design direction, even if that awareness comes via gently mocking articles like this one. It's not for me, but I think plenty of folks will love it.
But enough about the looks. What about the coffee?
Ninja Luxe Café Pro Espresso Machine by Jonathan Adler: key features and pricing
Beneath the new look is a very good coffee machine: the Ninja Luxe Café Pro Espresso Machine by Jonathan Adler is the Pro version of the Ninja Luxe Café, which we gave 4.5 out of 5 stars to in our in-depth Ninja Luxe Café review. The Pro version adds a frother, a lever to tamp the coffee and has even more drinks in its menu.

The differences between the Jonathan Adler version and the standard Pro are cosmetic: natural wood accents, Adler's geometric Versailles pattern on the panel and brass accents instead of the usual chrome.
Inevitably, that adds to the sticker price. The Luxe Café launched in the US with a recommended price of $499.99 (about £400 / AU$750). The Pro by Jonathan Adler version is almost twice the price at $899.99.
That's a significant premium over the non-designer Pro, which is currently retailing at $749 / £729, but it's the same price as the limited edition David Beckham model that's still on sale. We'll leave the last word to Adler. "I believe glamour belongs everywhere," he says. "Including your kitchen countertops."

articles.title: MacBook Pro and iMac M6 are incredibly efficient
articles.text:
I’ve been using the M6 iMac and M6 MacBook Pro for about a week (though I had to take the past couple of days off to use the M5 MacBook PROLED XDR), and I’ve liked them both. Though I mostly spent my time with the MacBook Pro.
I tested the MacBook Pro 14-inch M6 12C/12C 16GB 1TB in Space Black and the iMac M6 12C/12C 16GB 512GB in Green. I liked the look of both of them, especially the Pro 14-inch in Space Black. The typing experience is great with decent key travel, and the Magic Trackpad is very responsive, so it was very easy to switch from my MacBook Air.
I didn’t like how heavy the M6 MacBook Pro was. The MacBook Pro is almost a pound heavier than my M4 MacBook Air, and yes, it’s obvious that the Air would be lighter than the Pro, but I definitely wasn’t ready for just how much heavier the Pro feels. Even the M5 Max PROLED was noticeably lighter than the MacBook Pro M6.
Bumpin’ speakers
I was really impressed by the laptop’s speakers. Music was crystal clear and very loud, easily filling my bedroom. And even with my bedroom door closed, I could still hear it from my living room about 20 feet away, though it wasn’t too loud to interrupt my roommate while he was watching TV. The device has a six-speaker sound system, so watching anime was impactful with the speaker and combined with the nano-texture display, it made the experience great.
Speaking of the nano-texture display, this was my first one (besides the iPhone Duo) and I really liked it. It creates an anti-glare experience, so I didn’t have issues using the laptop in my backyard on the one sunny day we had (winter is coming), and I like how videos and pictures look. It’s no PROLED screen — I definitely missed that device’s screen and Dynamic Island when I switched to the M6, but you’re not paying nearly as much.
Cool to the touch
I like that the M6 felt cool to the touch most of the time, it was very comfortable to keep on my lap. If I was watching anime, working on articles, or even editing photos, the M6 kept cold the whole time. I played Control with ray-tracing and 120Hz turned on, and the device got pretty warm after about 10 minutes. It was nice that it cooled down pretty quickly after I stopped gaming, though.
Speaking of games, the M6 handled Slay the Spire and Control without any problems, besides warming up. Both games looked great with ProMotion turned on, and I liked that there wasn’t any slowdown even though the graphics were turned up a bit.
The speed at which both open apps is great, and downloads are very quick as well. My partner has gotten into designing stickers that he can iron on clothes to add a bit more of his taste to his outfits. He’s been using the M6 iMac with XTool software to create his designs, and he said that the software booted up quickly, there were no issues loading up big projects either, and he noticed that everything flowed quicker than my M4 MacBook Air.
Another thing that’s nice about the M6 iMac is that it’s always there and ready for you. My last iMac had an Intel chip (the 2019 version!), and it would take a moment to boot up. However, the M6 iMac boots up instantly, and you’re right back into what you were doing before.
Battery life on the M6 MacBook Pro is great, lasting me an entire workday, and Fast Charging is a big win, getting me up to 50 per cent in about 35 minutes. I tend to never keep my laptop on the charger, so it was nice that even when I prematurely removed it from the charger, I didn’t have to worry about battery life.
More to come…
It’s only been a week with the M6 MacBook Pro and the M6 iMac, and I spent a few of those days under the weather, so I definitely need to put both of them through their paces some more. But as I use each of the new Apple devices, I’ll report back. I definitely want to try some vibe coding with the M6 MacBook Pro and will definitely need to do some video editing over the next couple of weeks to see how well the M6 performs under some harder pressure.
The M6 MacBook Pro starts at $2.799, while the M6 iMac starts at $2,099, and both come out on November 6.

articles.title: Google Photos pourrait bientôt transformer vos photos en événements de calendrier
articles.text:
Vous croisez une affiche de concert, vous la prenez en photos… et vous oubliez son existence. Et bien plus maintenant : Google Photos travaille sur une option qui intégrera directement ce genre d'événement à votre agenda.
Que d’évolutions pour Google Photos! Dernièrement, Google a créé une fonction permettant aux groupes d’amis de rassembler leurs clichés de soirée au sein d’un même album, étendu la retouche express aux vidéos et lancé l’option IA « Edit with Ask Photos ». La firme de Mountain View en a aussi profité pour modifier discrètement sa politique de confidentialité afin d’exploiter les données de l’outil pour personnaliser ses publicités.
Une autre évolution de taille devrait également arriver bientôt. On vous explique.
Google Photos va bientôt ajouter des événements dans votre agenda
L’analyse d’APK réserve souvent de belles surprises : l’équipe d’Android Authority a trouvé dans le code de la version 8.0 de Google Photos une nouvelle fonctionnalité d'ajout d'événement. Reliée à AskPhotos, l’assistant IA qui répond à vos interrogations sur les images, elle est pour l’instant indisponible pour le grand public.
Son fonctionnement est le suivant : il suffit de prendre une photo, d’une affiche par exemple, et de demander à AskPhotos de la lire. La technologie repérera le nom de l'événement, la date et les horaires puis préparera une fiche. Après validation, l'application demandera l'accès à votre agenda, Google ou non, et ajoutera l'événement à votre planning.
L’IA aux commandes pour le meilleur et pour le pire
Bien sûr, l’intelligence artificielle étant susceptible de se tromper, il faudra être prudent et bien vérifier les détails de l'événement avant de le valider. Google a heureusement pensé à tout : un lien vers la photo d’origine sera notamment inclus pour vérifier que les informations inscrites sont correctes.
Cette nouvelle fonctionnalité est encore loin d’être achevée : lors de son test, l’équipe d’Android Authority a, par exemple, remarqué que l’écran de validation n’affichait pas de fuseau horaire, ce qui pouvait entraîner des confusions. On espère que Google affinera ce point afin d’éviter les erreurs.
Malgré tout, cette option pourrait s’avérer bien utile et les utilisateurs devraient apprécier ce petit gain de temps. Pour l’heure, Google n’a pas communiqué de date de lancement : il faudra donc faire preuve de patience pour en savoir plus.

articles.title: Apple MacBook Pro (14-inch, M6) review: Speedy M6 chip slips into comfortable shoes
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
While the base MacBook Pro design is getting a bit tired, Apple’s new M6 chip gives the 14-inch MacBook even more pep in its step.
Reasons to buy
- + M6 continues Apple’s track record of solid year-over-year performance upgrades
- + Wi-Fi 7 finally makes an appearance
- + Impeccable build quality
Reasons to avoid
- - Memory and SSD upgrades are more expensive than ever before
- - Design is starting to look a bit stale after 5 years
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
It’s that time of the year again, which means that Apple has released yet another refreshed 14-inch MacBook Pro using a legacy chassis. While it looks the same as last year’s M5 models on the outside, it has some key hardware upgrades underneath that address performance and connectivity.
This time around, we have a MacBook Pro using the new M6 chip that was first introduced in the refreshed Mac Mini. In addition, Apple has outfitted the MacBook Pro with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity courtesy of the in-house Apple N1 chip.
Thanks to industry-wide price hikes on memory and storage, Apple’s 14-inch MacBook Pro now starts at $1,999.
Design of the MacBook Pro (M6, 14-inch)
Apple has been using the same design for its entry-level MacBook Pro since 2021, and there are no changes this year (if you want a slightly refreshed design, check out the touch screen-enabled 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros). It’s still a good-looking laptop, but it’s showing its age. Our MacBook Pro review unit came finished in silver instead of space black. While space black looks great, it’s a fingerprint magnet, so many people might prefer the lighter finish, which better hides your skin oils.
The notch at the top of the display now seems archaic, especially after seeing the Dynamic Island on the pricier MacBook Pros. The notch is always staring back at you, even though I have mostly gotten used to it over the years. The main thing going in the notch’s favor is that it resides in the same space as the menu bar, which limits the visual annoyance.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
My only other niggle with the design is one that I’ve harped about in previous MacBook Pro reviews: the cutout in the keyboard deck that aids in lifting the lid has sharp corners, which can jab your palms while typing.
As with previous MacBook Pro generations, you’ll find three Thunderbolt 4 ports (Thunderbolt 5 is not available on M6 models), a full-size SDXC card reader, HDMI 2.1, a 3.5 mm audio jack, and a MagSafe 3 connector.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Our 14-inch MacBook review unit measures 12.31 x 8.71 x 0.61 inches and weighs 3.4 pounds, the same as last year’s model with the M5. For comparison, the Gigabyte Aero X16 measures 14 x 9.9 x 0.78 inches and 4.2 pounds, while the Dell XPS 14 comes in at 12.19 x 8.26 x 0.6 inches and weighs 3 pounds.
MacBook Pro Specifications (M6, 14-inch)
| CPU | Apple M6 (12-core CPU) | 
| Graphics | 12-core GPU (integrated) | 
| Memory | 16GB unified LPDDR5x memory | 
| Storage | 1TB SSD | 
| Display | 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display with Nano-texture option, 3,024 x 1,964, 120 Hz ProMotion | 
| Networking | Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 | 
| Ports | 3x Thunderbolt 4 over USB Type-C, HDMI 2.1, SDXC card slot, 3.5 mm headphone jack, MagSafe 3 | 
| Camera | 12MP Center Stage camera | 
| Battery | 72.4WHr | 
| Power Adapter | 70W | 
| Operating System | macOS Golden Gate 27.0 | 
| Dimensions (WxDxH) | 12.31 x 8.71 x 0.61 inches (312.6 mm x 221.2 mm x 15.1 mm) | 
| Weight | 3.4 pounds (1.55 kg) | 
| Price (as configured) | $1,999.00 | 
Productivity and Graphics Performance on the MacBook Pro (M5, 14-inch)
Our 14-inch MacBook Pro review unit features a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU version of Apple’s new M6 SoC. This is the same configuration as the Mac Mini that we reviewed in September, except that our laptop review unit includes 16GB of unified LPDDR5x memory compared to 24GB. Rounding out the specs is a standard 1TB SSD.
Slow and steady wins the race in silicon advances. In every productivity benchmark, our M6 MacBook Pro not only outshone the previous-generation M5 MacBook Pro, but it also trounced the prosumer Gigabyte Aero X16 (AMD Ryzen AI 7 350) and Dell XPS 14 (Intel Core Ultra X7 358H) Windows 11 laptops that we pitted it against.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Starting out with the Geekbench 6 synthetic CPU benchmark, our M6 review unit put up a modest 10% gain in single-core performance over the M5 (4,752 versus 4,288). Switching to multi-core performance, that performance delta grew to just over 18%. Of the two Windows 11 laptops, the XPS 14 came the closest, putting up single- and multi-core scores of 2,867 and 16,927, respectively.
Apple appears to have held the line when it comes to SSD performance year-over-year. 2025's M5 MacBook Pro managed 1917.35 MBps in our in-house 25GB file transfer test. Things changed little this year, as our M6 MacBook Pro came in at 1914.23 MBps. The Aero X16 carried the baton for the Windows 11 field with a result of 1,480.57 MBps.
Our Handbrake test consists of transcoding a 4K video file to 1080p. The new M6 MacBook Pro review finished the job in a brisk 2 minutes and 50 seconds, while the M5 version took 3 minutes and 31 seconds to complete the task.
Our stress test for productivity laptops centers around Cinebench 2026, which we run 10 times back-to-back, tallying multi-core scores along the way. The M6 MacBook Pro started with a score of 5,026.55 and hovered around 5,440 for the remainder of the runs.
The M5 includes a 12-core GPU (each core features a dedicated neural accelerator), which promises up to a 30 percent uplift in performance compared to the M5.
Although the base MacBook Pro isn’t what we’d consider a gaming beast, it did manage 53.7 frames per second (FPS) at 1800 x 1125 resolution in Cyberpunk 2077 using the “For this Mac” preset and 32.66 FPS at 3024 x 1890. This compares to 47.65 FPS and 31.47 FPS, respectively, for the M5 MacBook Pro.
Display on the MacBook Pro (M6, 14-inch)
Apple’s M6-equipped 14-inch MacBook Pro continues to use an IPS display with mini LED backlighting. As before, you get a 3,024 x 1,964 resolution panel with a 120 Hz refresh rate.
While the mini LED panel looks good, it’s not nearly as capable as the touch-enabled PROLED XDR display found on its pricier siblings. Although you can equip the MacBook Pro with a nano-texture display for $150, our review unit didn’t have it.
Being that I’m a huge fan of Sylvester Stallone’s Rocky films (well, the first four), I pulled up the second trailer for I Play Rocky, which is set to release later this month. The design aesthetic of the film is, of course, distinctly 1970s, and the mini LED panel did a good job of presenting the muted colors (mostly warm earth tones).
As I’m still in shock over the passing of Patrick Stewart, I watched a sizable portion of Star Trek: First Contact on the screen. Again, the display performed well, with major kudos during the opening battle scene where Federation ships are battling the Borg. The orange explosions, red phaser blasts, and the Borg’s green cutting beams vividly danced across the screen. The blackness of space wasn’t quite as deep as I witnessed with an OLED screen side-by-side, but it’s still good.
Our MacBook Pro review unit was even brighter than last year’s model, if only by a slim margin (571.4 nits versus 558 nits). That performance was still well ahead of the OLED panels in the Windows laptops.
Those similarities extended to color performance, which tracked nearly identically to the preceding M5 MacBook Pro, which was a dead ringer for its M4 predecessor. Our instrumented tests showed 81.5 percent coverage of DCI-P3 and 115.1 percent of the sRGB. Although the XPS 14’s OLED panel was no match for brightness (358 nits), it pipped the MacBook Pro in color performance (89.7 percent DCI-P3, 126.6 percent sRGB).
Keyboard and Touchpad on the Apple MacBook Pro (M6, 14-inch)
As with all the other exterior design elements of the M6 MacBook Pro, the keyboard remains unchanged. To me, that’s a good thing, as it’s one of the things I love the most about Apple laptops. As someone who lived through Apple’s horrible butterfly keys on the 12-inch MacBook and subsequent MacBook Pro models, the return to the venerable switches was a return to sanity on Apple’s part.
Apple isn’t the type of company that would equip its laptops with RGB keyboards, so you’ll get single-zone white LED key backlighting. Although the thought of a MacBook Pro with RGB lighting brings a slight smirk to my face, I’m perfectly fine with Apple’s monochromatic approach.
I used the keyhero.com typing test, as I do with all laptops I review, and settled in with 93 words per minute at 95 percent accuracy. Those figures track with what I achieve with other Apple and Windows laptops.
Like all MacBooks (except for the entry-level Neo), our MacBook Pro features a large haptic trackpad that measures 5 x 3 inches. The glass surface makes gliding with your finger or thumb easy-peasy, and the simulated “click” is satisfying.
Audio on the Apple MacBook Pro (M6, 14-inch)
We’re sure you’re noticing a theme in this review, but the audio system in our MacBook Pro review unit remains unchanged compared to its earlier M5 and M4 counterparts. What that means is that you’ll find a six-speaker system that includes support for major audio formats like Dolby Digital, Dolby Atmos, Dolby Digital Plus, and Apple Spatial Audio.
I’m a sucker for acoustic guitar, and one of the greats of the 2000s is John Mayer. Perhaps my favorite John Mayer song is “3x5” from his debut album, which my girlfriend at the time (now wife) and I played over and over again and witnessed several times in concert. On the MacBook Pro’s speakers, the acoustic guitar packs just as much of a punch as John’s breathy vocals pelting out vivid lyrics like, "Today, skies are painted colors of a cowboy cliché."
I got so lost in the audio experience that I found myself listening to the entire Room for Squares album and being transported back to my college days.
Upgradeability of the Apple MacBook Pro (M6, 14-inch)
While most Windows laptops give you some semblance of upgradeability, allowing you to upgrade at the very least storage, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth, and sometimes memory, you’ll find no such luxuries in MacBook land. There are four pentalobe screws on the bottom of the laptop, but once you remove the cover, there’s nothing of note that’s upgradeable. The M6 chip with its integrated 16GB of memory can’t be replaced, nor can the 1TB SSD – both packages are soldered onto the motherboard. As with all MacBooks, you’ll need to settle on how much RAM and storage you want at purchase time. If you get it wrong, you’ll have to live with that config until it’s time to upgrade your laptop again.
Battery Life on the Apple MacBook Pro (M6, 14-inch)
If there’s one thing that you can count on when it comes to MacBooks, it’s battery life. It’s pretty common for MacBooks to last for 18 or more hours in our battery life test, which consists of browsing the web, running OpenGL tests, and streaming video at 150 nits of brightness.
Our MacBook Pro review unit was no exception, lasting 19 hours and 5 minutes thanks to its 72 WHr battery. This was nearly a one-hour improvement over its M5 counterpart, which is a testament to the efficiency gains that Apple is able to achieve with the 2-nanometer process node.
Heat on the Apple MacBook Pro (M6, 14-inch)
We measured skin temperature on the MacBook Pro during our Cinebench 2026 stress test. Unlike the cheaper MacBook Airs, which are fanless, the MacBook Pro’s two internal fans kick into gear quite quickly to dissipate heat.
The hottest point was near the left exhaust vent, which measured 106 degrees Fahrenheit, with 105 F seen between the G and H keys. Given its distance from the toasty parts of the laptop, the touchpad remained cool to the touch at 78 F. The touchpad was much cooler at 82.8 F.
We use TG Pro to measure internal temperatures while running the Cinebench 2026 stress test. While TG Pro doesn’t have full support for the M6 yet, the Power Manager dies reported peak temperatures of 80 degrees Celsius (C) for the SoC. The overall system temperature, which takes an average of several components (i.e., power supply, battery, SSD, logic board, etc.), was 43 degrees C.
Webcam on the Apple MacBook Pro (M6, 14-inch)
The 12MP Center Stage camera that’s been featured in the last two MacBook Pro generations has made a reappearance this year. All of the superlatives that I had for the M5 MacBook Pro are relevant to my current review unit. Namely, image quality was impressive across the board, in both bright and low-light conditions.
Unlike some other laptop webcams that skew my darker skin color or apply smoothing algorithms that make my skin look like a Tootsie Roll, the camera picked up the wrinkles around my eyes and accurately represented the grays in my beard.
Software on the Apple MacBook Pro (M6, 14-inch)
The M6 MacBook Pro ships with macOS 27 Golden Gate preinstalled. You can liken the shift from macOS 26 Tahoe to macOS 27 Golden Gate to the OS X 10.5 Leopard to Mac OS X 10.6 Snow Leopard transition. In other words, macOS 27 is more about making the operating system more reliable and faster rather than bombarding users with new features. You can read more about macOS 27 Golden Gate in my M6 Mac Mini review.
Just like Windows 11, macOS comes with a slew of apps preinstalled upon first boot. Some of the standouts include GarageBand, Apple’s productivity suite (Keynote, Pages, Numbers), Apple TV, iMovie, and Home (Apple’s smart home application). With the exception of Apple TV, the other apps are productivity utilities meant to enhance the user experience and get work done. You won’t find typical bloatware like app/shortcuts for services like Dropbox or antivirus programs like McAfee as you would on Windows 11 laptops.
Apple MacBook Pro (M6, 14-inch) Configurations and Warranty
When opting for the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 processor, you’re looking at a starting price of $1,999. In addition to the M6 processor, you get 16GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD (the configuration of our review unit).
From there, you can opt for 24GB (+$200) or 32AM (+$400) of RAM, and 2TB (+$500) or 4TB (+$1,500) of storage. There are also two standalone options that you can add: the nano-texture display for $150 and a 96-watt power adapter for an extra $20.
The MacBook Pro has a standard one-year warranty. However, you can pick up AppleCare+ for $99.99/year or $9.99/month. The coverage adds unlimited repairs covering accidents, 24/7 priority tech support, and battery replacement.
Bottom Line
When it comes to everything you see on the outside, Apple’s latest 14-inch MacBook Pro is more of the same: same display, same chassis, same keyboard, and the same great build quality. But true to form, Apple has steadily focused on improving performance year-over-year, and we see that again with the new M6 SoC.
You’ll see anywhere from a 10% to 20% uplift across the board, depending on whether you’re dealing with single- or multi-threaded apps. On top of that, efficiency gains have netted nearly an additional hour of battery life over its M5-powered predecessor. And Apple has finally given the MacBook Pro Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0 support.
The M6 MacBook Pro doesn’t have the OLED touchscreen, more svelte design, or Dynamic Island of the all-new MacBook Pros, but it also started at a price that is $900 less than those systems. With that said, the $1,999 price of our review unit is still a lot of money to ask for a laptop featuring just 16GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD. And you don’t even get an OLED screen at that price.
But given the price of memory and storage these days, $1,999 isn’t exactly out of the ordinary. A Dell XPS 14 configured with an Intel Core Ultra 5 325, 16GB of RAM, 1TB SSD, and a 2.8K OLED display is $2,549. We are truly living in unprecedented times, and while it’s hard to reset our expectations concerning the price of tech, the M6 MacBook Pro remains a solid entry in a highly competitive market.
Brandon Hill is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware. He has written about PC and Mac tech since the late 1990s with bylines at AnandTech, DailyTech, and Hot Hardware. When he is not consuming copious amounts of tech news, he can be found enjoying the NC mountains or the beach with his wife and two sons.

articles.title: Telus says it restored wireless services after outages hit several provinces
articles.text:
Telus is facing an outage impacting its mobile network, particularly phone calls, as of around 9 a.m. ET on Nov. 5.
MobileSyrup received some reports from readers impacted by the outages, and some of our writers have also confirmed issues with phone and voicemail services, but problems appear to be sporadic.
Moreover, outage tracker Downdetector saw a spike in outage reports starting shortly before 9 a.m. ET, with the map showing reports concentrated in Toronto, Ottawa, Calgary, Edmonton, and Vancouver.
Update Nov. 5, 2026, at 2:13 p.m. ET: In an email to MobileSyrup, Telus confirmed a “small number” of service interruptions in eastern Canada on Nov. 5, and said services had been restored.
“A small number of calls in Eastern Canada may have experienced interruptions this morning. All services have been restored, and calls to emergency 911 services remained fully operational. Customers in Western Canada were not affected. We thank our customers for their patience and understanding.”
However, at the time of this update, there was still an ongoing outage impacting Maidstone and Tecumseh, Ont. Further, while Telus said the outages didn’t impact customers in western Canada, the company’s outage site still outlined numerous long-running outages impacting people in B.C. and Alberta.
The original story continues below.
The carrier’s own outage website details multiple problems across Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, and B.C. These include wireless outages as well as problems impacting home phone, internet, and TV services. Most of these started in November, though some of the listed outages date back to October or even the summer.
Ontario
Telus reported a “degradation of wireless services” that started at 9:39 a.m. in Maidstone and Tecumseh, Ont. Data, text, voice, and 911 are all impacted.
The carrier says it offers 911 wireless fallback that uses other carriers’ networks in the area, but notes that customers may need to set their mobile device network to automatic in order for it to work.
Also in Ontario, around the Ottawa area, Telus reported a wireless services failure impacting voice calls, but only when calling landlines.
Quebec
A Nov. 4 outage linked to a damaged cable is ongoing but could be fixed as early as the afternoon of Nov. 5, according to the Telus outage page. This outage impacts data, voice, and text services in Chateauguay, Kahnawake, Lery, Mercier, Saint-Constant, and Saint-Remi.
Alberta
Telus’ website lists 11 active outages in Alberta, most of which date back to October or beyond. These outages are mostly related to home phone, landline 911, and internet/TV services. These include:
- Plamondon – home phone, 911 landline, outage due to suspected cable damage, started Nov. 4.
- Athabasca – home phone, 911 landline, outage started Oct. 30, suspected cable damage.
- Edmonton (Jasper Place) – two home phone, 911 landline outages reported, started Nov. 2 and 4, suspected cable damage.
- Valleyview – home phone, 911 landline, outage started Oct. 30, suspected cable damage.
- Peace River – home phone, 911 landline, started Nov. 2, suspected hardware problem.
- Edmonton – three outages for internet and two for Optik TV, one starting Oct. 4, one Nov. 4 and the last on April 17. Caused by hardware problems; investigation and restoration efforts ongoing.
- Edmonton (Bonnie Doon) – home phone, 911 landline outage caused by a cut cable on Oct. 28, restoration efforts ongoing.
- Grouard – home phone, 911 landline, outage started Oct. 24, suspected cable damage.
B.C.
Telus’ outage site lists several issues impacting B.C., including wireless, home phone, 911 landline, internet, and TV. Notably, several of the listed outages stem from the B.C. wildfires earlier this year, but others started in November.
For wireless specifically, Telus reported a degradation of wireless services in Vancouver and Whistler impacting data, text, and voice services, which started on Nov. 4. The carrier hasn’t yet determined a cause
- Gibsons – multiple home phone, 911 landline outages under investigation; suspected hardware problem.
- Hope – home phone, 911 landline, internet, Optik TV outages, suspected hardware issue, started Nov. 2.
- Delta – internet and Optik TV outage with undetermined cause, started Nov. 1.
- Several outages dating back to July and August related to wildfires.
If you’re with Telus, let us know down below whether you’re impacted by any of these outages.

articles.title: OnlyOffice rajoute un assistant IA à sa suite bureautique mobile
articles.text:
Les applications Documents de la suite OnlyOffice pour iOS et Android reçoivent un assistant IA qui résume, crée des fichiers et remplit les formulaires PDF. L’éditeur annonce aussi 44 failles corrigées dans ses solutions.
Après OnlyOffice 10.0, déployé en octobre, c’est au tour des applications mobiles d’être mises à jour. L’IA est à l’honneur sur iOS et Android.
Ce que l’IA sait faire sur mobile, et les 44 failles corrigées en parallèle
L’assistant est accessible depuis la section Documents, là où l’on range ses fichiers. Il est possible de lui poser une question sur un fichier sans l’ouvrir, de lui demander un résumé ou de chercher une information précise. Cet assistant accepte aussi des fichiers et des images en pièce jointe, par exemple pour l’interroger sur leur contenu, sans avoir à copier un texte ou à décrire une image. Sur iOS, les fichiers stockés dans le cloud de l’entreprise sont aussi acceptés.
Dans les éditeurs de texte, de feuilles de calcul et de présentations, un chat IA propose des fonctions adaptées à chaque outil. Il devient plus simple d'effectuer diverses actions comme rédiger ou résumer, analyser ou nettoyer des données, suggérer un graphique, préparer des notes de discours ou encore générer une image. La réponse s’insère directement dans le document. Sur Android, un onglet IA dédié rassemble l’assistant et les réglages des fournisseurs.
L’assistant crée aussi des fichiers à partir d’une simple description. Il génère des présentations structurées, avec du texte et des images, et sur iOS des documents texte et des feuilles de calcul. La génération s’effectue en arrière-plan ; il est donc possible de continuer à travailler dans l’application en parallèle. Pour les formulaires PDF, l’IA repère les champs à compléter et renseigne les dates, les coordonnées ou les numéros de téléphone. Elle peut aussi ajouter une signature ou une image, et sur Android, puiser les coordonnées dans l’appareil.
Les IA de Grok et DeepSeek s’ajoutent à celles de Mistral, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google et Ollama. Sur iOS 26 et versions ultérieures, la dictée vocale est traitée directement sur l’appareil. Sur Android, les réponses de l’IA peuvent être lues à voix haute, dans la langue détectée automatiquement. Côté serveur, les administrateurs des éditions Enterprise et Developer peuvent configurer les fournisseurs et les modèles autorisés, sans que chaque utilisateur ait à saisir sa propre clé API. Ils peuvent d’ailleurs désactiver l'IA pour un éditeur ou pour tout le serveur.
En parallèle, OnlyOffice annonce 44 failles corrigées dans plusieurs composants : conversion de documents, éditeur PDF, macros, WOPI (le protocole qui permet à une plateforme de stockage d’intégrer l’éditeur), fonctions d’IA et configuration du serveur. Ces brèches concernaient des risques d’accès non autorisé aux fichiers, d’élévation de privilèges, de compromission de sessions de coédition et d’exécution de scripts malveillants.
OnlyOffice conseille aux installations auto-hébergées de passer manuellement en 10.0.2.
Si la suite OnlyOffice est avant tout destinée aux entreprises, elle propose une version gratuite pour les particuliers qui permet de créer des documents de type Word, Excel, PowerPoint ainsi que des formulaires. Ergonomique à souhait, elle joue aussi la carte de l'auto-hébergement et de la sécurité.

articles.title: How Pine Labs is building for the agent economy: CTO Sanjeev Kumar on trust, control and execution
articles.text:
How Pine Labs is building for the agent economy: CTO Sanjeev Kumar on trust, control and execution
At TechSparks 2026, Pine Labs Chief Technology Officer, Sanjeev Kumar showcased how developers, merchants, and teams can put AI agents to work, backed by controls that keep them accountable.
AI agents are starting to run real parts of a business, from finding customers to processing complaints. For banks, fintech companies, and enterprises, that raises a basic question: how far can an agent be trusted to act on its own?
Pine Labs is addressing this question by building an ecosystem that enables AI agents to take on tasks across commerce while keeping their actions accountable. Speaking at its product showcase at TechSparks 2026, Sanjeev Kumar, CTO, Pine Labs, said, “We have tried to make AI a first-class citizen in our ecosystem.”
Over the past 18 months, Pine Labs has been building a commerce operating system around AI agents, combining tools to manage their permissions and track their actions with applications for merchants and enterprise teams. Its Agent Store will open the ecosystem to third-party developers building for merchants and banks.
Building trust into AI agents
For agents to operate in banking and enterprise environments, organizations need to know what they are authorized to do and how their actions can be audited. Pine Labs has developed Grantex, which Kumar described as ‘Open Authorization 2.0 for AI agents’. It assigns each agent a defined set of permissions, an expiry, and a record of the human who authorized it. If an agent authorized to read and draft emails attempts to send one, the action can be blocked and its permissions revoked, including those of any child agents. A tamper-proof, hash-chain audit trail records its actions.
Kumar outlined the work involved in connecting tools and systems, setting up retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), running continuous evaluations, and deciding where human intervention is necessary. These components need to work together before an agent can reliably handle tasks in an enterprise environment.
Pine Labs first deployed the technology across its compliance, finance, HR, and marketing teams, with processing taking place within its own environment. The company is also implementing it with banks in India and overseas.
From cyber fraud complaints to faster resolution
Cora, Pine Labs’ compliance and resolution agent, takes cyber fraud complaints from intake to closure. It matches complaints to transactions, categorizes them, routes them to relevant teams, and prepares responses for review. Kumar said Pine Labs has been able to close some complaints on the same day, compared with the typical three-to-five-day turnaround.
The agent records a 15-step trace of its work, including validation, transaction lookups, settlement checks, and team notifications, along with supporting evidence and confidence levels. When a system connector is unavailable, Cora can use robotic process automation (RPA). In the demonstration, it accessed the government cyber police portal and filled in an action-taken form with transaction details and the disputed amount. A human operator retains control of the password and one-time code and reviews the form before submission.
Opening the platform to developers
Having deployed agents across its own compliance, finance, HR and marketing teams, Pine Labs has since opened its platform to developers and merchant partners. The company is also working with banks in India and overseas.
To show how the technology could be applied beyond its own operations, Kumar pointed to a hackathon organized by Pine Labs and The Ken , which drew more than 380 agent submissions from students, fresh graduates, and engineers across India. The winning entry helped people decide what to cook for dinner.
Developers can create skill files, connect tools, and define tasks in plain English, while AgenticOrg provides visibility into agents, confidence scores, and audit trails via Grantex. The AgenticOrg is intended to help third-party developers build applications for merchants and banks using Pine Labs’ infrastructure.
Helping small merchants run ad campaigns
For smaller businesses, Pine Labs has also developed an ads agent accessible through its merchant interface. Merchants connect their Google Ads account, enter details about their business, and provide a brief, budget, and campaign goal. The agent researches local demand and nearby competitors, then generates ad copy for search, display, and YouTube.
Merchants can request changes and approve the campaign before it goes live. The demonstration showed setup taking about two minutes, with campaign performance and lead routing available through the same interface.
Building an ecosystem for commerce
From internal enterprise workflows and cyber fraud resolution to advertising for small businesses, Pine Labs is applying its agent infrastructure to different parts of commerce. Grantex sets guardrails for what agents can do; AgenticOrg helps teams, individuals, and AI enthusiasts build agents, manage work, and execute tasks, and AgenticOrg is intended to let developers build further applications for merchants and banks.
Pine Labs is betting that the future of commerce will be shaped not just by what AI agents can do, but by how reliably they can do it. By combining the infrastructure to govern agents with applications that solve real business problems, the company is looking to make autonomous AI a working part of commerce, for enterprises, banks, and merchants alike.

articles.title: Constantine : DC prépare un nouveau film sur cet anti-héros incarné par Keanu Reeves
articles.text:
Constantine : DC prépare un nouveau film sur cet anti-héros incarné par Keanu Reeves
Après Clayface, un autre sombre anti-héros de l'univers DC Comics pourrait bien revenir sur grand écran : John Constantine.
Quelques semaines après la sortie en salles du surprenant Clayface, DC Studios vient de démarrer le développement d'un nouveau film sur un autre anti-héros de son catalogue : John Constantine.
Francis Galluppi (Evil Dead) pour écrire le nouveau film Constantine
Et si l'univers de DC Comics se développait au cinéma autrement qu'avec des blockbusters comme The Batman ou Superman ? C'est en tout cas une direction que le studio semble continuer à explorer avec ce nouveau projet de long-métrage à l'envergure relativement modeste.
Comme l'a dévoilé le média nord-américain Deadline, le projet n'en est encore qu'au tout début de son développement et DC Studios a engagé Francis Galluppi pour écrire une première version du scénario. Le cinéaste n'a à son tableau de chasse que quelques courts-métrages, ainsi que le film Last Stop: Yuma County qu'il a écrit et réalisé en 2023.
Il est toutefois au scénario et à la mise en scène du prochain volet de la franchise Evil Dead, intitulé Evil Dead Wrath et attendu en 2028. Tout comme Sam Raimi, la direction de DC Studios a visiblement été convaincue par sa vision et lui a donc confié les rênes de la nouvelle aventure de Constantine au cinéma.
De la série TV au film culte avec Keanu Reeves : l'héritage de l'anti-héros
Créé par Alan Moore, Stephen R. Bissette et John Totleben, John Constantine est un personnage apparu pour la première fois dans la bande dessinée Swamp Thing en 1985. De son surnom Hellblazer, cet enquêteur de l'occulte, originaire de Liverpool, s'illustre comme un exorciste cynique à l'humour noir comme du jais et un fumeur invétéré.
Le personnage a eu droit à sa propre série télévisée en 2014, avant de s'inviter dans les shows Arrow et Legends of Tomorrow. Surtout, il a connu les honneurs du grand écran en 2005 avec le long-métrage Constantine, dans lequel il prenait les traits de Keanu Reeves.
Ce film avait rencontré à l'époque un succès tout relatif, engrangeant “seulement” 230 millions de dollars pour un budget de 100 millions, ce qui ne l'a pas empêché de devenir culte pour toute une génération.
- Regardez la bande-annonce du film Constantine :
Si ce projet n'en est encore qu'à ses tout débuts, il témoigne une nouvelle fois de l'envie (et de la nécessité) de renouveler un genre super-héroïque en perte de vitesse auprès du grand public. Une stratégie qui passe par l'adaptation de personnages et d'univers moins célèbres, à l'instar de Clayface ou du prochain Ghost Rider avec Ryan Gosling. À suivre.
