articles.title: Bluetooth's new HDT technology delivers nearly four times the data transfer speed
articles.text:
Forward-looking: Bluetooth connectivity has never been regarded as a particularly fast means of exchanging files or handling other data-intensive wireless tasks. But now, the organization overseeing Bluetooth development is looking to improve the popular standard's data transfer speeds.
The Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG) recently unveiled the High Data Throughput (HDT) feature, describing the new solution as a significant milestone in the evolution of the popular wireless technology. The organization overseeing Bluetooth development said that HDT will introduce faster data transfer rates on newer Bluetooth devices. In turn, this performance improvement should make Bluetooth more capable and reliable than ever before.
Bluetooth HDT significantly expands the Bluetooth performance envelope, the group said. Introduced as an optional feature in the recently approved Bluetooth Core 7.0 specifications, HDT increases the maximum supported bit rate to 7.5 Mbps – nearly four times the data throughput available with the Bluetooth LE 2M PHY (LE 2M) technology.
Like Bluetooth LE 2M, HDT introduces a new physical layer (PHY) that should provide more robust frequency modulation schemes. Thanks to this new PHY, Bluetooth LE devices should be able to communicate more efficiently and carry "significantly" more data over an established Bluetooth link.
Beyond faster data transfers, Bluetooth HDT is also expected to improve performance and reliability across other "dimensions." The Bluetooth SIG said that HDT will increase capacity by improving spectral efficiency and allowing devices to exchange more data using the same wireless resources. HDT should also be more energy efficient, as it will move more data in less time, allowing radio transmitters to remain in lower-power states for longer.
Finally, Bluetooth HDT is expected to improve reliability by making wireless communications more robust and resilient. Devices should deliver more consistent performance and operate more effectively in demanding environments. According to Samsung vice-president Joonsuk Kim, HDT will enhance Bluetooth in ways that go well beyond faster data transfers.
"By advancing data throughput, capacity, energy efficiency, and reliability together, Bluetooth HDT gives developers and product makers a stronger foundation for building more capable products and richer wireless experiences," Kim said.
The Bluetooth SIG expects the first HDT-enabled products to arrive in 2027, with premium wireless audio peripherals likely to be among the first applications to adopt the new technology. Thanks to HDT, headsets and other audio products should benefit from greater efficiency without having to resort to non-standard communication solutions. Beyond audio, other applications expected to benefit from the improved data transfer rates include immersive and spatial computing, AI-powered devices, industrial wireless solutions, and everyday connected devices such as wearables and smart home products.
As for practical benefits across a wider range of Bluetooth products, HDT is likely still a few years away from widespread adoption, as is the case with any new wireless standard. Bluetooth SIG engineers were demonstrating HDT's capabilities more than a year ago, and the technology has now officially become part of the broader Bluetooth specifications.

articles.title: Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display review: The screen that every Mac deserves
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display has the best laptop screen I've ever seen, and other changes like reducing weight and moving from the notch to the Dynamic Island add to an excellent, albeit very pricey, machine.
Reasons to buy
- + Gorgeous tandem OLED screen
- + Noticeably lighter than existing model
- + Strong performance
- + Excellent speakers with deep bass
- + Dynamic Island is far more useful than notch
Reasons to avoid
- - Very expensive
- - Still no Face ID
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
Apple's fans know all about waiting. The company tends to polish features, especially in hardware, that some other laptop vendors release faster. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display ends the wait for two long-requested elements: OLED and touch, both on the platform for the very first time.
That comes at a price. The 16-inch version we have on review starts at $3,399 and is $7,899 as configured. 14-inch systems start at $2,899. Those are $400 bumps over the existing MacBook Pros with identical chips, making the OLED panel a pricey upgrade.
But those who can afford these high-end systems will get the best display on a Mac, if not laptops in general. Add in a significant reduction in weight and improved speakers, and you're getting a lot of small tweaks that add up over what was already one of the best laptops, even if many of the aesthetics haven't changed.
Design
From a distance, this new MacBook Pro doesn't look all that different from the existing models, which are still on the market, which may upset some people looking for a more sweeping redesign. They come in the same colors (space black, like our review unit, and silver) and they largely have the same design. Technically, the new OLED display stack allows for a thinner system, but our 16-inch review unit, at 16 mm thick, is just 0.8 mm shorter than an equivalent 16-inch MacBook Pro with Liquid Retina screen.
The aesthetic differences show up once you open the laptop. For one, the notch in the display is gone with the PROLED XDR models, replaced with the Dynamic Island from the latest iPhones. Let us rejoice; while the notch never bothered me on phones, it always felt in the way, dipping into the macOS menu bar. This isn't perfect, but it feels far more natural and has added functionality (see "Dynamic Island and macOS Touch Features" below).
Then there's the glowing Apple logo on the back of the lid. We haven't seen this for years, and while I could take or leave it, it's definitely going to make some fans nostalgic. The old glowing Mac logos used light from LCD backlights, getting the effect with no extra power. Because OLED panels only light up pixels when they're needed, Apple is making an aesthetic choice to power the logo with a bit of extra electricity this time. The glow matches the brightness of the display, which is a fun touch. I didn't see anything in settings to disable it.
Apple's bezels are thinner, which has let Apple stretch the display to 16.3 inches on this new 16-inch model (it's still 14.2 inches on the smaller one). The displays are now rounded on all four sides. On the Liquid Retina displays, they're rounded on top to match the curves in the chassis, but are squared on the bottom. It's not a huge change, but it does cut some pixels on the bottom of the screen and looks a bit like an iPad.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Otherwise, the system looks largely the same. You have the same ports: MagSafe 3, two Thunderbolt 5 ports, and a 3.5 mm headphone jack on the left; and an SD card reader, an additional Thunderbolt port, and HDMI output on the right.
But the OLED laptop feels different when you pick it up or put it in a backpack. Changes to cooling in the new 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR and the switch to an OLED screen get the laptop down to 4.1 pounds with M5 Max (4.0 pounds with M5 Pro), whereas the Liquid Retina versions are 4.7 pounds. You can really feel the half-pound difference. (The 14-incher is down from 3.5 pounds to 3 pounds, too.)
And that's lighter than some of its new competition, too. Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra with Nvidia's RTX Spark chip is 4.4 pounds and thicker at 0.75 inches. The Lenovo Pro 9n, also with RTX Spark and its own OLED screen, is a lighter 3.64 pounds and is thicker at 16.7 mm.
There has been talk of a sturdier hinge, but it does still wobble when you touch it. No one has gotten around that issue. Comparing it to my personal MacBook Pro with the old design, the display goes back ever so slightly more, which is nice for touch but not a game-changer. It would be nice to see a 180-degree hinge for people who really want to write or draw on a flat surface (Apple Pencil support would be nice for that, too). For now, people who want that will need to stick to an iPad.
I spent some of the time reviewing this laptop thinking of Microsoft's Surface Laptop Studio, a touch-focused workstation with a hinge that lets the screen sit in three positions: a standard laptop, pulled forward over the keyboard, or lying like a tablet. That didn't succeed (neither did similar designs from Acer), but it took a stab at changing how a touch-based laptop worked. The new MacBook Pro design isn't a radical rethink of the ergonomics that have plagued touch laptops for over a decade. It's just a powerful Mac that happens to have a touchscreen.
Specifications
| CPU | Apple M5 Max (18 cores: 6 super cores, 12 performance cores) | 
| Graphics | 40-core GPU (integrated) | 
| Memory | 128GB LPDDR5 unified memory | 
| Storage | 2TB SSD | 
| Display | 16.3-inch tandem OLED display (PROLED XDR), 3472-by-2266 native resolution, 254 PPI, touch, True Tone, ProMotion (VRR 10-120 Hz), Standard glass | 
| Networking | Apple N1 with Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread | 
| Ports | 3x Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C), 3.5 mm headphone jack, SD card reader, HDMI, MagSafe 3 | 
| Camera | 12MP Center Stage camera (1080p HD video recording) | 
| Battery | 99.6 WHr | 
| Power Adapter | 140W | 
| Operating System | macOS Golden Gate 27.2 | 
| Dimensions (WxDxH) | 14 x 9.62 x 0.63 inches (355.5 x 244.2 x 16 mm) | 
| Weight | 4.1 pounds (1.84 kg) | 
| Price (as configured) | $7,399 | 
PROLED XDR Display
We had to wait a long time to get OLED on a Mac. PROLED XDR is a silly name, but I'll give Apple this: The screen is absolutely stunning. It's the best screen I've ever seen on a notebook, and it makes me jealous when I look back at my personal system with plain old mini LED. Everything from the default wallpaper in macOS Golden Gate to videos and photos pop on this display. The blacks are deep, the colors pop, and it can get intensely bright.
Our review unit came with the 16.3-inch (slightly enlarged thanks to thinner bezels from 16.2-inches on non-PROLED models) with 3472-by-2266 native resolution, a variable refresh rate of 10 - 120 Hz, and, of course, touch support.
I used the PROLED XDR display to watch the finale of the latest season of Slow Horses. In one scene, where the mastermind of the season's plot shows up to a restaurant to meet with the head of MI5, I was wowed by the deep blacks. The restaurant was sparsely lit, and both characters were wearing black coats. The display brought out the highlights in the environment, as well as a few red accent walls.
In our instrumented testing, the PROLED XDR screen covered 83.6% of the DCI-P3 color gamut by volume and 118% sRGB, actually slightly lower than the mini LED version. I've seen them side-by-side. Trust my eyes; there's no contest here.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR measured 542.6 nits in our SDR brightness test, falling below the Surface Laptop Ultra, with its near-blinding 944 nits with its mini LED display. But again, PROLED simply looks better. The Surface Laptop Ultra has some light bleed and not enough local dimming zones to catch up.
The OLED panel on the Lenovo Pro 9n is the most vivid on each gamut by volume. I think it's a bit oversaturated, but if you prefer extreme pops of color, you may prefer that screen. The tandem OLED on the Dell XPS 16 was also more vivid on measurements, but was far less bright, which mutes the best aspects of OLED.
The PROLED screen showed how bright it could get with HDR content, outputting 1,964 nits in our 40% HDR test.
While I love how the display looks out of the box, Apple is offering more reference modes than ever before on a laptop, including various video, cinema, web and photography standards, and even DICOM medical imaging at 350 and 600 nits. There's also a display calibrator to fine-tune white points or perform full recalibration with external measurement tools.
Apple is far from the first company to add OLED (or, in this case, tandem OLED) to a laptop, but this stands out among the best OLED laptop displays I've seen in recent memory. The price hike to get it — $400 over mini LED models with the same chips, will be out of reach for many (though that hike also shaves half a pound off the weight). I desperately hope Apple starts bringing its brand of OLED down to the rest of the MacBook Pro and MacBook Air line, too. After all, the iPad Pro and iPad Mini both have it.
We tested the MacBook Pro with a standard screen. While I haven't spent significant time with a PROLED with the matte nano-texture display, I can tell you that this looks so good with a glossy finish that I'm not sure I could risk letting the matte displays (which I usually love!) take away any of the color saturation or context on display here. And as far as reflections go, they were minimal, even next to a window.
Dynamic Island and macOS Touch Features
Outside of OLED, there are two other additions to the MacBook Pro's screen.
The first is the Dynamic Island, a group of black pixels around the punch-hole webcam that can be used to show system alerts, notifications, and ongoing activities. (If you plug in a monitor, Dynamic Island activities show up to the left of your menu bar apps and icons.) It matches modern iPhones, and it's a huge change over the notch in other Macs, which took up far too much space in the menu bar. Now, the area around the camera is at least useful, though the camera still doesn't offer Face ID.
One of my biggest annoyances with the old design was that your mouse could fall behind the notch, with no indicator of where it was. The mouse can still move behind the Dynamic Island, but now the black area grows to indicate where the pointer is, and even wiggles if you make very small movements, to remind you where the cursor is.
The other much-discussed addition is the touchscreen. Apple hasn't reinvented the wheel here. Like most Windows and Chromebook makers, it added touch functionality onto a standard laptop. Apple's announcement mentions that the "touch sensor is built directly into the display panel — not layered on top of it," suggesting the use of technology similar to the iPhone and flagship Windows laptops.
Apple has made slight adjustments to macOS 27 Golden Gate to accommodate touch. My personal favorite is that the "traffic lights" for maximizing, minimizing, or closing a window expand when you tap on them, to ensure you can hit the right one. When you click on a menu with your finger, the spacing is larger for easier touch targets. Like the iPhone, you can swipe down from the dynamic Island to invoke Siri. You can also flick windows to the sides to organize your windows, though you can already do that with a mouse or keyboard.
Many gestures that work on the trackpad also work on the touchscreen, like pinch to zoom, accessing Mission Control (swiping up with three fingers), showing Notification Center (swiping left from the edge of the screen), and moving between virtual desktops by swiping left or right with three fingers. Many apps have already been optimized for touch, but if they haven't, touch translates to a click, so it all still works fairly well.
One of my many experiments with the touch screen included swiping across the timeline in Final Cut Pro. But in a sample project I put together, I didn't find it any better than using the keyboard and mouse — just another option. In Maxon's Cinema 4D, I felt the same way moving a model car and adjusting virtual cameras. It's an option, but it's no better than the existing way of doing things.
Perhaps my favorite use was in Blender, making adjustments to a 3D model I was sculpting. You could do everything I did with a mouse, but some features, like changing the angle of the sculpture, felt very natural with touch. That being said, after a few minutes, my arm was tired. I couldn't see using this all the time, as there are no changes to ergonomics over the usual laptop design.
For those who never want to use touch, you can turn it off in disability settings. That being said, as someone who would likely only use it for occasional scrolls, I don't see the harm in having it on, even if I don't see myself ever pulling to refresh on Safari when CMD + R is right there. (I do wish Apple included the polishing cloth with the glossy screen on our review unit and not just matte screens, however. Touch screens get fingerprints!).
I found touch most useful for iPad apps on the App Store that work natively on Mac. For instance, my go-to podcast app is Overcast, which is great on my iPhone but designed for touch on Mac. While I'm very used to navigating it with a mouse, the choice to use touch made sense here. It's also great for the iPhone simulator in Xcode, where developers can try out touch-based apps on their touchscreen Mac instead of using a pointer. The same goes for iPhone Mirroring.
There's no touch tutorial. Touch is clearly a feature on these new MacBook Pros, but not the feature. Keyboard and mouse are clearly still king.
Audio
The six-speaker sound system in the 16-inch MacBook Pro's new design, complete with updated woofers and tweeters, keeps the crown in Apple’s camp for the best laptop speakers I've ever heard.
When I listened to Justice's "Flower in a Hurricane" with the MacBook Pro, I was floored by the drums. While the rest of the speakers don't sound superbly better than the existing Pros, the low-end has improved, and deep drums and bass easily filled my apartment with deep, well-rounded sound. Everything sounded incredible, from the audio to the synths. This may be the best way I've heard this song since I've had it on a loop after its debut in a Grand Theft Auto VI trailer.
Apple has made some adjustments to how the speaker sounds with the lid shut, too. It's surprisingly good, with The Beaches' cover of "I Ran (So Far Away)" getting surprisingly loud, with the laptop plugged into a Thunderbolt dock and the lid shut, though the drums in that song weren't as snappy. Everything was slightly dampened until I opened the lid, but honestly, I could use it like this. It's still better than many other laptop speakers, with better bass.
Productivity Performance
We tested the new MacBook Pro with an M5 Max, 128GB of unified memory, and a 2TB SSD. That's the same chip and RAM as in the 14-inch MacBook Pro we tested earlier this year, though that had a 4TB drive.
The main competitors we looked at featured Nvidia's RTX Spark N1X chips, including the Surface Laptop Ultra (20-core version) and the Lenovo Pro 9n (18-core version). We also tossed in the Dell XPS 16 with a Core X7 358H — another 16-inch system with a Tandem OLED.
Unsurprisingly, this MacBook Pro can tear through most people's everyday workloads. Apple has re-tooled the cooling in this system, and it was often close to, if not ahead of, the M5 Max we tested earlier this year in a 14-inch chassis.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
On Geekbench 6, the 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR earned a score of 4,353 and a multi-core score of 29,430, coming close to the other M5 Max machine. Both of those scores are far ahead of the RTX Spark laptops and the Intel-based Dell.
The 2TB SSD copied roughly 25GB of files at a rate of 1,917.69 MBps, which is fast, though the 4TB SSD in the MacBook Pro we tested earlier this year was far faster. The Surface Laptop Ultra was ever-so-slightly ahead at 1,998.59 MBps.
On Handbrake, the 16-inch MacBook Pro transcoded a 4K video to 1080p in 1 minute and 43 seconds, the fastest of the bunch.
On the Xcode benchmark, in which Macs compile large code bases, the new 16-inch MacBook Pro beat the older 14-inch model with the same M5 Max by 7 seconds, completing the task in 80 seconds.
Our Cinebench 2026 stress test has systems go through ten runs of multi-core rendering, which is particularly stressful. In the automatic performance mode, Apple's default out of the box on macOS 27, the system started at a score of 9,080, before eventually settling in the 8,050's due to throttling. With high performance mode, which runs the fans harder and louder, the Mac started at a score of 9,647 and was far more stable, with its lowest score (9,479) at the very end. If you need to get some tough work done faster, switching to high performance mode could help, as long as you're OK with fan noise.
Gaming and Graphics
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display came with the same 40-core M5 Max GPU as the MacBook Pro we reviewed earlier this year.
In the new chassis, the M5 Max scored 4,355 on 3DMark Steel Nomad, beating the old system (3,865) as well as both configurations of the RTX Spark.
Running Cyberpunk 2077's benchmark at 1920 x 1200 using our typical test settings (Ray tracing ultra), the game ran at 36.24 frames per second. This is slightly faster than the 14-inch we tested earlier this year with the existing chassis, at 30.84 FPS. With the "For This Mac" preset, including MetalFX and a resolution of 2316 x 1448, the benchmark ran at 94.20 FPS.
Keyboard and Touchpad
Of all the things that haven't changed on the MacBook Pro, the most familiar are the keyboard and touchpad. That may be of some comfort to stalwarts of indirect input methods.
I was blazing fast on the keyboard, hitting 131 words per minute with a 99% accuracy rate on the monkeytype.com typing test. Both stats are on the high side for me, but I also can't blame Apple for making a comfortable keyboard with chiclet keys and a smart layout. I will praise any company that uses an inverted T for arrow keys as long as I live. Apple may not offer the deepest travel of the laptop market, but it does the job.
The massive trackpad features smooth glass, comfortable haptics, and intuitive gesture support in macOS. The 16-inch MacBook Pro's touchpad is luxuriously huge. After years of Windows laptops adding haptic trackpads to catch up, Apple's touchpad still feels great.
Upgradeability
While there are just four Torx Screws on the bottom of the MacBook Pro, there isn't much in the way of upgrading. Apple puts the RAM in the chip, and the storage is soldered down. If you need a repair, your best bet is probably Apple's Genius Bar.
Like other Macs, you should make sure you get the spec you need when you buy. Though, as you'll see in the configuration section, that could cost you quite a bit for some RAM and storage upgrades. Unfortunately, that's not unusual given the price of memory in the greater industry right now.
Battery Life
Apple's 99.6 WHr battery allows for a longer-lasting OLED laptop than its competitors, but in our testing, mini-LED model still lasts longer. On our battery test, laptops browse the web, run OpenGL tests, and stream video with the display set to 150 nits of brightness.
The 16-inch MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR display lasted 15 hours and 57 minutes, far ahead of the OLED screen on the Lenovo Pro 9n (10:30) and the tandem OLED panel on the Dell XPS 16 (13:03). It also beat the mini-LED screen on the Surface Laptop Ultra.
The nearly 16-hour runtime is slightly short of Apple's "up to 17 hours" claim for web browsing. The only laptop that did better on our battery test was the 14-inch M5 Max laptop we tested earlier this year. That machine, with a smaller, mini-LED screen, ran for just shy of 18 hours.
Heat
The MacBook Pro can get a bit toasty under heavy load, though it's nothing I would deem unusable. Heavy workloads are probably best on a desk, though. New cooling changes the direction of the airflow in the machine, moving it out and through the back rather than out from vents near the display, in order to extend the display's lifespan.
During our Cinebench 2026 stress test, the keyboard measured 106.6 degrees Fahrenheit, which is definitely hot enough to notice. The touchpad was a cooler 88 F, while the hottest point on the bottom measured 107 F.
Our usual monitoring was not able to identify the heat on the CPU yet (this may require some software updates), but the overall temperature from the computer's other sensors was an average of 51 degrees Celsius.
Webcam
The 12-megapixel Center Stage webcam on the MacBook Pro will serve you well even on the most professional call. It looked great in meetings, even in one difficult lighting scenario when I had a lamp on one side and post-Daylight Savings Time early evening light coming in from a window next to me. The system gracefully balanced the mix of warm yellow and the products of blue hour.
I could easily smooth that mix out using the MacBook Pro camera's studio light or edge light effects, too.
Software and Warranty
We tested this new MacBook Pro with macOS 27 Golden Gate, which we highlighted on the Mac Studio, with new Apple Intelligence features, and the new Siri based on Apple Foundation Models and Gemini.
Apple's software suite includes Safari, Messages, Photos, Maps, Notes, and Reminders. Its services, including News and Apple TV, also have applications. Pages, Keynote, and Numbers are still in the dock by default, but they're the Creator Studio subscription versions, which require a subscription to get full features, including AI functionality, royalty-free graphics, and additional templates.
Apple sells the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display with a one-year warranty. AppleCare+ extends protection for $17.99 per month or $179.99 per year, and also adds accidental damage and drop coverage.
Configurations
We reviewed the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display in a high-end, $7,399 configuration with an M5 Max (18 CPU cores, 40 GPU cores), 128GB of memory, and 2TB of storage.
The cheapest versions of these machines are a $2,899 14-inch system with a cut-down M5 Pro featuring 15 CPU cores and 16 GPU Cores or a $3,399 16-inch laptop with the M5 Pro featuring an 18-core CPU and 20-core GPU. Both base configurations come with 24GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, as well as the glossy screen option. (Adding the matte "Nano-texture" glass adds $150 and also nets you a polishing cloth, which isn't included with the glossy screen.)
Moving to the M5 Max moves you to $4,499 on the 14-inch laptop and $4,799 on the 16-incher for an 18-core CPU and a cut-down 32-core GPU. The full 40-core GPU is another $300.
RAM starts at 24GB, and costs $600 to goto 48GB or, on the 16-incher, $1,000 for 64GB. There's also 36GB and 128GB RAM options that also require 2TB of storage and an M5 Max (like our review unit). Storage prices are also astronomical, with a $1,000 jump between the 2TB and 4TB tier. (If you want 16TB, which I think will be a relatively rare choice, it's a $7,000 bump that requires the high-end M5 Max).
These are exceptionally expensive computers. Apple's 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros without the OLED screens are still there, however, starting at $1,999 for a 14-inch notebook with M6.
Apple sells the systems at full price, or divided up into 12 monthly payments through an installment plan. They're also available for lease through Apple Upgrade.
Bottom Line
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display isn't a radical redesign, but it has a bunch of small changes that add up to significant improvements over previous models. The tandem OLED screen is a treat to look at, and the weight reduction is significant for anyone carrying their laptop around on the go. Even the deeper bass from the speakers is a real treat.
Performance from the M5 Max is still strong, though if you're doing simple work, you can get much better single-core performance out of an M6 Macbook Pro (though you'll give up everything else).
With no major redesign, however, Apple hasn't done anything to make touching the laptop any more comfortable than its competitors. It ultimately does get tiring. That being said, the few gestures and adjustments Apple has made to macOS are helpful, if not revolutionary. Touch really is here because it's table stakes at this point. Some will use it and others won't. It's not the selling point, other than that it's a debut for the feature.
Far more Mac user deserves a screen this good, and I hope that some flavor of OLED, even if it's not tandem OLED, eventually makes it to the entry-level MacBook Pro and even the MacBook Air. Touch, too, could be popular with younger people who grew up with all touch screens and go for the Air or the MacBook Neo.
But the starting price for the systems with PROLED displays are high, and upgrades make them exceptionally expensive. For now, the best screens in the Mac lineup (and arguably the industry) are limited to just these systems. We've waited a long time for OLED on the Mac, and for many, they'll still be waiting until it gets more affordable.
Those with the deep pockets to make the investment, though, are in for one heck of a screen.
Andrew E. Freedman is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware focusing on laptops, desktops and gaming. He also keeps up with the latest news. A lover of all things gaming and tech, his previous work has shown up in Tom's Guide, Laptop Mag, Kotaku, PCMag and Complex, among others. Follow him on Threads @FreedmanAE and BlueSky @andrewfreedman.net. You can send him tips on Signal: andrewfreedman.01

articles.title: Billig-Tastatur oder Profi-Modell? Worauf es bei der richtigen Gaming-Tastatur ankommt
articles.text:
Schnelle Reaktion und individuelle Tastenbefehle: Welche Gaming-Tastaturen sich wirklich lohnen
Hinweis: Wir haben in diesem Artikel Provisions-Links verwendet und sie durch "*" gekennzeichnet. Erfolgt über diese Links eine Bestellung, erhält t3n.de eine Provision.
Einfache Tastaturen sind oft schon für unter zehn Euro erhältlich. Für die gelegentliche Online-Recherche oder das Verfassen von E-Mails kann ein solches Modell durchaus reichen. Wenn du allerdings am PC zocken möchtest, lohnt es sich, in eine spezielle Gaming-Tastatur zu investieren. Sie erkennt Tastenanschläge besonders schnell, was in Shootern oder anderen temporeichen Spielen den entscheidenden Unterschied machen kann. Viele Modelle verfügen außerdem über programmierbare Tasten, mit denen sich einzelne Befehle oder ganze Eingabefolgen festlegen lassen. Wir stellen dir drei empfehlenswerte Gaming-Tastaturen vor – vom günstigen Einsteiger- bis zum Profi-Modell.
Unter den Pioneers Picks stellen wir dir regelmäßig weitere praktische Tools und Gadgets vor.
Bei der Auswahl der passenden Tastatur solltest du einige Dinge beachten, die je nach Art deiner bevorzugten Games variieren können. Eine RGB-Beleuchtung und eine extrem hohe Polling-Rate sind nette Extras, aber nicht das Wichtigste. Was wirklich zählt, ist stattdessen das Tippgefühl, das Rollover sowie eine individuelle Tastenbelegung. Für reines Gaming sind lineare oder Hall-Effect-Switches meist die beste Wahl. Außerdem lohnt sich eine kabelgebundene Tastatur, weil der Akku nicht mitten in einer langen Gaming-Session schlapp machen kann. Zudem profitierst du von einer niedrigen Latenz und musst keine Funkstörungen befürchten.
Sharkoon Skiller SGK4: Gaming-Tastatur für unter 25 Euro
Die Skiller SGK4 von Sharkoon zählt zu den beliebtesten Gaming-Tastaturen für den kleinen Geldbeutel. Es handelt sich um eine Rubberdome-Tastatur: Unter jeder Taste sitzt ein elastischer Gummi-Dom, der beim Drücken nachgibt, den elektrischen Kontakt herstellt und die Taste danach wieder nach oben federt. Während andere Tastaturen dieser Sorte nur wenige Tastenanschläge gleichzeitig registrieren, beherrscht das Sharkoon-Modell N-Key-Rollover. Das heißt, du kannst beliebig viele Tasten gleichzeitig drücken – jede Eingabe wird korrekt erkannt. So behältst du auch bei komplexen Spielmanövern die volle Kontrolle. Zahlreiche Funktionstasten mit Multimedia-Aktionen runden das Erlebnis ab.
Über vier Profiltasten auf der Oberseite des Skiller SGK4 kannst du Spielprofile mit benutzerdefinierten Tastenbelegungen oder -effekten auswählen. Die deutsche Qwertz-Tastatur ist auf Windows-PCs optimiert. Mit Mac sind die Funktionen nur eingeschränkt nutzbar. Der Gaming-Modus mit deaktivierter Windows-Taste verhindert, dass die Technik beim Zocken dazwischenfunkt. Das Modell ist in der Farbe Schwarz erhältlich und mit einer RGB-Hintergrundbeleuchtung ausgestattet. Käufer:innen schätzen an dem Modell vor allem das gute Preis-Leistungs-Verhältnis und die individuell konfigurierbaren Einstellungsmöglichkeiten. Bei Amazon kostet die Gaming-Tastatur von Sharkoon 24,99 Euro.
Individuelle Qwertz-Gaming-Tastatur von Omoton
Die mechanische Gaming-Tastatur von Omoton lohnt sich, wenn du Wert auf ein flexibles und kompaktes Setup legst. Per Bluetooth kannst du sie mit bis zu drei Geräten verbinden. Der integrierte 4000-mAh-Akku sorgt laut Hersteller für eine lange Ausdauer im drahtlosen Betrieb. Die RGB-Beleuchtung zeigt den Akkustand an und erinnert rechtzeitig ans Aufladen. Alternativ kannst du in den latenzarmen Kabelmodus wechseln. Die Tastatur ist mit Windows und Mac sowie mit Playstation und Xbox kompatibel. Da das Modell auf den Nummernblock verzichtet, gewinnst du auch auf kleinen Schreibtischen Platz für präzise Mausbewegungen – ideal für Shooter oder Strategie-Games.
Die Tastatur unterstützt QMK und VIA und lässt sich damit sehr umfassend individuell anpassen. Du kannst beispielsweise Makros festlegen, also Abläufe, bei denen eine einzelne Taste mehrere Eingaben nacheinander auslöst. Außerdem erstellst du eigene Ebenen, auf denen dieselbe Taste unterschiedliche Aufgaben übernimmt. So stellst du jeden Tastenanschlag genau nach deinen Bedürfnissen ein. Ein zusätzlicher Multimedia-Knopf dient dazu, die Lautstärke zu regulieren oder den Ton stummzuschalten. Dank der Hot-Swap-Funktion kannst du die Tasten zudem einfach austauschen. Das Design zeichnet sich durch einen Farbverlauf in Anthrazit aus. Der Preis liegt bei 79,99 Euro.
Gaming auf Profi-Niveau mit der Logitech G Pro X TKL Rapid
Laut Herstellerangaben wurde die Logitech G Pro X TKL Rapid zusammen mit E-Sport-Athlet:innen entwickelt und richtet sich gezielt an Gamer:innen, die Reaktionsfähigkeit und Präzision auf Turnierniveau suchen. Sie arbeitet mit analogen Magnetschaltern, die auf dem Hall-Effekt beruhen und berührungslos über ein Magnetfeld messen, wie weit eine Taste gedrückt ist. Die Betätigungskraft beträgt 35 Gramm, sodass die Tasten mit wenig Druck auslösen. Das sorgt für flüssige Eingaben und eine zuverlässige Erkennung jedes Anschlags. Der Rapid-Trigger-Modus dieser Tastatur reaktiviert Tasten, ohne dass du sie vollständig loslassen musst. Das ist besonders bei First-Person-Shootern von Vorteil, in denen jede Millisekunde zählt.
Die Qwertz-Tastatur ist komplett individuell anpassbar. Mit den Modi der Funktionstaste legst du selbst fest, an welchem Punkt eine Taste auslöst. Außerdem kannst du jeder einzelnen Taste einen eigenen Befehl zuweisen und Tastenkombinationen erstellen, die mehrere Aktionen nacheinander auslösen. Die vollständig anpassbare RGB-Beleuchtung lässt sich mit der Musik oder dem Bildschirmgeschehen des Spiels synchronisieren und bietet so ein immersives Gaming-Erlebnis. Die Tastatur ist mit Windows, Linux und Mac kompatibel und in den Farben Schwarz, Weiß und Pink erhältlich. Die unverbindliche Preisempfehlung liegt bei 169,99 Euro. Bei Amazon ist das Modell aktuell schon ab 129,29 Euro erhältlich.

articles.title: GTA 6 : que nous révèlent les 39 nouvelles images dévoilées par Rockstar ?
articles.text:
GTA 6 est toujours attendu le 19 novembre 2026 sur PS5 et Xbox Series X|S, et à mesure que la date se rapproche, l’impatience grandit. L’occasion pour Rockstar Games de publier 39 nouvelles captures d’écran de GTA 6 ce 5 novembre, à seulement deux semaines de la sortie du jeu. On y découvre une multitude de détails sur Vice City, ses habitants, ses véhicules et les activités proposées dans ce nouvel épisode.
C’est probablement l’un des premiers éléments qui saute aux yeux : la densité de population semble particulièrement impressionnante dans GTA 6. On le savait déjà, mais le voir est toujours aussi impressionant. La capture d’écran prise dans une boîte de nuit montre une foule compacte, composée de nombreux personnages aux apparences différentes. Les visages, les vêtements et les morphologies varient considérablement, donnant l’impression que chaque PNJ possède sa propre identité.
Les fans, déjà très actifs sur Reddit, ont également repéré plusieurs personnages qui pourraient être inspirés de véritables personnalités de Floride. L’un d’entre eux ressemble notamment au rappeur Kodak Black, reconnaissable à ses tatouages.
Les amateurs de voitures devraient aussi apprécier ces nouvelles images, puisque plusieurs captures mettent en avant des véhicules modifiés, avec notamment des voitures de type « Donk », très populaires dans certaines régions des États-Unis. Les courses de rue avec personnalisation des voitures semblent ainsi occuper une place importante dans le monde ouvert.
Autre élément intéressant : les dégâts semblent poussés. Sur une voiture criblée de balles, les impacts traversent la peinture et laissent apparaître la couleur d’origine de la carrosserie. Un détail certes, mais qui montre encore le niveau de peauffinage des équipes de Rockstar. Les nostalgiques de Driver remarqueront également la présence de ponts-levis, qui pourraient donner lieu à quelques séquences intéressantes.
Vie nocturne à Vice City dans GTA 6
La vie nocturne semble particulièrement développée. Comme on l’a dit, les boîtes de nuit affichent une densité de population impressionnante et, GTA oblige, la musique, les fêtes et l’argent devraient occuper une place centrale dans l’ambiance de Vice City. Les affrontements entre gangs feront également partie du décor, avec une ville qui semble aussi festive que dangereuse.
Les captures laissent aussi entrevoir une certaine liberté dans la personnalisation des protagonistes. Bracelets et bagues pourront notamment compléter leurs tenues. La nudité semble par ailleurs faire partie des éléments que Rockstar souhaite mettre en avant dans cet épisode, dans la continuité de l’humour provocateur et de la satire sociale propres à la série.
Toutes les images ne se contentent pas de présenter les personnages ou les paysages. Certaines semblent directement tirées de séquences de jeu. Sur l’une d’elles, la police encercle notamment une propriété et un yacht appartenant à un personnage fortuné. Jason et Lucia sont visibles en train de prendre la fuite.
D’autres images montrent les héros avec différentes armes, dans des environnements variés. On retrouve notamment des scènes qui laissent entrevoir des activités criminelles, des affrontements et des moments de vie nocturne. Il reste difficile de déterminer précisément à quelles missions correspondent ces captures, mais semble réellement être une phase de gameplay.
Un autre détail intrigue les fans : la possibilité que Jason et Lucia puissent être accompagnés d’un chien. Une hypothèse à prendre avec des pincettes, mais qui s’inscrirait dans un monde ouvert où les animaux semblent avoir une place particulièrement importante.
Une faune et une flore impressionante dans GTA 6
Enfin, cette nouvelle galerie permet de découvrir un peu mieux les environnements de GTA 6. Au-delà des rues de Vice City, Rockstar met en avant des paysages naturels, des collines offrant une vue dégagée sur la ville et plusieurs zones sauvages. La faune et la flore semblent omniprésentes, avec de nombreux animaux visibles dans les différents environnements.
Les fonds marins ne sont pas oubliés. Les nouvelles images laissent entrevoir des eaux particulièrement détaillées et une vie sous-marine plus développée. De quoi laisser espérer de belles sessions de plongée et d’exploration sous-marine.
Ces 39 images ne dévoilent donc pas de nouvelle mécanique majeure à elles seules, mais elles permettent de mieux cerner les ambitions de Rockstar. Entre la densité des foules, les possibilités de personnalisation des véhicules, les activités criminelles, la faune et les environnements détaillés, le studio continue de miser sur un monde ouvert particulièrement riche. Il ne reste désormais plus que deux semaines avant de pouvoir découvrir tout cela manette en main : GTA 6 sortira le 19 novembre 2026 sur PS5 et Xbox Series X|S.

articles.title: Why AI’s biggest challenge lies beneath the model
articles.text:
Why AI’s biggest challenge lies beneath the model
At TechSparks 2026, Michael Cronin of Couchbase explained why fragmented data infrastructure remains a major barrier to enterprise AI adoption and why companies need to fix their data systems before scaling AI applications.
AI models are becoming increasingly accessible, but turning them into products that work reliably remains a challenge, particularly when enterprises are dealing with fragmented data infrastructure.
At TechSparks 2026, Michael Cronin, Vice President, Sales, Asia-Pacific, Japan & India, Couchbase, joined Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director – Strategic Content & Video, YourStory, for a discussion on moving AI beyond experimentation, production failures, governance challenges, customer experience, and India's growing role in AI innovation.
AI’s missing link: the data layer
Over the decades, large enterprises have adopted different databases and point solutions to address specific problems. While each solved an immediate need, the result has often been a fragmented data layer, with multiple systems that struggle to work together.
Cronin sees this fragmentation as a major barrier to AI adoption. Citing industry estimates, he said 70–80% of AI development projects never reach production, while an MIT study found that 95% fail to become profitable.
Couchbase’s operational data platform is designed to address this challenge by helping enterprises consolidate their data infrastructure.
Rather than trying to fix everything at once, Cronin advised companies to start small.
“My advice to founders and enterprises that are struggling with the fragmentation of the data layer is to pick your most critical use cases first,” he said.
Cronin cited the example of Tesco, the UK retailer with a large global Capability Center (GCC) in Bengaluru. Its multiple systems were affecting customer experience, particularly during busy shopping periods such as Black Friday and weekends.
Tesco began consolidating its data layer, starting with a single instance and use case before extending the effort across its technology stack.
The consolidation enabled the retailer to handle millions of transactions per second with sub-millisecond latency. According to Cronin, the example shows how companies can begin addressing fragmentation through a single use case before expanding the changes across their operations.
AI moves at machine speed. Can data keep up?
The pressure to develop AI products has led many enterprises to prioritize models and applications. However, pilots often run on small datasets in controlled environments, leaving organizations unprepared for the demands of production.
Cronin pointed to the growing scale of machine-generated traffic.
“Eighteen months ahead of schedule, machine traffic has overtaken human traffic on the internet. That’s the AI scale. That’s the machine speed scale that enterprises need to operate on,” he said.
When AI applications encounter real-world workloads, fragmented data systems can prevent them from operating reliably at scale.
The growing use of AI agents adds to the challenge. As agents become more autonomous and take on decision-making responsibilities, enterprises need to ensure they can access the right data while working within appropriate governance frameworks.
Fragmented systems can make communication and governance more difficult, limiting the ability of agents to operate autonomously.
Cronin also urged enterprises to reconsider how they allocate their AI investments. While models are evolving rapidly, enterprise data remains a critical asset.
“The models are rentable. Today’s best model is yesterday's newspaper. The true asset for the enterprise is the data,” he said.
More API layers aren't the answer
As enterprises began recognizing that fragmented data was holding back their AI initiatives, many responded by adding APIs and connectors to link existing systems.
Cronin cautioned that this approach could introduce further complexity rather than solve the underlying problem. Each additional connection brings latency, risk, and another potential point of failure.
Instead, he recommended consolidating the data layer so applications and AI agents can communicate with it more directly, bringing data closer to customers.
According to Cronin, many enterprises, including large GCCs in India, are now reassessing their architecture to address data fragmentation. Without these changes, further investment in AI development could lead to the same problems.
Consolidating data can also improve customer experience by helping systems manage growing demand, remain available and respond quickly.
As customers expect more from AI-powered services, having data available at the edge is becoming increasingly important.
India: From back office to innovation leader
Cronin observed that business cultures vary across the Asia-Pacific region, but fragmented data infrastructure remains a common challenge for AI adoption.
At the same time, India is becoming an important centre for AI innovation and decision-making.
He noted that 80% of Couchbase's top 50 global accounts have a significant presence in India, with much of their AI innovation and leadership based in the country.
Couchbase is also expanding its presence in India, with its Asia-Pacific headquarters moving to Bengaluru. Its Indian enterprise customers include Air India, Airtel, BigBasket, and Mahindra Finance.
According to Cronin, India’s role in global business has moved beyond cost savings, with innovation, leadership, and important business decisions increasingly taking place here.
He cited Air India's next-generation entertainment platform, which is being built on Couchbase. The platform aims to provide passengers with personalized shopping and entertainment experiences even when an aircraft is offline.
For Cronin, the project shows how Indian enterprises are using technology to improve customer experiences under real-world operating conditions.

Ces appareil de coiffage présentent le meilleur rapport qualité / prix de notre comparatif
Les appareil de coiffage Dreame AirStyle Pro s'affichent aujourd'hui à 199,00 € chez Boulanger.com. C'est actuellement le meilleur rapport qualité / prix de notre comparatif, selon les 12 modèles testés dans notre laboratoire.
Au tour de Dreame de sortir son styler. Polyvalent, l'AirStyle Pro permet de sécher, coiffer, lisser et boucler les cheveux d’un tour de main. Avec ses six embouts, il part à l’assaut d’un Dyson Airwrap de plus en plus concurrencé.
Dreame AirStyle Pro

Points forts
- Poids plume.
- Six embouts différents pour sécher et coiffer.
- Bonne maîtrise de la température du flux.
- Faible consommation.
- Niveau sonore contenu.
- Embouts aimantés.
Points faibles
- Panneau de commandes perfectible.
- Peut manquer de panache.

C’est la corde qui manquait à son arc. En sortant l'AirStyle Pro, Dreame signe son premier styler inspiré des modèles déjà présents sur le marché, Dyson Airwrap en tête. L’appareil est accompagné d’une myriade d’accessoires pour sécher et coiffer les têtes lisses et ondulées. En revanche, point de diffuseur pour coiffer les boucles au naturel. L'AirStyle Pro semble être un maniaque du contrôle et maîtrise sa température, son niveau sonore et sa consommation d’énergie. En revanche, il manque de puissance et peut sembler faiblard face à de longues et épaisses tignasses.

Une fois encore, Dyson utilise un puissant flux d’air pour sécher et lisser nos chevelures, tout en évitant les dommages thermiques. Son flux d’air est peu puissant, mais cette faiblesse est compensée par une philosophie 2-en-1 qui supprime l’étape du séchage préalable. En revanche, la technologie n’est pas parfaite, du moins pas pour tous. Les cheveux raides et ondulés pourront certes bannir les plaques chauffantes et jouir d'un résultat similaire avec l'Airstrait. articles.title: J'ai pris en main le Motorola Signature 27 : a-t-il de quoi inquiéter le Galaxy S26 Ultra ?
articles.text:
Après avoir officialisé son Signature 27 en septembre dernier, Motorola s’est décidé à le présenter ce jeudi 5 novembre. Nous avons pu prendre en main le nouveau smartphone haut de gamme de la marque, et il a de sérieux atouts à faire valoir face à ses concurrents comme le Galaxy S26 Ultra, l’iPhone 18 Pro ou encore le Google Pixel 11 Pro XL, pour ne citer qu’eux. Voici notre premier avis sur le Motorola Signature 27, en attendant notre test complet.
Un grand smartphone haut de gamme
Avec sa diagonale d’écran de 6,8 pouces, le Motorola Signature fait clairement partie des grands gabarits. Pour autant, il reste très agréable à utiliser à une main. Le smartphone est très fin pour sa taille et il garde un bon équilibre malgré son bloc caméra plus épais que le reste du téléphone. Le châssis est un mélange d’aluminium et de céramique qui fait très « premium » et le dos profite de deux finitions assez différentes.
La première finition se trouve sur le modèle noir charbon. Il s’agit d’un tissu texturé qui propose un bon « grip » une fois en main et qui fait un peu penser au kevlar que l’on retrouvait sur certains Motorola Razr. Le modèle vert olive du téléphone opte quant à lui pour une finition plus douce au toucher.
Côté ergonomie, on retrouve les boutons d’alimentation et de volume sur la tranche droite, un bouton dédié à l’IA sur la tranche gauche, ainsi qu’un système de haut-parleurs stéréo (en haut et en bas) conçu en partenariat avec Bang & Olufsen, et plus Bose comme sur le Motorola Signature.
Côté batterie, Motorola a mis les petits plats dans les grands en intégrant une batterie de 7000 mAh, compatible avec la charge filaire 90W et la charge sans fil 50 W. Aucun chargeur n’est fourni dans la boîte, il faudra donc en avoir un compatible.
Un écran Tandem OLED qui met une claque
L’écran est l’une des évolutions les plus impressionnantes de ce modèle. Le Signature 27 embarque une dalle Extreme AMOLED Duo de 6,8 pouces (LTPO 120 Hz, Dolby Vision). La grande nouveauté repose sur l’adoption de la technologie Tandem OLED (deux dalles OLED superposées), comme sur le dernier MacBook Pro. De quoi obtenir un contraste parfait et des couleurs éclatantes.
Motorola annonce une luminosité maximale pouvant atteindre 12 000 cd/m2 en mode automatique. Oui l’écran est impressionnant, mais cette prise en main ne nous a pas permis de le mettre à l’épreuve. Le 01lab s’en chargera pour notre test complet du Motorola Signature 27.
Performances et refroidissement : le chaud et le froid
Le Motorola Signature 27 embarque une puce Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 (ouf !) gravée en 2 nm, couplée à 16 Go de RAM LPDDR5X et jusqu’à 1 To de stockage UFS 4.1. On ne se fait pas beaucoup de soucis sur la capacité du téléphone à tout faire tourner comme une horloge, mais une telle puissance dans un smartphone aussi fin semble avoir demandé pas mal de travail au niveau du refroidissement.
Motorola a donc agrandi son système de refroidissement (qui était un des points faibles du précédent modèle). On retrouve donc une nouvelle chambre à vapeur, du métal liquide, du cuivre et un nouveau gel thermique. Là encore, nous verrons lors de notre test si ce système de refroidissement « ArcticMesh » tient ses promesses lorsque l’on repousse le téléphone dans ses retranchements.
Quatre modules photo
Pour son bloc caméra arrière, le Motorola Signature 27 muscle son jeu par rapport au modèle précédent. On retrouve ainsi :
- Un capteur principal de 50 Mpx (Sony LYTIA 910) avec stabilisation optique (OIS).
- Un téléobjectif périscope 200 Mpx offrant un zoom optique 5x et un zoom numérique jusqu’à 100x.
- Un ultra grand-angle 50 Mpx.
- Un capteur de mouvement dédié pour capturer les sujets en mouvement de la manière la plus nette possible.
Côté vidéo, le téléphone est capable de capturer jusqu’en 8K à 30 i/s.
Quelques photos prises avec le Motorola Signature 27. – © 01net
Et côté logiciel, ça donne quoi ?
Motorola promet 7 ans de mises à jour de l’OS et de sécurité pour son Signature 27. L’interface est assez épurée, ce qui n’est pas pour nous déplaire. On retrouve évidemment des fonctionnalités IA, avec notamment les outils de chez Google comme Gemini Gemini Omni pour la génération et l’édition de vidéos à partir de prompts, et Lyria pour la création musicale. Rambler, la dictée vocale survitaminée par l’IA du clavier Gboard est également de la partie.
Le téléphone est également compatible avec le système d’exploitation GrapheneOS, ce qui devrait plaire à ceux qui accordent beaucoup d’importance à la confidentialité et la sécurité.
Prix et date de sortie : on n’était pas prêts
Le Motorola Signature sera vendu au prix conseillé de 1899 € sur le site de Motorola. Vous avez bien lu. À titre de comparaison, l’iPhone 18 Pro Max est vendu à partir de 1629 € et le Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra à partir de 1469 €. Il sera également disponible chez Orange à partir de 839 € TTC si vous souscrivez un forfait 200 Go.
Les précommandes débutent le 16 novembre et se terminent le 2 décembre, date de lancement officielle du Motorola Signature 27.
De belles promesses à confirmer dans notre test complet
Cette première prise en main du Signature 27 nous a confirmé les ambitions de Motorola. Le produit est très prometteur, mais il faudra éclaircir ou confirmer certains points, comme l’autonomie, la qualité de l’écran ou encore les performances thermiques, lors de notre test complet afin de savoir si le Signature 27 a les épaules pour rivaliser avec les cadors du marché.
 👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.

articles.title: 4 reasons to check out the Canadian Black Friday perks from Fizz
articles.text:
You don’t need to look far if you’re searching for some serious savings this Black Friday. While the annual mega shopping event usually lasts for a single day or weekend, one Canadian mobile provider is kicking things up a notch.
Black Friday at Fizz is officially here, and that comes with incredible perks and member gifts. Hosted through November and December, Fizz members will be rewarded for just being members. Couple that with the already stellar deals at Fizz and, well, you’ve got a year-long Black Friday promo!
Here’s what Fizz offers members for Black Friday and beyond.
60GB of free data
Black Friday isn’t a one-day event at Fizz! It’s actually two months of extras and benefits. Starting on Nov. 4, members scored a literal mountain of data. That’s 40GB to be exact, absolutely free, and even more benefits are coming when the event concludes on Dec 8 with an extra 60 GB of free data.
Plus, three sets of deals and perks will be revealed as we get closer to the holiday shopping season.
That’s even more reason to become a Fizz member and reap the rewards. Already a member? Just wait to receive your Black Friday gift directly into your account to use whenever you’re ready.
Data rollover
You don’t need a Black Friday deal to score data rollover at Fizz. At the end of every month, your unused data transfers over to the next month, automatically. That means you can sign up for a plan with less data, at a more accessible price point, knowing that any unused data can still be used.
If the holiday season has got you feeling particularly festive, why not gift your extra mobile data? That’s right, you can gift your leftover data to a friend!
Lifetime pricing
No holiday miracles here, just lifetime pricing at Fizz. Sign up for a plan with a price that works best for you, and the price of that mobile plan will never increase. You get guaranteed pricing with zero surprise hikes, making budgeting even easier.
And with fully customizable plans, you can pick and choose the features that work best for you, without having to pay for the ones you don’t want. Don’t forget that Fizz doesn’t have any fixed-term contracts, meaning you can say bye-bye to any penalties for leaving or surprise fees like rate increases, roaming, or overage charges.
Loyalty program
Tis the season for perks! The robust Fizz loyalty program gives members access to cash discounts on their plans, plus free mobile data too. That means the value of your plan is actually increasing, while its price decreases. Now that’s a win-win.
Members can also get free data drops and exclusive offers from other brand partners.
Black Friday with Fizz
Who needs a Black Friday sale when Fizz is already giving members the ultimate deal? From incredibly affordable (and reliable) phone plans, a robust loyalty program, lifetime pricing, data rollover and gifting, Fizz is making Black Friday a 365-day affair.
But that doesn’t mean members don’t get rewarded for the occasion! Keep your eyes peeled for the three exclusive Fizz Black Friday drops and remember to sign up in time for eligibility.

articles.title: L'IA d'OpenAI découvre 948 failles dans Linux et développe des stratégies d'exploitation inédites
articles.text:
Une chaîne d'agents IA développée par OpenAI a découvert près de mille vulnérabilités dans le noyau Linux et réussi à les exploiter pour obtenir les privilèges les plus élevés du système. L'entreprise a également préparé des correctifs, dont plusieurs centaines ont déjà été transmis à la communauté Linux pour examen.
Repérer une vulnérabilité dans un logiciel est une chose. Prouver qu'elle permet de prendre le contrôle d'un système en est une autre. Dans une étude publiée le 4 novembre, OpenAI affirme avoir automatisé ces deux opérations, ainsi que la préparation des correctifs, grâce à une série d'agents alimentés par un modèle d'IA spécialisé dans la cybersécurité, dont la sortie est encore à venir. L'expérience, menée à la mi-octobre sur le noyau Linux, a permis de découvrir 948 failles distinctes permettant à un utilisateur disposant de droits limités d'obtenir les privilèges root, soit l'équivalent des droits administrateur sous Linux.
De la découverte de failles à l’élaboration de techniques d’attaque originales
Pour conduire cette expérience, OpenAI a d'abord chargé ses agents de repérer les parties du noyau qu'un utilisateur disposant de droits limités pouvait solliciter, afin de rechercher des failles qu’un attaquant serait capable d'exploiter sans posséder de privilèges élevés. Ce premier tri a permis de concentrer les recherches sur environ 7 % du code du noyau Linux, qu'une deuxième équipe d'agents a ensuite examiné.
Les erreurs suspectées ont été soumises à des tests dans des machines virtuelles isolées, puis les agents ont cherché à les exploiter pour obtenir les droits root. Au terme de la campagne, OpenAI a ainsi comptabilisé 948 vulnérabilités distinctes ayant permis d'accéder aux privilèges les plus élevés du système, sur une distribution Linux courante dont les principales protections de sécurité étaient activées.
A noter toutefois que pour exploiter ces failles, un attaquant doit déjà pouvoir exécuter du code sur la machine, par exemple après avoir compromis un compte utilisateur ou une application. Elles ne permettent donc pas, à elles seules, de pirater un ordinateur Linux à distance, mais peuvent transformer un premier accès limité en contrôle complet du système.
Au cours de leurs recherches, les agents auraient également élaboré au moins dix techniques d'exploitation inédites, que les spécialistes externes consultés par OpenAI ne connaissaient pas non plus. L'entreprise a choisi de ne pas en publier les détails techniques, mais ces découvertes suggèrent que les modèles sont désormais capables de concevoir leurs propres stratégies d'attaque, et plus seulement de répliquer des méthodes déjà documentées.
Linux à la peine face à l’avalanche de signalements générés par IA
Une démonstration impressionnante, qui confirme les progrès de l'IA dans la recherche de vulnérabilités, déjà illustrés récemment par Anthropic sur Linux, Chrome et Safari. Mais la multiplication de ces découvertes soulève aussi la question de leur traitement, alors que les responsables du noyau Linux alertent déjà sur l'afflux de rapports issus de recherches assistées par IA, souvent imprécis ou peu fiables, qui compliquent le travail des équipes de maintenance. En octobre, Google a même suspendu une partie de son programme de récompenses consacré aux logiciels open source, submergé par les signalements automatisés invalides.
OpenAI a bien tenté de répondre à ce problème en accompagnant ses découvertes de preuves d'exploitation et de propositions de correctifs, mais ses premiers essais ont quand même révélé que plusieurs patchs risquaient de dégrader les performances du noyau ou de passer à côté d'autres variantes d'une même vulnérabilité.
Après plusieurs ajustements et un examen par ses chercheurs, OpenAI a finalement transmis plusieurs centaines de rapports et de correctifs aux responsables du noyau Linux, en donnant la priorité aux failles les plus critiques. Pour l'heure, l'entreprise ne précise pas combien de ses correctifs ont été acceptés et intégrés au noyau.

articles.title: Qualcomm busca fuera del móvil lo que le quita la crisis de la memoria: coches, IA y antenas para SpaceX
articles.text:
Qualcomm lleva años diversificando negocio, pero por encima de todo, sigue siendo esa empresa de los procesadores Snapdragon para los móviles Android. No en vano, la propia compañía celebra un 'fiestón' cada año en Hawái para presentar sus procesadores para móviles (y también portátiles) más potentes de cara a los próximos meses, pero este año la cosa se ha enfriado debido a la sonadísima crisis de memoria.
Y, en un escenario en el que los envíos globales de móviles ha caído en picado, Qualcomm ha decidido reorientar el transatlántico. ¿Los objetivos más jugosos? Coches, antenas para SpaceX y la IA, cómo no.
En corto. Como tantas otras, Qualcomm ha presentado resultados financieros. En su caso, como en el de Apple, corresponden al último trimestre de su ejercicio fiscal y la cifra clave es la de 10.442 millones de dólares ingresados en este periodo, con unas ganancias operativas de 2.769 millones de dólares. Mucho dinero, pero un 7% menos que lo alcanzado en el mismo periodo del año anterior.
El beneficio por acción también fue un 28% inferior y el de las ganancias operativas también cayó un 27%. Y, aunque los ingresos superaron por "poco" los 10.140 millones de dólares que esperaba Wall Street, es evidente que hay cierta preocupación debido a que una de las patas principales del negocio se ha quedado coja.
Luces y sombras. Dentro del análisis presentado por la compañía podemos ver que la división de automoción ha aumentado un 89% hasta alcanzar los 1.990 millones de dólares. Es un subidón importante que, sin embargo, no consigue tapar que la división de chips para móviles "sólo" facturó 5.137 millones de dólares. Esto implica un 26% menos que en el mismo periodo del año anterior y refleja que la situación es la que es.
Lógico. Hemos venido hablando durante todo este año (y ya a finales del pasado, incluso) sobre cómo la crisis de memoria RAM y almacenamiento iba a provocar que el mercado de móviles se contrajera. Al principio teorizábamos con que las compañías volverían a apostar por modelos con menor cantidad de RAM, pero lo que ha terminado pasando es que la RAM se ha mantenido en su mayoría, pero los precios del dispositivo han aumentado.
También algo más drástico, como que se están fabricando y enviando menos móviles en una clara contracción del mercado. La International Data Corporation, una consultora especializada en tecnología y una de las fuentes más potentes junto a Canalys y Counterpoint, ya apuntó en agosto que los envíos mundiales de móviles iban a caer casi un 17% este año.
También señaló que el precio de la DRAM y la NAND había subido más de un 300% interanual y que el precio medio de un móvil había aumentado hasta un 28%. Esto hace no sólo que menos gente compre móviles y que los móviles sean también más caros, sino que Qualcomm está viendo que sus márgenes se reducen. Antes, el procesador era el componente más caro en un móvil, pero ahora es la RAM.
Playas prometedoras. El margen operativo de la división de Chips han caído del 29% de un año antes al 24%, y se estima que en el trimestre actual se quede entre el 20% y el 22%. Esto lleva a buscar soluciones, y aquí apuntan en tres direcciones:
- Coches. Ya hemos dicho que han crecido y esperan que sea una pata fuerte de cara al ejercicio de 2027.
- Centros de datos. Prevén más de 650 millones en este trimestre para los chips de centros de datos, con un objetivo de llegar a los 5.000 millones para el año fiscal completo. Para ello, tienen acuerdos como el de Amazon para chips de inferencia de IA.
- Antenas para SpaceX. Este mismo 4 de noviembre, Qualcomm anunció que iba a suministrar equipos de radio, unidades de banda base y software para la futura red 5G terrestre de Starlink Mobile en Estados Unidos. Desplegarán miles de torres a partir de 2027 y la propia Qualcomm (que ha fabricado chips 5G para Apple) describe la operación como "su mayor acuerdo 5G hasta la fecha". También es la base de la futura infraestructura 6G para la IA.
Girando el barco. El problema de esto es que las cosas están muy en el aire. Los chips y los coches son mercados que Qualcomm tiene asegurados, pero los ingresos tanto de SpaceX como de los centros de datos dependen de que se construyan esos centros de datos, de que no pinche la burbuja, de que los planes de SpaceX vayan como está previsto y de que las Big Tech como Amazon sigan apostando por esos chips de inferencia de Qualcomm en lugar de ir a por otro fabricante que aparezca con una solución más interesante.
Al margen de esto, es un ejemplo más de cómo la situación con la IA ha trastocado los planes de una compañía. A veces para mal (Qualcomm y los móviles), a veces para bien (Nvidia abandonando el gaming para centrarse en las GPU de IA o Micron dejando el segmento de consumo para producir únicamente RAM también para la IA).

Imagen | Federal Communications Commission
