articles.title: Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door Coupe first drive: Where tech and fun collide
articles.text:
The night before I drove the AMG GT 4-Door Coupe, I complained to a group of journalists that automakers don’t want to take chances and just build fun, weird cars anymore. About 12 hours later, Mercedes made me eat my words. Outside of all the bombastic extravaganza of the Los Angeles launch, the first true AMG powered exclusively by batteries is a technological triumph that’s as comfortable on the track as it is on the street. And it’s really very good on the track.
Triforce
One of the fundamental problems with EVs is weight. Batteries are heavy, and the old rule about an object in motion tending to stay in motion makes the notion of nimble cornering a difficult engineering problem. Mercedes loves an engineering problem, and after two days behind the wheel of the AMG GT EV, the company has mostly reduced the battery-weight tax that mires EV performance.
On the road and on the track, the vehicle is firmly planted to the roadway. Mercedes says various technologies make this possible. In addition to decades of producing high-performance vehicles, the automaker’s AMG.EA sports-car architecture does a lot of heavy lifting here, constantly adjusting power delivery from the three motors while guiding the Active Ride Control suspension, steering—including up to 6 degrees at the rear axle—and active aerodynamics to deliver the performance AMG customers have come to expect from a vehicle with the Affalterbach badge on the hood.
An exploded view of the axial flux motor.
Roberto Baldwin
An exploded view of the axial flux motor.
Roberto Baldwin
One of the AMG GT 4-Door Coupe’s battery cells.
Roberto Baldwin
One of the AMG GT 4-Door Coupe’s battery cells.
Roberto Baldwin
An exploded view of the axial flux motor.
Roberto Baldwin
One of the AMG GT 4-Door Coupe’s battery cells.
Roberto Baldwin
Of the technology added to the vehicle, the axial flux motors are the most intriguing. Three motors offer a lighter, smaller powertrain that unlocks a host of abilities: two that are 3.1 inches (79 mm) wide in the back, one that’s 3.5 inches (89 mm) wide in the front. Produced by Yasa, which Mercedes bought in 2021, the motors output up to 1,153 hp (860 kW) of peak power in the AMG GT 63, with a nominal output of 711 hp (530 kW) and 1,475 lb-ft (2,000 Nm). During Boost mode, the additional horsepower is available for 63 seconds—because it’s the AMG GT 63, obviously.
The AMG GT 55’s Boost mode lasts for 55 seconds, with a peak output of 805 hp (634 kW). The 55’s nominal output is 557 hp (415 kW) and 1,372 lb-ft (1,860 Nm) of torque. I was able to use the Boost modes of both trim levels multiple times in a row without issue. Indeed, zero to 60 mph (97 km/h) takes about 2.3 seconds, and zero to 124 mph (200 km/h) around 6.8 seconds.
Which means on track you can arrive at a corner going really quite fast.
The styling at the rear is… challenging.
Credit:
Mercedes-AMG
The styling at the rear is… challenging.
Credit:
Mercedes-AMG
Thankfully, the AMG GT’s speed can be tamed with regenerative braking and hydraulic brake-by-wire friction brakes: carbon ceramic discs at the front and steel ones at the rear. The system offered incredible stopping power when I decided to push the vehicle on the track and hit the brakes far too late for a tight left-hand corner. The deceleration was solid even as the vehicle was cresting a hill when I applied the brakes.
For drivers looking for an extreme amount of control over their vehicle, there’s the AMG race engineer control system (standard on the 63, optional on the 55) that consists of three dials in the center console: Response, Agility, Traction. They all go up to nine, which is a shame, because they could have added two more levels of control. At one, the settings are essentially for new drivers who really shouldn’t be behind the wheel of this vehicle. At nine, everything is turned up to (well, I’d like to say 11) the limit, and it’s a great way to fully unleash everything the vehicle has to offer and spend the day melting tires and struggling to keep the vehicle pointed forward around corners.
On the track, they had us dial it up to seven, which loosened up the rear end and increased throttle response to a level where we easily broke traction at the rear. Regardless of skill level, it’s a fun tool for track days where you can dial in exactly how you want the vehicle to respond.
Twist for fun.
Credit:
Roberto Baldwin
Twist for fun.
Credit:
Roberto Baldwin
Charging forward
Mercedes has moved to an 800 V system with the AMG GT 4-Door Coupe (yes, it’s a long name, but it distinguishes it from the current V8-powered AMG GT). The electrical architecture offers increased efficiencies and quicker charging, but because this is an AMG GT and it’s the automaker’s halo electric vehicle, they’ve decided to push the boat out and enable it to DC fast-charge at up to 600 kW. In a demo, one of the track AMG GT 63 vehicles hit a peak of 637 kW. At 60 percent state of charge, the car was drawing about 400 kW, and at 79 percent it was still pulling 252 kW. The vehicle went from 17 to 80 percent in about 10 minutes.
Charging quickly is great, but the same cooling technology in that battery pack also allows repeated Boost mode sessions. Mercedes is cooling its cylindrical batteries with a non-conductive oil that first flows by the connectors and then circles back past the center of the battery before returning to be cooled. Mercedes would not comment on the chemistry of the oil it uses, calling it a “secret.”
Mercedes has not shared range targets for the 106 kWh battery pack.
That sound
The driver’s displays are canted toward them.
Credit:
Mercedes-AMG
The driver’s displays are canted toward them.
Credit:
Mercedes-AMG
I want to hate the sound. I want to bat it away as a gimmick meant to appease drivers still clinging to a world of V8 power and loud exhausts.
Instead, the roar of the AMG GT R (C190 generation) comes flooding out of the speakers and activates actuators in the seats, and it’s delightful. It won me over, and the sound placement in the cabin re-creates a sort of mid-engine location for my brain. The result is, I’m driving an all-electric AMG with a fake mid-engine V8 noise, and I’m having fun.
The V8 growl appears when you walk up to the vehicle and when it’s turned on. In Comfort, Sport, and Race mode, it’s gone, but in Sport+, it rears its throaty head. When the vehicle is placed into Boost mode, the V8 noise gets louder (as it should).
It doesn’t sound real. It sounds close to real. It’s the difference between listening to a cassette tape of your favorite band and going to see them live. There’s an audio fidelity that’s not quite there, particularly in the low end. But you still enjoy that tape. It’s not necessary, but it’s delightful.
Inside (or finally a use for the passenger screen)
The interior is outfitted with all the luxury bits you expect from a Mercedes. All the usual suspects are there: the quilted door panels, the comfortable seats, and the array of available materials. This includes the screens and, yeah, the passenger screen.
Now this is useful information on a passenger screen.
Credit:
Roberto Baldwin
Now this is useful information on a passenger screen.
Credit:
Roberto Baldwin
But I finally found a use for that screen. It can display all the technical information of the vehicle, including nerdy data points about the amount of Nm a motor is outputting. I’ll never watch a video or play a video game on that screen outside of testing the latest version of MBUX 4.0, but I will stare at it while it shares details about the vehicle.
The seats are very comfortable, and the lumbar support and side bolsters are controlled on-screen. Usually I find this annoying, but the level of fine-tuning this affords the driver and passenger is impressive, and I’ll give it a pass. Also, at 6 feet, 3 inches (1.9 m), I fit comfortably in the back seat. The large trunk should allow for a group of four to head out for a nice weekend away. Or maybe pick up the kids from soccer practice.
Kids love fun. Adults love fun. At least they should. Mercedes-AMG built a fun but very expensive vehicle. The AMG GT 55 starts at $145,000 (destination is an additional $1,550) and will be available by the end of the year. The AMG GT 63 starts at $175,000 (destination fee unavailable at this time) and will be available at the beginning of 2027. Regardless of the 401(k)-emptying price, the electric coupe should squelch the “all EVs drive the same” discourse.
A coupe can have four doors, because it just means “cut” in French, as in the roofline has been cut.
Credit:
Mercedes-AMG
A coupe can have four doors, because it just means “cut” in French, as in the roofline has been cut.
Credit:
Mercedes-AMG
The AMG-GT Four-Door Coupe delivers the promise of an AMG as an EV that drips with nerdy and driver joy that can also get very, very sideways.

articles.title: The ex-Secret Service agent who flipped a hacker is now raising a second $250M cybersecurity fund | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Every time venture capitalists write a check, they’re secretly running numbers in their heads about different exit scenarios. It’s their job as fiduciaries. But nearly all will tell you (publicly, anyway) that every portfolio company is headed for an IPO.
Stephen Ward, the co-founder of Brightmind Partners, a two-year-old cybersecurity fund in New York, says otherwise outright. “You have to sell on the way up,” he says.
Ward’s unvarnished pragmatism is one reason he stands out. Another is the size of his firm’s debut fund late last year: a whopping $250 million fund, which he closed with co-founder Gur Talpaz. A third reason is his resume, which includes a stint with the Coast Guard, nine years in the Secret Service, and CISO jobs at TIAA and Home Depot before he ever thought about investing.
One proof point that suggests the combination is working is SGNL, the identity security startup CrowdStrike agreed in January to buy for $740 million, 11 months after Brightmind led its Series A.
Now, Ward is raising a second fund, targeting roughly the same size as the first one. This time, though, he’ll be doing it without Talpaz, who left in April along with another early colleague, leaving Ward as the firm’s sole general partner. He’s betting on himself at a moment when early-stage cybersecurity startups are raising more money than later-stage rivals for the first time in more than a decade.
His unemotional approach to exits traces back to an unlikely career. Ward says he grew up in northwest New Jersey between two farms, in a family that couldn’t afford college for his older brothers. After high school, he joined the Coast Guard, inspired by a commercial of a man jumping out of a helicopter, though he says he barely knew how to swim at the time. He spent four years in search and rescue.
Afterward, he studied criminal justice at Seton Hall in New Jersey and thought half-heartedly about law school. “I didn’t know what I wanted to do,” Ward told me last week over Zoom, wearing a pale hooded sweatshirt and looking more like a basketball coach than a venture capitalist. “I was kind of lost. I missed the military and the camaraderie and all of that.”
After graduating in 1998, he says, he mailed out some 300 resumes but no one responded. A Seton Hall professor who was also a chaplain to Secret Service personnel, as well as to members of the FBI and CIA, began introducing him around, and the Secret Service called first.
The Secret Service has two primary missions: protecting people and investigating financial crimes. Ward gravitated to investigations, then to “cyber” after the September 11 attacks in 2001. That year, he married a former college classmate, an American-born Syrian Muslim. Colleagues warned him the background check would be “miserable.” (They’re still happily married.)
What came next took Ward’s life down an unexpected path. Stationed in New York, he arrested a hacker who’d pulled off the largest credit card data theft of that era. Instead of charging him, however, Ward flipped him, turning him into an informant and running him for about three years. But the hacker kept hacking behind Ward’s back, and after he was caught again, he told the agency, as a diversionary tactic, that Ward was in on it.
By that time, Ward had left for the private sector, and he ultimately spent roughly 18 months clearing his name. “It was hard to get out of bed,” he said of that period, describing the investigation as “almost like a spouse cheating on you,” given his love of the agency. The hacker ultimately received a 20-year sentence, and Audible bought the rights to the story, turning it into an eight-episode podcast called “Operation Firewall.”
Ward’s corporate career has been a success by most measures, though he describes it as a series of jumps he really wasn’t qualified to make. His first private-sector job at J.P. Morgan, where he was recruited in 2007 to build a cybersecurity unit, was the hardest transition of his career, he says. He felt like “the dumbest person in the room,” missed his Secret Service crew, and twice thought about going back, unaware he was still under investigation. He stuck it out and now calls the investment bank the “best management school.”
Six years as CISO at the financial services company TIAA followed, and then two years at Home Depot starting in 2019. But in 2021, feeling burned out, he quit without anything lined up for the first time since age 16.
That chapter didn’t last long. The founders of Wiz, whose security software Ward had used at Home Depot, put him on a short list for a job at their company. Jeff Horing, a venture capitalist at Insight Partners, which had co-led Wiz’s $100 million Series A round in late 2020, interviewed Ward for the role, then offered him one at Insight instead.
It’s a good-news, bad-news story, given that Wiz was acquired last year by Google for $32 billion. When I asked him about it last week, Ward observed that the friend who took the Wiz job “made life-changing money,” but said it doesn’t bother him.
Regardless, he spent just three years at Insight, where he says he worked on Wiz, Abnormal Security, and Elisity, which IonQ agreed in October to buy for up to $1.3 billion. Then, at age 49, he thought about striking out on his own for the first time.
He says people told him it was a young man’s game. He left anyway and began cold-emailing limited partners. Ultimately, fewer than 20 LPs filled the fund, including Horing.
Ward started Brightmind in 2024 with Talpaz, a CrowdStrike corporate development executive whose deals overlapped with Ward’s during his time at Insight. Tayler Sipperly, another CrowdStrike corporate development alum, was the firm’s third employee.
The partnership ended this past spring. Asked what happened, Ward, using carefully worded legalese, cited “differences in opinions regarding operations and the future of Brightmind.” In August, Talpaz and Sipperly co-founded a new venture firm with Elia Zaitsev, CrowdStrike’s global CTO for the past three years. Called Cognition, it’s now reportedly targeting a $170 million first fund to back cybersecurity startups.
Brightmind’s first fund has made 14 investments to date, with one exit: that SNGL sale.
Some investors asked why Brightmind didn’t ride out that bet even longer. But Ward says he’s seen enough across his career that he feels confident in warning founders when they’re “going to race past the turn.”
In cybersecurity, he says, the best sales come between a startup’s third and seventh years. Indeed, he says his team tracks every security acquisition and what buyers are building versus buying. If Palo Alto Networks is likely to buy something, he says, CrowdStrike will experience “FOMO, then Zscaler is going to look over and go, ‘What did they just do? I should probably do the same thing.’”
Understanding how the pieces fit together is the trick, Ward explained, offering some hypotheticals. If CrowdStrike is building a product, he said, it’s unlikely to buy a portfolio company that makes something similar. Palo Alto Networks might love a company, but not if buying it would force its customers to switch away from something it bought five years ago.
“It’s very easy to go, ‘Good match,’ ‘terrible match,’” he said. “And that’s really what we spend a ton of time figuring out.”
He has timing on his side, at least. Early-stage cybersecurity startups are out-raising their later-stage rivals for the first time in more than a decade, according to PitchBook, which counts $4.7 billion worth of seed-through-Series B deals through September.
That total is already ahead of the entirety of 2025, even though the number of deals fell to 248 from 358 last year. Seed rounds in particular are ballooning, per PitchBook. The average cybersecurity seed round jumped to $8.4 million in the first nine months of this year, from $5.54 million a year earlier.
Ward questions how much of that money is really going to AI security. By PitchBook’s count, 278 deals in the first half of 2026 were bucketed as such, but his team’s manual review found only 30 true ones. He doesn’t think Anthropic or OpenAI will “take over the security world,” but instead will do “just enough.”
For real-time protection, which he terms “zero second,” he favors cyber-specific models that run locally on a customer’s own systems, like that of Empirical Security. He also looks for startups that could trounce established companies that he considers vulnerable, name-checking 27-year-old Qualys and 24-year-old Tenable.
Ward says Brightmind’s second fund won’t be entirely cybersecurity, focusing about 20% on AI infrastructure deals. He expects a meaningful number of teams to come from Israel, too. (Roughly 40% of the debut fund’s startups are based in Tel Aviv.)
Asked about the founders he’s most comfortable backing, the response is immediate: second-time founders who stick together.
Brightmind is comprised of five people right now: COO Iva Messy, also a Seton Hall graduate, came from venture firms Felicis and Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) on the recommendation of Ward’s cousin, Carl Eschenbach, a former Workday CEO who is now back at Sequoia. Sven Wollschlaeger, a Midwesterner whom Ward calls one of the hardest-working people he’s known, spent three years alongside Ward at Insight, and is a principal at Brightmind.
CTO Jamie Mneimneh, whom Ward first hired at Home Depot as a distinguished engineer, is the most technical person of the team. He built the cloud computing environment on AWS where the firm tests startups’ products. Mneimneh also built the AI agents that now source most of Brightmind’s deal flow, which is how the firm avoids hiring a bench of analysts and keeps management fees down, says Ward.
Taylor Cleveland, Ward’s chief of staff at Home Depot, joined the firm a few months ago.
For all the career changes, Ward says the real force driving him hasn’t changed. He grew up without money and still worries it could happen again, saying he’s being paid to produce a “3x net fund,” and he’s “not going to celebrate until we get that.”
Said Ward: “I don’t know what’s wrong with me. I have a level of being very naive to like, not being qualified to do something. I’ve just always looked at people and been like, ‘Okay, you know more than me today, but tomorrow, it’s going to be a little less, and the day after that, it’s going to be less, and eventually, I’m going to catch you and surpass you, and I’m going to know more than you.’ That’s how competitive I am.”

articles.title: Cat Wu, jefa de producto de Claude Code, dejó Anthropic y a los pocos días se sumó a OpenAI
articles.text:
Cat Wu, la responsable de producto de Claude Code en Anthropic, se sumó a OpenAI pocos días después de dejar la empresa. Wu anunció en la red social X que dirigirá la gestión de producto de los productos centrales de OpenAI, la compañía que compite directamente con Anthropic en herramientas de programación con IA.
La noticia la dio primero Business Insider. Según el medio, Wu dejó Anthropic el viernes 30 de octubre y comunicó su salida el martes 3 de noviembre. Anthropic confirmó la partida a ese medio. En su mensaje de despedida, Wu no explicó los motivos ni mencionó su próximo destino.
Wu lideró el producto de Claude Code y de Cowork, la herramienta de Anthropic para tareas que van más allá de la programación. Business Insider la describe como una de las dos grandes voceras del producto junto con su creador, Boris Cherny, y como una de las caras públicas de Claude Code en las redes.
En OpenAI trabajará con Thibault Sottiaux, jefe de los productos centrales de la compañía. Wu escribió que respeta a OpenAI porque mostró que escalar los modelos funciona, porque llegó a más de 1.000 millones de personas y porque trata los buenos productos como parte de su misión. Greg Brockman, presidente de OpenAI, le dio la bienvenida.
Su meta, dijo, es crear agentes, asistentes de IA que ejecutan tareas por su cuenta, sin quitarles el control a los usuarios. A un usuario que le preguntó en X si se tomaría seis meses de descanso, le respondió con una broma: “post agi!”, en alusión a una IA de nivel humano.
Tres salidas del equipo en diez días
Wu es la tercera persona clave de Claude Code que se va en ese plazo. El 24 de octubre, el ingeniero Thariq Shihipar anunció que dejaba Anthropic tras más de un año en el proyecto y que quería tomarse un descanso antes de emprender algo nuevo. Ese mismo día, Anthony Morris, creador de la versión de escritorio, también se despidió.
Morris escribió que su último día fue el 23 de octubre. Según el sitio Dealroom, Shihipar recomendó en su despedida seguir a Wu para conocer las novedades del producto, y Anthropic no había comentado esas dos salidas.
Wu se había unido a Anthropic en 2024. En su despedida contó que, hace dos años, cuando Claude Code era una herramienta interna pequeña, le pidió que construyera un entorno para entrenar IA con aprendizaje por refuerzo y la guió durante decenas de horas sin escribir una línea de código a mano. Eso la convenció de sumarse al equipo.
También describió cómo cambió el uso. Al principio, la mayoría aprobaba a mano cada permiso y usaba a Claude sobre todo para responder preguntas y escribir pruebas. “Hoy, lo habitual es confiar en el criterio de Claude para aprobar automáticamente”, escribió. Según Wu, la herramienta ahora hace migraciones grandes y construye productos nuevos.
Una herramienta que sostiene los ingresos de Anthropic
Claude Code superó los USD 2.500 millones de proyección de ingresos anualizados en febrero de 2026, según informó Anthropic. Business Insider sostiene que el producto le dio a la empresa un éxito viral que impulsó sus ingresos y le permitió acceder a más financiamiento para capacidad de cómputo.
OpenAI tiene un producto equivalente, Codex, que según Business Insider también impulsó su crecimiento y que se usa cada vez más en tareas ajenas a la programación. El fichaje pone a la responsable de uno de los productos rivales al frente de la estrategia de producto del otro.
Los movimientos coinciden con un momento delicado para Anthropic. Business Insider informó que la empresa se encamina hacia una salida a bolsa a fines de este mes de noviembre, con el equipo de Claude Code ya sin tres de sus integrantes más visibles.

articles.title: Vols de câbles : 850 stations de recharge visées en France, les opérateurs appellent l'État à l'aide
articles.text:
L’association Charge France, qui réunit les principaux opérateurs de bornes de recharge, a publié le 3 novembre un bilan qui montre l’ampleur prise par le phénomène. Depuis le début de l’année, 850 sites de recharge ont été visés par des vols de câbles, soit environ 10 % du réseau de recharge rapide français, pour un préjudice estimé à 18 millions d’euros. Auprès du Figaro, son secrétaire général, Matthieu Dischamps, évoque même un millier de stations touchées fin octobre, plus de 15 % du réseau de recharge rapide et 21 millions d’euros de préjudice, contre une centaine de stations sur toute l’année 2025. Les voleurs s’attaquent au cuivre que contiennent ces câbles, particulièrement épais sur les bornes rapides.
Le butin est pourtant plutôt maigre, puisqu’un câble sectionné leur rapporterait entre 30 et 80 euros à la revente. En revanche, son remplacement coûte environ 1 500 euros à l’opérateur, sans compter l’intervention des techniciens et les recettes perdues pendant l’immobilisation de la station.
Pour les conducteurs, la conséquence est très concrète. Une station dont les câbles ont été coupés ne peut tout simplement plus recharger et TotalEnergies indiquait à BFM remplacer les câbles en une quinzaine de jours. Le problème pèse d’autant plus que 71 % des conducteurs de voitures 100 % électriques utilisent la recharge publique, selon une enquête Enedis-CSA d’octobre citée par l’association. Sur les grands axes, où les stations peuvent être espacées de plusieurs dizaines de kilomètres, il est recommandé de vérifier la disponibilité d’une borne sur l’application dédiée ou le planificateur de bord avant de s’y rendre.
Des vols de plus en plus organisés
Les opérateurs estiment que ces vols sont surtout le fait de réseaux organisés équipés de coupe-câbles hydrauliques sur batterie et des meuleuses de chantier, qui opèrent de nuit sur des sites isolés et sans surveillance. « Sur notre réseau de plus de 450 stations, nous constatons presque chaque semaine un ou plusieurs actes de vol de câbles », explique Gautier Chatelus, président de Driveco, qui déploie progressivement des gaines en Kevlar intégrant des puces GSM. D’autres opérateurs misent sur la vidéosurveillance, les alarmes ou les alertes en temps réel, et Ionity dit recourir à une protection physique renforcée, à des technologies de suivi et à des systèmes de marquage à l’encre.
La justice commence néanmoins à sévir et Charge France recense quinze mises en examen depuis janvier, dont sept depuis septembre. Les tribunaux de Toulouse et de Troyes ont prononcé des peines de deux ans de prison ferme, assorties d’interdictions du territoire de cinq et dix ans, et celui de Nantes une peine de seize mois ferme, avec à chaque fois l’indemnisation des opérateurs. Pour l’association, ce n’est pas suffisant.
Elle demande aux ministères de l’Intérieur et de la Justice de croiser les enquêtes entre parquets pour démanteler les réseaux, de renforcer les contrôles chez les ferrailleurs pour fermer les filières de recel, et de mobiliser rapidement les forces de l’ordre en cas d’alertes d’une borne. « On ne peut pas demander aux Français de passer à l’électrique et les laisser face à des bornes rendues inutilisables par des vols », alerte Matthieu Dischamps, secrétaire général de Charge France, tout en interpellant aussi les candidats à l’élection présidentielle de 2027.
Les bornes bientôt classées infrastructures critiques ?
Le sujet est aussi remonté à l’Assemblée nationale et dans une question écrite adressée le 3 novembre au ministre de l’Intérieur, la députée Olga Givernet (Ensemble pour la République) fait état de 637 plaintes et d’environ 14 millions d’euros de préjudice déclarés par 27 opérateurs. Elle plaide pour classer les stations les plus stratégiques parmi les infrastructures critiques, au sens de la directive européenne de 2022 sur la résilience des entités critiques, afin de mieux les protéger.
Charge France appuie cette demande en prenant pour modèle le Portugal, où le phénomène aurait disparu après la condamnation d’un voleur à neuf ans de prison ferme. Dans ce pays, les bornes sont considérées comme des infrastructures énergétiques critiques. Aucune décision n’a été annoncée à ce jour en France. En attendant, les opérateurs paient à la fois les réparations et les nouvelles protections, tout en finançant l’extension du réseau. On comptait environ 40 000 points de recharge rapide fin septembre en France.

articles.title: VC funding into Indian B2C ecommerce companies dips 33%: Tracxn
articles.text:
VC funding into Indian B2C ecommerce companies dips 33%: Tracxn
Late- and seed-stage funding nearly halved in the period between January 1 and November 3 this year, while early-stage funding remained stable compared to last year.
Venture capital funding into business-to-consumer (B2C) ecommerce companies in India dropped 33% in the ten months of the year, according to a report by Tracxn.
The report titled 'India B2C E-Commerce' noted that, between January 1, 2026 and November 3, 2026, B2C ecommerce companies raised $1.6 billion across 356 rounds, compared with $2.4 billion from 621 rounds in the similar period of 2025.
According to the report, funding and rounds declined, with late- and seed-stage funding nearly halving, while early-stage funding remained stable in 2026 compared to 2025.
The key funding rounds during the period included FS Life ($110 million), Ultrahuman ($65 million), Yulu ($63 million), Snabbit ($56 million), FirstClub ($55 million), and Nua ($50 million).
Early-stage funding reached $872 million in 2026, up 3% from $846 million in 2025. In contrast, late-stage funding declined 51% to $587 million from $1.2 billion, while seed-stage funding fell 50% to $169 million from $339 million. Early-stage accounted for 54% of total funding in 2026, with 97 rounds, compared with 125 in 2025.
Bengaluru raised $686 million in 2026, accounting for 43% of the $1.6 billion raised for the year till now. Mumbai ranked second, with $286 million, while the third place was taken by Gurugram at $199 million.
On the exit front, acquisitions declined to 19 in 2026 compared with 25 in 2025, while IPOs nearly halved to 7 compared to 13 in 2025. L’Oréal’s acquisition of Innovist for $434 million was the largest acquisition of the year by deal value, while Purple Style Labs recorded the highest market capitalisation among companies that went public in 2026, at $488 million. Astrotalk was the only new unicorn in 2026 from the ecommerce category.

articles.title: Transformer de la ferraille « sale » en super-métal : l'incroyable trouvaille de l'IA
articles.text:
Des chercheurs utilisent les impuretés du métal recyclé pour améliorer ses propriétés. Sur 17 variantes de fonte proposées par leur méthode d’apprentissage automatique, puis fabriquées et testées, 14 offrent un meilleur compromis entre résistance et capacité à se déformer avant de casser.
Pour obtenir un bon alliage recyclé, les industriels diluent souvent les impuretés de la ferraille avec du métal neuf. Une équipe réunissant plusieurs universités chinoises et l’Institut Max-Planck pour les matériaux durables a choisi de tirer parti de ces éléments indésirables. Ses travaux, publiés dans Science Advances, utilisent l’IA pour trouver les compositions et les traitements qui leur donneront un rôle utile.
Composer avec les impuretés plutôt que les diluer
Ajouter du métal primaire aide à retrouver les propriétés recherchées, mais sa production consomme de l’énergie et émet du CO2. Une partie de l’intérêt environnemental du recyclage se perd donc dans l’opération. Avec leurs « dirty alloys », ou alliages « sales », les chercheurs veulent conserver davantage de ferraille dans le mélange et utiliser certains éléments qu’elle contient pour renforcer le matériau.
Mais comment trouver les bonnes proportions ? Avec l’IA, pardi ! Pour faire ses calculs, l’IA s’appuie sur deux bases de données : une première de 330 entrées détaillées et une seconde d’environ 2 400 entrées associant compositions et propriétés mécaniques. Un algorithme explore différentes compositions et fait aussi varier les paramètres de fabrication, notamment les températures du métal et les durées des opérations de fonderie. Des réseaux de neurones prédisent ensuite la résistance à la traction et l’allongement à la rupture, qui mesure la capacité du matériau à s’étirer avant de casser. La recherche vise un équilibre entre les deux propriétés.
Un second modèle, entraîné sur davantage de données, affine la sélection. Les candidats retenus sont alors fabriqués et soumis à des essais mécaniques. Les mesures rejoignent ensuite la base de données pour améliorer les prédictions au tour suivant. Le laboratoire fournit ainsi de nouveaux résultats à l’IA qui s’en sert pour proposer les prochaines compositions.
Jusqu’à 15,2 % de résistance en plus
L’équipe a commencé par une fonte à graphite sphéroïdal, aussi appelée fonte ductile, déjà connue pour sa tolérance aux impuretés. Parmi les 17 variantes testées, 14 améliorent les compromis entre résistance et déformabilité par rapport aux fontes recyclées de référence recensées dans les données.
À allongement comparable, la résistance à la traction progresse jusqu’à 15,2%. À résistance comparable, l’allongement avant rupture augmente jusqu’à 73,2%. Ces maxima correspondent donc à des compromis différents selon les alliages. Les auteurs annoncent également un coût de fabrication inférieur de 8,1% à celui du procédé conventionnel mêlant ferraille et fer primaire.
Ces résultats concernent pour l’instant une seule famille de fonte. Les chercheurs envisagent d’étendre leur méthode aux aciers recyclés ainsi qu’aux alliages d’aluminium et de cuivre.
Pour une fonderie, la perspective serait de fabriquer des pièces de qualité avec les lots de ferraille disponibles en ajoutant moins de métal neuf pour les corriger. Ou comment faire des économies en obtenant un bien meilleur alliage.
Source : Institut Max-Planck pour les matériaux durables via Heise

articles.title: KI-Hacker nutzen alte Technik: Die unterschätzte Gefahr für Unternehmen
articles.text:
Immer mehr Cyberattacken mit KI-Unterstützung: Warum alte Technik die größte Gefahr ist
In Supermärkten in ganz Europa heizen Hacker Tiefkühltruhen auf bis zu 50 Grad hoch. Dafür brauchten sie keine KI, nur veraltete Steuerungstechnik, die offen im Netz hängt. Zur gleichen Zeit greift eine China zugeordnete Hackergruppe mit einem KI-Werkzeug mehr als 200 Organisationen weltweit an. Beides zeigt, wohin die Reise geht: KI erfindet keine neuen Angriffe, aber sie macht sie schneller, billiger und massenhaft möglich. Wie groß ist die Gefahr wirklich und wie können wir uns schützen?
Noch vor wenigen Jahren wäre das Science-Fiction gewesen: Ein auf Cyberangriffe spezialisiertes KI-Modell von OpenAI ist während eines Tests aus seiner isolierten „Sandbox“ ausgebrochen, hat einen Server gehackt, sich Administrator-Rechte dafür verschafft und von dort aus über das Internet den auf offene KI-Modelle spezialisierten Online-Dienst Hugging Face angegriffen. Auch dort nutzte der von OpenAIs KI gesteuerte KI-Agent eine Sicherheitslücke, über die er Zugriff auf das System bekam. Dort erweiterte er seine Zugriffsprivilegien, erschlich sich schließlich Zugang zu vertraulichen Daten, und verschleierte anschließend seine Spuren. Ein Mensch hätte das nicht besser machen können.
Dieser Text erscheint in der Ausgabe 7/2026 von MIT Technology Review. Darin beschäftigen wir uns damit, wie KI die IT-Sicherheit auf den Kopf stellt. Das Heft erscheint am 25.9.2026 im Zeitschriftenhandel.
Seitdem sind eine Vielzahl ähnlicher Fälle gemeldet worden: Antrophic, Meta und Moonshot AI gaben bekannt, dass ihnen ihre Modelle ebenfalls ausgebrochen sind und fremde Server angegriffen haben. Was für andere Branchen ein PR-Desaster wäre, ist für die KI-Entwickelnden eine gigantische Werbekampagne: Seht her, unsere KI ist so gefährlich, dass niemand sie unter Kontrolle halten kann. Nicht einmal wir selbst.
Häufigere Cyberattacken mit KI-Unterstützung?
Auch wenn das alles durchaus im Verdacht steht, nur Show zu sein – sicher ist: Die wachsenden Fähigkeiten von KI-Modellen verändern nicht nur die legale Wirtschaft. Auch die Schattenwirtschaft im Cybercrime-Untergrund macht sich den technischen Wandel zunutze. „Die zunehmende Verbreitung von KI hat die Bedrohungslandschaft grundlegend verändert“, warnt etwa Interpol in einem aktuellen Bericht.
Auf die Frage, wie das weitergehen wird und ob wir vor einer massiven Welle KI-gestützter Verbrechen stehen, gibt es im Moment mehr Antworten als Expertinnen und Experten. Das hängt nicht nur damit zusammen, dass Berater:innen, Firmen für IT-Sicherheitssoftware, Behörden, Forschende und KI-Provider jeweils ihre eigenen Interessen verfolgen. Es liegt auch daran, dass IT-Sicherheit ein weites Feld ist, das die beteiligten Akteure in der Regel nur aus ihrer spezifischen Perspektive betrachten: Ein bisschen so, wie in der indischen Legende von den drei Blinden, die einen Elefanten beschreiben sollen und von denen jeder eine eigene Sicht auf die Wahrheit hat.

articles.title: Aspiration, lavage et entretien du rouleau : le Dreame H15 Pro passe sous les 250 €
articles.text:
L’aspirateur laveur Dreame H15 Pro est à 249,16 € (-45 %)
Avec son format inclinable à plat et son rouleau autonettoyant, le Dreame H15 Pro passe à 249,16 € chez Amazon, soit 45 % sous le prix conseillé.
Vendu et expédié par Amazon, ce modèle neuf bénéficie de la livraison gratuite. L’économie atteint 199,84 € face au prix conseillé de 449 €. Le tarif est également inférieur de 48,83 € au plus bas des 30 derniers jours indiqué par le marchand, de 297,99 €.
Un nettoyage jusque sous les meubles
Le H15 Pro aspire les poussières et lave les sols durs avec son rouleau humide. Sa conception inclinable à 180° permet d’atteindre le dessous des meubles bas. Une raclette mobile accompagne les mouvements pour récupérer les petites saletés et limiter l’eau laissée au sol.
Sur sa base, le rouleau bénéficie d’un autonettoyage avec de l’eau chauffée jusqu’à 100 °C, suivi d’un séchage à l’air chaud. Ces températures concernent l’entretien de la brosse sur la station. Les réservoirs séparés permettent de conserver l’eau propre à l’écart de l’eau récupérée.
Une bonne autonomie, mais un poids sensible
Lors de notre test, nous avons mesuré près de 44 minutes d’autonomie. Les réservoirs ont permis environ 39 minutes de nettoyage avant de nécessiter une intervention. Nous avons également apprécié l’efficacité de l’autonettoyage du rouleau et le ramassage des petites poussières le long des murs.
Ses 5,8 kg restent toutefois sensibles malgré les roues motorisées, particulièrement dans les virages serrés. La raclette peut aussi repousser les gros déchets. Ce modèle convient donc surtout à l’entretien régulier des sols durs, avec une bonne endurance entre deux charges.

articles.title: Apple quiere que Siri IA esté en todas partes. Al mismo tiempo, limita a 200 dólares el gasto de tokens para sus empleados
articles.text:
Apple quiere que sus usuarios usen todo el rato la nueva Siri AI en sus dispositivos. Apple lo vende como su gran remontada en IA. Pero de puertas para adentro, alguien ha mirado el Excel (o Numbers, en su caso) de gastos en IA de sus empleados y ha empezado a meterle la tijera a los presupuestos diarios de tokens que los equipos de Apple pueden usar para mejorar su trabajo.
Este recorte en el presupuesto de tokens para sus empleados no es cosa solo de Apple. Muchas de las empresas que hasta hace solo unos meses invitaban a sus empleados a usar la IA en su trabajo, han recibido ya su primera factura de esos tokens consumido. El susto ha debido ser tan grande que les han cerrado el grifo.
Apple mete la tijera a los tokens. De acuerdo a lo publicado por Bloomberg, el mes pasado Apple redujo de forma discreta el límite diario de uso de tokens de algunos ingenieros de 300 a 200 dólares. Ahora, la compañía de Ternus estudia rebajarlo todavía más y dejarlo en 100 dólares para determinados equipos.
Fuera de ingeniería, algunos grupos de empleados pasarían de 100 dólares en tokens a 25 dólares diarios. Quien necesite más puede pedir una excepción y se estudiará su uso. Los empleados de Apple disponen de acceso a Claude, ChatGPT y Gemini. Aun así, algunos equipos ya habrían recibo la consigna de usar modelos más baratos o que funcionen de forma local en el propio dispositivo.
¿Tan cara es la factura? Este recorte presupuestario para el uso de IA entre su plantilla llama la atención por venir de la tecnológica con mayor capitalización del mercado. ¿Si Apple no puede pagar la barra libre de tokens para sus empleados, quién puede?
Según sus cuentas, la compañía gastó 45.765 millones en I+D en su último ejercicio, un 32% más que en el anterior. Apple atribuye esa subida en parte a la inversión en IA. Entonces, ¿por qué recortar? Empleados citados por Bloomberg sostienen que "pocos trabajadores utilizaban la totalidad de su asignación diaria de 300 dólares", por lo que el ahorro real puede ser mínimo. Otros empleados manifestaban su temor a que esta limitación presupuestaria pueda ser la antesala de mayores recortes o posibles despidos, como está sucediendo en otras empresas tecnológicas.
Nvidia piensa justo lo contrario. Jensen Huang lo dejó claro en el podcast All-In. Le preocuparía mucho que un ingeniero con 500.000 dólares de sueldo gastara menos de 250.000 dólares en tokens de IA. Cuando le preguntaron si Nvidia gasta unos 2.000 millones al año en tokens para sus ingenieros, el CEO respondió: "Lo estamos intentando".
Las declaraciones de Huang tienen su lógica. Nvidia vende los chips donde se ejecutan esos modelos, por lo que cada token que se quema supone un poco más de inversión en potencia de cómputo y más ventas para sus chips. En Cupertino, que solo pagan la factura, el mensaje es muy diferente.
Apple no es la primera. El frenazo en el fenómeno conocido como tokenmaxxing viene de meses atrás. En Meta hubo una carrera interna por ser quien más tokens gastaba. En Amazon cerraron un ranking parecido en mayo. Su memorando posterior desaconseja el tokenmaxxing, pero la empresa asegura que no ha puesto límites.
En Microsoft, un solo empleado llegó a quemar 28.000 dólares en tokens en solo un mes. Microsoft reaccionó. Su vicepresidente Jay Parikh escribió en un correo interno al que tuvo acceso 404 Media que "el tokenmaxxing no es lo que estamos optimizando".
Revolut cambia de modelo. Con las facturas de los tokens en el punto de mira, algunas empresas buscan otra salida. Revolut ha puesto a unos 2.000 ingenieros a programar por defecto con GLM, un modelo chino de pesos abiertos. Sus parámetros son públicos y se pueden ejecutar en servidores propios, lo cual contribuye a reducir considerablemente el coste en tokens.
El responsable de infraestructura de Revolut, David Abitbol, contó que pagan una décima parte de lo que cuestan los modelos de frontera. Además, la factura es fija y no sube con cada petición. Antes, los 300 dólares mensuales por ingeniero para Claude Code no duraban todo el mes, ahora el límite de consultas la definen sus propios servidores.

articles.title: Motorola's new Signature 27 smartphone aims to set a higher flagship standard
articles.text:
Bottom line: Motorola is looking to make a statement with its latest flagship smartphone. The Signature 27 is not a foldable, but you'd be forgiven for thinking that just by looking at the price tag.
The traditional slab-style handset features a 6.8-inch Extreme AMOLED Duo, a 120Hz display that Motorola claims is the brightest available on any smartphone. Indeed, the 12,000 nits of peak brightness is impressive, but note that it only hits this mark in specific scenarios and that sustained performance while viewing most content will be far more average.
The device is powered by Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 Mobile Platform (that's a mouthful) and is paired with 12GB of RAM – not quite the 16GB we saw some phones ship with just before the memory crunch, but still ample given continued inventory shortages. Buyers also get 512GB of onboard UFS 4.1 storage.
Motorola says the Signature 27 includes its most advanced camera system to date. The rear array consists of a 50MP Sony Lytia L910 main camera with f/1.6 aperture, a 50MP ultrawide shooter with f/2 aperture lens, and a 200MP periscope telephoto camera with 3x optical zoom, alongside a dedicated event-based vision sensor to help capture fast-moving subjects. There's also a 50MP camera with f/1.9 aperture up front for video calling and selfie duties.
DXOMARK currently has the Motorola Signature 27 ranked second behind the Huawei Pura 80 Ultra in terms of overall camera quality.
Other noteworthy features include Bang & Olufsen audio, Corning Gorilla Glass Ceramic 3, a massive 7,000mAh battery that supports 90W wired charging, and a six-antenna design to enhance 5G download speeds. A 12-minute charge is enough to "restore power for the day," we're told. Motorola promises seven OS updates and up to seven years of security updates starting from its global launch date.
Speaking of, the Motorola Signature 27 goes up for pre-order on November 19 in your choice of coal smoke or capulet olive and launches a week later on November 26. Pricing starts at $1,599.99.

articles.title: ¿Cuál es el precio de las principales criptomonedas de hoy 5 de noviembre?
articles.text:
Las criptomonedas son un activo digital innovador que han experimentado un crecimiento monumental en los últimos tiempos debido a varios elementos que contribuyen a ello, entre ellos que algunos gobiernos hayan decidido darles una oportunidad como moneda de curso legal; no obstante, también han sufrido descalabros que han puesto en duda su viabilidad, como el más reciente episodio conocido como el "criptoinvierno".
Pese a este panorama, cada vez más personas han empezado a adquirir criptomonedas para poder invertir en algo "seguro" y "fiable" tanto a corto como a largo plazo, a pesar de los niveles extremos de inestabilidad que sufre constantemente.
Sin embargo, invertir o comprar en criptodivisas es más fácil de lo que parece. Hay que recordar que se trata de monedas virtuales, por lo que serán controladas en carteras o monederos que comparten esa particularidad, pues a diferencia del dinero corriente, no tienen un soporte físico.
El precio de las criptomonedas hoy
Esta es la cotización de las criptodivisas más destacadas en este momento.
El Bitcoin, cotiza a 80.535,28 dólares, lo que implicó un cambio de 0,162% en las últimas horas.
La segunda criptomoneda más popular del mercado, Ethereum, ha mostrado un movimiento de 0,014% en las últimas 24 horas, por lo que su valor se ubica en 2.422,66 dólares.
En el caso de TetherUs, su precio es de 1 dólares, por lo que en el último día tuvo un movimiento de 0,04%.
Por su parte, BNB, tiene un valor de 713,48 dólares, con un cambio de 2,14%, en cambio el Litecoin cotizó a 56.138 dólares, tras una variación de 3.300497.
Finalmente, el Dogecoin, una de las monedas virtuales que fue impulsada por Elon Musk, tiene un valor de 0,08 dólares tras presentar un cambio de 2,2% en las últimas 24 horas.
Qué pasa con las criptodivisas
Luego de que en las primeras semanas de mayo del 2022 se viviera el "criptocrash" o "criptoinvierno" que dejaron al descubierto la enorme volatilidad de estas monedas digitales, ha llegado un nuevo periodo de relativa estabilidad.
Bitcoin, ethereum y BNB han mostrado variaciones "controladas", puesto que no se han disparado los precios como en semanas previas. Por ejemplo, a inicios de agosto, las mencionadas anteriormente tuvieron un cambio menor del 2%.
Por otra parte, algo que esta llamando la atención en el mundo de las criptomonedas es que China está ablandando sus restricciones y podría comenzar a permitir su uso. Específicamente sería Hong Kong en donde este cambio se haría presente.
Sumado a ello, la plataforma de transacciones digitales PayPal anunció su propia stablecoin llamada PayPal USD (PYUSD), que cuenta por el respaldo de depósitos en dólares, bonos del Tesoro de Estados Unidos a corto plazo y activos equivalentes.
La compañía ha afirmado en su declaración que permitirá la transferencia de fondos a monederos digitales de terceros y proporcionará detalles sobre cómo integrar su servicio en exchanges centralizados y descentralizados, con el objetivo de ser utilizado en Finanzas Descentralizadas (DeFi, por sus siglas en inglés). Por lo tanto, es muy probable que se utilice ampliamente en la industria Web3.
Criptomonedas en Latinoamérica
Criptomonedas en México: el Banco de México (Banxico) ha determinado que ninguna de las instituciones que participan en el sistema financiero nacional podrá hacer uso o deberá permitir operaciones de ninguna clase a través de este medio de pago.
En territorio mexicano el empresario Ricardo Salinas Pliego, uno de los más ricos del país, ha mostrado interés en las criptomonedas y ha asegurado que varios de sus negocios aceptarán bitcoin en el futuro, incluido su banco; hasta el momento una de sus tiendas más populares ya lo hace.
Criptomonedas en Perú: el Banco Central de Reserva del Perú (BCR) ha dejado en claro que su misión no es ser el primero ni el segundo banco central que regule el uso de las criptomonedas, ello debido a la inestabilidad que las caracteriza. Sin embargo, hace días el presidente del (BCR) aseguró que el BCR trabajaba en un proyecto de moneda digital propia.
Criptomonedas en Colombia: en la nación sudamericana hay más de 500 sitios donde es permitido pagar con criptodivisas. Colombia ocupa el puesto 14 entre 26 países de adopción de criptomonedas, según el informe de Finder.
Criptomonedas en Centroamérica: en el gobierno de El Salvador, el bitcoin, que en septiembre de 2021 se convirtió en moneda de curso legal, ha perdido oficialmente este estatus en este enero del 2025 tras una reforma aprobada por la Asamblea Legislativa del país. Según informó la prensa local, la modificación de la Ley Bitcoin fue impulsada por el gobierno del presidente Nayib Bukele y respaldada por la mayoría oficialista en el órgano legislativo. Este cambio marca el fin de una política que había colocado al país centroamericano en el centro del debate global sobre las criptomonedas.
¿Cómo crear una criptomoneda?
Al momento de crear una criptomoneda es importante primero determinar qué se desea tener: una moneda o un token. La primera usa su propia blockchain, mientras que la segunda se basa en una red preexistente.
De acuerdo con el sitio de Binance, para crear una criptomoneda se necesita de un gran equipo de desarrolladores y expertos; mientras que para el token sí se requieren conocimientos técnicos pero es posible crearlo en minutos a través del uso de otras blockchains como Ethereum o BNB, que son las más populares.
Los costos de creación, el tiempo requerido y el uso de fuerza de trabajo dependerá de si se opta por hacer una moneda virtual o un token. En éste último caso también se puede usar un código establecido para crear tokens o pagar para usar un servicio de creación de monedas.
Es importante saber que antes de crear una criptomoneda se debe considerar su utilidad y estado legal.
En el caso de elegir crear una criptomoneda, entonces se debe elegir una blockchain, posteriormente se debe hacer un plan acorde al funcionamiento y la funcionalidad de la blockchain para diseñar los nodos y la interfaz.

articles.title: ¡Que 'GTA 6' llegue ya! Rockstar calienta el lanzamiento del juego con estas espectaculares imágenes
articles.text:
Faltan solo 2 semanas para el lanzamiento de GTA 6 y Rockstar Games está calentando motores al máximo. El estudio ha aprovechado para lanzar hoy una nueva colección de imágenes tanto de los escenarios como de los protagonistas del juego, y son verdaderamente espectaculares.
La llamada "Galería de lanzamiento" de GTA 6 incluye decenas de capturas de pantalla hasta aquí nunca vistas. Estas permiten ver con absoluto detalle tanto a Vice City y otras ubicaciones de Leónida, como a Jason, Lucía y demás personajes involucrados en la historia.
Al igual que con materiales previos, las nuevas imágenes de GTA 6 se ven impresionantes. Entornos como la ciudad de Vice City, la playa, el puerto y las discotecas son alucinantes y están llenos de detalles. Esto es una prueba más (como si hiciese falta) de que la experiencia en el mundo del nuevo Grand Theft Auto VI será prácticamente inacabable y que todo el tiempo permitirá descubrir elementos nuevos.
A continuación puedes ver todas las nuevas imágenes de GTA 6, palpitando las últimas dos semanas hacia su lanzamiento en PS5, PS5 Pro y Xbox Series X|S.
Las espectaculares nuevas imágenes de GTA 6
GTA 6 se lanza el próximo 19 de noviembre, aunque la precarga del juego estará disponible con más de una semana de anticipación en ambas plataformas. Vale recordar que en el caso de la PlayStation 5, cada jugador podrá iniciar la descarga anticipada el 10 de noviembre, a partir de las 00:00 de su zona horaria. Quienes lo jueguen desde una Xbox Series X o Series S, en cambio, podrán comenzar el proceso el mismo día a las 00:00 (GMT); es decir, la 01:00 de España, las 21:00 del 9 de noviembre en Argentina o las 18:00 del 9 de noviembre en México.
La apuesta de Rockstar Games por GTA 6 es inmensa y promete suspender todo lo que hemos visto hasta ahora en materia de experiencias de mundo abierto. Una de las revelaciones más curiosas que hemos tenido recientemente es que los jugadores podrán usar hasta caca de perro para atacar a un NPC.
Se espera que el 19 de noviembre millones de personas se ausenten de sus trabajos para disfrutar de GTA 6. Expertos creen que esto se puede traducir en pérdidas por productividad por más de 1.000 millones de dólares en un solo día.
Todavía no hay anuncios oficiales sobre cuándo llegará GTA 6 a PC. No obstante, una filtración sostiene que podría darse en el transcurso del primer trimestre de 2027, aunque hay que tomarla con pinzas. También se espera que el nuevo juego tenga su versión de GTA Online en algún momento del próximo año.

articles.title: I tested the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G, and it's built like a tank — just don't expect flagship performance
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G trades raw performance and UX polish for industry-leading toughness. With an IP69K rating, serious drop resistance, and a massive 6,500mAh battery, it easily out-toughs mid-range rivals like the Pixel 10a and Galaxy A57. It won't set speed records, but if you have chronic butterfingers — or know someone who does — this is the ultimate peace-of-mind purchase for the price.
Reasons to buy
- + Built like a literal tank with 2.5m drop resistance
- + Flagship IP68 / IP69K dust and water resistance
- + Huge 6,500mAh battery lasts for days
- + Charges to full in 40 minutes thanks to 100W fast charging
- + Strong 200MP main camera
Reasons to avoid
- - HyperOS is bogged down by ads and bloatware
- - No wireless charging or USB 3.0 fast speeds
- - No telephoto, an average ultra-wide, and poor selfie video
- - Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 chipset stutters in day-to-day use
- - Aggressive screen dimming outdoors
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G review: Two-minute review
You may not have heard of Redmi, but you likely know its parent company, Xiaomi, which regularly features in our coverage of the best phones.
While Xiaomi focuses on premium smartphones and tablets, Redmi offers solid mid-range smartphones that aim to compete with the similarly priced competition from Google, Samsung, and Nothing.
Indeed, the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G stands squarely against the Google Pixel 10a, Samsung Galaxy A57, and Nothing Phone 4b in the mid-range category. But while those devices stand out for camera, design, or overall polish, Redmi has chosen to focus on raw durability with the Note 15 Pro Plus 5G.
The star feature is an SGS 5-star certified Titan Durability frame with Gorilla Glass Victus 2, offering up to 2.5-meter drop resistance alongside flagship-level IP68 and IP69K dust and water resistance. That’s paired with a large 6,500 mAh battery with 100W fast charging — both market-leading at the phone's £350 price point.
Still, at that price, there’s always a catch. The Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G prioritizes tough hardware over software refinement. The 6.83-inch 120Hz display is sharp and supports Dolby Vision, but aggressive auto-dimming hampers outdoor visibility. The 200MP main camera takes great daylight shots, but the 8MP ultra-wide is mediocre, and there’s no dedicated telephoto lens.
Meanwhile, the mid-range Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 processor struggles under heavy gaming loads; Xiaomi’s HyperOS has a bundle of ads through native apps, and there’s a general lack of UX refinement, all of which lead to a more sluggish experience than you'll find on other phones.
You'll notice these trade-offs throughout daily use, but the phone's excellent battery life and solid drop protection make it a champion in its own right.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
If you can live with less polish and the usual mid-range trade-offs, you’ll get something that can withstand much more than most phones. And if you know a chronic butterfinger who can’t keep a phone in their hands — my sister, for instance — the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G is the exact phone you should buy them.
Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G review: price and availability
- Launched for £429 in January 2026
- Currently available from ~£349 in the UK and Europe
- Not officially sold in the US or Australia
The Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G was announced in December 2025 and launched in January 2026 at £429 in the UK. It was quickly followed by launches in India and across Asia, but like many Xiaomi phones, it's not available in the US or Australia.
Six months later, at the time of writing, the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G has dropped to around £350 for the model with 8G of RAM and 256GB of storage, the latter of which is double that of its three key competitors — the Pixel 10a, Galaxy A57, and Nothing Phone 4b.
The upgraded version with 12GB of RAM and 512GB of storage costs just £50 more, offering excellent value for money, especially given the ever-increasing cost of RAM and storage driven by AI. A price of £479 is relatively unheard of in this price bracket, as phones with 512GB usually cost considerably more.
Like most Redmi phones, there are a few colors to choose from. Mocha Brown features a vegan-leather rear panel paired with a gold frame and matching camera-ring accents. However, this model is slightly thicker and heavier than the Glacier Blue and Black versions, which both feature a fiberglass back with a matte texture and color-matched side rails.
- Value score: 5 / 5
Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G review: specs
| Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G specs |  | 
|---|---|
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Header Cell - Column 1 | 
|---|---|
| Dimensions: | 163.3 x 78.3 x 8.2 mm | 
| Weight: | 207g | 
| Display: | 6.83-inch AMOLED (1280 x 2772), 120Hz, 3,200 nits peak brightness | 
| Chipset: | Qualcomm Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 | 
| RAM: | 8GB / 12GB RAM | 
| Storage: | 256GB / 512GB | 
| OS: | Android 15, but Android 16 is now available | 
| Primary camera: | 200MP, f/1.7 1/1.4-inch sensor PDAF, OIS | 
| Ultra-wide camera: | 8MP, f/2.2, 120° 1/4-inch sensor, | 
| Selfie camera: | 32MP, f/2.2 1/3-inch sensor | 
| Battery: | 6,500mAh | 
| Charging: | 100W wired | 
| Colors: | Glacier Blue, Mocha Brown, Black | 
Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G review: design
- A sleek, modern phone, not a bulky industrial brick
- IP68 and IP69K water resistance ratings
- 2.5-meter drop resistance onto hard granite
- Touchscreen remains responsive in pouring rain or with wet hands
If there’s one area where the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G truly stands out, it’s design — specifically, durability.
What makes this device unique is the sheer lengths Xiaomi/Redmi went to in order to build one of the most durable smartphones on the market without incurring the classic "rugged phone" penalty. Instead of resembling a heavy industrial power tool, the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G looks and feels like a standard, stylish mid-ranger.
Underneath that homogeneous exterior sits a “Titan Durability” frame, certified by SGS, with a 5-star rating for drops from up to 2.5 meters onto granite. Add full IP68 and IP69K water and dust protection — a high-temperature, high-pressure rating that many of the best smartphones skip — and you have an absolute durability champion.
The Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G proves that drop-proof hardware doesn't have to look industrial. Offered in either a faux-leather finish or two matte fiberglass backings with color-matched frames, it demonstrates that extreme durability can coexist with different aesthetic styles.
This achievement becomes obvious when put side-by-side with its direct rugged price rivals:
- Samsung Galaxy XCover 7 (~£320): Wrapped in a heavy black rubber casing with chunky bezels, the XCover measures 10.2mm thick and weighs 240g. The Redmi is 2mm thinner, 33g lighter, has a higher drop rating (2.5m vs 1.5m), and superior water protection.
- Nokia XR21 (~£360): Matches the IP69K rating, but caps drop protection at 1.8 meters while measuring a thicker 10.4mm and weighing 231g.
- Doogee S200 (~£330): Offers solid protection, but at a massive 16mm thick and 369g — nearly double the Redmi's weight. It looks like an archetypal construction-site brick, whereas the Redmi comfortably slides into standard jeans pockets.
The Redmi's durability is further enhanced through software features like water ejection, which works the same way as a smartwatch by ejecting water from the speakers using low-frequency sound/vibration, and screen algorithms optimized for use with wet hands.
The Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G is attractive enough to appeal to casual buyers who aren’t looking for a rugged phone, but its build stands head and shoulders above its rugged competition.
- Design score: 5 / 5
Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G review: display
- Vibrant 6.83-inch 1.5K AMOLED panel with Dolby Vision and HDR10+
- Smooth 120Hz refresh rate and ultra-high 3840Hz PWM dimming
- 3,200 nits peak brightness is bright enough for outdoor use but…
- … aggressive thermal auto-dimming makes it much harder to use in direct sunlight
The display on the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G is a strong performer for a mid-range phone. You get a large 6.83-inch 1.5K AMOLED panel (2772 x 1280) that delivers crisp details, rich 12-bit colors, and deep contrast. With both Dolby Vision and HDR10+ support included, media streaming looks noticeably punchier than on baseline 1080p mid-range screens.
In daily use, scrolling feels fluid thanks to the adaptive 120Hz refresh rate. Xiaomi also equipped the panel with 3840Hz PWM dimming to reduce eye strain during late-night scrolling — a thoughtful touch rarely prioritized at this price point.
The Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G falls short in Xiaomi’s aggressive thermal management in direct sunlight. While Xiaomi claims a massive 3,200-nit peak brightness — which is higher than most phones at this price point — the company employs aggressive auto-dimming that kicks in quickly when outdoors to protect the panel from overheating. It’s fine for basic tasks, but it won't maintain its peak brightness in sustained summer heat, and it is definitely less enjoyable to watch content on while outdoors.
That aside, this screen is a solid upper-mid-range offering, and it further reinforces that you can have a great display in a rugged phone.
- Display score: 4 / 5
Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G review: cameras
- 200MP primary camera (1/1.4" sensor) with OIS delivers detailed daylight stills
- Effective 2x somewhat compensates, but you do miss the telephoto
- 8MP ultra-wide lens is a noticeable drop in sharpness and color fidelity
- Video tops out at 4K/30fps on the main camera and 1080p on the front selfie camera
The Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G camera is the epitome of mid-range compromise, with a single main camera doing all the heavy lifting to compensate for weak or missing additional cameras.
The 200MP main camera features an f/1.7 aperture and OIS. In daylight and great lighting conditions, it uses 16:1 pixel binning to capture 12.5MP photos with a wide dynamic range and punchy colors. The high-resolution choice means the 2x and 4x zoom options achieved via in-sensor cropping are fairly capable for casual portraits and macro shots, but the lack of a dedicated telephoto lens means this doesn’t stand out for its zoom capabilities.
Beyond the main sensor, the camera quickly falls apart. The 8MP ultra-wide camera lacks the detail and color accuracy of the primary lens, with soft detail and noticeable grain even in challenging lighting. Nor is the Redmi Note 15 Pro+ 5G a champion at video, with 4K recording at 30fps limited to the rear cameras, and the 32MP selfie camera locked to just 1080p video.
- Cameras score: 3.5 / 5

Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G review: performance
- Powered by Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 (4nm) processor
- Up to 12GB of RAM is great, with other phone makers cutting back or increasing costs
- Paired with older UFS 2.2 storage speeds
- Handles daily tasks and media smoothly, but stutters under heavy load
The Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G has an admirable 8GB or 12GB of RAM, and this is ultimately necessary to provide a somewhat smooth day-to-day experience. However, under heavy loads, the 4nm mid-range Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 starts to struggle, and you are quickly reminded that this is a mid-range phone.
Xiaomi is quite generous by offering 256GB of storage as the base option, but it uses slower UFS 2.2 storage, which means app installations, accessing storage in apps, and heavy gaming loads are noticeably slower than on rivals using UFS 3.1 or UFS 4.0 standards.
The 5,200mm2 vapor chamber does keep the phone relatively cool during heavy gaming sessions, which is a pleasant surprise, but as we covered before, it doesn’t prevent the screen from aggressively auto-dimming in response to high temperatures in direct sunlight.
Overall, this is about the experience you’d expect from a mid-range phone, and if you’re coming from a phone with a flagship processor, you’ll definitely notice the difference. Compared to its rugged rivals, though, the performance package is above average.
- Performance score: 3 / 5
Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G review: software
- Ships with HyperOS 2 built on Android 15
- 4 major OS updates and 6 years of security patches beats most rugged rivals...
- ... but falls short of the 6–7-year policies on the Pixel 10a and Galaxy A57
- Preloaded bloatware is annoying
- Has features like Circle to Search, Google Gemini, and IR Blaster
Xiaomi isn’t known for offering the longest support or fastest updates across its smartphone range, and the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G firmly sits at the lower end of the update spectrum for modern mid-rangers. Yes, Xiaomi is offering four major OS updates and six years of security patches — which easily beats niche rugged rivals — but Xiaomi is notorious for slow regional rollouts.
Considering the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G launches on Android 15 while non-durable competitors at this price point will soon be receiving Android 17, the software commitment doesn't feel particularly future-proof. At best, you’ll get Android 19 support, but it won’t be particularly fast to roll out.
Further, Xiaomi’s HyperOS 2 remains one of the more frustrating aspects of the user experience. Out of the box, it comes cluttered with preloaded bloatware and opt-out system ads tucked inside native utility apps. Yes, you can uninstall many of them quite easily, but it’s a frustrating first impression.
On the positive side, HyperOS 2 isn't short on practical utility. You get Google’s native Circle to Search feature and solid Gemini Integration, while Xiaomi’s Hyper Connect suite allows for handy cross-device clipboard sharing and PC integration. The pre-installed Mi Remote app also makes great use of the top-edge IR blaster.
However, the overall software experience would be far more appealing if Xiaomi adopted a lighter, cleaner approach.
- Software score: 3 / 5
Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G review: battery life
- 6,500mAh silicon-carbon battery delivers genuine two-day endurance
- 100W fast charging charges to full in 40 minutes
- 22.5W reverse wired charging
- No wireless charging support
Many people turn to rugged phones because their large batteries are worth the obvious trade-offs in features and design. There are also many customers who would like the larger battery but are not willing to accept the same trade-offs.
The Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G sits in the Goldilocks zone between these two camps, with a 6,500mAh battery that’s much larger than those of its non-rugged competition at this price, and also bigger than the batteries in several key rugged rivals. Yes, it’s not as large as the 10,000 mAh battery you’ll find in the Doogee S200, but the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G strikes the best balance of capacity, longevity, and overall design.
In real-world usage, this 6,500mAh battery delivers genuine multi-day battery life, with the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G regularly lasting two full days with between 10 and 11 hours of screen time. This is among the best battery life you’ll reliably get on a smartphone, and even if it does run low, it’s fast to recharge.
The 100W superfast charging is faster than most of the competition, rugged or otherwise, and takes around 40 minutes for a full charge. This gives it an average speed of 162.5 mAh/min, which is among the fastest of any phone I’ve tested.
There’s also the option of 22.5W reverse-wired charging, which is fast enough to charge your accessories, or even your friend’s phone in a pinch. In many ways, the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G is almost the perfect smartphone if you like to go camping for a weekend, as it’s versatile enough for many use cases.
- Battery score: 5 / 5
Should you buy the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G?
| Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G scorecard |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Design | Combines a stylish, non-rugged look with top-tier IP68/IP69K water resistance and 2.5m drop protection. | 5 / 5 | 
| Display | A vibrant 120Hz AMOLED screen, marred only by aggressive thermal auto-dimming in direct sunlight. | 4 / 5 | 
| Performance | Solid for everyday average tasks, but the Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 and older UFS 2.2 cause the phone to stutter under heavy loads | 3 / 5 | 
| Camera | A great 200MP main camera, but below-average ultra-wide, no telephoto, and poor selfie video.. | 3.5 / 5 | 
| Battery | Outstanding 6,500mAh battery delivers true multi-day battery life, while 100W charging is among the fastest of any smartphone. | 5 / 5 | 
| Software | HyperOS 2 includes Google AI features, but has a lot of preloaded bloatware and questionable software longevity. | 3 / 5 | 
| Value | Unbeatable bang-for-your-buck; 256GB base storage for ~£349 is double the entry storage of main mid-range rivals. | 5 / 5 | 
Buy it if...
You (or someone you know) has chronic butterfingers 
With IP68/IP69K ratings and 2.5-meter drop resistance onto granite, this phone offers elite peace of mind without forcing you to carry a bulky industrial brick.
You want multi-day battery life and superfast charging
The 6,500mAh battery easily delivers two full days of use (10–11 hours of screen time) and tops up from 0 to 100% in just 40 minutes via 100W HyperCharge.
You want maximum storage value for money
Starting at ~£349 for 256GB storage (or just £50 more for 12GB RAM / 512GB storage), it offers double the base capacity of most mid-range competitors.
Don't buy it if...
You want a clean software experience free of bloatware
HyperOS 2 comes loaded with third-party app bloatware and native system ads out of the box, and Xiaomi’s regional update rollouts lag behind those offered by Google and Samsung.
You spend a lot of time outdoors in bright sunlight
While the screen is rated for 3,200 nits peak brightness, Xiaomi's aggressive thermal auto-dimming reduces brightness quickly in sustained summer heat.
You need high-end gaming performance or versatile zoom optics
The Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 processor and UFS 2.2 storage struggle under demanding 3D games, and the camera setup lacks a dedicated telephoto lens.
Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G: also consider
There are four real competitors to the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G worth considering, but each has its compromises.
Google Pixel 10a (~£449): 
If camera quality and clean software take priority over rugged toughness, the Pixel 10a delivers superior image processing, Google AI features, and seven years of software support. However, it offers much slower charging and standard battery life.
Read our full Google Pixel 10a review
Samsung Galaxy A57 (~£450): 
A more rounded mainstream choice with a cleaner UI, long-term software support, and a vibrant screen. It won't match the Redmi’s drop resistance or 100W charging speed, but it provides a more polished daily experience.
Read our full Samsung Galaxy A57 review
Nokia XR21 or Samsung Galaxy XCover 7 (~£320–£360):
Choose one of these devices if you specifically want a traditional rugged phone with removable parts or rubberized bumpers. Just be aware that both options are significantly thicker, heavier, and offer inferior screens, batteries, and performance compared to the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G.
How I tested the Redmi Note 15 Pro Plus 5G
- Review test period: ~2 weeks
- Testing included: Daily driver usage, including GPS navigation, web browsing, social media feeds, photography, casual and 3D gaming, video streaming, music playback, and outdoor brightness checks.
- Tools used: Synthetic benchmarks (Geekbench 6, 3DMark), battery drain logs, native Android stats, official Xiaomi chargers, and real-world drop tests.

articles.title: SpaceX, Qualcomm team up to build a Starlink Mobile 5G network
articles.text:
SpaceX has partnered with Qualcomm in order to build out a 5G mobile network.
Under a new multi-year deal, SpaceX will bring Qualcomm’s Dragonwing Cellular Infrastructure tech to what is described as “tens of thousands” of 5G cell towers across the U.S., with the first deployments set for 2027.
With the Qualcomm partnership, SpaceX will use Dragonwing to boost network coverage, capacity, and efficiency. As expected, SpaceX will pair this technology with its satellite constellation.
This essentially means that the aeronautics company is pushing to make Starlink Mobile a major carrier in the U.S., with intentions to compete directly with T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon.
According to The Verge, the company has already bought a large number of spectrum licenses, and other recent reports note that it was actively exploring a purchase of U.S. telecom company Boost Mobile.
While the news is U.S.-focused, it’s notable since SpaceX is partnered with Rogers in Canada, with the carrier using Starlink to power its satellite-to-mobile features. It’ll be interesting to see what SpaceX’s carrier push will mean for that partnership, or what a Starlink Mobile could mean for the broader Canadian telecom industry.
This news comes as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney shared a desire to move away from Starlink.
Source: Qualcomm via The Verge
Image Credit: Qualcomm
