articles.title: Microsoft rechazó duplicar su contrato con Nscale, una empresa de centros de datos que va a salir a bolsa
articles.text:
Microsoft rechazó una opción para duplicar el contrato con el que alquila capacidad de cómputo de IA a Nscale en un centro de datos de Texas, informó el Financial Times. El acuerdo potencial valía decenas de miles de millones de dólares, y la empresa británica prepara su salida a bolsa en Nueva York.
El diario basó la información en tres personas familiarizadas con el asunto. La opción afectaba al sitio del condado de Ward, en Texas. Nscale debe ahora conseguir nuevos clientes para esa capacidad o perder miles de millones de dólares de ingresos futuros.
La empresa tecnológica británica discrepó con parte del relato. Mencionó a Financial Times que la opción era de unos 500 megavatios, y no de 700 como indicaba el reporte, y que correspondía al alquiler de capacidad adicional en su propio terreno. El rechazo no altera su cartera de contratos pendientes, de USD 103.000 millones.
Otro rechazo de Microsoft
Es el segundo revés con Microsoft en pocas semanas. El 18 de octubre, The Telegraph y Bloomberg informaron de que la empresa estadounidense había abandonado el acuerdo para ser el cliente principal del primer centro de datos de Nscale en el Reino Unido, en Loughton, en el condado de Essex.
Las autoridades habían advertido a la firma británica de que el sitio no tendría conexión eléctrica hasta la década de 2030. La empresa respondió entonces que su relación con Microsoft seguía siendo “fuerte y de largo plazo” y que buscaba otras fuentes de energía y otros terrenos en el país.
El peso de Microsoft explica la importancia del episodio. El prospecto de la salida a bolsa, presentado ante el regulador bursátil de Estados Unidos el 18 de septiembre, indica que Microsoft y Anthropic concentran cerca del 85% de los contratos de Nscale, según Bloomberg.
Según el prospecto, los contratos con Microsoft prevén pagos de hasta USD 43.800 millones hasta diciembre de 2033, y los firmados el 25 de agosto con Anthropic suman hasta USD 44.600 millones. Ambos montos dependen de que Nscale cumpla plazos de entrega y niveles de disponibilidad.
Microsoft sigue siendo cliente. El mismo documento prevé que la firma británica instale para esa empresa más de 66.000 chips de Nvidia en un campus de Portugal a partir de fines de 2027, además de los equipos ya desplegados en el primer edificio de ese sitio.
Pérdidas, retrasos y plazos que pueden costar contratos
El Financial Times informó que Nscale perdió USD 1.000 millones en el primer semestre de 2026, con ingresos de USD 141 millones. Para este tipo de empresas, los contratos nuevos son clave para seguir tomando deuda con la que financiar la construcción de centros de datos.
El prospecto, citado por la revista financiera, reconoce otro riesgo: si la empresa incumple los plazos de entrega en Virginia Occidental, Anthropic podría cancelar ese tramo sin responsabilidad. Al presentar el documento, la compañía admitió que aún no tenía compromisos vinculantes para financiar esa obra.
El diario añadió que ese proyecto sufre retrasos de construcción y oposición local, y que las firmas negocian ampliar el acuerdo con un segundo centro de datos de 460 megavatios en el mismo campus.
El rechazo de Microsoft llega cuando los inversores miran con más cautela a las empresas que construyen y alquilan capacidad de cómputo para la IA con deuda. Además, el diario recordó que los gobernadores demócratas electos, entre ellos el de Texas, pidieron una moratoria inmediata a la construcción de centros de datos.
Nscale firmó en septiembre un contrato con la empresa de robots Figure y tiene otros acuerdos sin divulgar en el sitio de Ward. Una persona cercana a la compañía dijo que negocia con varios clientes potenciales para esa capacidad.

articles.title: iPhone 18e : voici la seule amélioration qu'Apple proposerait sur son « iPhone pas cher »
articles.text:
Fin février 2025, Apple sortait son iPhone 16e, remplaçant de sa gamme SE, avec un téléphone moins cher que les autres iPhone, tout en proposant des compromis sur sa fiche technique. Rebelotte l’année d’après avec l’iPhone 17e, avec la même recette. Apple semble bien parti pour sortir son iPhone 18e en même temps que l’iPhone 18, en mars ou en avril prochain. Parmi les changements attendus, la seule vraie amélioration serait au niveau de la puce.
Une meilleure puce et c’est tout ?
C’est le leaker Fixed Focus Digital qui a publié un message sur le réseau social chinois Weibo pour nous en dire plus sur l’iPhone 18e. Il a indiqué que l’iPhone 18 et l’iPhone 18e partageraient certains procédés de fabrication, sans qu’on sache lesquels. Mais il a surtout insisté sur le fait que le seul changement majeur serait une nouvelle puce ; et c’est le seul changement qu’il dit confirmer.
Récemment, un autre leaker du nom de Digital Chat Station avait indiqué que l’iPhone 18e serait équipé d’une puce A20, gravée en 2 nm. Pour le moment, cette puce est inconnue, puisque que les iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max, iPhone Duo et iPad mini de 2026 sont tous équipés d’une A20 Pro. On peut supposer que l’A20 serait une version un peu moins puissante (et moins chère) de cette puce haut de gamme.
Fixed Focus Digital en a profité pour rappeler qu’il avait vu juste avec l’iPhone 17e. Alors que beaucoup de rumeurs évoquaient l’arrivée de la Dynamic Island, il avait toujours laissé entendre que ce ne serait pas le cas. De quoi subtilement sous-entendre que l’iPhone 18e en serait aussi dépourvu, au profit de l’encoche qu’on connaît bien.
Ce qu’on sait de l’iPhone 18e
Jusqu’à maintenant, les autres rumeurs n’ont pas évoqué de grands changements sur l’iPhone 18e. Rien ne changerait sur l’écran : il s’agirait toujours d’une dalle Oled de 6,12 pouces, toujours limitée à 60 Hz. Côté mémoire vive, ce modèle serait équipé de 9 Go de RAM. Avec la puce A20, cela devrait offrir de meilleures performances, notamment pour les usages d’IA générative en local.
Quant au volet photo, il faudrait toujours compter sur un seul capteur à l’arrière de 48 Mpx, sans ultra-grand-angle, ni téléobjectif. À l’avant, Apple ferait un petit effort : le capteur selfie passerait de 12 à 24 Mpx. Cet iPhone 18e est attendu pour le premier trimestre 2027, vraisemblablement en mars, aux côtés de l’iPhone 18 standard ainsi que de l’iPhone Air 2. Quant au prix, impossible de le connaître pour le moment, mais au vu de la crise des composants, on peut s’attendre à une augmentation : pour rappel, l’iPhone 17e avait été lancé à 719 euros.

articles.title: 7.000 mAh en menos de 8 mm: el Motorola Signature 27 demuestra que fino ya no significa poca batería
articles.text:
La delgadez estaba reñida con la autonomía, al menos hasta la llegada de las baterías de silicio-carbono. Esta combinación de componentes ha logrado auténticas pilas con pantalla y cámara de fotos, sin desmerecer ninguna de las características clave de un smartphone premium. Y creo que pocos lo orquestan igual de bien como el nuevo Motorola Signature 27. Si ya me gustó el Motorola Signature del año pasado, creo que la marca ha sabido cómo elevar lo que ya era muy bueno.
Si el segmento de los móviles de categoría ya tenía serios aspirantes al podio de 2027, Motorola entra de lleno como competencia gracias al Signature 27. Sobresale en varios aspectos importantes, como en ser el primer smartphone comercial que monta lo mejor de Qualcomm: el Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. Y hay otro detalle curioso con el que el móvil destaca a nivel de software: es compatible con GrapheneOS.
Ficha técnica del Motorola Signature 27
|  | Motorola Signature 27 | 
|---|---|
| PANTALLA | Panel Extreme AMOLED Duo de 6,78 pulgadas Refresco de hasta 120 Hz 12.000 nits de pico de brillo 100 % del espacio de color DCI-P3 Dolby Vision y HDR10+ Water Touch | 
| DIMENSIONES Y PESO | 162,01 x 77,04 x 7,99 mm 227 gramos | 
| PROCESADOR | Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 | 
| RAM | 12 / 16 GB LPDDR5X Hasta 24 GB con RAM Boost | 
| ALMACENAMIENTO | 256 / 512 GB UFS 4.1 | 
| CÁMARA FRONTAL | 50 MP, f/1.9, PDAF | 
| CÁMARA TRASERA | Principal: 50 MP, f/1.6, OIS (Sony LYTIA L910) Gran angular: 50 MP, f/2.0, 122° Teleobjetivo periscópico: 200 MP, zoom óptico 3x, OIS Vídeo hasta 8K a 30 fps | 
| BATERÍA | 7.000 mAh (silicio-carbono) Carga de 90 W Carga inalámbrica de 50 W Carga inversa inalámbrica de 5 W y por cable de 4,5 W Cargador en la caja | 
| SISTEMA OPERATIVO | Android 17 Gemini Intelligence y Qira | 
| CONECTIVIDAD | 5G eSIM + SIM física GPS, Galileo, QZSS, BeiDou, NavIC y GLONASS | 
| OTROS | Certificación IP68 e IP69 MIL-STD-810H Refrigeración ArcticMesh con cámara de vapor de 8.384 mm² Altavoces estéreo con sonido de B&O y Dolby Atmos Funda protectora en la caja | 
| PRECIO | 1.899 euros | 
Un móvil diseñado para destacar ocupando lo mínimo
Si el primer Signature me sorprendió por su delgadez y sus acabados, mientras no prescindía de batería gigantesca, en este Signature 27 Motorola ha redondeado esa relación con el diseño, tanto por fuera como por dentro. El nuevo móvil se corona por la parte alta del catálogo con una batería de 7.000 mAh en un cuerpo de solo 7,99 mm. Eso sí, con algo de trampa, ya que en el área de cámaras es más grueso. No deja de ser lo habitual.
El Motorola Signature es delgado sin que esto merme la autonomía, que debería de situarse en unas dos o tres jornadas de uso moderado. Y cuando toque enchufarlo, su carga de 90 W promete un día de uso en solo 12 minutos; también admite carga inalámbrica de 50 W. Eso sí, que sea delgado no implica que también sea ligero, porque la calidad "pesa". 227 gramos, concretamente.
¿Quieres más números colocados en el móvil para impresionar? Motorola asegura que la pantalla del teléfono alcanza 12.000 nits de brillo. Eso sí, de brillo pico: está medido sobre un 1 % de la pantalla. Motorola no ha facilitado el brillo HBM del Signature 27, que es el interesante de verdad.
De potencia debería ir sobrado, no en vano estrena la mejor versión del SoC de referencia de Qualcomm. Esto apunta a una mayor calidad en juegos compatibles; regados con los hasta 120 Hz de tasa de refresco que aporta la pantalla del teléfono, de 6,78 pulgadas.
El Motorola Signature 27 es una declaración de amor a la potencia, la versatilidad y las posibilidades. Por fuera es un teléfono bonito, con acabados que solo suelen verse en Motorola y con los colores Pantone que tan bien le sientan a las distintas versiones del teléfono. Además, no solo destaca por fuera, ya que la marca ha sellado una colaboración poco habitual: el Signature 27 es el primer móvil de Motorola compatible con GrapheneOS.
Este sistema operativo es una adaptación de Android orientada a la seguridad y a la privacidad. GrapheneOS viene limpio de las apps y servicios de Google, aunque admite su instalación posterior sin demasiado problema. Motorola lo ha desarrollado junto a la Fundación GrapheneOS y dará más detalles en los próximos meses.
Que Motorola haga compatible con él su móvil más premium es una excelente noticia, y no solo por dar alternativas: es la demostración de que el Motorola Signature 27 puede convertirse en el teléfono de quienes se preocupan en mayor medida por su privacidad. Y que pueden tener ese móvil sin prescindir de capacidades, como bien demuestra su conjunto de cámaras.
Rendimiento en hardware y software más que sobrados. ¿Y en cámara? Pues tanto de lo mismo, al menos eso dice el papel: el Motorola Signature 27 estrena un sensor Sony LYTIA L910 de 50 megapíxeles como principal. Apunta a ser luminoso y a mantener el detalle, también los colores y la naturalidad: el teléfono combina su apertura f/1.6 y su estabilización óptica de 3,5° con la tecnología LOFIC, que amplía el rango dinámico para que el vídeo no se queme en un concierto o en una calle iluminada con neones.
Otro aspecto importante es el telefoto: además de incluir un objetivo periscópico, el Motorola Signature 27 monta un sensor de 200 megapíxeles para así obtener más detalle incluso de los objetos más lejanos. Ofrece 3 aumentos ópticos y llega hasta los 100 aumentos con el Super Zoom Pro, que se apoya en la IA para conservar el color y la nitidez.
Completan el conjunto un ultra gran angular de 50 megapíxeles (agrupa cuatro píxeles en uno, por lo que las fotos salen a 12,5 MP efectivos) y una cámara frontal también de 50 megapíxeles que graba vídeo 4K. Y hay una curiosidad: según Motorola, es el primer móvil con un sensor de acción EVS dedicado, un sensor de visión por eventos que detecta los cambios de luz en cada píxel para congelar sujetos rápidos con la función Action Shot
Motorola ha refinado su visión del smartphone definitivo con una propuesta que intenta incorporar lo máximo posible en un grosor mínimo. Creo que es la definición de "móvil Air" a recomendar, ese que te entrega una experiencia premium en todos los detalles. Algo que también se paga: el Motorola Signature 27 se pone por detrás del Motorola Fold en cuestión de coste.
Precio y disponibilidad del Motorola Signature 27
Es un móvil de la máxima categoría y así se muestra a la hora de pagarlo, ya que va en linea de su competencia: 1.899 euros. Para aliviar el lanzamiento, Motorola regala el Watch Ultra y unos Motorola Flow Buds valorados en 628 euros. En cuanto a la compra, el Signature 27 es oficial en España y podrá adquirirse próximamente. No sabemos la fecha definitiva.

articles.title: Un dinosaurio que nunca llegó a nacer quedó preservado durante más de 66 millones de años: está encogido dentro del huevo igual que un pollito
articles.text:
Una de las imágenes más llamativas de la paleontología reciente es la de "Baby Yingliang", un embrión de dinosaurio que murió dentro de su huevo cuando estaba a punto de salir y que ha llegado hasta hoy prácticamente intacto. El fósil tiene entre 66 y 72 millones de años, procede de Ganzhou, en la provincia china de Jiangxi, y lo describió en 2021 un equipo de China, Reino Unido y Canadá en un estudio publicado en la revista iScience.
Lo que lo más ha llamado la atención de los investigadores es la postura de este bebé de dinosaurio. La cabeza queda por debajo del cuerpo, con los pies a cada lado y la espalda curvada contra el extremo romo del huevo, una posición que nunca se había visto en un dinosaurio no aviano y que recuerda mucho a la de un pollo poco antes de nacer. Y es que, como explicaba Fion Waisum Ma, investigadora de la Universidad de Birmingham y coautora del trabajo, en la nota de prensa de su universidad: “Los embriones de dinosaurio son de los fósiles más raros y la mayoría están incompletos, con los huesos dislocados. Estamos muy emocionados con el descubrimiento de Baby Yingliang: está muy bien conservado y nos ayuda a responder muchas preguntas sobre el crecimiento y la reproducción de los dinosaurios”.
Quince años olvidado en un almacén
La historia del hallazgo también es curiosa. El huevo se recuperó como posible fósil hacia el año 2000 y pasó años guardado sin que nadie supiera lo que había dentro, hasta que en 2015 Kecheng Niu, conservador del Museo de Historia Natural Yingliang Stone, se fijó en él.
Lida Xing, una de las autoras del estudio, lo contaba así: “Durante la construcción del museo, en la década de 2010, el personal revisó el almacén y descubrió los especímenes. Se identificaron como fósiles de huevos de dinosaurio. Se prepararon los fósiles y, finalmente, apareció el embrión que estaba oculto dentro del huevo. Así salió a la luz Baby Yingliang”.
El embrión mide unos 27 centímetros de la cabeza a la cola y está enroscado dentro de un huevo de 17 centímetros, que hoy se conserva en el museo que le da nombre en China. Por su cráneo alto y sin dientes, los investigadores lo identificaron como un oviraptorosaurio, un grupo de dinosaurios terópodos con plumas, muy cercanos a las aves actuales, que vivió en Asia y Norteamérica durante el Cretácico. Darla Zelenitsky, paleontóloga de la Universidad de Calgary especializada en huevos de dinosaurio y coautora del estudio, reconocía a National Geographic: “No podía creer lo que veían mis ojos, porque está perfectamente conservado”.
La misma postura que un pollo antes de romper el cascarón
La postura en la que se encontró el fósil recuerda a la que adoptan los pollitos antes de nacer. Hacia el día 17 de incubación, el embrión adopta una posición previa, y el día 20 se encoge del todo, en lo que se conoce como “tucking”. Al día siguiente rompe el cascarón. Ese movimiento lo controla el sistema nervioso central y es clave para que la eclosión salga bien, y la postura de "Baby Yingliang" se parece mucho a la de un pollo de unos 17 días.
Al comparar este embrión con los de otros oviraptorosaurios, con saurópodos de cuello largo y con aves, el equipo plantea que ese comportamiento, que se creía exclusivo de las aves, apareció primero en los terópodos, los dinosaurios de los que descienden. Parte del cuerpo sigue cubierta de roca, así que su idea es estudiarlo con técnicas de escaneo avanzadas para ver el esqueleto completo, cráneo incluido.
Steve Brusatte, paleontólogo de la Universidad de Edimburgo que también firma el trabajo, lo resumía así: “Este pequeño dinosaurio prenatal se parece muchísimo a un pollito acurrucado en su huevo, lo que es una prueba más de que muchos de los rasgos característicos de las aves actuales aparecieron primero en sus antepasados dinosaurios”.
Fotos | Julius Csotonyi - University of Birmingham

articles.title: Qui a donné à l’IA l’accès aux données sensibles ? Seuls 36 % des décideurs IT peuvent l’affirmer avec certitude
articles.text:
Selon une étude de Delinea, spécialiste de la sécurité des identités, presque tous les responsables IT affirment que leur entreprise a une politique formelle sur les données auxquelles l’IA peut accéder (99,7 %). Pourtant, seuls 36 % peuvent toujours retrouver qui a autorisé un accès sensible à un chatbot.
Delinea a interrogé 2 254 responsables IT et sécurité, ainsi que 2 250 salariés hors IT, dans des entreprises d’au moins 500 personnes. Huit pays sont couverts, dont la France, mais le rapport ne détaille pas de résultats propres à l’Hexagone.
Des règles écrites, mais peu de moyens de savoir qui a validé quoi
En théorie, tout est en place et les entreprises sont fin prêtes. Mais en pratique, ce n’est pas vraiment la même chose. Seules 51 % des organisations comparent les accès de l’IA à cette politique en temps réel, et moins d’une organisation sur cinq (19 %) remarque sur le moment qu’un agent a accédé à des données qu’il n’était pas censé consulter. 87 % des responsables IT affirment qu’un outil ou un agent IA est sorti de son périmètre au cours de l’année écoulée. Pour trois quarts de ces derniers, cela s’est d’ailleurs confirmé. Concernant les accès à des données sensibles, seuls 36 % des personnes interrogée sont en mesure de remonter systématiquement jusqu’à la personne ayant accordé l’autorisation. Pourtant, presque tous disent que leur entreprise exige l’accord d’une personne nommée avant qu’une IA accède à une nouvelle source confidentielle, au moins pour certains usages.
Côté salariés, 60 % disent avoir déjà ressenti une pression pour utiliser l’IA sur des données sensibles ou confidentielles, sans pour autant être sûrs que cela soit permis par leur employeur. Près de la moitié (48 %) affirment accéder toujours ou régulièrement à des données de l’entreprise via l’IA sans approbation formelle. Côté IT, 34 % reconnaissent que le dernier accès donné à une IA est passé par une équipe métier sans supervision ou par un salarié sans validation formelle.
Dans la moitié des cas, l’entreprise ne donne pas à l’agent des droits d’accès propres et limités. Elle le laisse agir avec les droits de la personne qui l’a lancé. La “limite” de ce que l’agent peut consulter est donc en théorie celle de son utilisateur. 42 % des organisations n’ont aucun moyen automatique de couper l’accès d’un agent à la fin d’une session.
L’étude distingue six environnements :
- Le stockage cloud ;
- les applications en ligne ;
- les bases de données internes ;
- les serveurs de fichiers internes ;
- les chaînes de déploiement automatique du code (CI/CD) et
- Kubernetes, l’outil qui gère les applications sur les serveurs.
47 % des organisations n’ont pas de contrôle au moment de l’action dans au moins deux de ces six environnements
Delinea rappelle l’incident ayant touché PocketOS en avril dernier. Dans un environnement de test, un agent de programmation a rencontré une erreur d’identifiants, puis trouvé une clé d’API sans rapport avec sa tâche. Il s’en est servi pour supprimer en neuf secondes la base de production et les sauvegardes de l’entreprise.
En décembre 2027, l’AI Act rendra obligatoire l’audit des actions menées par l’IA.
Source : étude Delinea

articles.title: The EIC confirms €1.8 billion for startups in 2027, with expanded defence and women-led startup support | EU-Startups
articles.text:
The European Commission has adopted the 2027 European Innovation Council (EIC) Work Programme, allocating €1.8 billion to support DeepTech startups, scale-ups and researchers across Europe.
The funding package aims to help promising technologies move from early-stage research to commercialisation, while improving access to investment for women-led and DefenceTech companies.
Ekaterina Zaharieva, Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation, says: “This is how it puts our Startup and Scaleup Strategy into action: mobilising more capital, stimulating customer deals, cutting complexity, and making bold investments on the technologies that will shape our future. And, as we shape the next EU research and innovation programme, our task is to turn Europe’s scientific excellence, talent and industrial strength into new companies and lasting competitiveness.”
The programme marks the final EIC funding package under Horizon Europe 2021–2027, the EU’s research and innovation framework.
A significant part of the programme focuses on expanding access to growth capital. This includes completing the €1 billion commitment to the Scaleup Europe Fund, launched in 2026 and managed by investment firm EQT. The fund aims to attract at least €4 billion from other investors and support European technology companies through investments averaging more than €100 million.
Alongside this initiative, the EIC will continue supporting startups through its STEP Scale Up scheme, targeting companies developing strategic technologies. The 2027 programme also completes funding allocations of €200 million for defence investments and €25 million for the Advanced Innovation Challenges pilot, both introduced in 2026.
These measures form part of the EU Startup and Scaleup Strategy and the Competitiveness Compass, two initiatives intended to strengthen Europe’s innovation ecosystem and address obstacles faced by technology companies seeking to grow.
Established under Horizon Europe in 2021, the EIC has a budget exceeding €10 billion for the 2021–2027 period. Since its launch, it has supported more than 800 companies and nearly 700 research projects, providing financial assistance at different stages of technological development.
Its investment arm, the EIC Fund, has already invested close to €2 billion in more than 375 deep tech startups, attracting approximately 3.5 times that amount in co-investment.
The programme also expands support for women-led startups through a redesigned Women TechEU initiative, doubling individual grants to €150k. A new European Prize for Women Innovators in Quantum will also be introduced, complementing the existing European Prize for Women Innovators and recognising female entrepreneurs working in quantum technologies.
Another priority is helping EIC-backed startups secure their first customers. New measures will connect companies with public and private procurers, allowing them to test emerging technologies and explore potential commercial applications.
Support for dual-use and defence technologies will remain part of the EIC’s activities, reflecting the EU’s interest in strengthening its technological capabilities across strategic sectors.
At the same time, the Commission intends to reduce administrative complexity and make funding more accessible to innovators at different stages of development.

articles.title: « La pire interface jamais conçue par Google » : le nouveau YouTube sur mobile fait déjà polémique — Frandroid
articles.text:
YouTube n’en finit pas d’évoluer ces derniers et mêmes ces dernières semaines. Récemment, la plateforme a lancé Ask YouTube, sa recherche conversationnelle par IA, sur smartphone en octobre, puis a testé une interface qui range le bouton « Je n’aime pas », et elle préparerait même un réseau social à part, baptisé Tamba. Et désormais, elle s’apprête à changer l’ergonomie principale de son application mobile.
Depuis une dizaine d’années, l’application mobile de YouTube s’organise autour d’une barre de cinq boutons en bas de l’écran. L’un d’eux, l’onglet Abonnements, rassemble les vidéos des chaînes qu’on suit. Google avait annoncé sa disparition en octobre, et c’est désormais fait : ce jeudi 5 novembre, 9to5Google a vu la nouvelle interface arriver sur Android, et de nombreux utilisateurs l’ont aussi vu débarquer sur iOS. Les vidéos des abonnements restent accessibles, mais il faut maintenant aller les chercher dans l’onglet Accueil, elles n’ont plus d’onglet dédié via le menu principal en bas de la fenêtre.
Une nouvelle interface déjà controversée
YouTube abandonne ainsi sa barre à cinq boutons pour une navigation qui met en avant les Shorts, ses vidéos verticales façon TikTok, et la création de vidéos. Le nouvel onglet Accueil regroupe les recommandations et une section consacrée aux abonnements, qu’on ouvre en swipant sur la droite.
Sur le fond, l’accès ne change donc pas beaucoup, mais comme le mentionne 9to5Google, ce sont des années de mémoire musculaire qui sont mises à mal. Surtout, le changement passe par les serveurs de Google, sans mise à jour à installer : la nouvelle interface peut apparaître du jour au lendemain.
Sur r/youtube, le forum Reddit consacré à la plateforme, des internautes qualifient la nouvelle interface de « bâclée », de « dégoûtante », voire de « pire interface jamais conçue par Google ». Des réactions quelque peu disproportionnés si vous voulez notre avis, surtout qu’un simple swipe du doigts permet d’accéder à ses abonnements.
Beaucoup reprochent à YouTube d’avoir pensé son application pour ce que la plateforme veut leur faire faire, alors que nombre d’entre eux ouvrent surtout YouTube pour retrouver les chaînes auxquelles ils sont abonnés, et non pour créer du contenu.
Tous nos articles sont aussi sur notre profil Google : suivez-nous pour ne rien manquer !
Et le second meilleur moyen de nous donner un coup de pouce, c’est d’ajouter Frandroid à vos sources préférées sur Google.

articles.title: The 2023 Chinese rule that may have stalled OPay's US listing
articles.text:
OPay’s October 9 Initial Public Offering (IPO) prospectus suggested that the company did not expect to require approval from Chinese regulators to list on the New York Stock Exchange. But a last-minute regulatory inquiry from China, shortly before its planned $304 million public offering, has raised questions about whether the fintech company underestimated its exposure to Beijing’s securities rules.
On October 30, 2026, OPay decided not to complete its much-anticipated IPO following a regulatory inquiry involving a jurisdiction it described as immaterial to its business operations. The company had priced 16 million American Depositary Shares (ADSs) at $19 each, valuing it at approximately $4 billion.
On Wednesday, Bloomberg reported that a Chinese regulator’s inquiry prompted the Nigeria-focused payments company to halt its IPO just hours after setting the price. OPay said in an earlier statement it was confident the inquiry would be resolved satisfactorily “in the near future” but did not identify the regulator or disclose the nature of the inquiry.
However, in its IPO prospectus first released on October 9 and amended on the 23, OPay said it was not required to obtain approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) or complete its filing procedures under China’s 2023 overseas listing rules.
“We are not required to obtain regulatory approval from the CSRC or go through the filing procedures under the CSRC Filing Rules before ADSs can be listed or offered in the United States because we did not generate any revenues within mainland China in 2025, being the most recent accounting year, and all of our operating assets are located outside of mainland China, our business activities are conducted outside mainland China, and our places of business are located outside mainland China, and our senior managers in charge of our business operation and management are predominantly non-PRC citizens or not domiciled in mainland China,” the company said in its prospectus.
China’s Trial Administrative Measures of Overseas Securities Offering and Listing by Domestic Companies, introduced in February 2023 and effective from March 31 that year, require domestic companies seeking to list overseas to complete filing procedures with the CSRC. The rules also cover certain offshore-incorporated companies whose underlying businesses are substantially connected to mainland China.
Opay did not respond to a request for comments.
The OPay Chinese connection
OPay’s connection to China is largely through Zhou Yahui, its Chinese founder. The fintech is incorporated in the Cayman Islands and headquartered in Singapore, while Nigeria accounts for most of its business. According to its prospectus, Nigeria generated 88.1% of its revenue in 2025 and 89.5% in the first half of 2026.
Under Article 15 of China’s Trial Administrative Measures, an offshore company can fall within the rules’ scope if at least 50% of its operating revenue, total profit, assets, or net assets comes from mainland Chinese companies and it meets specified operational or management criteria. The regulation requires the determination to be made on a “substance over form basis”, meaning regulators can look beyond an offshore corporate structure to examine where a company’s business actually operates.
OPay argued in its prospectus that it did not meet these conditions because it generated no revenue in mainland China in 2025, held no operating assets there, and conducted its business activities and management predominantly outside the country. However, the company acknowledged that uncertainty remained over how the rules would be interpreted and implemented.
“We cannot assure you that we are not, or will not be, subject to such filing requirements for this contemplated offering and listing in the United States and our securities offering in the future, in which case we may not be able to get clearance from the CSRC in a timely manner, or at all,” the company said.
The Chinese regulatory connection also extended to OPay’s underwriting arrangements. In its prospectus, the company named China International Capital Corporation (CICC) Hong Kong Securities Limited as one of four representatives of its underwriting syndicate, alongside Citigroup, Deutsche Bank and Standard Bank.
Article 21 of China’s overseas listing rules requires an overseas securities company acting as a sponsor or lead underwriter for a qualifying overseas offering by a domestic company to file with the CSRC within 10 working days of signing its first engagement agreement. The firm must also submit an annual report detailing its previous year’s business activities relating to such listings.
However, CICC was absent from OPay’s October 30 IPO pricing announcement, which named Citigroup, Deutsche Bank and Standard Bank as joint book-running managers, alongside B. Riley Securities and Needham & Company as co-managers. Bloomberg subsequently reported that CICC had been taken off the deal.
In a factsheet shared with TechCabal on Monday, OPay still listed CICC as part of its underwriters.
“JPMorgan Chase was part of the advisory team in the early planning stages earlier in the year. However, the actual lead underwriters managing the active NYSE registration and pricing were Citigroup, Deutsche Bank, Standard Bank, and CICC,” the factsheet read.
The regulation also places responsibilities on securities companies and law firms involved in overseas listing transactions. Article 20 requires them to thoroughly examine and verify filing documents, including ensuring that they establish whether an issuer meets the conditions for an indirect overseas listing under Article 15. Where the filing rules apply, this makes the issuer’s regulatory assessment relevant not only to the company but also to the intermediaries facilitating the transaction.
It remains unclear whether CICC’s removal from the underwriting syndicate was connected to the Chinese regulatory inquiry or whether the bank’s role triggered any filing obligations under Article 21.
OPay has yet to publicly identify the regulator behind the inquiry or confirm that it concerned China’s 2023 overseas listing rules.
“Furthermore, changing regulatory requirements and any failure of us to fully comply with new regulatory requirements may significantly limit or completely hinder our ability to offer or continue to offer the ADSs,” the company said in its prospectus.
Whether the inquiry was connected to those rules remains unclear. However, it has left unanswered questions about the regulatory risks OPay could face in its next attempt to access US capital markets.

articles.title: Bank Phishing Sites Show Fake ‘Suspended’ Pages to Evade Takedowns
articles.text:
A threat actor has been relying on fake ‘suspended account’ notices to hide phishing content from users revisiting its look-alike bank websites, cybersecurity firm Kela reports.
The campaign, active since May, has been relying on more than 300 fake domains, including 248 impersonating 189 US financial institutions. The first were registered in late 2025, but most of them appeared between July and September 2026.
As of October 25, 183 of the targeted organizations still had live look-alikes, mainly targeting mid-sized regional banks. Last week, 49 new domains appeared.
“What ties them together is one mechanism: the kit remembers every visitor’s IP address, so the first visit gets a bank login page, and any return visit gets what looks like a closed hosting account. We call this cluster the ‘Suspended’ infrastructure,” Kela notes.
Most of the identified domains follow a similar naming pattern containing a keyword such as ‘secure’, ‘disable’, ‘protect’, ‘cancel’, ‘authorize’, ‘terminate’, ‘credentials’, and ‘commercial’ followed by a hyphen and the targeted bank’s name.
“A smaller, growing group uses help-desk, live-support, treasury-portal, and ‘primary device’ names built on the bank’s name. About half of the 49 domains that went live in the week to October 25 use these templates, including help-desk and live-chat look-alikes of JPMorgan, Citi, BMO, and Santander,” Kela notes.
While the cybersecurity firm has not discovered how victims are lured to the phishing pages, it did conclude that the campaign is largely targeting business banking and treasury logins rather than personal accounts.
First-time visitors are served pages that contain the targeted bank’s branding, ask for a user ID and password, and may show a reCAPTCHA.
The tab title, “Attention required”, copies Cloudflare’s challenge page name, while a script on the page blocks the browser’s developer tools.
Users who visit the page again are shown a ‘This account has been suspended’ page that copies the notice a hosting provider shows after an account has been closed.
“That design targets exactly the people who could shut a site down. A victim typically follows a link once. A scanner, a security team, or a takedown provider checks a reported site, then checks it again to confirm, and the second check shows what looks like a completed takedown. In practice, a takedown provider can mark a look-alike domain as down while it is still serving the phishing page to new visitors. Seeing the live content requires a new IP address for every check,” Kela notes.
While the fake suspended page was seen across multiple phishing domains, some of them served other fake notices, while others redirected to Google instead, preventing public scanning services from capturing the full campaign.
The domains sit behind Cloudflare, but some briefly resolved to their real servers, which allowed Kela to trace their actual hosting and to discover that the campaign also targets victims in the UK, Australia, and New Zealand.
“Four things make this infrastructure hard to stop: a naming formula simple enough to repeat for any bank; Cloudflare, which hides where the sites are hosted; a kit that shows anyone checking twice a fake ‘suspended’ screen, so a live domain can pass for an inactive one; and shared servers that outlast any single domain,” Kela notes.

articles.title: Canada’s drone ambitions put domestic manufacturers to the test | BetaKit
articles.text:
To anyone pitching themselves as a Canadian drone manufacturer, Josh Ogden has a question: If you’ve assembled IKEA furniture, are you a manufacturer?
“If we’re going to build, let’s be honest about what that means. Building means building our own product.”
Josh Ogden, AVSS
It may sound like a joke, but the co-founder and CEO of AVSS is making a serious point as Ottawa looks to expand its drone fleet and build a domestic supply chain to support it. If Canada wants control over the technology it needs to defend itself, Ogden says, it needs people who know how it was built and can change and adapt it quickly when required. Just being the people who put a drone together from someone else’s design doesn’t give the country that sovereign control.
“If we’re going to build, let’s be honest about what that means. Building means building our own products,” Ogden said in an interview with BetaKit.
His comments come as federal spending opens new opportunities for the sector. In September, Ottawa announced its Defence Drone Initiative Marketplace, a digital procurement platform for the Canadian Armed Forces and Coast Guard to acquire drones and counter-drone systems. AVSS, which operates in Ottawa and New Brunswick, was among six Canadian companies awarded initial contracts collectively worth up to $50 million.
Now, with nearly 400 suppliers qualified for the marketplace and further requests for proposals expected, Ogden sees an opportunity for those purchases to strengthen Canadian engineering and manufacturing. He wants buyers to consider who owns the technology, where the expertise is, and whether a supplier can make changes without turning to a foreign partner for permission or advice.
“If there’s a shortage in one chip, you should be able to go and have your designs done so that you can modify that chip without talking to anybody,” he said.
Designing for disruption
Ogden doesn’t have to look far for an example of why sovereign capability matters; his own company had to learn how to keep manufacturing through the supply-chain disruptions of COVID-19.
AVSS brought its first product to market in 2020, after three years developing and testing parachute safety technology that helps drones meet strict aviation requirements to fly over people. As the pandemic took hold, the company ran into chip shortages, unpredictable component prices, and injection-moulding suppliers laying off staff.
AVSS began stockpiling parts, but the experience also changed how its engineers learned how to design future products. Modular design, for instance, became a priority, giving the team room to swap components as supplies and costs shifted.
“What COVID taught us was how to design for potential shortages, price increases, and making modifications,” said Ogden.
He sees that experience as a vital part of what established Canadian manufacturers bring to defence work. “Any company that existed before COVID—and made it through COVID—is already tougher. They’ve already got the calluses.”
Owning the innovation
The same ability to make changes proved useful when AVSS received a request from the avalanche industry.
The company had become the first in Canada approved to drop explosives from drones for avalanche mitigation, carrying out demonstrations in Alberta’s Jasper National Park. Its system dropped five pounds, but the feedback was to develop a way to release a 50-pound bag of explosive material.
AVSS received the request in March, and, over the following months, its engineers redesigned the new release system. Ogden said the company has now produced three product lines ready for testing in the mountains.
Making those changes quickly and accurately required detailed knowledge of the hardware, including the strength of attachment points and the forces acting on them.
“You can’t do that when you don’t own the IP, and you don’t know how it was built and how you can modify it,” said Ogden.
A company licensing foreign technology may have to pay ongoing fees and accept limits on where it can sell. Owning the technology gives Canadian manufacturers more freedom to reach customers abroad and keep more of each sale to invest in products and jobs at home.
Building domestic expertise
AVSS is ready for a busy 2027, with the recent expansion activities finalized and new contracts to deliver more than 1,000 drones and associated equipment to the federal government over the year. That’s on top of a commercial business that sold more than 2,500 units of its parachute safety technology, avalanche tech, and integrated systems worldwide this year.
The company is increasing its workforce to support its growth. AVSS currently has approximately 50 staff in Ottawa and five in New Brunswick, with plans to reach 70 by December. An expansion that triples its facility space is also nearly complete, and Ogden is already planning to grow it fivefold next year.
AVSS is also developing the engineers it will need. Junior staff spend two years working on technology alongside senior colleagues and without the commercial deadlines handled by more experienced team members.
“That is what it takes to build a sustainable company,” he noted.
For him, every purchase is a chance to build up Canadian expertise so the country can develop, produce, and adapt the technology it needs without depending on anyone else.
“We’re building capability so that when someone comes to me and says, ‘Can you modify this drone?’ The answer is yes, and I could do it that day.”

articles.title: Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics | TechCrunch
articles.text:
It feels like AI is cracking a new math problem every week. Last month, OpenAI released 719 manuscripts claiming solutions to some of the field’s hardest problems. Even the computer checks can slip. After years of AI slop, it’s fair to wonder whether math is next.
Axiom Math is betting math can avoid that fate, not by slowing down, but by standing on firmer ground. The $1.6 billion startup wants to build a verified foundation that AI agents can rely on to write software and, eventually, do science.
On Wednesday, the company announced it had formally verified the Stacks Project, one of the largest bodies of mathematics ever written by humans. Mathematicians often hold Stacks in rare regard — Columbia mathematician Peter Woit has claimed there’s “nothing else really comparable,” comparing the project to “the famous Bourbaki books,” a series that rebuilt math from its foundations in the 20th century.
Woit’s Columbia colleague Johan de Jong started the Stacks Project in 2005 as an open source reference. Mathematicians have contributed to it ever since, building out results from college-level algebra all the way up to the field’s most advanced ideas across algebra, geometry, and number theory.
The company’s fleet of AI agents translates the library’s roughly 7,654 pages into about 16 million lines of computer-checked code.
Formalizing math is a way of making sure the structure underneath it is sound. Mathematicians rewrite the proof as code in a programming language called Lean, and a program called a proof assistant checks the code line by line. If the proof passes, mathematicians can trust that it’s logically sound.
Engineers use the same idea, called formal verification, to confirm their chip designs work, while researchers in France have used it to catch bugs in software that calculates family benefits.
For a library like the Stacks Project, checking each theorem is only part of the job. The theorems and definitions in Stacks are interconnected, and each one builds on the ones before it. Like a family tree, many results in Stacks trace back to the ones that came before it.
That interconnectedness made Axiom unsure the project would work at first. The team had to keep every connection intact across about 16 million lines of Lean code.
“Things that are big and things that are delicate in life just don’t go together,” Axiom CEO Carina Hong told TechCrunch. “[Stacks] is a collection of mathematical results that is the foundation of mathematics. You want [theorems] to be consistent and not, like, paradoxical. You want the definitions to not fight with each other.”
The 25-year-old CEO dropped out of a Stanford math PhD program and founded the company in March 2025. In March, Axiom raised a $200 million Series A led by Menlo Ventures.
“We were not sure if vibe coding would be able to preserve the beauty of Stacks,” Hong said.
To pull off the project, the team gave its agents a loose structure and let them run in parallel. “With Stacks, we imposed a hierarchy … [but] it was not, like, a complete hierarchy of dictating what every single agent was doing,” said Ashvin Swaminathan, a member of Axiom’s technical staff. “The agents were finding tasks for themselves and identified things that they could work on in parallel.”
Axiom also trained its own models to be good at math, an approach Hong said most other verification startups haven’t taken. At first, the team relied on one of its in-house Lean experts to teach the agents a human sense of taste. Over time, Hong said, the agents have picked up taste on their own.
The result fills one of the biggest gaps in formalized math. “When you look at what has been formalized in mathematics, there’s this huge black hole. And that black hole covers algebraic geometry,” Swaminathan said.
Until now, researchers who wanted to check new work in algebraic geometry with Lean had little to build on, Swaminathan said. “Well, now they do.”
Axiom argues that each verified result becomes a building block, so future proofs can lean on checked math instead of starting from scratch. Terence Tao, the UCLA mathematician and Fields Medal winner, has made the general case more simply: “The more formalized proofs you have, the more formalized proofs you can make.”
Mathematicians aren’t Axiom’s only intended audience. Developers have long struggled to guarantee that their code is free of bugs and security holes. That problem grows as AI agents write more of the world’s code.
Axiom is betting that the software of the future will need to rest on verified foundations, the way Stacks now does.
“We believe that mathematics is the domain where you start building these things and that it’s a transferable skill,” Swaminathan said. “Agents can read our code, understand it, and build new infrastructure on top of it. Our Lean formalization is now the substrate that agents can build upon.”
The way Axiom’s agents built Stacks, working in parallel and picking their own tasks, is how Hong expects much of AI’s future work to happen. AI agents, she argues, will need a well-built, reusable body of knowledge to keep from producing slop.
“You want [agents] to have a reusable library for them to build on and keep pushing the frontier,” Hong said. “If you slop drop in a way that’s bad engineering choices in the beginning, then it’s very hard for them to grow that boundary.”
Hong is confident enough in that approach to issue a dare. “I openly challenge all the coding companies to work on formalization at this scale.”

articles.title: Two dead, five injured in Taiwan PCB factory explosion — Panasonic Industrial Devices Materials facility fire prompts emergency response
articles.text:
Two dead, five injured in Taiwan PCB factory explosion — Panasonic Industrial Devices Materials facility fire prompts emergency response
We don't know if or for how long the facility will be out of action.
An explosion and fire at a PCB factory situated in Taiwan’s Silicon Valley have left two people dead and five injured, reports Reuters. The tragic incident took place at a Panasonic Industrial Devices Materials-owned facility on Wednesday. Panasonic is investigating the details and the cause of the accident. Initial reports suggested that five were injured in the post-explosion fires in the Hsinchu factory. However, an update today confirmed that two missing people had been found dead.
Local media have more details about this sizable accident. Focus Taiwan reveals that the fire broke out at 2 am local time on Wednesday. The five-story building where PCBs are produced had 20+ staff on the production lines at the time of the accident.
Five injured men were conscious and taken to hospital shortly after the incident occurred. However, as mentioned above, two were missing. 12 vehicles and 23 firefighters were dispatched to dig through factory debris using heavy machinery. Only then were the two missing employees found dead.
Panasonic’s explosion and fire-damaged facility “conducts research and development and manufactures printed circuit boards and semiconductor packaging materials,” notes Focus Taiwan. It had passed a safety inspection as recently as August. The news follows a Deadly Intel Fab 28 explosion in Israel, which killed two people last month.
Initial reports pointed to the use of flammable chemical solvents, including methanol and methyl ethyl ketone (MEK), in the plant as a probable accident vector. However, the precise cause of Wednesday’s incident is still being investigated.
While our thoughts are with the dead and injured, and their families, some will be wondering about the potential implications for the AI industry-induced PCB shortage that recently hit the headlines. We aren’t sure about how important this particular factory is to the wider electronics components supply chain. Moreover, no reports discuss how long the facility may be out of action in the wake of this tragic accident.

articles.title: Has Samsung learnt something from its ill-fitting Buds 4 Pro? These leaked buds sound like something from the company's historic Gear range, to fix the fit issue and then some
articles.text:
Samsung seems to have even more earbuds on the way, but these hark back to the forgotten, sports-specific Gear range
Let's get geared up for new Galaxy Buds
- FCC listings hint to another pair of Samsung earbuds coming soon
- This pair looks set to have exercise hooks
- Samsung may be aiming at sporty users, as open earbuds go mainstream
If you cast your mind back to a time Before The Pandemic, you might remember that Samsung used to release products with the 'Gear' name. These were smartwatches and earbuds designed for fitness (see the Samsung Gear Icon X for reference, also in the main image of this piece), but the line was retired when the company started making its all-in-one Galaxy gadgets which could do everything, making its fitness-specific tech all-but obsolete.
But it looks like Samsung's Gear range could be back — in spirit.
An FCC filing for an as-yet-unreleased pair of Samsung earbuds have been spotted. No, these aren't the Galaxy Buds On open-ears, because they're already out in many parts of the world. This is another pair of mystery earbuds.
The documents refer to them as the Samsung Galaxy T1, though that's possibly a code-name. Either way, it points to a new pair of earbuds coming from the company soon, and a previous leak pointed to the T1 earbuds having sports loops.
Earbuds with sports loops are, naturally, made for fitness users, as they keep the buds locked in place when you're running or jumping up and down. So these could be the first pair of exercise-designed buds from Samsung since the Gear line was ditched (it's worth noting that Gear earbuds didn't actually use sports loops, just ear ridges to lock them in place, like in the picture above).
It's unlikely that Samsung will revive the Gear name itself, but if it did put out some exercise earbuds, they'd be Gear in spirit.
Samsung's return to fitness earbuds
Since it stopped making Gear earbuds, Samsung hasn't made bespoke workout headphones. Instead, it pitches its standard buds like the Samsung Galaxy Buds 4 Pro as being great for running, and as someone who's tried to work out with them, their fit issues ensure this is not the case.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Perhaps that's why the tech giant began branching into the world of open-ear headphones. These non-noise-blocking buds are bought for a range of safety and awareness reasons, but their initial (and, to my eyes, still primary) use case was for running in busy areas while remaining aware of your surroundings.
As we covered recently, stats show that open ears are massively surging in popularity, so the release of the Galaxy Buds On makes sense. But what about noise cancelling exercise earbuds? I can't find any sales figures that suggest this kind of bud is 'booming', more than just growing at roughly the same rate as the entire market is.
Discounting open earbuds, the bespoke sports earbuds market is a rather quiet one. Options from brands such as Skullcandy, JBL, JLab and Soundcore mark some of the few in-ear buds with sports loops, and new releases aren't afforded the attention or buzz that non-sports-buds are.
Does Samsung know something we don't? Hopefully. It has its own research and sales figures that we're not privy to, and so any decision to release sports-specific headphones or earbuds likely points to the market segment being bigger than we realize.
That would also explain why Sammers also supplements its fancy premium smartwatches, such as the Galaxy Watch 9, with cheaper options like the Galaxy Fit 3: it knows sports users want their own tech, not just jacks of all trades. It's as true in wearables as it is in hearables.
When I tested the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro, their in-ear fit was the big issue. If Samsung released them but with a sports loop to lock them in place, they could be the best headphones on the market... for exercise users and normies alike.

articles.title: Más problemas para One UI 9, que rompe el WiFi y las redes móviles de varios Samsung Galaxy
articles.text:
Si tu Samsung Galaxy ha comenzado a tener problemas severos de conectividad, es posible que la culpa sea de One UI 9. Usuarios de dispositivos del fabricante coreano están reportando inconvenientes en varios modelos tras instalar la más reciente versión de la capa de personalización de software, que trae la actualización a Android 17.
El presunto fallo en One UI 9 está provocando fallos en el WiFi de los equipos afectados. Según recoge Android Authority, este es el inconveniente que más se repite entre el público, pero no golpea a todos de la misma forma. Algunos usuarios hablan de que ya no pueden conectarse a su red doméstica, pero que en otras conexiones guardadas funciona todo con normalidad. Otros, en tanto, mencionan que el WiFi funciona bien en redes 2.4 GHz, pero no así en las de 5.0 GHz.
Pero la cosa se vuelve todavía más complicada, pues otros usuarios de móviles Samsung Galaxy están teniendo problemas con las redes móviles tras instalar One UI 9. En algunos casos se menciona que falla la conexión con la cobertura celular y que no hay forma de cargar apps o sitios web hasta usar una red WiFi. En otros, directamente no se reconoce la SIM.
Al momento de redacción de este artículo, Samsung no se ha pronunciado respecto de los problemas de conectividad que están azotando a los móviles Galaxy. La causa concreta de los fallos todavía es un misterio, pero que todos los dispositivos afectados hayan comenzado a sufrirlos tras actualizar a One UI 9 genera señalamientos lógicos contra el software.
Móviles Samsung Galaxy experimentan fallos de conectividad severos con One UI 9
Entre los dispositivos actualizados a One UI 9 que se han registrado fallos de WiFi, redes móviles y tarjetas SIM, están estos modelos:
- Galaxy S24,
- Galaxy S24 Plus,
- Galaxy Z Fold 7,
- Galaxy A56,
- Galaxy A52s
- Galaxy A36.
En ninguno de los casos reportados hasta el momento se ha logrado una solución permanente, lo cual es una preocupación adicional porque implica que sí o sí hay que esperar una intervención de Samsung para que se resuelva.
Si la causa de los problemas está en un bug de One UI 9, como todo apunta, no sería el primer inconveniente de gravedad que están experimentando los dispositivos recientemente actualizados. A finales de octubre se supo que el software estaba arruinando la autonomía de los Galaxy S24 y S25 en todas sus variantes. Usuarios impactados reportaron que sus teléfonos se quedaban sin carga tras apenas 3 horas y fracción con la pantalla activada.
Estaremos atentos a cualquier novedad sobre los nuevos fallos de conectividad. Si Samsung confirma que se trata de un problema en One UI 9, seguramente veremos pronto un parche para enmendarlo. Aun así, no podemos aventurar tiempos reales de demora para una solución.

articles.title: Turning Conv2D Into A Practical GPU Compute Pattern
articles.text:
A reusable optimization mindset for engineers building GPU compute kernels.
Convolution is one of the foundational operations in modern machine learning, but it is also a useful example of a broader engineering idea: many apparently specialized tensor operations can be reorganized into well-understood compute patterns that are easier to implement, optimize, and scale.
This article explains a practical way to implement 2D convolution by treating it as a structured form of matrix multiplication. The goal is not to promote a specific product or benchmark result, but to show a reusable optimization mindset for engineers building GPU compute kernels.
Key idea: A 1×1 convolution is effectively a matrix multiply, and larger K×K convolutions can be expressed as a sequence of matrix-like accumulations with careful attention to cache behavior and loop ordering.
Conv2D is everywhere in inference pipelines, image models, and feature extraction stages. Yet the implementation challenge is often less about the mathematical definition and more about the execution strategy: how data is laid out, how work is grouped, and how memory traffic is controlled.
A useful approach is to avoid treating convolution as a completely unique primitive. Instead, interpret it as a compute pattern closely related to matrix multiplication. This can reduce implementation complexity and create a clearer path for optimization.
A standard Conv2D operation can be described as applying a learned filter tensor across an input tensor to produce an output tensor.
C = A * B
Where:
A is the input tensor of size N × H × W × C_in
B is the weight tensor of size H_filter × W_filter × C_in × C_out
C is the output tensor of size N × H_out × W_out × C_out
In practice, one of the most important simplifications comes from looking at the data in a way that matches the compute engine rather than the original mathematical notation.
A 1×1 convolution is the cleanest place to see the matrix multiplication analogy. At each spatial position, the input contributes a feature vector of length C_in. The weights map that vector into an output vector of length C_out.
If the input tensor is already stored in NHWC order, each spatial feature vector is naturally arranged in a way that can be interpreted as rows of a matrix, without requiring explicit data rearrangement.
Practical takeaway: For NHWC input, a 1×1 convolution can be treated directly as a matrix multiply from C_in to C_out, producing output in NHWC order with no transposition step.
This matters because unnecessary data movement is often one of the fastest ways to lose performance. When the original layout already matches the desired access pattern, the implementation can stay simple and efficient.
Once the filter grows beyond 1×1, each output element depends on multiple spatial locations. A 3×3 convolution, for example, combines nine separate spatial contributions. Conceptually, this becomes a set of matrix-like products that are accumulated together.
That means the problem is no longer just “do matrix multiplication,” but “do repeated matrix-like accumulation while minimizing memory waste.”
For a 3×3 filter, there are nine C_in × C_out contributions per output location. A naive implementation can achieve good arithmetic utilization, but it may repeatedly flush and reload input data through the cache hierarchy. That is where execution order becomes critical.
One of the most useful lessons in convolution optimization is that equivalent mathematics can produce very different memory behavior.
A straightforward ordering may process each filter position as if it were a separate matrix multiply and accumulate the result. While this is simple, it can cause the same input region to be fetched repeatedly into L1 cache and potentially L2 as well.
Reordering loops can improve locality, reduce refetch traffic, and increase effective cache reuse. In other words, the arithmetic stays the same, but the memory system sees a much friendlier pattern.
Optimization principle: When a kernel is already compute-valid, one of the highest-value changes is often to restructure loop nesting to improve data reuse before attempting low-level instruction tuning.
The following sample illustrates the core structure of the convolution loop nest. The details are implementation-specific, but the pattern is broadly recognizable: load weights, compute input coordinates, read vectorized input values, synchronize local memory, and accumulate partial products.
1	VEC_TYPE out_vec = 0.0;  // accumulator for results, with _N_STRIDE length
2	while ((idx_x += 2) < K_STEPS * 2) {
3	  for (int fh = 0; fh < F_H; ++fh) {
4	    for (int fw = 0; fw < F_W; ++fw) { 
5	     int idx_in2 = 
6	          IDX_FROM_4D(fh, fw, F_W, idx_x * 4 + load_in2_k_offset, CI, load_in2_n_offset, CO); 
7	     ((__local float *)localBuf)[local_idx] = (load_in2_n_offset >= CO) ? 0 : in2[idx_in2];
8	 
9	      const int hi = h * STRIDE_H + fh * DILATION_H - PAD_TOP;
10	      const int wi = w * STRIDE_W + fw * DILATION_W - PAD_LEFT;
11	 
12	      idx_y = IDX_FROM_3D(b, hi, IN_H, wi, IN_W);
13	      input1_8.lo = (float4)read_imagef(in1, samp, (int2){idx_x, idx_y});
14	      input1_8.hi = (float4)read_imagef(in1, samp, (int2){idx_x + 1, idx_y});
15	      barrier(CLK_LOCAL_MEM_FENCE);
16	      batch8_F32_MM(input1_8, (__local float16 *)localBuf, (float2 *)&out_vec,
17	                    (float2 *)&out_vec);
18	      barrier(CLK_LOCAL_MEM_FENCE);
19	    }
20	  }
21	}
This kind of kernel is useful to study because it highlights where performance usually lives:
Real convolution kernels are shaped not only by filter math, but also by parameters such as padding, stride, and dilation. These affect both correctness and performance.
Zero padding is the most common approach and is the one reflected in the source implementation. A typical boundary-safe pattern checks whether the computed input coordinate falls within valid image bounds before issuing the read.
1	float8 input1_8 = 0;
2	if ((hi >= 0) && (hi < IN_H) && (wi >= 0) && (wi < IN_W)) 
3	{
4	  input1_8[i] = { ... }
5	}
This is correct and easy to reason about, but a branch inside a hot loop can be expensive. One alternative is to move boundary handling outside the innermost loop by redirecting out-of-range reads to a dummy zero-filled line or buffer. That trades branch cost for setup logic and is often worth testing.
Important: Boundary checks are not just a correctness concern. Their placement in the loop nest can have a measurable effect on throughput.
Filter size and stride also shape performance in less obvious ways.
These effects are often indirect rather than absolute. A larger filter does not automatically make a kernel faster, and a larger stride does not automatically make it slow. But both influence the balance between arithmetic work and memory traffic, which is exactly where many Conv2D kernels are won or lost.
The most transferable value in this Conv2D implementation is not a single micro-optimization. It is the method behind it.
This approach tends to produce implementations that are easier to reason about and easier to evolve. It also creates a stronger foundation for future acceleration, because many hardware platforms already invest heavily in dense linear algebra patterns.
When turning Conv2D into a matrix-like GPU kernel, several mistakes come up repeatedly:
Caution: A mathematically elegant implementation is not always a performant one. Equivalent formulations can behave very differently on real hardware.
If you are designing or reviewing a GPU convolution kernel, it helps to think in three layers:
Strong kernels usually come from aligning all three layers, not from over-optimizing only one of them.
Conv2D is often presented as a special-purpose deep learning primitive, but from an implementation perspective it can often be understood as structured matrix multiplication plus careful accumulation across spatial neighborhoods.
That framing is powerful because it simplifies design decisions. It encourages reuse of proven compute patterns, reduces unnecessary data motion, and puts optimization effort where it usually matters most: locality, loop order, and bandwidth efficiency.
For engineers working on GPU inference and tensor kernels, that is the bigger lesson. Good performance does not begin with heroic low-level tuning. It begins with choosing the right interpretation of the problem.
