articles.title: Xbox muscle son cloud gaming avec deux nouveautés, dont une manette connectée en Wi-Fi
articles.text:
Xbox continue d’améliorer son service Cloud Gaming avec deux nouvelles fonctionnalités en phase de test. La première permet d’utiliser son smartphone comme manette sur un téléviseur compatible alors que la seconde promet de réduire la latence grâce à une connexion Wi-Fi directe entre la nouvelle (et toute petite) manette Nano et les serveurs de Microsoft.
Dans une annonce publiée sur son blog officiel, Xbox présente deux nouvelles possibilités actuellement en phase de test concernant son service de jeu en streaming, avec une attention toute particulière portée à la petite manette Nano, récemment dévoilée.
Le smartphone pour remplacer la manette Xbox
La première nouveauté pourrait intéresser ceux qui utilisent Xbox Cloud Gaming sur leur téléviseur. Sur les Smart TV compatibles, le géant américain teste la possibilité de transformer un smartphone Android ou un iPhone en manette virtuelle.
Le fonctionnement est assez simple, et lorsqu’un joueur lance un jeu sans avoir de manette physique connectée, une option lui permet d’utiliser son téléphone. Les commandes apparaissent alors directement sur l’écran tactile, après association préalable avec le téléviseur.
Une solution pratique pour lancer rapidement une partie sans devoir chercher sa manette au fond du canapé, au détriment toutefois d’une précision digne de ce nom en fonction des jeux. Une option en cours de déploiement sur les téléviseurs compatibles (et dans les pays où Xbox Cloud Gaming est disponible).
La Xbox Nano se connecte directement aux serveurs en Wi-Fi
L’autre nouveauté concerne la Xbox Nano, cette toute petite manette de poche présentée récemment par Microsoft. Elle bénéficie d’une fonction baptisée Cloud Connect, qui lui permet de communiquer directement avec le serveur exécutant le jeu, en passant par le réseau Wi-Fi.
Avec une connexion Bluetooth classique, la manette communique d’abord avec le téléviseur, qui transmet ensuite les commandes au serveur distant. Selon Xbox, cette liaison directe pourrait réduire la latence, rendre les parties plus réactives… et éviter donc de continuer à rejeter systématiquement la faute sur la manette !
Il faudra toutefois patienter avant de pouvoir en profiter en France, puisque cette expérimentation est pour l’instant réservée aux joueurs américains. Elle nécessite également de configurer la manette via l’application Xbox Beta sur Android ou Xbox Accessories sur PC (avec une inscription au programme Xbox Insider dans ce dernier cas).
La fonction reste également limitée à une flopée de téléviseurs compatibles, et ne prend pas encore en charge toutes les expériences Cloud Gaming.
Ces deux nouveautés sont encore en phase de test, mais alors que le futur Project Helix devrait prochainement se dévoiler, Microsoft semble bien décidé à s’attaquer à deux obstacles bien concrets du jeu en streaming, à savoir la simplicité d’accès et la réactivité des commandes.
- La rétrocompatibilité au top
- Le Quick Resume, difficile de revenir en arrière
- Taillée pour l'avenir (HDMI 2.1, dolby vision/atmos, VRR)

articles.title: Windows-Sicherheitslücke: Ausgerechnet Microsoft Paint wird zum Einfallstor für Hacker
articles.text:
Windows-Sicherheitslücke: Ausgerechnet Microsoft Paint wird zum Einfallstor für Hacker
Im Rahmen seines Oktober-Patchdays hat Microsoft über 1.400 Schwachstellen in Windows, Office und weiteren Microsoft-Produkten geschlossen. Eine der adressierten Lücken betraf eine Schwachstelle in dem Windows-eigenen Zeichenprogramm Paint.
Microsoft: Paint-Lücke sehr komplex
Die als CVE-2026-83844 registrierte Sicherheitslücke erreicht einen hohen Schweregrad von 8.1 von 10. Dass Microsoft die Einstufung nicht auf kritisch gesetzt hat, liegt daran, dass die Ausnutzung der Lücke sehr komplex ist und „fundierte Kenntnisse des Systems“ voraussetzt.
Der Softwarekonzern selbst bezeichnet eine Ausnutzung daher als „weniger wahrscheinlich“. Hinweise darauf, dass die Sicherheitslücke aktiv ausgenutzt wird, gibt es laut Microsoft bisher nicht.
Angreifer könnten Schadcode ausführen
Nutzer:innen sollten die Paint-Schwachstelle dennoch nicht auf die leichte Schulter nehmen. Denn sie ermöglicht es Angreifer:innen theoretisch, Schadcode auszuführen, indem sie ein speziell gestaltetes Datenpaket über das Netzwerk senden. Eine Authentifizierung oder eine Interaktion der PC-Nutzer:innen sind demnach nicht erforderlich.
Wie Windows Latest berichtet, hat Microsoft eigentlich einen Patch für die Sicherheitslücke bereitgestellt. Nutzer:innen, die auf die Paint-Version 11.2609.401.0 updaten, sollten auf der sicheren Seite sein.
Probleme mit Paint-Update
Das Problem ist, dass im Windows-Store kein entsprechendes Paint-Update zur Verfügung steht. Und auch bei Aktivierung der Auto-Update-Funktion scheint Paint laut dem Bericht nicht auf die neueste Version gebracht zu werden. Auf Reddit bestätigen mehrere IT-Admins das Fehlen des von Microsoft genannten Updates.
Möglich also, dass ein Bug verhindert, dass das Paint-Update auftaucht. Oder Microsoft hat aus Versehen eine falsche Softwareversion genannt. Der Konzern hatte die Versionsnummer zuvor schon einmal von 11.2605.91.0 auf 11.2609.401.0 korrigiert.
Aber auch Letztere ist offenbar nicht erhältlich. Laut den offiziellen Release Notes zu Paint stammt das bis dato letzte Update, eine Beta-Preview für sogenannte Windows-Insider, aus dem Juni 2026 und trägt die Versionsnummer 11.2605.61.0.
Sicherheitslücke betrifft nur Store-Version
Das Oktober-2026-Update ist jedenfalls keine Hilfe. Denn die Sicherheitslücke in Paint betrifft offenbar nur die via Microsoft-Store ladbare Version des Zeichenprogramms. Wer sich unsicher fühlt und Paint derzeit nicht benötigt, kann die kostenlose App vorübergehend löschen und einfach später wieder installieren.
Um zu checken, welche Paint-Version aktuell auf dem PC läuft, können Nutzer:innen Powershell nutzen. Dort einfach Get-AppxPackage Microsoft.Paint | Select-Object Name, Version eingeben, und das Programm gibt die Versionsnummer aus.

articles.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 05, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 05, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Thursday, November 05, 2026.
From how KumaonKhand, a social enterprise building a hemp-based ecosystem in Uttarakhand, began as a college project and became a full-time venture in 202, to how PhysicsWallah and Lenskart's doubled their profit in the second quarter of FY27, here are the latest developments across sectors.
Featured Stories
How KumaonKhand is building a hemp ecosystem in Uttarakhand
KumaonKhand, a social enterprise building a hemp-based ecosystem in Uttarakhand, began as a college project and became a full-time venture in 2021 with his mother, Sangeeta and Anuj Sharma, the founder and CEO of Alsisar Impact, a social impact incubator and investment firm.
A problem-mapping exercise through an environmental and social lens pointed toward hemp as a solution.
Latest News
altM raises $10.3M in Series A funding
Specialty chemicals startup altM has raised $10.3 million in a Series A funding round, with Rainmatter by Zerodha and Mela Ventures joining as new investors. Existing backers Omnivore, Theia Ventures, Aureolis Ventures and Spectrum Impact also participated in the round, along with strategic angel investors.
The Bengaluru-based company said it will use the funds to expand its manufacturing capacity, strengthen research and development, support customer qualification programmes, and grow its engineering and commercial teams. The investment will help altM transition from pilot-scale production to commercial manufacturing.
Funding News
Venomics AI raises $2.7M pre-seed round led by Speciale Invest, South Park Commons
Bengaluru-based Venomics AI, a biotechnology startup spun out of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), has raised $2.7 million in a pre-seed funding round co-led by Speciale Invest and South Park Commons, with participation from Operators Studio. Co-founded by Kartik Sunagar and Vinay Prabhu, the company uses artificial intelligence, venom biology and laboratory screening to identify venom-derived molecules with therapeutic potential.
The funding will be used to expand its Venom Atlas molecular dataset, strengthen AI and experimental screening capabilities, hire across research and computational science, and validate promising molecules. The startup aims to build a drug discovery platform for global markets.
Other News
Zoho launches restaurant POS platform in India
Zoho has launched a point-of-sale (POS) platform for restaurants in India, with Kolkata-based sweet shop Asha Sweets becoming its first customer. The product is being offered free of charge to restaurants with annual billing of up to Rs 12 lakh, as part of Zoho’s push to bring smaller food businesses onto digital platforms.
In a post on X, Zoho co-founder Sridhar Vembu said Asha Sweets began using Zoho POS for Restaurants during the festive rush. Zoho’s team visited the outlet to observe how the platform was being used during one of its busiest periods.
Prodigi Connect partners with Indonesia's Lokanima to develop AI-powered animation for Fun Cican
Dubai-headquartered AI video production company Prodigi Connect has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Lokanima, a creative venture of Indonesia's Singhasari Special Economic Zone, to develop animated content based on Indonesian children's entertainment property Fun Cican.
The partnership will combine Prodigi Connect's AI-native production capabilities and India-based operations with Lokanima's intellectual property access, local creative direction and Indonesian production talent. Prodigi Connect has already produced an approximately one-minute animation sequence as an initial demonstration. The collaboration aims to reduce the cost and time associated with conventional animation production while expanding the company's presence in international character-based intellectual property development.
75% of Gen Z and Millennials more likely to travel across generations, finds Airbnb survey
Airbnb's 2026 intergenerational travel survey found that 75% of Gen Z and Millennial respondents are more likely to travel with family members across generations. The findings highlight a growing preference for holidays centred on shared experiences, with 55% citing creating memories and 51% strengthening family bonds as key motivations.
Airbnb reported a more than 55% year-on-year increase in domestic searches for stays by groups of five or more travelling with children or infants. The survey also found that 63% of respondents prioritise relaxing together at their accommodation over sightseeing. Bangalore, Goa, Hyderabad, The Nilgiris and Pondicherry feature among popular domestic destinations.
This article will be updated with the latest news throughout the day.

articles.title: Taxe au gigaoctet : déjà sortie du budget 2027, peut-elle encore revenir ?
articles.text:
Votée le 30 octobre par 11 voix contre 10, dans un hémicycle qui ne comptait que 35 votants, la taxe au gigaoctet ne figure déjà plus dans le budget 2027. Le 4 novembre, l’Assemblée nationale a rejeté la première partie du projet de loi de finances, celle des recettes, par 458 voix contre 0 et 2 abstentions. Les amendements adoptés dans cette partie disparaissent avec elle, et c’est le texte initial du gouvernement, sans cette taxe, que le Sénat doit examiner, selon LCP. Deux des onze députés favorables, les insoumis Éric Coquerel et Abdelkader Lahmar, avaient d’ailleurs fait savoir après le vote qu’ils voulaient respectivement voter contre et s’abstenir, sans que cela modifie le résultat officiel.
L’amendement du député socialiste Laurent Lhardit reprenait une idée du programme du Parti socialiste, qui fixait cet été le tarif à 0,10 euro. Il prévoyait de faire payer aux fournisseurs de contenus 0,055 euro pour chaque gigaoctet envoyé aux abonnés français, dans la limite de 15 % de leur chiffre d’affaires en France ou de 2 % de leur chiffre d’affaires mondial. Une heure de film en 4K sur Netflix, qui peut consommer jusqu’à 7 Go, aurait ainsi coûté près de 40 centimes à la plateforme. Son auteur en attendait 10 milliards d’euros par an, en s’appuyant sur les 200 milliards de gigaoctets que l’Arcep estime envoyés chaque année vers les abonnés. Les grandes plateformes auraient payé l’essentiel de la facture : selon l’Arcep, Akamai, Netflix, Amazon, Google et Meta représentaient fin 2025 à eux cinq 49 % du trafic à destination des internautes français. Le gouvernement, opposé à la mesure, estimait toutefois que la moitié de la somme pèserait sur des fournisseurs de contenus plus petits, notamment français.
Les opérateurs ne voulaient pas compter les gigaoctets pour le fisc
Dans ce dispositif, les fournisseurs d’accès à internet n’auraient rien payé, mais ils auraient dû mesurer les volumes envoyés par chaque émetteur et transmettre ces relevés à l’administration fiscale chaque trimestre. Un rôle dont la Fédération française des télécoms (FFT), qui représente notamment Orange, SFR et Bouygues Telecom, mais pas Free, ne veut pas. « Pour nous, c’est d’abord problématique parce que c’est une très grosse charge administrative pour les opérateurs », a expliqué son directeur général, Romain Bonenfant, à L’Usine Digitale. Le mécanisme reviendrait selon lui à constituer « une espèce de grand registre de tous les flux internet entre tous les émetteurs, tous les clients ».
La fédération estime que les outils nécessaires n’existent pas aujourd’hui, notamment pour les réseaux de diffusion de contenus (CDN), qui stockent une partie des vidéos au plus près des abonnés, parfois directement chez les opérateurs. Elle pointe aussi un enjeu de confidentialité : « Savoir qui consulte quoi, etc. Tout ça n’est pas trivial. » Laurent Lhardit assurait au contraire que des technologies existantes permettaient ce comptage. Le ministre de l’Action et des Comptes publics, David Amiel, avait lui aussi mis en doute la faisabilité d’une mesure qui « obligerait à disposer de capteurs de flux, ou, à tout le moins, à mesurer ceux-ci au niveau des terminaux individuels de réception ».
Les opérateurs défendent une autre piste, qu’Orange réclamait déjà en 2021 avec d’autres opérateurs européens et qui est aujourd’hui débattue à Bruxelles dans le cadre du Digital Networks Act : négocier directement avec les grandes plateformes le prix de l’acheminement de leurs données, avec un arbitre indépendant en cas de désaccord. « Nous, on reste dans le monde du commercial, c’est-à-dire qu’on a des coûts, on veut juste faire payer des coûts », résume Romain Bonenfant. L’argent irait alors aux entreprises qui déploient la fibre et la 5G, et non au budget de l’État. La FFT rappelle que les opérateurs paient déjà 1,7 milliard d’euros par an de fiscalité spécifique aux télécoms, sans que cette somme soit affectée aux réseaux. Free, qui ne siège pas à la fédération, s’est exprimé par la voix de son fondateur, Xavier Niel, qui a qualifié d’« ignares incompétents » les députés qui ont voté la taxe.
Une taxe qui pourrait revenir au Sénat ?
Pour réapparaître, la taxe devrait être réintroduite par les sénateurs ou par le gouvernement. Le Sénat doit examiner le budget du 20 novembre au 8 décembre, avant un vote solennel le 9 décembre, puis une commission mixte paritaire tentera d’écrire une version commune avant la mi-décembre. En cas de recours au 49.3, le gouvernement choisirait lui-même les amendements à conserver, et il avait donné un avis défavorable à celui-ci. Au 5 novembre, aucun de ces acteurs n’a annoncé vouloir le relancer, selon NosParlementaires. Sollicités par L’Usine Digitale, Google, Amazon et Netflix n’ont pas souhaité commenter le dispositif, tandis qu’une pétition déposée le 2 novembre sur le site de l’Assemblée réclame toujours le retrait de l’amendement et une étude indépendante de ses effets, avec 853 signatures ce jeudi matin, loin des 100 000 nécessaires. Le débat sur la contribution des géants du numérique au financement des réseaux, lui, reste entier.

articles.title: Google é processado por conversas sobre suicídio entre IA e garota de 13 anos
articles.text:
Os pais de uma adolescente de 13 anos estão processando o Google nos Estados Unidos após descobrirem que a filha passou meses conversando com ferramentas de inteligência artificial (IA) da empresa sobre depressão, automutilação e suicídio. A família acusa a companhia de expor crianças a riscos psicológicos sem oferecer alertas adequados aos responsáveis e às instituições de ensino.
O caso aconteceu na Carolina do Norte (EUA), onde a estudante utilizava um Chromebook fornecido pela escola. Segundo a ação judicial, apresentada em um tribunal da Califórnia (EUA), a jovem trocou milhares de mensagens com ferramentas de IA do Google, principalmente o Gemini e o Modo IA integrado à Busca.
Identificada pelo pseudônimo Emma no processo, a adolescente começou a utilizar os recursos para tirar dúvidas escolares no segundo semestre de 2025. Entretanto, o volume de interações aumentou significativamente em dezembro, período que coincidiu com a disponibilização do modelo Gemini 3 Flash.
De acordo com os pais, as conversas passaram a abordar questões pessoais, incluindo ansiedade, depressão, transtornos alimentares e diferentes métodos de suicídio.
A denúncia também afirma que a IA orientou a menina sobre como esconder sinais de automutilação dos familiares e de outras pessoas próximas.
A família sustenta que o Google incorporou ferramentas generativas aos produtos utilizados por estudantes sem apresentar informações claras sobre os riscos envolvidos. Os responsáveis também questionam a falta de mecanismos capazes de identificar situações de sofrimento psicológico e alertar adultos responsáveis.
Como os pais descobriram as conversas?
- Segundo informações da Reuters e da Bloomberg, a família só tomou conhecimento da situação depois que um sistema de monitoramento da escola identificou um documento escrito pela adolescente com referências ao próprio funeral;
- O alerta permitiu que os responsáveis descobrissem a gravidade do conteúdo produzido pela estudante;
- A denúncia afirma que a escola levou semanas para identificar os registros e comunicar os pais, que desconheciam a utilização do computador escolar para conversas sobre sofrimento psicológico;
- Outro ponto levantado pela família envolve o acesso ao histórico das interações. Segundo a ação, contas escolares não oferecem aos responsáveis a mesma possibilidade de consultar integralmente o histórico de conversas disponível em contas pessoais;
- Com isso, os pais afirmam ter encontrado dificuldades para reconstruir o que aconteceu durante os meses de utilização das ferramentas;
- O processo busca responsabilizar o Google pelos danos alegados e pede indenização financeira. A empresa informou que está analisando as acusações.
Leia mais:
- ChatGPT ganha ferramenta para criar e editar GIFs
- Startup chinesa tenta contornar restrições dos EUA para acessar chips da Nvidia
- Claude agora pode acessar contas bancárias para analisar gastos
Google muda regras para IA nas escolas
O processo chega em momento de crescente pressão sobre o uso de IA em instituições de ensino.
Nesta semana, o Google anunciou mudanças nas configurações de suas ferramentas para contas escolares. A empresa pretende desativar o Gemini por padrão para estudantes, permitindo que instituições de ensino decidam se desejam manter o acesso.
A medida também envolve recursos de IA incorporados à Busca, como resumos gerados automaticamente. Segundo a Reuters, escolas que quiserem preservar o acesso dos alunos ao mecanismo de pesquisa ainda precisarão lidar com a presença dessas funcionalidades.
O debate não se limita ao caso da adolescente. Uma pesquisa da organização Common Sense Media já havia apontado riscos relacionados ao uso de ferramentas de IA por crianças e adolescentes. Entre as preocupações estão a dificuldade dos sistemas em identificar sinais indiretos de pensamentos suicidas e a possibilidade de respostas que normalizem comportamentos associados a transtornos alimentares.
Especialistas também alertam que conversas prolongadas com chatbots podem criar falsa sensação de acolhimento. Com isso, crianças e adolescentes podem acreditar que estão recebendo apoio suficiente e demorar a procurar ajuda de familiares ou profissionais especializados.
Segurança de chatbots volta ao centro do debate
O processo contra o Google se soma a outras ações judiciais que questionam a responsabilidade de empresas de tecnologia sobre os efeitos de seus chatbots.
Em 2025, os pais do adolescente Adam Raine processaram a OpenAI, alegando que o ChatGPT contribuiu para a morte do filho, de 16 anos, ao fornecer informações relacionadas a métodos de suicídio.
A Character.AI também enfrentou processos após a morte de Sewell Setzer III, de 14 anos, que desenvolveu relação emocional com um personagem controlado por IA.
Em janeiro de 2026, Google e Character.AI concordaram em princípio em encerrar diversas ações judiciais relacionadas a esses casos, sem que isso representasse necessariamente uma admissão de responsabilidade.
As novas acusações reforçam o debate sobre os limites da IA em ambientes frequentados por menores de idade, especialmente quando as ferramentas passam a ser utilizadas como confidentes para questões emocionais e psicológicas.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Smart appliances need power and Wi-Fi. A look at who in Africa has both
articles.text:
LG leads South Korea’s laundry and refrigeration markets, and is now pushing connected appliances in the Middle East and Africa, where it already sells other products like home entertainment devices. But where power cuts are common, internet access is patchy, and budgets are tight, paying extra for a smart fridge is a hard sell. Wealthier urban households, hotels and developers are the likely first buyers. In this edition of Delve into AI, Kenn Abuya toured LG’s model home in Seoul and its factory in Busan, and asks what manufacturers must prove before the connected home becomes an everyday purchase on the continent.
The curtains opened as I walked into the model home at LG Electronics’ headquarters in Seoul, South Korea’s capital. The lights came on a beat later. Someone from the LG team said a command and the room changed mood, while a washing machine hummed away in the background, doing its thing. The fridge, dishwasher, and air conditioner were all hooked into the same system, and one interface ran the lot.
It’s a neat party trick, and a serious bet. Appliance makers want to be the software layer in your home, not just the thing that keeps your milk cold. Euromonitor puts LG’s 2025 share of home laundry appliances at 44%, ahead of Samsung’s 37%. In refrigeration, it’s 39% to Samsung’s 34%. Both are now fighting over whose platform you’ll use to run it all.
LG wants to sell its connected appliances across the Middle East and Africa, where the conditions look very different. Power can be unreliable, internet access patchy and household incomes tight. Even people who can afford a connected appliance may find half its features useless without a stable connection. Asking customers to pay extra for smart features is a tough sell where a fridge that simply stays on can’t always be taken for granted.
LG’s regional headquarters in Dubai oversees 75 markets across the Middle East and Africa. Its East African operation, based in Nairobi, covers 16 countries across East and Central Africa, according to LG Electronics East Africa.
The company sells everything from basic household appliances to connected models in the region, but does not disclose how many African customers use its ThinQ app, which controls its connected appliances, or how much it earns from them.
World Bank data for 2024 show that 62.5% of Nigeria’s population had access to electricity, compared with 90.2% in South Africa. In Nigeria, Afrobarometer found in 2024 that only 13% of respondents had reliable electricity from the national grid.
A smart home powered by LG ThinQ services. Image: TechCabal
The model home also raised a question I kept coming back to: what do manufacturers actually mean when they call an appliance AI-powered? Connected appliances can be monitored remotely, switched on or adjusted through an app, and set to send alerts. Some also use data, such as the weight of a laundry load or a household’s usage habits, to suggest settings and tweak how they run.
But connected isn’t the same as intelligent. Curtains that open when you walk in can run on a motion sensor and a pre-programmed routine. A washing machine you can start from your phone is connected, and that’s about it. Even one that weighs the load and picks a cycle may just be working from sensors and preset rules.
Manufacturers charge a premium for the AI label, yet buyers may see little reason to pay extra for features that only work online. In homes that deal with power cuts, the priority is an appliance that keeps food cold or washes clothes once the electricity comes back. Remote controls and automated settings matter less if the machine can’t do its job reliably. Internet access is the same story. A connected appliance can still do its basic work offline, but much of what’s sold as the smart-home experience goes missing.
Juhyun Liu, marketing communications lead at LG’s Home Appliance Solutions, told me the appliances run without an internet connection and work with home automation systems from other manufacturers. Lose connectivity, though, and users lose remote controls, alerts, and data-based settings. The machines can still wash clothes and chill drinks, but they stop being smart.
The limits of the African market
Mobile connectivity is far more common than fixed broadband across much of Africa, while data costs and network quality vary widely by market. For appliances that rely on Wi-Fi, that gap could limit how often people use connected features after they buy the device. Their appeal will depend partly on how well they cope with patchy connections.
Connected features require a compatible appliance and a Wi-Fi connection. Owners can control supported devices remotely, receive notifications, and monitor operation through an app. Much of that is lost in homes that cannot keep a steady connection. Power cuts hit the appliances themselves, whether or not the owner can reach them through the app.
Cost is another hurdle, since smart appliances typically cost more than basic models, and the extra features may not justify the premium. A household buying a fridge is paying, first of all, to keep food cold. Remote temperature monitoring and maintenance alerts come second, especially where budgets are tight.
Some of the smart home appliances need a reliable internet connection and power supply to work well. Image: TechCabal
South Africa offers a glimpse of the market available to manufacturers. Statistics South Africa’s 2024 General Household Survey found that 80.9% of households owned a refrigerator, while 88.3% had an electric stove. Internet access reached 82.1% of households. The figures suggest a consumer market with the basic infrastructure and appliance ownership needed to support connected products, although they do not measure smart-appliance adoption.
Nigeria presents a different proposition. About 61% of Nigerians had access to electricity in 2023, according to the World Bank, compared with 87.7% in South Africa, and supply remains unreliable even for those connected. Internet use stands at 45.5% of the population, compared with 79.6% in South Africa, according to DataReportal. Buyers of connected appliances are likely to be concentrated among wealthier urban households and businesses with dependable power and internet.
Hotels, serviced apartments and property developers could also provide a market. Connected appliances can be useful in properties where operators manage several units and want to monitor equipment, schedule maintenance or control energy use. Such customers may find a stronger business case than households buying individual devices.
The factory behind the appliances
LG’s AI push goes beyond what it sells in shops. In Busan, South Korea’s second-largest city, the company showed the visiting media team the factory floor where its appliances are made.
Photography was not allowed on the tour, but the automation was hard to miss. Machines moved parts between stations, took on the repetitive jobs, and kept watch over the line, with few people on the floor.
LG is now selling that technology and skill. In 2024, the company set up a smart factory division that sells factory planning, automation and operations software to other manufacturers, built on the systems it runs in its own plants.
For African countries courting manufacturers, that cuts both ways. Automated plants can lift output and quality, but they need fewer hands and different skills. Kenya, Nigeria, Egypt and South Africa will have to decide what they’re willing to trade for investment.
Copying Busan also takes more than buying machines. It needs steady electricity, workers who can run and repair the kit, and the data infrastructure behind it. Across much of Africa, those are still missing.
Selling a practical benefit
LG must show African consumers that connected appliances are worth the extra cost. Voice-controlled lighting and appliances that communicate with one another may appeal to wealthier households, but lower electricity bills, reduced water consumption and cheaper repairs offer more concrete benefits.
A washing machine that adjusts its cycle to the laundry load could use less water and electricity. A refrigerator that detects faults early could prevent food spoilage and expensive repairs. These are benefits consumers can measure, unlike the convenience of controlling appliances through a phone.
Some home appliance products at a store in Seoul. Image: TechCabal
ThinQ also depends on Wi-Fi for its connected features. Power interruptions, internet costs, and limited support for African languages could restrict its appeal. Pricing will be another factor, particularly where conventional appliances already stretch household budgets.
Early buyers are likely to be wealthier urban households, hotels, and property developers. Reaching beyond them will take lower prices and products that cut bills under local conditions. That isn’t an African problem alone; a fully connected home still isn’t an everyday purchase anywhere. But with shakier grids and tighter budgets, the gap between premium and mainstream could take longer to close here.

articles.title: Anthropic toma medidas drásticas contra los clones de videojuegos de IA hechos con Claude
articles.text:
El mundo de los videojuegos está viviendo una revolución debido a la IA. Muchos grandes estudios la usan, con exponentes tan extremos como una Epic Games que hasta se ha vibecodeado la tienda, pero lo que las grandes productoras ven como una herramienta, en el mundo independiente es visto como una bomba. La muestra es el último festival de demos de Steam, donde la idea era dar a conocer demos de juegos futuros para que los usuarios los tengan en el radar y añadan a la lista de deseados que tanto ayuda a estos desarrolladores.
En la última edición, la cantidad de contenido hecho con IA eclipsaba a los lanzamientos desarrollados por personas, pero lo peor no es eso: lo peor es que hay desarrolladores que no quieren subir demos por miedo a que alguien con IA copie todo su trabajo antes de que el juego legítimo salga a la venta. Anthropic va a tomar medidas, pero el problema es que es complicado que sirva para algo.
En corto. A través de The Verge, vemos que Anthropic ha actualizado el sistema de Claude Code para que las instrucciones internas que orientan al modelo antes de cada conversación no deje recrear videojuegos existentes. Ha sido un usuario de Twitter el que señaló este cambio de condiciones hacia el 27 de octubre, localizando las nuevas reglas de la herramienta bajo el identificador "tengu_heron_brook".
Esta regla permite crear juegos originales, juegos pertenecientes a un género y juegos basados tanto en diseños como en recursos propios del usuario. Lo que no deja es reconstruir un juego específico, aunque se le cambie el nombre o se presente como algo original. Este usuario afirma que es una regla que no se puede desactivar y la propia Anthropic ha confirmado el cambio.
¿Y si se equivoca? También en Twitter, Addy Osmani, que es miembro del equipo técnico de Anthropic, explicó que añadieron dos frases al prompt de Claude Code sobre Opus 5.5 para que no pueda recrear el juego concreto de otra persona. Es algo que va contra sus propias políticas de uso, pero deja ver que puede haber fallos en el programa y que rechace algo propio. En ese caso, Osmani afirma que pueden escribir al soporte.
El porqué. La razón ya la hemos dicho: propiedad intelectual. Y el problema es que, como apuntan en PC Gamer, Opus 5.5 es extremadamente bueno en hacer ingeniería inversa de código. Esto ha alimentado varias cosas, desde una ola de juegos de consolas recompilados (reconstruidos para que sean ejecutados en PC de forma nativa) hasta clones descarados que roban el contenido original de juegos. Incluso aquellos que no se han lanzado.
Problema. Antes hablaba del festival de demos de Steam, algo conocido como Steam Next. Se trata de un evento que estaba pensado para que los desarrolladores (tanto grandes como pequeños) lanzaran demos de sus juegos con la esperanza de que destacaran y llamaran la atención de los jugadores. Si alguien jugaba una demo de tu juego y le gustaba, había probabilidades de que lo añadiera a la lista de deseados, lo que podría convertirse en una futura venta cuando el juego se acabara.
Y el problema de la última edición no es la cantidad de basura hecha con IA, sino que hay desarrolladores que trabajan "a mano" que no han lanzado demos por miedo a que llegue otro con la IA y les copie el juego. No es un temor a la ligera:
- Alliance Arts canceló la demo de 'Drunken Goddess Reflux'por miedo a que aparecieran copias hechas con IA antes del lanzamiento del juego. Lo sustituyó por un periodo de beta cerrada por sorteo.
- Digital Sun Games canceló la prueba de 'ReVamp' por el mismo motivo, alegando que una demo pública es un riesgo demasiado alto.
- Studio Bitdot tiene 'Needle in a Haystack Simulator' y han aparecido una cantidad obscena de clones, hasta el punto de que en la ficha de Steam, el original ha puesto una etiqueta de "original".
Puertas al campo. Hay desarrolladores que se están planteando incluso retrasar tráileres para no mostrar esa mecánica, estilo artístico o idea que hacen que sus juegos sean especiales por el miedo a que alguien con IA lo clone sin pudor, y este es un problema mayúsculo porque las demos y la promoción intensa son claves para que los estudios pequeños logren hacerse un hueco. 'GTA VI' no necesitó ni un gameplay para que las reservas explotaran, pero 'Cairn', por poner un ejemplo, necesitaba toda la carne en el asador para ser atractivo.
La propia Valve, responsable de Steam, reconoció que esto es un problema y dos de los responsables del equipo de negocio apuntaron que los clones existían desde antes de la IA y que no querían ser los guardianes. ¿La recomendación? Que los juegos no dependan sólo de una mecánica fácil de copiar, algo mucho más fácil de decir que de hacer.
Y el problema es que esto cubre Claude Code sobre Opus 5.5, una sola herramienta que sí, puede ser la más capaz en estos momentos, pero el resto de grandes empresas de la IA tienen su propio brazo de programación y, a medida que se hagan más y más capaces, más clones descarados y 'slop' aparecerán en las tiendas digitales. Y luego está por ver si, realmente, cambiar esas líneas de código servirá para algo... o quien quiera copiar algo podrá dar la vuelta a la petición para seguir haciéndolo.

articles.title: CPPIB takes $50-million USD stake in AI holding firm Beacon Software | BetaKit
articles.text:
The Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPPIB) is taking an equity stake in Toronto AI company Beacon Software, contributing to an upsizing of the company’s previously announced Series C fundraising round.
The news: Beacon Software, a holding company that acquires software companies and integrates AI into their operations, announced an investment from CPPIB of $50 million USD ($69 million CAD) on Thursday. The investment comes from CPPIB’s Growth Equity Unit, and will be used to further accelerate Beacon’s acquisitions and hire “frontier AI engineers” to build out the company’s shared AI operating system.
From the source: Beacon’s portfolio boasts 45 companies, primarily serving sectors like logistics, education, finance, manufacturing, and utilities. It now reports more than $200 million USD in consolidated annual revenue and is valued at $1.75 billion USD ($2.4 billion CAD), according to The Globe and Mail.
The context: CPPIB’s investment is one part of a larger expansion to Beacon’s Series C raise. Announced last June, that raise netted Beacon $225 million USD and was led by Silicon Valley-based investor General Catalyst and Boston’s HarbourVest Partners, as well as Toronto’s Intrepid Growth Partners. This recent upsizing, which includes CPPIB’s $50 million investment, brings Beacon Software’s Series C to $425 million USD.
Beacon’s rollup strategy—sometimes compared to the celebrated Canadian software firm Constellation Software—not only brings AI integration into already established operations, it also provides portfolio companies with a shared tech platform and advisors from tech heavyweights like Instacart (of which CEO and co-founder Nilam Ganenthiran is an alumnus), Meta, OpenAI, and Shopify.
Final thought: Founded just two years ago, Beacon has seen remarkably quick growth, raising more than $750 million, according to The Globe and Mail, and opening offices in New York and San Francisco. The company claimed last June to be acquiring new portfolio companies on a near-weekly basis. That success likely contributed to the CPPBI’s interest in taking an equity stake at such an early point in the startup’s career, particularly on the heels of other, later-stage investments in Canadian success stories like Cohere and Wealthsimple.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Feature image courtesy Beacon Software.

articles.title: Bluesky hit peak usage for the year on election night | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The blue wave swept Bluesky on Tuesday night as the microblogging platform recorded its highest daily number of posts, replies, and likes in 2026.
“We’re seeing a wave of new people joining and old friends coming back,” Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider posted.
According to Schneider, posts and likes doubled during the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday.
COO Rose Wang told TechCrunch that usage began to peak between 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. PT, when many election results were rolling in. Daily posts and likes increased 30% and 70%, respectively, compared to the previous 30-day averages; clicks on links also spiked 20%.
According to open source data, Bluesky reached 44 million likes, 4.8 million posts, and 2 million new follows on November 4. This nearly eclipsed Bluesky’s all-time record 45 million likes in a single day, set in November 2024.
This jump was especially visible in Bluesky’s data traffic, which was 200% higher than usual, reaching up to 35.8 GB/s.
Bluesky is — sometimes snidely — referred to as “Twitter for the left,” given that its user base seems to skew that way politically. This isn’t a coincidence; Bluesky’s most concentrated period of user growth occurred after Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election, so it makes sense that those users would post actively during a night of overwhelming victories for the Democratic party.

articles.title: Motorola asalta la gama alta con un nuevo móvil de casi 2000 euros llamado Signature 27 y su impresionante sistema de cámaras
articles.text:
Motorola pone al día su catálogo de smartphones con un nuevo modelo con el que busca llevar la mejor tecnología de la marca a un mercado cada vez más competitivo en la gama alta. La compañía apuesta por este segmento con el nuevo Motorola Signature 27, al que ha bautizado como el más avanzado hasta la fecha.
Y razones no le faltan. La propuesta de Motorola con el Signature 27 parte de un diseño bastante diferenciador en su parte trasera, nuevos materiales de fabricación premium y mucha IA. Sin olvidar, eso sí, un sistema de cámaras totalmente renovado y con el sello de Gold Label de DxOMark.
Aunque, como decimos, su punto fuerte es su sistema de cámara, uno de los grandes protagonistas del Motorola Signature 27 es su pantalla. Monta una Extreme AMOLED Duo con tecnología tándem, la más brillante disponible en un smartphone. Su cerebro es un Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 refrigerado con el sistema ArcticMesh de Motorola, y remata el conjunto un sistema de audio con la firma de Bang & Olufsen.
El Motorola Signature 27 quiere plantar cara en la gama alta con sus cámaras
Destaca, sobre todo, su sistema de cámaras, compuesto por una cámara principal Sony LYTIA L910 de 50 MP con la tecnología LOFIC, un teleobjetivo periscópico de 200 MP con Super Zoom de 100x, un sensor de acción EVS dedicado en un smartphone y una cámara ultra gran angular de 50 MP, además de una cámara frontal de 50 MP. Respecto al vídeo, el Signature 27 cuenta con el Video Enhancement Engine de Motorola, que utiliza la IA para optimizar de forma inteligente y en tiempo real el color, el contraste y el rango dinámico y es totalmente compatible con Dolby Vision.
Además, todo trabaja en conjunto con la estabilización electrónica de imagen de Qualcomm y el estabilizador óptico (OIS) de 3,5° de la cámara principal, por lo que promete algunas de las fotos más nítidas del mercado, al menos sobre el papel. La calidad de imagen de las fotos también se traslada a la pantalla, que incluye la tecnología necesaria para ver esas imágenes y vídeo a máxima calidad: 12.000⁴ nits de brillo máximo, resolución 1,5K Super HD y, como decimos, Dolby Vision.
Respecto a su autonomía, el Motorola Signature 27 incorpora una batería de silicio-carbono de 7.000 mAh, un 35 % mayor que la de la generación anterior, y carga TurboPower de 90 W.
Respecto a su precio y disponibilidad, el Motorola Signature 27 estará disponible en dos colores, Coal Smoke y Capulet Olive, a un precio recomendado de 1.899 €, aunque llegará con una oferta de lanzamiento que incluye un Moto Watch Ultra y los Moto Sound Flow, valorados en 628 €.
Motorola también tiene nuevos smartwatch y auriculares con sello de Bose
Además, Motorola también ha presentado los nuevos auriculares moto buds 2 ultra que siguen con la firma de Bose e incluyen sus dos tecnologías más importantes: Bose SoundDesign y Bose QuietControl ANC para ofrecer una experiencia de audio inmersiva y una cancelación de ruido avanzada.
Incluye un sistema de seis micrófonos de alta relación señal-ruido (SNR) y dos unidades de captación de voz (VPU), que, según la compañía, consiguen una captura de voz de gran calidad y estrenan nuevas funciones inteligentes como AI Live Translate y gestos con la cabeza. Tienen hasta 8 horas de reproducción continua con una sola carga y hasta 37 horas en total con su estuche de carga. ¿Su precio? 199 €.
Junto con estos nuevos auriculares, Motorola también ha presentado el nuevo Moto Watch 2 Fit, un reloj inteligente de nueva generación que combina análisis deportivos avanzados con tecnología de Polar y promete 12 días de autonomía.
Algunas de estas funciones de análisis incluyen opciones muy interesantes como Running Index, que ofrece una puntuación basada en la forma aeróbica y la eficiencia de carrera, Daily Activity Goal y Daily Activity Score, que ofrecen objetivos y datos personalizados según el nivel de actividad de cada usuario, para ayudar a crear hábitos deportivos.
constantes, Active Intensity Zones, que divide la actividad física en niveles de intensidad ligera, moderada e intensa, y una especialmente interesante llamada Energy Sources, que muestra cómo utiliza el cuerpo las grasas, los hidratos de carbono y las proteínas durante el ejercicio.
Cuenta con protección IP68 2 y resistencia al agua 5 ATM, pantalla gOLED de 1,85" con 1500 nits y marco de aluminio. Todo por un precio de 99 euros.

articles.title: A System-Level Approach To Protecting 3D-IC Signal Integrity
articles.text:
Accurate SI analysis must account for interactions across vertical interconnects, interposers, silicon bridges, package transitions, and neighboring high-speed channels.
By Muhammad Hassan, Mahmoud Mahany, and Mohamed Saleh
The semiconductor industry is rapidly transitioning to chiplet-based architectures to meet the performance, bandwidth, and power demands of AI and high-performance computing (HPC). Technologies such as TSMC CoWoS, SoIC, Samsung I-Cube, X-Cube, Intel EMIB, and Foveros enable designers to integrate multiple compute, memory, and I/O dies into a single package, dramatically increasing system capability while reducing development risk.
As these architectures become more complex, signal integrity has emerged as a critical design challenge. High-speed die-to-die (D2D) interfaces, dense microbump arrays, silicon interposers, TSVs, and advanced package substrates introduce electromagnetic effects that can significantly impact performance, power efficiency, and product yield.
Traditional design methodologies that verify dies, packages, and interconnects independently are no longer sufficient. Success requires a system-level approach capable of validating complete communication channels spanning dies, interposers, package substrates, and memory stacks.
Signal integrity ensures reliable communication between heterogeneous chiplets and HBM stacks operating at high data rates. Unlike traditional 2D SoCs, 2.5D/3D systems—such as TSMC Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate with a Silicon Interposer (CoWoS), SoIC, and Chip-on-Wafer (CoW), together with Intel Embedded Multi-Die Interconnect Bridge (EMIB), EMIB-T, and Foveros technologies—feature multiple interconnect structures, including D2D interfaces, microbumps, TSVs, RDLs, interposers, bridges, and advanced substrates. Each transition introduces impedance discontinuities, parasitic coupling, and return-path disturbances that cross process nodes and dense interconnects. Mitigating these effects requires a system-level view of the entire communication channel rather than isolated analysis of individual blocks.
Fig. 1: TSMC’s CoWoS-S on the left and Intel’s EMIB on the right.
Advanced packaging platforms introduce sophisticated, highly coupled routing topologies. At multi-gigahertz frequencies, accurate SI analysis must account for interactions across vertical interconnects, interposers, silicon bridges, package transitions, and neighboring high-speed channels. Unlike traditional PCBs, D2D interfaces exhibit distinct mathematical loss properties.
Fig. 2: Typical lossy channel loss profile in silicon interposer.
The channel’s low-pass frequency response heavily attenuates high-frequency harmonics, blunting the signal’s rise and fall times. In the time domain, this high-frequency roll-off manifests as severe ISI and increased jitter, directly shrinking the vertical eye height (Y) at the receiver pad as shown in Figure 3.
Fig. 3: Received signal highlighting channel bandwidth limitation.
The emergence of advanced D2D communication standards is placing even greater emphasis on early signal integrity verification. Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) is an open industry specification defining physical layers, protocols, compliance, and multi-vendor interoperability for 2D, 2.5D, and 3D packages. It offers up to sub-2 ns physical layer latency, a highly scalable modular architecture, and maximum cost-effectiveness by mixing heterogeneous chiplets. The specification fundamentally bifurcates into two packaging tiers.
Enforcing the UCIe open standard shifts validation onto strict hardware-level compliance protocols; channels must maintain an extraction frequency response (S₂₁) strictly above a mandatory voltage transfer function mask.
Figure 4 compares representative UCIe bump maps for the two packaging tiers: UCIe-AP (advanced packaging) and UCIe-SP (standard packaging), illustrating their different bump densities and Tx/Rx lane organizations.
Fig. 4: UCIe bump maps: (a) UCIe-AP bump map and (b) UCIe-SP bump map.
Unlike traditional fiberglass PCBs that tolerate minor thickness variations and use coarse trace geometries (>50), silicon interposers utilize a non-laminate, planarized back-end stack-up derived from semiconductor foundry manufacturing. Microscopic copper traces (0.5 to 2 µm) are embedded within a perfectly flat matrix of deposited silicon dioxide (SiO2) or low-k dielectrics. Because the interposer bridges sub-micron chiplet nodes, any surface waviness or conformal warping causes lithographic mask misalignment and snaps the microscopic wires. Consequently, foundries rely on expensive chemical vapor deposition and chemical mechanical planarization to polish every single layer down to an absolute mirror-like plane.
Accurately modeling these structures requires automated workflows to ingest highly detailed stackup data. Foundries distribute this structural data in specialized semiconductor formats, like iRCX, MiPT, and ITF. Effortlessly converting these formats into native EDA electromagnetic (EM) solver inputs is highly challenging. The target EM software must map the 2D process profiles into precise 3D boundary-value solver definitions while maintaining computational efficiency. Attempting this translation manually introduces severe risks of human error, as omitted layer rules or misconfigured thickness parameters create critical modeling inaccuracies later in the signal integrity sign-off phase.
Silicon interposers utilize GDSII and OASIS formats because they are manufactured using standard semiconductor foundry lithography rather than mechanical PCB drilling and routing. These sub-micron features (0.5 to 2 µm trace widths) require the exact geometric language of the chip foundry optimized for advanced silicon manufacturing.
Importing raw foundry GDSII or OASIS layout data into 3D EM simulation engines triggers three severe performance bottlenecks:
Siemens’ Innovator3D IC solution suite addresses these complexities by providing a unified, system-level environment that aggregates several proven technologies into a seamless workflow spanning architecture exploration, electromagnetic extraction, channel simulation, protocol compliance verification, and final system-level signoff.
Fig. 5: Signal integrity workflows for 3D IC using Innovator3D IC Integrator cockpit.
As AI and HPC architectures rapidly adopt chiplet designs built on advanced platforms—such as TSMC CoWoS, SoIC, and Intel EMIB, EMIB-T, and Foveros—signal integrity verification must evolve from component-level validation to full system-level channel analysis. High-speed D2D interfaces like open-standard UCIe and proprietary NVLink-C2C demand high-precision EM modeling, strict protocol compliance verification, and package-aware channel optimization.
Siemens delivers a comprehensive, unified signal integrity platform. This end-to-end workflow enables early architectural exploration, accurate 3D EM extraction, automated stackup compilation, and robust protocol compliance verification—ensuring confident, first-time-right signoff for next-generation 2.5D and 3D IC designs.
To learn more about Siemens’ end-to-end 3D IC solution can help your team achieve first-pass silicon success while accelerating time-to-market, please download the new whitepaper, 3D-IC signal integrity: From silicon interposers to system signoff.
Mahmoud Salah Mahany is a senior software development engineer in Central Engineering solutions at Siemens focusing on signal and power integrity, developing and optimizing SI/PI flows for 3D ICs to support advanced nodes and complex semiconductor ecosystems. He received the B.Sc. degree in Nanotechnology and Nanoelectronics from Zewail University of Science and Technology in 2018 and the M.Sc. degree in Electronics and Communications from the American University in Cairo in 2024.
Mohamed Saleh Abouelyazid is a senior technical manager and R&D architect in Calibre, Design to Silicon Department at Siemens since 2009. Mohamed has authored or coauthored publications and patents focusing on physical verification, data modeling, and electronic design automation. He received the B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in electronics engineering from the Faculty of Engineering, Cairo University, Cairo, Egypt, in 2009 and 2013, respectively, and the Ph.D. degree from the School of Sciences and Engineering, The American University in Cairo, Cairo, in 2022.
