articles.title: Marvell to buy Lumentum in $115 billion all-stock deal — combined company to supply scale-up and scale-in optics for AI data centers
articles.text:
Marvell to buy Lumentum in $115 billion all-stock deal — combined company to supply scale-up and scale-in optics for AI data centers
The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2028.
Marvell Technology Inc. has signed a definitive merger agreement to acquire Lumentum for an enterprise value of $115 billion, combining two of the biggest players in the data center optics market into one company. According to a joint press release on November 2nd, Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each share they own, which the companies put at about $1,132 per share. This figure represents a 23.9% premium over the company's unaffected closing price on October 28, the last trading day before reports of the deal affected prices.
The agreement — which leaves Marvell's current shareholders with about 67% of the combined company and Lumentum's with about 33% — is reportedly the second-largest tech transaction deal ever after the SpaceX-xAI merger, according to Bloomberg. Both boards have approved the deal unanimously, and it is expected to close in the first half of 2028, pending regulatory and shareholder approval.
The acquisition represents another significant expansion of Marvell's optical infrastructure portfolio, following its $10 billion acquisition of Inphi in 2021 and its $3.5 billion upfront purchase of optical interconnect startup Celestial AI, completed in February 2026. All three mergers and acquisitions involved companies handling different parts of one of the most critical AI infrastructures: optical connectivity.
As AI infrastructure continues to scale, optical connectivity is becoming increasingly important for moving vast amounts of data between processors, racks, data centers, and even on the accelerator board itself. With the acquisition of Lumentum, Marvell, which already supplies optical DSPs, silicon photonics, and high-speed SerDes, is positioning itself as one of the industry's major suppliers of optical interconnect technologies, spanning scale-across and scale-out networking to emerging scale-up and scale-in connections.
Why AI infrastructure is moving towards optical connectivity
Modern AI data centers house thousands of interconnected accelerators exchanging enormous volumes of data. As data volume, speed, and travel distance scale, copper interconnects, the conventional medium for inter-rack connections, hit physical limits, becoming impractical at around one to two meters. The industry's solution has been a transition to optics, moving data as light instead of electrical signals.
First, optical transceivers and fiber optics replaced copper for inter-rack connections and beyond. Pluggable transceivers containing a laser chip, digital signal processor (DSP) chips, and several optical components convert the accelerator's electrical signals into light for transmission over fiber, then convert them back into electrical signals at the receiving end.
The industry is also looking to bring optics into the accelerator package itself with co-packaged optics and near-packaged optics. In conventional packages, signals from the logic chip have to travel inches along copper traces across the board to reach the transceiver. Co-packaged optics takes the optical engine out of the pluggable module and places it as a photonic integrated circuit (PIC) chip directly on the switch or accelerator package, shrinking the electrical path.
These shifts to optics have made optical interconnects one of the most critical AI infrastructure markets, driving several multi-billion-dollar deals and major partnerships among industry players across the different technologies and processes involved.
From silicon to lasers: What Marvell and Lumentum bring to the table
The optical interconnects market encompasses several critical technologies. On the electronics side, semiconductor chips such as high-speed serializer / deserializers (SerDes) and optical DSPs prepare and process electrical data signals. Electronics also include analog components such as drivers and transimpedance amplifiers (TIAs) that interface with the optical hardware. Photonic integrated circuits (PICs) use microscopic optical components such as waveguides, modulators, and photodetectors to manipulate light, encode information onto it, and convert received light back into electrical signals, combining all of this into a single chip.
Whether an optical engine sits inside a pluggable transceiver or directly on the board, it still needs a laser, either integrated into the assembly or supplied externally, which brings us to another specialized branch of semiconductor manufacturing: laser technology. Lastly, fiber optic cables and associated passive optical components transmit and distribute light while optical circuit switches redirect optical connections through a network.
Marvell already covers most of the electrical and electronics side, with a portfolio that includes custom AI accelerators, Ethernet switches, high-speed SerDes interfaces, DSPs, optical drivers, TIAs, and silicon photonics. Lumentum, on the other hand, supplies many optical components, including high-performance lasers, modulators, photodetectors, optical transceivers, and optical circuit switches. Combining these portfolios and processes allows Marvell to develop more complete solutions, designing and optimizing electrical and optical components as part of the same system.
Perhaps the most strategically important part of Lumentum's business is its expertise in compound semiconductors, particularly indium phosphide (InP), which is critical for laser and other optical chips. Unlike conventional silicon, which has an indirect bandgap and is inefficient at generating light, InP-based semiconductor structures can efficiently emit and detect light, making the material well suited for manufacturing high-performance lasers and other optical components used in high-speed communication systems.
Lumentum is also bringing its manufacturing experience to the merger. Unlike Marvell's predominantly fabless semiconductor business, Lumentum directly controls its front-end semiconductor fabrication processes, owning and operating specialized InP fabrication facilities, which its CEO Michael Hurlston described as the world's largest InP manufacturing footprint during the acquisition announcement. If the deal closes in 2028, Marvell will transition into a hybrid model, inheriting Lumentum's internal factories while keeping its chip side outsourced. The combined company would also gain access to gallium arsenide (GaAs) technologies.
A $115 billion bet and a long road to 2028
Over the years, Marvell — already one of the biggest custom ASIC suppliers, with clients such as Google, AWS, Meta, and Microsoft — has also strategically positioned itself as a major player in the optical interconnects market, supplying the largest optical transceiver manufacturers. In March 2026, Nvidia invested $2 billion directly in Marvell in a partnership that brings Marvell’s custom XPUs and scale-up networking into Nvidia’s NVLink Fusion ecosystem.
Marvell's biggest optics competitor, Broadcom, also supplies custom AI accelerators, networking silicon, and optical connectivity components, offering both the electronic chips and the optical components. Acquiring Lumentum would give Marvell a more comprehensive portfolio similar to Broadcom's. Nvidia’s separate $2 billion stake in Lumentum would also convert into Marvell shares, consolidating its two $2 billion bets into a single holding.
A key question is how vertical integration affects existing customers, as Marvell supplies optical module manufacturers, while Lumentum sells optical components to companies that also compete with its transceiver business. Merging operations could create concerns among customers that depend on the companies for critical components. Marvell CEO Matt Murphy addressed this issue during the company's November 2 investor conference call, stating that the company intends to maintain its existing component supply model. Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston also emphasized that supplying competitors is already an established part of the optical industry's business model.
Financially, Marvell expects the combined company’s total addressable market to reach about $550 billion by 2030 — roughly $60 billion more than the two companies’ standalone estimates combined. The companies also expect more than $1 billion in annual run-rate cost synergies, primarily from cost of goods sold. Combining Marvell’s current-quarter guidance with Lumentum’s latest results, the companies put the merged business at about $17.7 billion in annualized revenue.
According to Murphy, pairing Lumentum’s next-quarter guidance with analyst consensus for Marvell’s next quarter lifts that figure to more than $21 billion. Lumentum's recent performance shows the growing demand behind these projections. The company reported $1.26 billion in revenue for its first fiscal quarter of 2027, a 136.5% year-over-year increase. It also announced a second major near-packaged and co-packaged optics design win, which Hurlston said he expects to generate more than $5 billion in revenue.
However, the merger's huge valuation raises questions about whether future growth will justify the acquisition price. Investors reacted negatively to the announcement, with Marvell shares closing down 12.7% at $171.41 on November 2 and Lumentum falling 18.6% to $684.40. For now, the agreement is subject to a lengthy review, with an outside date of November 1, 2027, and options to extend to February 1, May 1, and finally August 1, 2028, if regulatory approvals are still pending. If the deal then fails on regulatory grounds alone, Marvell owes Lumentum $3.2 billion. However, if either board backed out or took a rival offer, Marvell would pay $5.8 billion, and Lumentum $2.9 billion.

He is a mechanical engineer and senior technical writer with over nine years of experience in documentation and reporting. He is deeply passionate about all things engineering and technology, and is an expert in gadgets, manufacturing, robotics, automotive, and aerospace.

articles.title: Dafne Keen confiesa lo más trágico de Hollywood siendo una niña: "Me ofrecían cocaína"
articles.text:
La actriz española Dafne Keen, estrella de la película Logan de Marvel y la saga X-Men, ha sorprendido con unas impactantes declaraciones sobre su paso por Hollywood. La madrileña, de 21 años, saltó a la fama mundial siendo solo una niña cuando protagonizó aquella cinta junto a Hugh Jackman. Y muy pronto tuvo que aprender lo que se cuece de verdad en la industria detrás de las cámaras.
En una entrevista concedida al podcast Inside of You, Dafne Keen ha confesado que incluso a esas edades ya le proponían consumir drogas. "Me ofrecían cocaína en las fiestas de fin de rodaje", revela, "yo era muy pequeña, tendría 11, 12 o 13 años". Por suerte, asegura, siempre rechazó esas proposiciones. "Vi lo que era y pensaba: 'No me interesa mucho'. Afortunadamente, les decía que no".
A su vez, ha confirmado que siempre ha tenido los pies en la tierra y ha sido bastante responsable con el consumo del alcohol. "Creo que nunca he estado lo suficientemente borracha como para tener resaca. Tengo mucho control con eso", cuenta la joven actriz. Incluso afirma que ha mentido en varias ocasiones diciendo que ya había bebido suficiente solo para poder mantenerse sobria. En definitiva, Dafne Keen parece querer alejarse de los excesos de Hollywood.
Quizá uno de los responsables de su visión responsable con respecto a la industria sea el mismísimo Hugh Jackman. Y es que, según cuenta, siempre la protegió mucho. "Fue increíblemente protector y maravilloso. Se aseguraba de que nadie abusara de mis horarios, de que me divirtiera en el rodaje y que no fuese consciente de las tensiones que pudiera haber detrás de escena", recuerda agradecida. "Lo sentía como una especie de figura paterna, de verdad", promete.
¿Volverá Dafne Keen como X-23 a Marvel?
Aunque Dafne Keen conquistó al mundo entero como X-23 en Logan, los problemas de 20th Century Fox con la saga X-Men y su posterior fusión con Disney truncaron la carrera de la actriz como la joven mutante. La compañía quería colocarla como una de sus grandes protagonistas, pero todo acabó cuando La Casa del Ratón adquirió el estudio.
En cualquier caso, Dafne Keen tuvo una nostálgica y emotiva aparición en Deadpool y Lobezno hace solo unos pocos años, regresando a su querido personaje. Y, a raíz de ese cameo, los fans han vuelto a pedir una y otra vez su retorno al UCM. Algo que ella misma abrazaría sin pensarlo. "Lo haría durante el resto de mi vida, al 100%", revelaba hace meses en una entrevista.
De hecho, su presencia en Avengers: Doomsday o Avengers: Secret Wars no está para nada descartada. Pero pase lo que pase, lo cierto es que a Dafne Keen no le ha faltado el trabajo en Hollywood. A lo largo de los años, la madrileña ha aparecido en series como La materia oscura, Star Wars: The Acolyte o, en solo unos días, en la tercera temporada de Percy Jackson y los dioses del Olimpo.

articles.title: A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure
articles.text:
A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure
The midterms are over, and the next big fight could be over permitting reform.
A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.
With the dust barely settled on this week’s momentous midterms, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on November 9. It’s a plan that could finally start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved, as part of something called permitting reform. People on both sides of the political aisle have been pushing for this type of change for some years.
The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still.
The federal permitting system is designed to protect the environment against industrial pollution from large projects like power plants, transmission lines, and natural-gas pipelines. Today, permitting is governed by a range of laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. And if there’s one thing you might know about the current state of permitting in the US it’s that it’s slow and incredibly complicated.
So in its 417 pages, BAAJA attempts to tighten things up. The bill has provisions that narrow the sorts of projects that need to apply for federal permits and others that enact deadlines in hopes of speeding up a process that today can take years. (There are also specific provisions about transmission planning, mining, and the rest of the kitchen sink; this thing is dense.)
One thing to know about this bill is that it’s largely technology neutral: It opens the doors for the buildout of projects involving both fossil fuels and renewables. So there’s a weird mishmash of legislators and outside groups supporting it.
The bill’s four sponsors in the Senate are two Republicans and two Democrats. The White House has backed this permitting reform bill, with its Council of Economic Advisors finding that it would reduce review times and have economic benefits like boosting GDP.
Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s analysis finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid.
Some environmental groups, however, oppose the bill, or parts of it. An assessment from the Natural Resources Defense Council says the parts about transmission could have substantial benefits for the grid, but the narrowing of environmental reviews could be damaging for public and private lands.
Many in the climate world have long been calling for permitting reform, arguing that renewables stand to benefit more than fossil fuels. The thinking is that solar and wind power are some of the cheapest sources available today, so if we unlock the ability to build more energy, they are likely to win out economically.
A few early analyses have tried to quantify just what BAAJA would mean for emissions in the US. One, from the think tank Rhodium Group, found that in the best-case scenario, the bill would cut economy-wide emissions by 4%, reduce annual energy bills by $78 per household, and add 200 gigawatts of new clean energy by 2040. In the worst case, emissions would stay about the same.
Another report, from the nonprofit research group Resources for the Future, found that the bill could cut power-sector emissions 6% by 2041 and save more than $350 billion on system costs by midcentury.
But there are some concerns that this permitting bill’s real effect would be to open the floodgates for new natural-gas plants. As data centers have put more pressure on the grid, a wave of such plants have been announced.
“You get down to a trade-off between essentially growing the clean electricity industry on the one hand and then, as a compromise, growing the fossil-fuel industry on the other,” says Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.
To quantify that trade-off, Kircher also modeled the potential emissions effects of the bill and found that if BAAJA had been in place in 2025, energy sector emissions would have been higher than the actual baseline. Health and mortality risks associated with air pollution would also have increased.
This bill is scheduled for a Senate vote on November 9, well before the next Congress takes control. It’s not clear what the dramatic victories for Democrats might mean for the legislation, which was expected to pass the Senate with largely Republican support if a few Democrats got on board. Democrats could decide to wait for next year, when they’ll have control of both chambers. But any deal would ultimately need to win Trump’s signature, limiting what a future bill might be able to change.
In a world where permitting new projects is easier, we’ll see more clean energy, but we’ll see more natural gas, too. And while prices could get lower, that could push demand for electricity higher, leading to more emissions overall.
Simplifying the permitting system and cutting red tape is a worthy goal. But when it comes to emissions, it still really matters what, exactly, you want to build.

articles.title: Muse has a voice mode now
articles.text:
Meta now lets you have voice conversations with your Muse AI agent in real time, CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced today.
Muse has a voice mode now
Muse AI agent now has voices and ‘expressive’ avatars that animate while chatting with you.
The feature has been rolled out to me, and I gave it a spin on the iOS app while writing this article. As you chat with your Muse agent, the avatar at the top of your conversation animates in time with the words that it’s saying. You can also change the tone of the voice by just asking your agent about what you want and letting it decide or by browsing through a bunch of options in the avatar settings.
In my brief tests, my Muse agent responds quickly over voice, though it occasionally pauses while it’s looking up information or checking something for me (like it would with a text chat query). It also animates what it’s saying well, though for my particular avatar, it’s been a little uncanny. I set my Muse agent’s avatar to look like Mark Zuckerberg as a constant reminder that I’m chatting with a Meta service (I refuse to be charmed by a Jolly!), and seeing the digital Zuckerberg facsimile actually talk with me is quite weird. I also can’t get my Muse agent’s voice to sound exactly like Mark Zuckerberg.
Muse’s voice mode and expressive avatars are rolling out now in the US for the app, Meta says. They’re coming “soon” for Meta’s AI glasses and will also be available for its forthcoming Muse Charm gadget, which is supposed to ship this year.

articles.title: Fitting AI Models To Edge Applications
articles.text:
Compression can shrink AI models, but efficient edge deployment starts with matching the architecture to the workload and hardware limits.
Key Takeaways:
Today’s AI industry faces two very different challenges. On one side, enormous AI data centers and AI factories are seeking more efficient ways to process high-parameter large language models (LLMs), with bandwidth and memory as the key bottlenecks. On the other side are smaller AI models running locally on edge devices, where there isn’t enough area, power, or memory for complex, higher-parameter LLMs.
“This has led to a gold rush with people raising huge amounts of capital to build mega data centers, but has also sparked innovation on the edge,” said Ed Plowman, CTO at Imagination Technologies. “People are trying to work out how they can cram an entire container of liquid into a very small cup, and that has been driven by the fact that compute resources are not the main problem at the moment. It’s bandwidth, and that’s why RAM has gotten so expensive. That triggered a whole bunch of researchers to look at what the key problems are and what we can do about it. That triggered innovations around quantization — reducing activations and weights simultaneously — to make the models even smaller but still maintaining the output capability of the model.”
AI models come in many shapes and sizes to fit a wide range of edge devices, from earbuds to phones, home appliances, industrial IoT, robotics, and automotive systems. Designers need to choose a model with the right number of parameters because an oversized model can slow the device down or cause it to overheat. On the flip side, if the model is too small, the product may not be smart enough.
The first step in right-sizing an AI model for an embedded application is to define its purpose. “You have to start from the point of view of what you want the model to do, but then there are a million and one things we can throw at it to make it smaller,” said Plowman. “Quantization and self-compression are very effective tools. Distillation is another approach, and it works better on transformers than on traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs). All these things are starting to combine to get us to a point where the gold rush for bigger and bigger GPUs is less prevalent. The enablement in embedded systems and the progression towards quite intelligent models being able to run on truly embedded platforms is becoming more realistic.”
| Technique | How It Works | Key Characteristics | 
|---|---|---|
| Distillation | Trains a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher. | Transfers learned behavior into a smaller model. | 
| Pruning | Removes low-impact weights, neurons, heads, or layers. | Structured (whole units) or unstructured (individual weights). | 
| Quantization | Uses fewer bits for weights and activations. | Retains network structure; correction limits accuracy loss. | 
| Self-compression | Gradually reduces precision, potentially to zero bits. | Managed compression that can target proprietary hardware. | 
Fig. 1: Common ways to compress AI model
The model size must be considered alongside the system. “The hard part is designing a model that is sophisticated enough to solve the problem but small enough to fit the device,” said Magnus Gedda, CTO and chief product officer at Imagimob, an Infineon Technologies company. “On top of that, the model usually shares memory and compute with the rest of the application, so the available resources are smaller than the spec sheet suggests. Optimization techniques like pruning and quantization can shrink a model, but they are applied after design and usually after training, and they cost some accuracy. You need to pick an initial architecture that is the right size from the start so that its optimized version still fits the device and meets the performance target. Getting those three things to line up — problem fit, size, accuracy after optimization — is where most of the effort goes.”
Others agree that system-level efficiency is the central challenge. “Edge AI is ushering in a shift from ‘largest model wins’ to ‘experience per watt,'” said Steve Woo, distinguished inventor and fellow at Rambus. “Techniques such as compression, pruning, and lower-precision arithmetic help shrink models to fit local resources, but deployment remains difficult because memory capacity and bandwidth are often limiting factors. Getting a model onto the device is just the beginning. Making it run efficiently within tight power and latency budgets is where the engineering challenge begins.”
Choosing the wrong AI model can lead to extra work after deployment or a substandard product. “Once you have the optimized model, deployment is not that hard,” said Infineon’s Gedda. “The model is converted to C code, compiled for the target, and flashed to the device. The challenge is using the hardware to its full potential, so that inference is energy-efficient and low-latency. Edge hardware is extremely varied — MCUs, accelerators, NPUs, DSPs — and standards are somewhat lacking. So without the right tooling you end up with a generic, inefficient deployment, or a lot of manual work per target.”
These deployment constraints make model selection an application-specific exercise. The right architecture depends on the functions the device must perform and the workloads it must support.
Functions and workloads determine the correct model
Edge device and physical AI workloads vary considerably across sectors, from medical to industrial, automotive, home, or personal. The specific modalities of the collected sensor data are the primary driver for selecting the optimal AI model type and size.
“Right-sized inference for physical AI is critical,” noted Mick Posner, senior product marketing group director for chiplets at Cadence, in a recent blog. “Intelligent physical systems do not have a one-size-fits-all compute profile. Some workloads require always-on, low-power inference. Others require higher-performance multimodal processing across cameras, radar, lidar, audio, environmental sensors, and system-state data.”
Each hardware function and end-device feature needs to be considered and defined. “The best techniques for right-sizing AI models for edge AI are being able to categorize your functionality so that you don’t need a big model,” said Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI at Siemens EDA. “A 4-billion [parameter] model on a sensor is huge, even though we’re now talking 1 trillion [in the cloud]. Being able to bake that model into less than a billion parameters and have it in each of the sensors is doable. We need to define the highest-priority, must-have function, and train it well in an SLM (small language model). It could even be an ML (machine learning) model or a neural network model. It doesn’t need to be an LLM.”
After defining the must-have functions, designers can start building the AI core, then slowly add more features, including must-have, critical, or nice-to-have.
“Those are the three categories I see people defining in terms of how they do it architectural-wise, and where they fit in what intelligence,” said Balasubramanian. “Once you have determined those categories, the must-haves should be very close to the sensor. You can’t make everything must-have. You really need to prioritize and design it in a way that [the system] is able to be in a self-contained sensor loop with the local compute, local memory requirement, and sometimes even a local backup environment. Everything is cut up. You also need to have at least an hour or two of power envelope available so that the device doesn’t slow down or shut down.”
In the automotive sector, companies are increasingly deploying AI models for certain tasks and functions, though much of that industry is still using CNNs from about three or four years ago, Plowman noted. “They haven’t fully moved to transformers yet, or embraced the latest compression techniques. But certain external bodies have produced image segmentation object recognition systems, which use transformers.”
For IP providers tasked with optimizing these models, one challenge is that they may not get to see the actual model their customers are using. “The automotive guys train their own models, and they’re very secretive about them, for safety, security, and proprietary IP reasons,” said Plowman. “We don’t get to see them. We get a lot of proxies about what they look like or proxy functions that they want to accelerate, but it’s very rare that we get an entire model to play with.”
Fig. 2: IP modules for edge AI and physical AI. Source: Synopsys
For right-sizing, each IP block needs to be weighed against the model size. “Right-sizing a model for the edge is a systems problem, not a single-point optimization,” said Licinio Sousa, senior director of product management at Synopsys. “Techniques like quantization help the model fit, but real-time latency, power, cost, and functional safety all have to be balanced together. As AI models evolve faster than silicon development cycles, systems also need enough flexibility to support not only today’s workloads, but the models that come next.”
Once the model and system architecture are aligned, designers must determine which compression techniques can meet those constraints without sacrificing critical accuracy or performance.
Challenges of various compression techniques
Designers typically use a variety of compression techniques to right-size a model, and each has pros and cons.
For example, distillation enables drastic shrinking but potentially more loss. “You interrogate the model to find and see which bits of it light up,” said Imagination’s Plowman. “You do a similar exercise where you trim things off, but there is always loss from the teacher-student model. The student is trying to refine from the big model the essentials of what the teacher model knows. That’s why there’s potentially more inherent loss, but you retain much more of the reasoning capability. It drastically shrinks the size of the model, but there’s only so far you can go with that without going to quantization.”
Quantization makes models take a roundabout path to their destination instead of a direct one. “When applying an input to a network, there is a starting point for navigation,” said Plowman. “Then, depending on the values that you’ve given it, you need to navigate to an endpoint. Every time you do a layer you’re nudging the transform in a slightly different direction. With a full-width value such as FP32 or FP16, you’re going much more directly to a given point.”
Full-width values travel as the crow flies, while quantization is closer to city-block navigation. “We go up one, over one, up one, over one, but eventually you end up in exactly the same place,” said Plowman. “The trick with quantization is making those small, more angular steps mean the same thing as the direct navigation, but without the overhead power, memory, and other costs of the associated mathematics. It starts off with all the weights in the model, and it starts fitting them into buckets that match the quantization. There are lots and lots of different ways of doing the quantization. That’s a very brutal way of doing it.”
A gentler way is self-compression. “Self-compression techniques understand that, as a model is being trained, certain pathways will be very popular while others will be less popular,” explained Plowman. “You never know what this dimensional shape will look like. It’s random every time you retrain. You can maneuver the space to recreate certain desirable shapes you want every time, or get close to them, but there is an element of randomness. You get certain pathways that become critical as scaffolding for the rest of the system, but they’re not pathways that will matter in the end. We look for the sensitivity to those pathways, then quantize and quantize and quantize them down to zero bits. If nothing changes in the model and you still get the same outcomes, there was likely very small, or infinitesimally small, or no contribution from [those pathways].”
Fig. 3: A quantized transformer architecture. Source: Imagination
For quantization and self-compression, the complexity lies in managing the loss. “You need to make sure you’re not throwing away things that you really need, and that you’ve got good data coverage in the training set for the quantization flow,” Plowman observed.
For example, in automotive, engineers need to avoid losing long-tail data on edge cases or rare training samples that let an autonomous system navigate unusual road conditions.
Conclusion: Trending smaller
Small language models and other compact models suit resource-constrained edge devices, but they require system-level design and optimization to deliver the functions and features a specific product needs.
Ultimately, successful edge AI deployment starts with defining the workload and choosing an appropriately sized architecture — not simply shrinking the largest available model. Compression can help close the remaining gap, but its value depends on preserving accuracy while meeting the device’s power, memory, latency, cost, and safety requirements. As models and hardware evolve at different rates, flexible system design will be essential to support current applications and future workloads.

articles.title: How CNC Machines Quietly Changed the Way Furniture Gets Made - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Walk into a furniture workshop today and the first thing you notice is what’s missing. The noise. Not the absence of it, exactly, but the pattern. Instead of the stop-start rhythm of a circular saw and someone swearing at a mitre, there’s a steady mechanical hum that lasts twenty minutes and then stops.
That hum is a CNC router. And over the past fifteen years or so, it has rewritten how cabinets, tables, shelving and shopfitting get built, without most people outside the trade noticing.
From Pattern Templates to Code
CNC stands for computer numerical control, which is a dull name for something fairly clever. A designer draws a part on screen. Software converts that drawing into coordinates. A spindle spinning at 18,000 RPM then follows those coordinates across a sheet of material, cutting shapes to within a fraction of a millimetre.
Before this, repeat work meant templates. A cabinetmaker building forty identical kitchen doors would make a jig from plywood, clamp it down, run a router around the edge, unclamp, reposition, repeat. Accurate enough, but the jig wore down. Part number one and part number forty were never quite twins.
Digital files don’t wear out. That single fact changed the economics of small-batch furniture completely.
Why Tolerances Suddenly Mattered
Flat-pack assembly only works if every hole lines up. Cam locks, dowels, screw-in feet, European hinges with their 35mm boring cups; all of it depends on holes landing exactly where the instruction diagram says they will.
Hand-drilling that lot across hundreds of panels is miserable work with a decent error rate. A CNC machine with a drill bank punches the whole pattern in seconds and does it the same way every time. That reliability is the hidden reason IKEA-style assembly became tolerable rather than infuriating.
The Material Side of the Story
Machines are only half of it. CNC routers reward materials that behave predictably, and that pushed engineered sheet goods to the front of the queue.
Solid timber moves. It expands across the grain in humid weather and shrinks when the heating goes on. Lovely stuff, but a nightmare if you’ve programmed a toolpath that assumes the sheet is exactly where you left it. Plywood is more stable but has voids and grain direction to think about.
MDF sits in the sweet spot. It has no grain, no voids and a consistent density right through, which means a router bit cuts the same resistance in every direction. Cut a curve in MDF and you get a clean edge you can paint straight away. Cut the same curve in solid oak and you’ll be sanding out tear-out for an hour.
Thickness choice matters more than people expect. An 18mm sheet is the default for carcass work, but 15mm MDF has become a favourite for drawer boxes, cabinet backs, shelving and anything where shaving three millimetres off the wall thickness buys useful internal space without compromising strength. It’s also noticeably lighter to lift onto a machine bed, which the people doing the lifting appreciate.
Nesting and the War on Offcuts
Here’s where software earns its keep. Nesting algorithms arrange every part of a project onto a sheet like a jigsaw, rotating and shuffling shapes to squeeze out maximum yield.
Manual layout on a 2440 x 1220mm sheet might achieve 70 per cent material usage on a complex job. Good nesting software regularly hits 85 to 90 per cent. Across a year, that difference pays for a lot of machine time.
Less waste means lower material spend and smaller skip bills
Fewer handling steps because parts come off the bed labelled and ready
Faster quoting since the software tells you exactly how many sheets a job needs
What It Did to Small Workshops
The common assumption was that automation would hand everything to the big factories. The opposite happened in a lot of cases.
Entry-level CNC routers now start around the $15,000 mark, with capable production machines in the $40,000 to $80,000 range. That’s a serious outlay, but it’s within reach of a two-person workshop in a way that a factory-scale beam saw never was.
The result is a wave of small outfits doing bespoke built-ins, curved reception desks and one-off retail fitouts; work that used to be either prohibitively expensive or simply declined. A custom radius bookcase is no longer a heroic hand-shaping exercise. It’s a file and a sheet.
The Skills Shifted, They Didn’t Disappear
Plenty of old hands worried the craft would die. It didn’t. It moved.
Knowing which bit to use, what feed rate stops burning, how to hold a thin part down without it chattering loose, where to leave material for hand-finishing; none of that comes from the software. CAD knowledge joined the toolkit rather than replacing it.
Where This Is Heading
Machine learning is starting to creep into toolpath optimisation, and five-axis routers are slowly becoming affordable enough for mid-sized shops. Expect more curved, sculptural furniture at ordinary price points.
What won’t change is the basic trade-off. Good design and good material still decide whether the finished piece is worth owning. The machine just stopped being the bottleneck.

articles.title: Zoho launches restaurant POS platform, offers free plan for small businesses
articles.text:
Zoho launches restaurant POS platform, offers free plan for small businesses
Zoho has launched its restaurant POS platform in India, offering free access to outlets with annual billing of up to Rs 12 lakh, with Kolkata-based Asha Sweets becoming its first customer.
Zoho has launched a point-of-sale (POS) platform for restaurants in India, with Kolkata-based sweet shop Asha Sweets becoming its first customer. The product is being offered free of charge to restaurants with annual billing of up to Rs 12 lakh, as part of Zoho’s push to bring smaller food businesses onto digital platforms.
In a post on X, Zoho co-founder Sridhar Vembu said Asha Sweets began using Zoho POS for Restaurants during the festive rush. Zoho’s team visited the outlet to observe how the platform was being used during one of its busiest periods.
"The first customer for any new product is special. When that customer is a sweet shop, it is even more special," Vembu said, announcing the launch at Zoholics India.
Zoho POS for Restaurants is a cloud-based platform that brings billing, order management, menu management, kitchen operations and inventory tracking under one system. It is designed for quick-service restaurants, cafes, bakeries, cloud kitchens, casual dining establishments and businesses operating multiple outlets.
The platform consolidates orders from dine-in, takeaway and food delivery channels such as Swiggy and Zomato through a single interface. It also supports QR code-based digital menus, table management and kitchen order tickets (KOTs), which help restaurants track orders and their preparation.
The software supports offline billing, allowing restaurants to continue processing transactions during internet disruptions, with data synchronised once connectivity is restored. It is compatible with Windows and Android devices and integrates with Zoho Books for accounting. Payment integrations include Zoho Payments, Paytm, Pine Labs, and PhonePe.
The product is available under four subscription plans—Free, Essentials, Signature and Premium. While the free plan includes basic billing and inventory management features, capabilities such as food aggregator integrations, table management, self-ordering kiosks and customer loyalty programmes are offered through paid plans.
The launch is part of Zoho's broader expansion into vertical software-as-a-service (SaaS), through which the company is developing industry-specific applications alongside its existing business software. Zoho has identified seven sectors for this expansion, including retail, automotive, banking and financial services, education, real estate and restaurants.

articles.title: Renault écrase la concurrence en octobre : la Twingo championne des ventes électriques suivie de près par la R5
articles.text:
Les voitures électriques continuent leur percée sur le marché français en représentant plus de 4 ventes sur 10 en octobre. Leurs immatriculations ont ainsi augmenté de 81,7 % par rapport à octobre 2025. Les véhicules essence, eux, ont vu en parallèle leurs livraisons se contracter avec une baisse de 44,2 %. Ce ralentissement profite naturellement aux nouveautés françaises qui inondent le top 10. Renault a notamment de quoi sourire.
La dernière Twingo tient en effet sa première victoire en arrivant en tête des ventes avec 4 747 exemplaires sur le mois d’octobre, et 19 230 ventes depuis sa commercialisation au printemps. Ancienne favorite, la R5 garde toujours la forme en décrochant la deuxième place avec 4 666 modèles écoulés, ce qui lui permet de talonner la grenouille. Et entre janvier et octobre, 36 664 exemplaires de la citadine ont encore été vendus.
Peugeot et Citroën distancés par l’offensive au Losange
Cela représente une hausse de 39,5 % par rapport à la même période l’année passée. Elle tient donc le pavé comme la Peugeot e-208, qui a enregistré 3 221 livraisons. La lionne est suivie des 3 037 exemplaires du Renault Scénic. Ce dernier devrait d’ailleurs connaître une nouvelle dynamique grâce à sa version restylée fraîchement commercialisée. En cinquième place pointe la Citroën ë-C3 avec 2 736 modèles vendus.
Le Peugeot e-3008 s’empare de la sixième place avec 1 875 unités écoulées, suivi des 1 786 exemplaires de la Renault 4. Le petit SUV est d’ailleurs le modèle connaissant la plus forte hausse de ses immatriculations avec 145,4 % de ventes en plus sur la période comprise entre janvier et octobre 2026 par rapport à la même période en 2025. Premier modèle étranger du classement, le bien connu Tesla Model Y arrive en huitième position.
Allemandes hors du Top 10 : le réveil annoncé du groupe Volkswagen
Ses 1 748 unités écoulées en octobre lui permettent d’arriver devant le nouveau Kia EV2 et ses 1 506 exemplaires. Le Peugeot e-2008 clôture le top 10 avec 1 412 modèles vendus. Ironiquement, la chinoise la plus vendue est l’anonyme Leapmotor T03 avec 832 exemplaires en 19ème position. Et comme on peut le voir, le groupe Volkswagen n’a pas non plus réussi à intégrer le haut du classement. Son modèle ayant le mieux performé n’arrive qu’à la 13ème place. Il s’agit du Skoda Elroq et ses 1 067 unités.
Un petit passage à vide, donc, qui devrait cependant être rapidement compensé avec l’arrivée des petites électriques connaissant un succès retentissant. Nul doute que nous verrons apparaître dans les prochains mois les Volkswagen ID. Polo, Cupra Raval et Skoda Epiq dans les tableaux. Cette belle dynamique est donc appelée à perdurer avec de futurs modèles électriques toujours plus abordables.

articles.title: OpenSSH flaw lets attackers log into password-disabled Linux accounts
articles.text:
A newly disclosed flaw involving OpenSSH and musl, dubbed "*sshole," allows attackers to log in to certain Alpine Linux and other musl-based Linux accounts configured to block password authentication simply by entering an oversized password.
The flaw only affects OpenSSH servers running on Linux distributions that use the musl C library, including Alpine Linux, OpenWrt, Buildroot, and Yocto, under certain authentication configurations.
Security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, who discovered and released details on the vulnerability today, says the flaw has existed since 2016 and stems from how OpenSSH handles password verification errors on systems using the musl C library.
Linux accounts can be configured to prevent password logins by replacing their password hash with an asterisk (*) in the /etc/shadow file. Because this is not a valid password hash, no password should allow access to those accounts.
However, a patch introduced in OpenSSH in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210 changed how OpenSSH handled accounts without usable password hashes.
To prevent attackers from identifying valid usernames through different response times, OpenSSH was modified to perform password hashing even when an account had no usable password hash, including accounts configured with * to block password logins.
The problem is that the musl C library's crypt() function also returns * when password hashing fails, including when a submitted password exceeds its 256-byte limit.
This means an attacker can submit an oversized password and cause OpenSSH to compare the returned * against the account's stored *, resulting in a successful login.
To be clear, the flaw does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes.
Kultekin says exploitation requires the following conditions:
- OpenSSH is running on a musl-based Linux system, such as Alpine Linux, OpenWrt, Buildroot, or Yocto.
- PAM authentication is disabled, as it is by default in Alpine Linux's openssh-server package.
- SSH password authentication is enabled.
- At least one account has an asterisk (*) as its password hash.
- Another account has a valid password hash.
The researcher warns that Alpine Linux's official AWS and Azure cloud images have an affected default 'alpine' account with passwordless 'doas' privileges, which could allow attackers to gain root access.
Systems using glibc, including Debian, Ubuntu, and Fedora, and those using PAM authentication are not vulnerable to this attack.
Kultekin says he discovered the vulnerability using AI agents that ran about 17,600 authentication tests with different OpenSSH configurations, malformed password hashes, and oversized passwords.
The vulnerability has been fixed in OpenSSH 10.6p2, and Alpine Linux administrators are advised to update their OpenSSH packages using apk upgrade openssh.
Admins who can't immediately install the update can mitigate the issue by turning off SSH password authentication with PasswordAuthentication no in their SSH server configuration and restarting SSH.
Kultekin says admins can also check for signs of exploitation by examining SSH authentication logs for password-based logins for accounts that should not allow them.
On Alpine Linux, the following command can reveal successful SSH password logins:
grep "Accepted password" /var/log/messages
If the logs show a successful password login for the alpine account, administrators can check whether that account has password authentication disabled:
grep '^alpine:' /etc/shadow
If the account's password field contains *, but SSH logs show a successful password login, it could indicate that the vulnerability was exploited.

articles.title: Kurz vor historischem Meilenstein: Kontakt zu Voyager 1 steht wieder
articles.text:
Kurz vor historischem Meilenstein: Kontakt zu Voyager 1 steht wieder
Aufatmen bei der Nasa: Voyager 1 hat sich zurückgemeldet. Die Raumsonde, die seit 49 Jahren im Weltall unterwegs ist, hatte kurzzeitig nicht auf Kommunikationsversuche des Deep Space Network auf der Erde reagiert.
Voyager 1 reagierte zweimal nicht auf Kontaktversuche
Das Funk- und Kommunikationsnetzwerk der Nasa hatte am 18. und 19. Oktober Voyager 1 kontaktiert. Doch die Raumsonde blieb bei beiden Kontaktversuchen stumm.
Wie die US-Raumfahrtbehörde kürzlich bekannt gab, löste sich das Problem aber von selbst. Am 20. Oktober meldete sich Voyager zurück. Seitdem ist die Kommunikation stabil. Die Nasa versucht nun herauszufinden, was zu dem Ausfall geführt hatte. Es handelte sich schließlich um den ersten Vorfall dieser Art.
Als erstes menschengemachtes Objekt ein Lichttag von Erde entfernt
Der Wackler kam zur Unzeit, denn bald erreicht Voyager 1 einen Meilenstein, der die Kommunikation noch schwerer macht. Die Raumsonde wird als erstes menschengemachtes Objekt einen Lichttag von der Erde entfernt sein. Dies entspricht etwa 25,9 Milliarden Kilometern.
Wie das Wort Lichttag schon sagt: Das Licht, das von einem Objekt in dieser Distanz ausgestrahlt wird, benötigt 24 Stunden, um die Erde zu erreichen.
„Wartet zwei Tage, bis man endlich eine Antwort bekommt“
Ein Radiosignal, das die Kontrollstation auf der Erde in Richtung Voyager abschickt, ist dann ebenfalls einen ganzen Tag unterwegs. Das sorgt für massive Delays in der Kommunikation.
„Wenn man ‚Voyager ‚Hallo‘ sagen will, schickt man seine Nachricht ab, geht nach Hause und wartet zwei Tage, bis man endlich eine Antwort bekommt“, sagte Suzanne Dodd vom Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) der Nasa in der Mitteilung.
An diesem Tag erreicht Voyager 1 den historischen Meilenstein
Die Nasa hat den Moment, an dem Voyager 1 einen Lichttag von der Erde entfernt sein wird, bereits exakt berechnet. Demnach ist es am 18. November um 5.16 Uhr US-Ostküstenzeit so weit.
Zu diesem Zeitpunkt wird die Distanz der Sonde zur Erde exakt 25.902.068.356 Kilometer betragen.
Voyager 1: Seit fast 50 Jahren im Einsatz
Voyager 1 startete am 5. September 1977 von Cape Canaveral aus. Seitdem bewegt sie sich mit einer Geschwindigkeit von über 60.000 Kilometern pro Stunde durchs All.
Voyager 1 erforschte zunächst Jupiter und Saturn. Im Sommer 2012 trat sie als erstes von Menschen geschaffene Objekt in den interstellaren Raum ein.
Zahn der Zeit nagt an Voyager 1: Nur noch zwei Intrumente aktiv
Doch ein Jahr vor ihrem 50. Geburtstag nagt der Zahn der Zeit an der Sonde. Deswegen musste die Nasa im Frühjahr 2026 ein weiteres Instrument abschalten, den Teilchenmesser LECP. (Low-energy Charged Particles).
Die Abschaltung spart Energie, die der Sonde ein Jahr weiterer Lebensdauer verschaffen soll. Von ursprünglich elf Instrumenten an Bord der Voyager 1 sind damit nur noch zwei aktiv.
Interessant! Aber… die NASA Kontaktiert am 18.10. und die Sonde blieb still…
2 Tage auf eine Antwort warten, dann am 20.10. eine Antwort.
also, nicht still geblieben, oder? Aber genug für einen spannenden Artikel… denke ich!

articles.title: Hologrammes décevants, mais batterie bluffante : on a testé les futurs prototypes Mercedes — Frandroid
articles.text:
Votre voiture pourrait-elle, demain, expliquer aux autres automobilistes pourquoi vous vous arrêtez ? Ou vous laisser regarder un film directement sur le pare-brise, sans le moindre écran devant vous ? Ce sont quelques-unes des pistes explorées par Mercedes-Benz, qui nous a invités dans son antre dédié à la R&D de Sindelfingen, près de Stuttgart, pour découvrir plusieurs technologies en cours de développement, que le constructeur a officiellement présentées ce mardi 3 novembre.
Une visite au cours de laquelle nous avons également découvert comment Mercedes teste ses voitures et les soumet à toutes sortes d’épreuves bien avant qu’elles soient sur la route, comme nous vous l’avons raconté dans un précédent article. Nous avons aussi pu assister à un spectaculaire crash-test entre deux Mercedes CLA lancées chacune à 56 km/h, auquel nous avons consacré un autre article.
Mais le constructeur allemand nous avait réservé d’autres démonstrations, moins destructrices cette fois. Au programme : des affichages intégrés aux vitrages, un dispositif holographique et une nouvelle technologie de conversion électrique. Trois innovations encore expérimentales, qui sont loin de nous avoir toutes convaincus.
Des messages lumineux sur les vitres : une bonne idée, mais une réalisation encore expérimentale
Comment une voiture peut-elle communiquer directement avec les autres automobilistes ? Mercedes travaille sur l’intégration d’affichages lumineux dans les vitrages, capables de faire apparaître des informations à la demande tout en restant presque invisibles le reste du temps.
Le constructeur explore deux technologies. Les mini-LED, adaptées aux grandes surfaces comme la lunette arrière, permettent notamment d’afficher des feux de freinage, des pictogrammes d’avertissement ou des informations liées à la circulation. Les micro-LED, plus précises, se prêtent davantage aux animations sur des surfaces réduites. Dans les deux cas, les éléments lumineux sont intégrés directement dans l’épaisseur du vitrage.
Nous avons découvert ces dispositifs sur une Classe S de démonstration. À commencer par l’affichage intégré à la lunette arrière.
Imaginez que vous vous arrêtiez pour laisser traverser un piéton. Plutôt que de laisser le conducteur derrière vous s’impatienter, voire vous coller au pare-chocs, votre voiture pourrait lui expliquer la raison de cet arrêt grâce à un message lumineux. De quoi améliorer la compréhension entre automobilistes et, potentiellement, la sécurité. Les messages possibles sont variés : un rappel des distances de sécurité pour l’automobiliste qui vous suit de trop près sur autoroute, un triangle rouge pour signaler un freinage d’urgence, ou encore une flèche accompagnée d’un « P » pour indiquer que vous allez vous garer, et de quel côté. Utile pour éviter que le conducteur distrait derrière vous s’avance trop et vous bloque la place.
Pas question, en revanche, de laisser le conducteur choisir ses messages en temps réel. Comme nous l’ont expliqué les équipes Mercedes, c’est la voiture qui sélectionnerait automatiquement les informations adaptées à la situation. Une approche logique pour éviter toute distraction supplémentaire.
Sur le papier, l’idée est donc séduisante. Mais il suffit de regarder la Classe S d’un peu plus près pour comprendre que nous sommes encore loin d’une intégration dans une voiture de série. En se penchant à l’intérieur, on distingue les fils qui relient les différents éléments du dispositif. Quant à la zone d’affichage, elle conserve un aspect légèrement fumé, et donc pas totalement transparente, même lorsque les LED sont éteintes.
On ne peut pas dire que le rendu visuel soit franchement futuriste non plus. Avec ses messages lumineux, le système évoque davantage les anciennes enseignes LED de pharmacie qu’une technologie automobile de dernière génération. On comprend toutefois que ce rendu tient en partie à des considérations de sécurité. Bref, l’idée convainc bien davantage que sa mise en œuvre actuelle.
Une vitre latérale transformée en écran : pour quoi faire ?
Sur cette même Classe S, Mercedes nous a également présenté un affichage intégré à une vitre latérale, utilisant cette fois des micro-LED pour diffuser des animations. Il faut reconnaître que la qualité d’image nous a semblé la meilleure de toutes les démonstrations d’affichage.
Son utilité, en revanche, nous paraît moins évidente. Parmi les démonstrations proposées figurait l’affichage du niveau de charge de la batterie, visible depuis l’extérieur. Pourquoi pas, mais certains véhicules disposent déjà de témoins lumineux indiquant l’avancement de la recharge, tandis que l’information, si tant est qu’on en ait absolument besoin, peut également être consultée sur une borne ou une application liée à la voiture.
Quant à la possibilité de diffuser des animations ou des vidéos à destination des passants, elle nous laisse franchement perplexes. D’autant que la zone d’affichage reste, là encore, légèrement fumée, au détriment de la transparence du vitrage.
Ces deux applications montrent assez bien les limites de l’exercice. Sur la lunette arrière, Mercedes semble avoir identifié un véritable usage, mais la technologie doit encore progresser. Sur la vitre latérale, c’est presque l’inverse : l’affichage est plus convaincant, mais son utilité reste à démontrer.
Un affichage holographique sur le pare-brise qui peine à convaincre
La deuxième grande innovation présentée par Mercedes nous a nettement moins convaincus. Cette fois, nous doutons autant de sa réalisation que de son intérêt. Le constructeur travaille sur un affichage holographique capable de transformer le pare-brise en écran, sans installer de dalle supplémentaire dans l’habitacle.
Le principe repose sur un projecteur intégré à la planche de bord et un film transparent incorporé au vitrage. Celui-ci utilise des éléments optiques holographiques, ou HOE (Holographic Optical Elements), capables de réfléchir sélectivement les longueurs d’onde lumineuses émises par le projecteur.
Mercedes promet ainsi une image visible même en plein soleil, mais uniquement depuis certains angles. Le conducteur et son passager pourraient donc consulter des contenus différents, sans voir ce qui s’affiche de l’autre côté. Navigation, informations sur les points d’intérêt, visioconférence ou films : les applications envisagées sont nombreuses.
Sauf que Mercedes propose déjà, notamment avec son MBUX Hyperscreen, un véritable écran face au passager. Pour regarder une vidéo, difficile de faire mieux qu’une dalle offrant une image nette et lumineuse. Nous avons testé le dispositif holographique à l’arrêt puis dans une voiture en mouvement, depuis le siège passager du véhicule de démonstration. Une vidéo tournait en boucle sur le pare-brise. Franchement, l’expérience a été assez désagréable.
Premier souci, l’image prend la forme d’un trapèze plutôt que d’un vrai rectangle. Surtout, il nous a fallu de longues secondes pour parvenir à faire correctement la mise au point avec nos yeux sur ce que nous étions censés découvrir. Une sensation étrange, presque comme si l’on devait loucher pour regarder la vidéo. Une fois l’image enfin perceptible, sa qualité restait très inférieure à celle d’un écran traditionnel. Le problème vient sans doute du fait que contrairement à un affichage tête-haute que l’on trouve déjà dans nombre de modèles, l’image est projetée très proche, trop proche. Dans le cas d’un HUD, les informations de conduite s’affichent comme si elles étaient projetées à plusieurs mètres devant la voiture.
À la sortie du véhicule, la personne en charge du projet nous a demandé ce que nous avions pensé de la démonstration. Difficile de lui répondre que nous avions été convaincus. Mais surtout, nous lui avons posé la question qui nous taraudait : à quoi bon développer une telle technologie alors qu’un écran classique fait déjà parfaitement le travail ?
Sa réponse permet de mieux comprendre la démarche de Mercedes. Certains clients pourraient souhaiter conserver une planche de bord élégante, avec de belles finitions en bois par exemple, plutôt que de multiplier les écrans. L’affichage holographique permettrait alors de faire apparaître des contenus uniquement lorsqu’ils sont nécessaires, sans modifier l’esthétique de l’habitacle.
Autre argument avancé : le confort des passagers sujets au mal des transports. En affichant une vidéo dans leur champ de vision, avec la route toujours visible en arrière-plan, Mercedes espère leur permettre de conserver des repères visuels sur les mouvements de la voiture.
Même si l’on comprend donc mieux l’intention de Mercedes, qui est de proposer une alternative aux écrans omniprésents dans les habitacles modernes, il ne s’agit ni plus ni moins que d’un écran de plus. Contrairement à ce que son nom pourrait laisser imaginer, il ne s’agit pas non plus d’un hologramme en trois dimensions « façon Star Wars ». Entre la qualité d’image décevante, la difficulté à faire le point et le confort visuel discutable, nous avons surtout eu l’impression de découvrir une solution technologique à un problème qui n’existe pas vraiment.
Mercedes n’est d’ailleurs pas le seul à explorer cette piste. L’équipementier coréen Hyundai Mobis a présenté au CES 2025 son propre pare-brise holographique, développé avec l’opticien allemand Zeiss, et vise une commercialisation dès 2027. Une échéance qui dira si la technologie a progressé depuis ce que nous avons vu à Sindelfingen.
Power Converter : l’innovation la plus intéressante était peut-être celle qu’on ne voyait pas
Après les affichages futuristes, Mercedes nous a présenté une technologie nettement moins spectaculaire, mais potentiellement bien plus importante pour l’avenir de ses voitures électriques. Derrière l’appellation assez générique de Power Converter se cache une nouvelle manière de gérer l’énergie au sein d’une batterie.
Pour comprendre son intérêt, rappelons que la tension d’une batterie dépend notamment du nombre de cellules assemblées en série. C’est cette architecture qui permet de concevoir des systèmes électriques fonctionnant autour de 400 ou 800 volts. Mais la tension varie également selon l’état de charge et les caractéristiques des cellules.
Mercedes explore une autre approche, reposant sur de petits convertisseurs électroniques programmables, capables de gérer les flux d’énergie au niveau de chaque cellule ou groupe de cellules. Plusieurs de ces modules, fonctionnant en parallèle, pourraient ainsi fournir une tension de sortie stable, indépendamment de l’état de charge ou du vieillissement de la batterie.
L’intérêt ? Découpler en partie la tension utilisée par la voiture de l’architecture même de sa batterie. Autrement dit, ne plus dépendre uniquement du nombre de cellules branchées en série pour obtenir la haute tension nécessaire au fonctionnement du véhicule. Ce serait alors l’électronique de puissance, pilotée par logiciel, qui se chargerait de fournir la tension souhaitée.
Mercedes sait déjà atteindre 800 volts, une architecture présente sur ses voitures électriques récentes ; l’objectif est ici de maintenir cette tension indépendamment de la configuration et de l’état de charge de la batterie. Une approche qui pourrait offrir davantage de liberté aux ingénieurs pour concevoir les futures batteries, sans pour autant garantir une recharge plus rapide.
Cette technologie pourrait également réunir plusieurs fonctions aujourd’hui assurées par des composants distincts, notamment certaines conversions entre courant alternatif et courant continu. Mercedes envisage aussi des applications liées à la recharge bidirectionnelle, pour alimenter une habitation (Vehicle-to-Home) ou réinjecter de l’électricité dans le réseau (Vehicle-to-Grid).
Le gain le plus concret pourrait venir de la disparition d’une pièce. Comme le relève Electrive, ces micro-convertisseurs savent gérer eux-mêmes la conversion entre courant alternatif et continu, ce qui permettrait de se passer du chargeur embarqué séparé et de gagner du poids, de la place et des coûts de production. Le média spécialisé pointe toutefois deux revers possibles : une électronique plus complexe logée au plus près des cellules pourrait compliquer les réparations, et des fonctions comme la recharge bidirectionnelle ou la puissance de charge maximale pourraient être pilotées uniquement par logiciel, ce qui ouvrirait la porte à des déblocages payants à distance.
À terme, le constructeur espère concevoir des systèmes électriques plus compacts, plus modulaires et plus efficaces, avec de possibles bénéfices sur la consommation et l’autonomie. Aucun gain chiffré n’a toutefois été communiqué.
La génération actuelle du Power Converter atteint une puissance de 3 kW et prend en charge des applications en courant alternatif comme en courant continu. Un chiffre encore très éloigné des puissances nécessaires à la propulsion ou à la recharge rapide d’une voiture électrique moderne, et même inférieur aux 7,4 kW d’une borne domestique classique. Mais l’architecture étant modulaire, plusieurs convertisseurs pourraient être associés pour atteindre des puissances plus importantes.
Mercedes n’avance aucune date de commercialisation. Ce Power Converter pourrait néanmoins répondre à de véritables enjeux techniques : simplifier l’architecture électrique, améliorer son efficacité et faciliter l’intégration de nouvelles fonctions de recharge. Des bénéfices encore théoriques, tant qu’aucun modèle équipé n’a été annoncé.
Des innovations qui ne se valent pas toutes
Cette visite dans les laboratoires Mercedes nous aura finalement laissé une impression contrastée. D’un côté, des technologies d’affichage qui cherchent à réinventer notre rapport aux écrans, mais dont certaines peinent encore à convaincre. De l’autre, des travaux beaucoup moins visibles sur l’électronique de puissance, qui pourraient avoir des conséquences concrètes sur les futures voitures électriques.
Il faut évidemment rappeler que nous avons découvert des prototypes de recherche, sans calendrier de commercialisation annoncé. Pour autant, la démonstration la plus spectaculaire est aussi celle qui nous a le moins convaincus : l’affichage holographique peine à justifier sa place face à un simple écran, quand le Power Converter, invisible à bord, répond à des besoins bien concrets d’architecture électrique et de recharge.

articles.title: WoW Forever : Blizzard officialise sa toute première arme légendaire inédite pour son « nouveau » MMORPG
articles.text:
La scène avait quelque chose d’un peu émouvant pour qui a connu les premiers jours de World of Warcraft, il y a plus de vingt ans. Pour accompagner le lancement de WoW Forever, et montrer l’engouement de la communauté autour de ce « troisième » WoW, le studio a partagé une animation assez hypnotisante à regarder.
Selon Blizzard, cette animation en forme de carte montrait les joueurs et les joueuses se connectant à WoW Forever depuis les différentes régions de départ, côté Alliance ou côté Horde. Un point clignotant par brave rejoignant le serveur, d’après le studio. Mais ce n’était pas là la seule animation que l’entreprise avait prévue autour de la sortie de WoW Forever.
Une autre surprise a également été conservée pour le jour J : alors que le jeu a fait ses débuts dans la nuit de ce mercredi 4 à ce jeudi 5 novembre (les serveurs ont ouvert à minuit, heure de Paris), le compte officiel de Warcraft sur X a présenté vers 23h… la toute première arme légendaire inédite propre à World of Warcraft Forever.
Et l’item en question est un bâton à deux mains appelé Taldramir, aussi surnommé The Whispering Wood (qu’on traduirait par Le Bois Murmurant). Juste avant, lors d’un direct sur Twitch, l’atelier néo-zélandais Wētā Workshop (à qui l’on doit les armes et armures du film Warcraft de 2016) en avait assemblé une réplique grandeur nature.
L’officialisation de Taldramir comme arme légendaire dans WoW Forever est triplement notable.
D’abord parce qu’un tel équipement est accompagné, dans l’immense majorité des cas, de statistiques exceptionnelles, et bénéficie au passage d’une direction artistique très souvent admirable. Deux critères qui attisent, forcément, bien des convoitises.
Ensuite parce que dans le WoW d’origine, ces armes se comptent sur les doigts d’une main (Sulfuras, Lame-tonnerre ou Atiesh, qui était déjà un bâton…). Qui plus est, leur obtention demandait des semaines, voire des mois de jeu, et passait par des activités de haut niveau en groupe, comme les raids. Et il valait mieux avoir l’appui de toute une guilde pour y parvenir.
Enfin, et surtout, le bâton est la première arme légendaire pensée spécialement pour Forever. Blizzard avait évidemment prévu d’ajouter du contenu pour ce troisième WoW, comme de nouvelles quêtes, des régions inédites et des items supplémentaires. Celui-ci est le premier de très haut niveau à être mis en avant.
On notera au passage que ce bâton apparaît dans une illustration du jeu publiée dès le 29 octobre, dans l’actualité annonçant la sortie du MMORPG.
Taldramir, un bâton légendaire pour… druide ?
Compte tenu du design de l’arme (tout en branches noueuses et en bourgeons naissants) et de son nom (qui rappelle l’ambiance des elfes de la nuit), on présume que la classe druide sera capable de se servir du bâton. Cela étant, Blizzard n’a rien dit des classes qui pourront le porter ni de ses effets, rappelle le site spécialisé Wowhead.
Du côté du data mining, c’est-à-dire l’extraction des données cachées dans les fichiers du jeu, des pistes ont été trouvées. D’après Icy Veins, ce bâton serait tourné vers les soins, et sa quête passerait par le raid du sommet d’Hyjal, le cratère d’Un’Goro (deux zones où la présence des druides peut se justifier) et le Cercle cénarien, la faction des druides.
Des indices de cette quête étaient déjà apparus dans les fichiers de la bêta en septembre, au moment où Blizzard promettait une nouvelle suite de quêtes légendaire pour le printemps 2027. Ces étapes restent non confirmées.
