articles.title: Five Ways NVIDIA Co-Design Maximizes the Value of Every Byte in the AI Factory | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
In an AI factory, high bandwidth memory (HBM)is the fastest, most expensive, and most contested memory tier. Every byte spent on a redundant weight copy, an idle session’s KV cache, or a recomputed prefix is a byte that is not being used to produce tokens. The question is no longer how much memory a GPU has, but how much useful work each byte delivers.
The generational data in Figure 1 below shows why. From GB300 to NVIDIA Rubin, capacity held at 288 GB while bandwidth rose to 19.2 TB/s.
agentic throughput per megawatt grew far faster. On SemiAnalysis AgentX, which replays recorded coding-agent sessions with real tool-call gaps and growing context, NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 then delivers up to 30x the throughput per megawatt of GB300 NVL72 at 160 tokens per second per user.
Capacity alone cannot explain a 30x gain delivered from the same 288 GB per GPU. The difference is how much useful work each byte delivers.
NVIDIA treats this as a co-design problem that spans GPU architecture, the scale-up interconnect, serving software, the CPU, and storage. This post examines five ways that co-design maximizes the value of each byte of memory, from the bits that encode a single weight to the shared storage that preserves and reuses context across agentic turns and nodes.
1. How does NVFP4 store more intelligence in fewer bytes?
The most direct way to raise the value of a byte is to make each value smaller without losing what it encodes. NVFP4 does this with a 4-bit E2M1 element and two levels of scaling: Every 16-value micro-block shares an FP8 (E4M3) scale factor, and a per-tensor FP32 scale sits on top. The result is a format that is small enough to free significant HBM, yet granular enough to preserve accuracy where naive 4-bit formats fall short.
Applied to weights, NVFP4 reduces the model footprint by approximately 3.5x relative to FP16 and 1.8x relative to FP8, freeing memory for what agentic inference needs most: more KV-cache capacity, larger batches, and higher concurrency. NVFP4 has become the default precision for open agentic benchmarks with strict accuracy requirements, including AA-AgentPerf, SemiAnalysis AgentX, and MLPerf Endpoints. Across these benchmarks and leading mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, it delivers up to 4x the throughput of an FP8 baseline at the same interactivity (Figure 3 below).
The same principle extends to the KV cache itself. NVFP4 KV cache cuts the cache footprint by up to 50% compared with FP8, so approximately 2x more context stays resident on device. Fewer evictions mean higher cache-hit rates during prefill, while a smaller cache means less bandwidth consumed during decode.
NVFP4 shrinks the bytes. The next question is where those bytes live, and how many copies of them the AI factory has to keep.
2. How does the NVLink scale-up domain turn 72 GPUs into one memory pool?
MoE models activate only a subset of parameters per token, but every expert’s weights must still live somewhere in HBM. When experts are packed onto a small number of GPUs, each GPU spends a large share of its memory on weights, and each decode step pays a heavy weight-loading cost for the MoE GroupGEMMs. The bytes are resident, but they are not working hard.
Wide expert parallelism (Wide-EP) in NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM changes that ratio by spreading experts across eight or more GPUs. With DeepSeek-R1 at EP64, each GPU holds four experts per layer, or 232 expert blocks across 58 MoE layers out of 14,848 in the full model. Fewer expert weights per GPU means:
- Capacity: More HBM per GPU is left for KV cache, larger batches, and higher concurrency.
- Arithmetic intensity: GroupGEMM kernels reuse each loaded weight across more tokens, raising FLOPs per byte.
- Balance: The Expert Parallel Load Balancer (EPLB) redistributes hot and cold experts between forward passes, so no GPU’s memory is overcommitted while another sits idle.
This only works because the scale-up domain makes remote bytes nearly as useful as local ones. Every MoE layer triggers all-to-all dispatch and combine traffic, and without a high-bandwidth fabric, those collectives would erase the gains. On GB200 NVL72, 130 TB/s of aggregate NVLink bandwidth absorbs that traffic, and large EP (EP32) delivers up to 1.8x more output tokens per second per GPU than small EP (EP8) at 100 tokens per second per user.
Vera Rubin NVL72 extends the same design point. Each Rubin GPU brings up to 288 GB of HBM4 and 3.0 TB/s of NVLink 6 bandwidth, for roughly 20.7 TB of HBM4 across the rack. Rubin also adds inline memory tensor acceleratory (TMA) descriptor updates, so one shared descriptor can serve every expert with a common layout, reducing the metadata overhead that grows with expert count.
Wide-EP decides where weight bytes live. The next lever decides whether KV cache bytes, once computed, are ever computed again.
3. How does NVIDIA Dynamo make every cached byte count?
The key-value (KV) cache stores intermediate attention calculations from previously processed tokens so the model can reuse them instead of recomputing them. This inference state is ephemeral and can be evicted and recomputed when needed, but KV cache is only valuable if it is reused. Agentic workloads are full of reuse opportunities: system prompts, tool schemas, shared documents, and the growing history of a multistep task. But if a request lands on a GPU that does not hold its prefix, or if that prefix was evicted moments earlier, the system pays for prefill again. The bytes existed; they were just in the wrong place.
NVIDIA Dynamo is the distributed serving layer that closes this gap. It treats KV cache as a fleet-wide resource rather than a per-GPU side effect, and it does so through three co-designed capabilities:
- KV-aware routing: The Dynamo router tracks where KV blocks reside and considers both cached-prefix overlap and worker load when placing requests. It balances existing context against the cost of sending work to an utilized GPU and turns potential recomputations into cache hits.
- Disaggregated serving: Prefill and decode run on separate GPU pools, each sized for its own compute and memory profile. Decode GPUs can dedicate HBM to KV cache and batch size rather than reserving headroom for bursty prefill.
- KV Cache Runner (KVCR): This tracks where every block lives across configured GPU, pinned CPU, and storage tiers, including local SSDs and mounted network filesystems. A prefix preserved outside HBM can be restored when a later request needs it, allowing useful context to survive GPU eviction and continue saving prefill work. KVCR uses the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) for its storage-transfer paths, allowing cached blocks to move while the GPU processes other work. KVCR also enables distributed reuse, with router-provided hints helping a selected worker retrieve cached context from a peer, while the inference engine retains control of GPU memory and local host offloading. The additional KVCR-Guard feature preserves committed KVCR-managed host-memory cache across an engine failure as long as the guard service and host remain available.
Dynamo’s KV-cache offloading depends on fast retrieval: Preserving a prefix outside HBM saves time when loading it is faster than repeating prefill. NIXL connects this offloading path to external storage systems. In separate validation tests, storage vendors VAST Data and WEKA demonstrated 35 GB/s to one H100 GPU using GPUDirect Storage and up to 270 GB/s of aggregate read throughput across eight H100 GPUs through a custom NIXL plugin, respectively. These tests showed that external storage could supply KV cache to the tested GPU systems without becoming the transfer bottleneck, supporting cache capacity beyond HBM. A separate VAST test demonstrated the response-time benefit: Using vLLM and LMCache on a DGX H100 system, loading stored KV cache instead of recomputing it reduced time to first token for Qwen3-32B with a 130K-token prompt.
Dynamo coordinates where cached bytes go and when they come back. The next two levers expand the capacity available for that context, starting with CPU memory.
4. How does the NVIDIA Vera CPU keep idle context from wasting HBM?
Agentic inference does not run in one uninterrupted pass. A single session alternates between GPU model steps and CPU-side work: tool calls, code execution, retrieval, database queries, and sandboxed evaluation. During each of those gaps, any session KV cache retained in HBM occupies capacity without serving active token generation, while other requests compete for the same bytes.
In a fully subscribed AI factory, the GPU does not wait. It takes on new requests while the tool call runs, and the longer the gap, the more likely the original session’s KV cache is evicted to make room. When the tool returns, the GPU may have to rebuild that context through a full prefill rather than resume from a cached state. A slow CPU therefore costs HBM twice: first as idle residency, then as recomputation.
The NVIDIA Vera CPU attacks both sides of this problem:
- Shorter gaps: 88 Olympus cores deliver 1.8x faster single-threaded performance, 40% lower peak loaded latency than x86 CPUs, and up to 14 GB/s of memory bandwidth per core. Faster, more predictable tool calls shrink the window in which KV cache is exposed to eviction pressure.
- A fast place to park context: Each Vera CPU provides up to 1.5 TB of LPDDR5X, more than 5x the HBM4 capacity of a single Rubin GPU. NVIDIA NVLink-C2C connects it coherently to Rubin at 1.8 TB/s, roughly 7x the 256 GB/s of an x16 PCIe Gen 6 link.
Together, these capabilities change the economics of an idle session. Instead of holding its KV cache in HBM or discarding it, Dynamo’s KV Block Manager can stage it in Vera memory for the duration of the tool call and bring it back over NVLink-C2C when the agent resumes. HBM stays dedicated to sessions that are actively generating tokens, and the paused session avoids paying for prefill twice.
Vera memory is the warm tier, sized for context that will return within a turn. For context that must survive across turns, agents, and nodes, the AI factory needs a tier that is larger still.
5. How does NVIDIA CMX extend context memory across the pod?
Keeping every reusable KV-cache byte in GPU or host memory limits capacity for active inference, but discarding it can force recomputation.. Multi-turn sessions, long-horizon tasks, and multi-agent workflows that share working memory all generate KV cache that will be needed again, often minutes later and often on a different node. Longer context windows and more concurrent sessions increase KV-cache capacity requirements beyond GPU HBM (G1 in Figure 9 below) and host memory (G2). The traditional hierarchy was not designed for this data. Local SSDs (G3) are bound to one node, while shared enterprise storage (G4) is built for durable data and carries replication and metadata overhead that ephemeral KV cache does not need.
NVIDIA CMX context memory storage closes this gap with a new G3.5 tier: Ethernet-attached flash, shared at the pod level, and optimized specifically for KV cache. It is built on the NVIDIA STX reference design and co-designed across four layers:
- Storage processing: The NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Storage Processor manages the NVMe SSDs, runs storage services, and offloads KV-cache data movement, data integrity and encryption. Its integrated NVIDIA Vera CPU accelerates CPU-side storage processing, extending the same CPU architecture used for agent execution into the storage data path.
- Networking: NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet provides low-latency, high-bandwidth RDMA access between compute nodes and CMX storage nodes.
- KV-aware services: NVIDIA DOCA Memos provides KV-aware services and I/O control on BlueField-4, treating context as a first-class resource for placement and sharing.
- Serving integration: Dynamo and NIXL make CMX appear as one seamless context tier across the pod, prestaging context and routing requests to where KV cache already resides.
The pod-level design is what raises the value of each byte. A prefix computed once on one node can be reused across compatible model instances in the pod, so agents that share documents, tools, or working memory can avoid duplicate prefill. Pooling context storage across the pod reduces KV-cache duplication and stranded capacity across nodes, extending effective GPU memory for inference. By prestaging reusable context into GPU or host memory, CMX reduces inference stalls, while its KV-cache-optimized storage tier lowers the power overhead of serving that context. Together, these capabilities help CMX deliver up to 5x higher tokens per second and up to 5x better power efficiency compared with traditional storage for long-context inference.
How do the five levers work together?
Each lever removes a different kind of waste. NVFP4 removes bits a value does not need, Wide-EP removes redundant weight copies, Dynamo removes recomputation, Vera removes idle residency during tool calls, and CMX enables KV-cache sharing and reuse across nodes. Because these levers are designed as one memory system, not as independent parts, the gains stack: A 4-bit KV block saves space in HBM, in Vera memory, and in CMX alike.
The result is an AI factory that measures memory not by capacity alone, but by the useful tokens each byte produces. Vera Rubin NVL72 shows what that looks like: up to 30x the throughput per megawatt of GB300 NVL72, from the same 288 GB per GPU. As agentic workloads grow, every byte counts.
Learn more
This work was made possible through the expertise and engineering contributions of Wei-ming Chen, Shiyang Chen, Chao Ni, Mengdi Wang, and Jeff Pool.

articles.title: Ces entreprises ont failli échapper à la facturation électronique, mais tout a basculé en 24 heures
articles.text:
Les députés avaient adopté une exemption de grande ampleur pour les petites entreprises et les agriculteurs. Mais dès le lendemain, le rejet du budget 2027 a effacé cette mesure. Pour les professionnels concernés, le calendrier de la réforme reste inchangé.
Décidément, les députés ne s'ennuient pas avec les dossiers qui touchent au numérique et aux entreprises ces derniers temps. Après avoir adopté à une voix près la fameuse taxe sur les gigaoctets, ils ont voté mardi 3 novembre un moratoire sur la facturation électronique pour les petites entreprises. Deux décisions importantes, et finalement le même sort : le rejet du volet recettes du budget 2027, mercredi soir, a effacé ces deux mesures. Pour les millions de professionnels qui espéraient un répit, c'est donc le retour au calendrier initial.
Une exemption qui aurait profondément changé la réforme
Tout est parti de l'amendement n° I-3426, déposé le 10 octobre par la députée Mathilde Hignet et le groupe La France insoumise. Adopté le 3 novembre par 101 voix contre 74, malgré l'avis défavorable du gouvernement et du rapporteur général du budget, il prévoyait d'exclure les microentreprises, les PME et les exploitants agricoles des obligations de facturation électronique et de transmission des données à l'administration fiscale, aussi appelée e-reporting.
La portée du texte allait donc bien au-delà d'un simple report de quelques mois. Son adoption définitive aurait remis en cause une partie importante du dispositif, dont la première étape est entrée en vigueur le 1er septembre 2026.
Les auteurs de l'amendement dénonçaient notamment le recours obligatoire aux plateformes agréées par l'État. Ils souhaitaient maintenir ce moratoire au moins jusqu'à la mise en place d'un véritable service public permettant aux entreprises de gérer gratuitement leurs factures électroniques.
Une revendication qui renvoie à l'abandon, en octobre 2024, du projet de portail public permettant directement l'émission et la réception des factures. L'infrastructure publique conserve deux fonctions techniques, l'annuaire des destinataires et la centralisation des données fiscales, mais ne proposera pas ce service aux entreprises. La loi de finances pour 2026 a d'ailleurs supprimé du Code général des impôts les références à ce portail public de facturation.
L'amendement pointait également les risques de sécurité liés à la multiplication des intermédiaires. Une préoccupation ravivée par la fuite de données ayant touché VosFactures fin septembre, qui avait conduit l'administration à suspendre temporairement ses échanges avec la plateforme agréée associée au service.
Et ce n'était pas le seul texte adopté. Deux amendements identiques du groupe Droite républicaine, les n° I-1729 et I-2894, prévoyaient aussi, à compter du 1er janvier 2027, de dispenser du passage par une plateforme agréée les opérations dont le client bénéficie de la franchise en base de TVA ou réalise exclusivement des opérations exonérées sans droit à déduction. Une mesure qui concernait notamment certains microentrepreneurs, sans pour autant les exclure totalement de la réforme.
Le budget rejeté, les obligations restent inchangées
Le répit envisagé aura finalement tourné court. Mercredi 4 novembre au soir, les députés ont rejeté la première partie du projet de loi de finances pour 2027, consacrée aux recettes, par 458 voix contre, aucune pour et deux abstentions.
Ce vote a entraîné le rejet du budget à l'Assemblée nationale, emportant les dispositions ajoutées pendant les débats. Le moratoire sur la facturation électronique, tout comme les amendements de la Droite républicaine, disparaît donc du texte. Le Sénat examinera la version initiale du gouvernement.
Concrètement, aucune obligation n'a été suspendue. Les entreprises assujetties à la TVA, y compris les microentrepreneurs bénéficiant de la franchise en base, doivent être capables de recevoir des factures électroniques depuis le 1er septembre 2026, lorsqu'elles leur sont adressées par des fournisseurs soumis à l'obligation d'émission.
Les grandes entreprises et les entreprises de taille intermédiaire sont déjà tenues d'émettre leurs factures électroniques pour les opérations concernées. Pour les PME et les microentreprises, cette obligation d'émission, ainsi que celle de transmission des données de transaction et de paiement, entreront en vigueur le 1er septembre 2027.
Reste une nuance importante concernant les sanctions. Dès le lancement de la réforme, le gouvernement s'est engagé à ne sanctionner aucune entreprise jusqu'à la fin de l'année 2026. David Amiel, ministre de l'Action et des Comptes publics, a réaffirmé cette volonté d'accompagnement ces dernières semaines. Il s'agit toutefois d'un engagement administratif, qui ne modifie pas les sanctions inscrites dans la loi et ne constitue pas une garantie juridiquement opposable.
Or, les montants prévus peuvent rapidement grimper. Le défaut d'émission d'une facture électronique, lorsque cette obligation s'applique, est passible d'une amende de 50 euros par facture, plafonnée à 15 000 euros par an. Une première infraction peut toutefois échapper à la sanction si elle est régularisée spontanément ou dans les 30 jours suivant une demande de l'administration, sous les conditions prévues par le Code général des impôts.
Pour les entreprises qui ne respectent pas l'obligation de recevoir leurs factures via une plateforme agréée, le mécanisme est différent : une mise en demeure leur accorde d'abord trois mois pour se mettre en conformité. Passé ce délai, une amende de 500 euros peut être prononcée. Si le manquement persiste, elle passe à 1 000 euros après trois mois supplémentaires, puis 1 000 euros à chaque nouvelle période de trois mois, sans plafond global prévu pour cette sanction.
Le dossier n'est toutefois pas définitivement clos. Le Sénat doit examiner le projet de budget à partir du 20 novembre, et les parlementaires pourront remettre sur la table certaines des dispositions écartées. D'ici là, les entreprises ont tout intérêt à poursuivre leur préparation : un amendement voté ne vaut pas une réforme suspendue.

articles.title: How a car-importing problem led Sheriff Adedokun to build Clea
articles.text:
In car importing, business owners must find the vehicle and pay the auction house, which could be in another country. This proved harder than expected for Sheriff Adedokun, a serial entrepreneur who founded Clea, a cross-border payments platform for African businesses.
Africa’s fragmented cross-border payments landscape was not new. Businesses trading internationally had relied on banks or other financial intermediaries to move money between markets. By 2022, when Adedokun started importing vehicles from the United States, Nigerian fintechs were building products to make international payments easier. However, the available options did not always work for the transactions he needed.
“I tried to use some of the fintech platforms in Nigeria, but it didn’t work because most of my payments were rejected,” Adedokun told TechCabal in an interview. “Then I had to go to the bank, fill a form, and try to do the transfer. There was also a limit on sending international transfers from Nigerian banks.”
He explained that US vehicle auction platforms required payments to come directly from the person or business buying the car, as third-party transfers could be rejected.
Car importation was one example of a deluge of businesses that had to pay suppliers before their orders could be shipped. Total imports stood at over ₦15 billion ($11.1 million) in the first quarter of 2025, according to National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) data.
In 2024, Adedokun founded Autoclear, a business that helped customers source vehicles and pay US auction platforms. While working with importers, he noticed they also had to pay shipping companies, freight forwarders, and brokers, each with its own payment requirements and separate from the auction houses where they buy the cars.
So, he teamed up with his longtime friend Sidney Egwuatu to build Clea, a cross-border payments platform to serve African businesses importing goods from overseas. The company developed the product in stealth before publicly launching in December 2025.
How Clea moves money across borders
Clea allows businesses to manage international supplier payments from a single platform. After signing up and completing verification, a business can fund its account in naira from a Nigerian bank account, convert the funds into the required currency, and add its overseas supplier as a beneficiary. During a live product demonstration, Adedokun showed that the platform supports currencies including the US dollar, British pound, euro, and Chinese yuan.
To add a new supplier, a customer provides details such as the recipient’s address, country, and the nature of their relationship with the beneficiary. After adding the beneficiary, the customer can initiate a payment using the available payment routes for that destination. Adedokun said payments to US beneficiaries could go through ACH, Fedwire or the Real-Time Payments (RTP) network, while payments to other destinations could be routed through SWIFT.
Stablecoins form part of the infrastructure Clea uses to move value between the different parts of this payment process. Adedokun said the platform is designed to keep this complexity out of sight, allowing customers to focus on funding their accounts in naira and ensuring suppliers receive the agreed foreign currency. Customers can also fund their dollar wallets directly with stablecoins, including USDT and USDC, through supported blockchain networks.
Africa’s cross-border payments ecosystem has seen growing stablecoin use for remittances and business settlements. Flutterwave, a Nigerian payments infrastructure company, has begun exploring an integration of USDC settlement into its payments infrastructure. In February, Onafriq partnered with Conduit to use USDC for cross-border payments and payouts to international partners.
“Stablecoins are also part of our settlement infrastructure,” Adedokun explained. “They allow value to move efficiently between parts of the payment stack, but our customers don’t need to understand stablecoins or interact with crypto. They simply know that they were funded in naira and their supplier received dollars, pounds, euros or yuan.”
In August, Clea launched a Vendor Payments feature for businesses that regularly pay the same overseas companies. Adedokun said the product emerged from a deeper understanding of customer needs, shaped by observing how businesses used the platform. Clea serves wholesalers, manufacturers, electronics distributors, fashion businesses, machinery importers and African businesses that depend on international suppliers.
“Initially, we thought speed and FX access were the biggest problems,” he said. “ They are still very important, but once customers started using Clea repeatedly, we realised that trust, payment identity, reconciliation and supplier management are equally important.”
With Vendor Payments, customers can select the supplier from a list of preconfigured vendors whose payment information the platform maintains. They still need to provide the transaction-specific reference the supplier requires, such as a buyer number or lot number, before authorising the payment.
According to Adedokun, Vendor Payments supports US-dollar payments to selected suppliers in the United States, including vehicle auction platforms Copart and IAA.
“If thousands of importers are paying the same shippers, auction companies and suppliers, it doesn’t make sense for every importer to establish that relationship independently every time,” he said. “Once the vendor already exists on Clea, we can simplify the transaction for both sides: fewer incorrect account details, faster reconciliation, better visibility and potentially much faster settlement.”
Clea is betting on importers
Clea makes money primarily from transaction fees and the margin between the exchange rate it sources foreign currency at and the rate it offers customers. Adedokun said the company is building a transaction-driven business, where higher payment volumes and more efficient infrastructure can help lower its underlying costs and improve pricing over time. Since its launch, Clea says it has processed more than $50 million in payments.
“We have to be very disciplined about pricing because our customers understand FX extremely well. These are businesses moving significant amounts of money, so even a small difference in the exchange rate matters,” Adedokun said.
Clea is competing with fintechs such as Verto, Raenest and Grey, which offer businesses multi-currency accounts and international payments. In February, Olayemi Cardoso, Nigeria’s Central Bank (CBN) governor, stated that the country’s average monthly diaspora remittance inflows are about $600 million, showing the scale of cross-border money movement in Nigeria. Adedokun argued that Clea’s focus is narrower: it is building around the specific needs of importers, rather than offering a general-purpose international payments product.
“We don’t think of Clea as another generic international money-transfer product. We are building specifically around the workflow of an importer,” he said. “Our objective is to stay competitive on FX and fees while giving customers speed, reliability, transparency and proper payment documentation.”
When asked about regional expansion, Adedokun said the company is prioritising growth in Nigeria. Its immediate plans include expanding the vendor network, strengthening its payment infrastructure, improving transaction efficiency and reducing the underlying cost of payments.
“There’s a temptation with an African fintech company to announce ten countries very quickly, but there is still a huge amount of market for us to capture in Nigeria,” Adedokun said. “Our immediate priority is to deepen our presence in Nigeria, where we still see considerable opportunities to serve businesses involved in international trade. Ultimately, we want Clea to become the preferred financial infrastructure partner for African businesses trading globally.”

articles.title: The Enough Phone is a $499 Android with a small screen, a removable battery, and fewer distractions
articles.text:
First look: The conversation about increasing smartphone screen sizes has mainly centered on phablets and foldables, but standard-sized phones have also grown over the years. A recent Kickstarter aims to gauge interest from users who want to reverse the trend with an Android device smaller than all but the tiniest currently supported iPhones.
The makers of the Sleke phone have launched a Kickstarter for a new model that packs its deliberately low-key feature set into a more compact form factor. Expected to ship in mid-2027, the device highlights how much smartphones have grown since Apple debuted the original iPhone nearly two decades ago.
Early iPhones measured just 3.5 inches with a 320 x 480 pixel resolution before gradually growing past the four-inch mark. Apple's first phablet, the iPhone 6 Plus, expanded to 5.5 inches, but later standard and phablet-sized phones outgrew it by shrinking the bezels.
The iPhone X, for example, reached 5.8 inches, while the iPhone 17 and 18 now sit at 6.3 inches, just two-tenths of an inch smaller than the iPhone 11 Pro Max and nearly twice as large as the original iPhone. However, Apple still supports a few models in the same ballpark as the Enough Phone's 5.3-inch screen: The iPhone 13 mini is just one-tenth of an inch bigger, at 5.4 inches, while the 3rd-generation iPhone SE is still only 4.7 inches.
However, the Enough Phone also targets users looking for an essentials-only smartphone experience wiFth fewer distractions. The phone comes with either a standard Android 17 installation or Sleke's Odyssey OS, an Android fork that supports only communication and utility apps, with pared-back browser functionality.
Measuring just 133 x 64 x 12mm with a 1,500 x 720 screen resolution and a matte finish, the Enough Phone features a MediaTek Dimensity 7500 processor, clocked at 2.4 GHz, a removable 3,500 mAh battery, 8GB of memory, 128GB of storage, and microSD card support. It includes a 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera and a 32MP front camera that supports face unlock. The power button also supports fingerprint unlock. Software support is planned through 2032.
Pricing starts at $499, with shipments expected to begin in May 2027. However, the creators admit the Enough Phone is still undergoing product tooling, and working samples have yet to be produced. Some technical specs could change before mass production, which is set for April.

articles.title: HP lanza ofertas en todos estos ordenadores portátiles, de sobremesa y all-in-one que son ideales para estudiar o trabajar
articles.text:
Se acerca el Black Friday y se nota en el número y calidad de ofertas que estamos encontrando, incluso en algunas tiendas oficiales de marcas. Un buen ejemplo lo tenemos en HP que ha lanzado descuentos en un buen surtido de ordenadores con distinto formato y que son ideales para estudiar y trabajar. Además, todos ellos vienen con Windows 11 Home o Windows 11 Pro.
- HP OmniBook 3 por 699 euros, un ordenador con pantalla 2K y 16 GB de RAM.
- HP OmniBook 5 Flip por 1.049 euros, un convertible con 1 TB de SSD y pantalla OLED 2K.
- HP ProBook 4 por 1.208,79 euros, un portátil de 16 pulgadas con Windows 11 Pro.
- HP All in One por 999 euros, un ordenador todo en uno con pantalla de 27 pulgadas.
- HP ProDesk 4 por 1.238,01 euros, un ordenador de sobremesa que incluye ratón.
HP All in One

articles.title: El Ejército de EE UU apuesta por Alex, un robot humanoide con protección balística para misiones peligrosas.
articles.text:
El Ejército de EE.UU. está explorando cómo utilizar robots humanoides para realizar tareas que ponen en peligro a sus soldados, y uno de los candidatos que ha llamado su atención es Alex. Desarrollada por el Instituto de Cognición Humana y de Máquinas de Florida (IHMC), Alex es una máquina que acaba de ser seleccionada entre los cinco ganadores del concurso xTechHumanoid.
Su particularidad principal es que incorpora protección balística y combina IA con control humano para desenvolverse en escenarios complicados, aunque todavía no forma parte de ninguna unidad militar operativa. Además, Alex cuenta con 29 articulaciones y mecanismos de movimiento diseñados específicamente para facilitar sus desplazamientos por terrenos irregulares.
Según explica el IHMC en su documentación oficial, el robot dispone de sus sistemas de procesamiento propios, sensores y alimentación energética. Gracias a ello, puede trabajar fuera de instalaciones preparadas para estas máquinas. De hecho, sus desarrolladores quieren que pueda moverse por edificios, superar obstáculos y acceder a lugares con escaleras o escombros en los que enviar a una persona podría suponer un riesgo considerable.
El Ejército busca robots capaces de asumir tareas peligrosas
La selección de Alex forma parte de xTechHumanoid, un concurso que recibió 103 propuestas y reunió a sus finalistas en la base militar de Quantico durante septiembre. Junto al humanoide del IHMC, también ganaron premios tecnologías relacionadas con el almacenamiento y generación de energía, los sensores táctiles y los programas de control.
Así, el Ejército pretende aprovechar estas iniciativas para acelerar el desarrollo de nuevas herramientas, aunque no ha detallado qué impactos puede soportar la protección de Alex ni tampoco confirmó su futuro despliegue. Sorprendentemente, el interés por estas máquinas no es exclusivo de Estados Unidos, dado que una investigación de Reuters reveló en septiembre que China está estudiando aplicaciones militares de los humanoides que van desde tareas de reconocimiento hasta operaciones en entornos urbanos.
De momento, una parte importante de estos proyectos continúa en fase experimental, pero la selección de Alex refleja hasta qué punto los ejércitos están interesados en desarrollar máquinas que puedan acompañar a sus soldados o, por otro lado, entrar primero en zonas especialmente peligrosas.

articles.title: Hackers publish over 320,000 files stolen from 39 Bristol schools on the dark web
articles.text:
Hackers publish over 320,000 files stolen from 39 Bristol schools on the dark web
Bristol school breach has made it to the dark web
- Cyberattack on Bristol schools leads to the online leak of more than 320,000 stolen files from 39 schools
- Officials warn students, parents, and staff to expect phishing attempts and other fraud using exposed data
- Investigation continues as authorities determine whose information was compromised and the extent of the breach
Threat actors have leaked hundreds of thousands of records they stole from Bristol schools in September 2026 onto the dark web.
Bristol city council has issued a warning urging both students and parents to expect phishing attacks and other internet scams, and to be vigilant with incoming communications.
“Following ongoing investigations into the cyber-attack affecting the school's IT network, evidence has been found that data taken during the incident has been published online by the criminals responsible for the attack,” the council said in a new statement. “Specialist investigations have identified a significant number of files believed to have been taken from the network and made available online.”
Data leaks online
Reports of a cyberattack against Trading with Schools (TwS), a service operated by Bristol City Council providing schools with shared IT infrastructure and a range of administrative and operational support services, including financial administration, payroll, HR, and more, emerged in October 2026.
At the time, the council said it first suspected foul play on September 21, and decided to shut down the service four days later, on September 25. Following an initial investigation, it was discovered that someone had planted malware, and that the breach affected 87 schools. Back then, council leader Tony Dyer told the BBC that the investigation “had not identified any evidence that data has been stolen.”
However, it seems that not only that the data was stolen - it also leaked on the dark web. Usually, leaks follow a failed extortion attempt, but we don’t know who the threat actors are or if they actually tried to get the council to pay for the data.
The announcement does not put a figure to this “significant number” of files, but according to the BBC, it’s more than 320,000 files, stolen from 39 schools.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Right now, no one knows the nature of the stolen data, or how much of it includes personally identifiable information (PII). Director of Education and Skills at Bristol City Council, Vik Verma, said its officers were "working through a large amount of material as quickly as possible" to determine what was stolen, the publication wrote.
The BBC says that the 39 schools whose data was stolen “heavily” relied on the system for everyday tasks such as scheduling, lesson plans, recording staff details and payroll information.
Therefore, students and pupils might not be the only ones worrying about potential phishing attacks - school staff could be targeted, as well. To make matters worse, since TwS was shut down, many digital tools and services are unavailable making teachers’ jobs harder, and their working hours longer.
The council has notified Avon and Somerset Police and the Regional Organised Crime Unit, and has brought in third-party specialist cybersecurity advisers to help with the investigation.
Only Bristol schools affected
“At present, it is not possible to confirm all schools or individuals affected by the theft,” the council said. “Officers are working to audit the published files and establish this picture as quickly as possible.” Apparently, only Bristol schools were hit.
Parents and students are now being advised to be careful with unexpected emails, text messages, and even phone calls, and especially if they’re claiming to come from a trusted source. They’re also told not to click on links or open attachments in such messages, and to be wary of requests to reset passwords, “verify” account details, or otherwise provide personal or financial information.
They were also told to use strong and unique passwords for important online accounts, and to turn on multi-factor authentication whenever possible, and to keep a close eye on online accounts and bank statements.

articles.title: Cisco, WatchGuard Release Patches; SonicWall Won’t Fix GMS Flaws
articles.text:
Cisco and WatchGuard this week announced patches for a handful of vulnerabilities in their products, including remote code execution (RCE) and authentication flaws.
WatchGuard published five advisories, including four describing critical-severity bugs. The most severe is CVE-2026-98432 (CVSS score of 9.8), a use-after-free issue in the IPv4 networking code of the Linux kernel.
Fireware OS and WatchGuard AP contain the vulnerable Linux kernel versions, but are not affected by the RCE exploit chain it opens the door to. Dimension runs a vulnerable Ubuntu version, but patches are not available yet, WatchGuard says.
The company rolled out fixes for three critical authentication issues (CVE-2026-121639, CVE-2026-121638, and CVE-2026-121640) and a high-severity integrity validation bug (CVE-2026-121637) in AuthPoint Authentication Gateway.
Cisco released fixes for CVE-2026-76506, a high-severity vulnerability in UCS Central Software that could allow authenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely or leak information.
Both WatchGuard and Cisco say they are not aware of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild.
On Wednesday, Cisco also updated its advisory on CVE-2026-111497, dubbed Node2Shell, HTTP2Shell, and Broccoli2Shell, the exploited out-of-bounds write flaw in Google’s Brotli data compression library that organizations have been scrambling to patch.
Per the updated advisory, 19 Cisco products are affected by Node2Shell, and the company is still investigating dozens more. The security defect also impacts nearly a dozen Splunk products.
This week, SonicWall warned that its legacy centralized management platform Global Management System (GMS), which reached End-of-Life (EOL) in October 2025, is affected by two vulnerabilities that will remain unpatched.
The first, CVE-2026-109593, is a critical-severity file read bug that can be exploited without authentication, while the second, CVE-2026-109594, is a medium-severity SQL injection that could allow attackers to access and modify information in the GMS database.

articles.title: Top 50: Women business angels shaping European Tech | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Europe’s startup ecosystem is home to a growing community of women business angels who back promising founders, support early-stage innovation, and help shape the next generation of successful companies. Beyond providing capital, these investors bring valuable industry expertise, entrepreneurial experience, and networks that help startups grow.
While venture capital often dominates conversations about startup funding, business angels play an important role in Europe’s technology ecosystem, particularly at the earliest stages. It is no surprise therefore that a 2025 report by the European Parliamentary Research Service identifies business angels as a major component of the EU’s innovation ecosystem.
From established investors with extensive portfolios to entrepreneurs-turned-angels backing emerging technologies, this alphabetical list highlights 50 women shaping the European Tech landscape today.
Ana Barjasic is the founder and CEO of Connectology, an angel investor and an ambassador for the European Innovation Council. She supports early-stage companies through investment, fundraising expertise and initiatives connecting European founders with international capital.
Andrea Sinclair is a UK-based angel investor, member of the HERmesa investment syndicate and Venture Partner at Ascension. With extensive early-stage investment experience, she was individually named as an investor in women’s health startup PeriPear’s 2026 pre-seed funding round.
Annegien Blokpoel is the founder and Managing Partner of PerspeXo and founder of Catalyst Impact Investment Club, focusing on early-stage impact investing and sustainable technologies. She was named Europe’s Female Angel Investor of the Year in 2024.
Bettine Schmitz is the co-founder and General Partner of Auxxo Female Catalyst Fund and a co-founder of the Evangelistas angel network. With her investments, Bettine supports women-led and mixed-gender founding teams across Europe’s technology sector.
Céline Lazorthes is a French entrepreneur, angel investor and founder of Leetchi, the FinTech business behind Mangopay. She backs early-stage technology companies, with personally attributed investments in HealthTech startups Lucis and DermaScan during 2026.
Christina Caljé is the founder and CEO of TINTT, an independent angel investor and startup adviser. Her historical investment portfolio includes Lalaland, Newcon and Lucky Sweater, reflecting her interest in emerging technology and consumer businesses.
Cintia Mano is a Portuguese angel investor, COREangels partner and former CEO of COREangels International. She has personally invested in more than 30 startups and was recognised as Europe’s Female Angel Investor of the Year in 2025.
Constanze Buchheim is the founder and Managing Partner of i-potentials, a German leadership advisory firm, and an experienced business angel. Her historical startup investments include Delivery Hero and Empion, alongside her work advising technology companies on leadership and scaling.
Debbie Wosskow is a British entrepreneur, angel investor and co-chair of the Invest in Women Taskforce. A co-founder of WJV and Executive Chair of The Better Menopause, she has backed early-stage businesses including Hybr and advocates for greater access to investment capital for women founders.
Deepali Nangia is a Partner at Speedinvest, co-founder of Alma Angels and an experienced independent angel investor. Her personal investments include PensionBee and Planera, and she works to increase women’s participation in early-stage investing across Europe.
Emilie Dellecker is the co-founder of FoodHack, HackGroup and HackCapital, supporting investment and entrepreneurship in the food technology sector. She invests through the FoodHack angel syndicate and was individually named among the angels participating in Bright Biotech’s 2022 funding round.
Fiona Pathiraja is the Managing Partner of Crista Galli Ventures, a former NHS doctor and an experienced HealthTech angel investor. She has backed early-stage healthcare businesses including Skin Analytics and Jude, focusing on technologies that improve healthcare delivery and patient outcomes.
Georgie Smallwood is the Chief Product and Technology Officer at Moonpig Group, founder of Auxilia Global and an early-stage technology investor. Her investment experience includes backing emerging startups such as LiSA, alongside supporting women in technology and entrepreneurship.
Gesa Miczaika is the co-founder and General Partner of Auxxo Female Catalyst Fund and an experienced business angel. She has personally backed early-stage businesses including Lilio Health and focuses on expanding investment opportunities for female and mixed-gender founding teams.
Gloria Bäuerlein is the founder and General Partner of Puzzle Ventures and an experienced early-stage angel investor. Having previously made more than 25 angel investments, she now backs emerging technology businesses through her venture capital firm.
Helen Oldham is the co-founder of Lifted Ventures, a board member of the UK Business Angels Association and an experienced angel investor. Her personal startup portfolio includes Future Greens and BindEthics, while Lifted Ventures helps connect women-led businesses with early-stage investment capital.
Helena Torras is a Spanish entrepreneur, business angel and Managing Partner of PaoCapital. She has personally invested in early-stage technology companies including Abiquo, Marfeel and TeamEQ, alongside holding board and advisory positions in the Spanish startup ecosystem.
Ilinca Paun is a Romanian angel investor, startup adviser and founder of Bravva Angels, a community supporting women-led and mixed-gender founding teams. Her personal investment portfolio includes Flip, Bright Spaces, Unfrosen and Spark School.
Itxaso del Palacio is a General Partner at Notion Capital and an experienced independent angel investor. Her historical personal investments include BridgeU, Trouva and Leaf.fm, alongside her institutional investment experience supporting European business software companies.
Jane Walerud is a Swedish entrepreneur, DeepTech angel investor and Partner at Walerud Ventures. An early backer of technology companies including Klarna, Lensway and Bluetail, she also serves as co-founder and Executive Chair of climate technology company Paebbl.
Janneke Niessen is the Founding Partner of CapitalT, a serial technology entrepreneur and an experienced angel investor. She supports early-stage technology companies and advocates for greater diversity and inclusion within Europe’s startup and investment ecosystems.
Jessica Holzbach is a German FinTech entrepreneur, co-founder of Penta and Partner and CEO Germany at 0TO9. She also invests personally in early-stage FinTech, artificial intelligence and DeepTech businesses, with documented angel-investing activity as recently as 2024.
June Angelides is a Venture Partner at Samos Investments, founder of Levare Ventures and an experienced angel investor. Her historical personal investments include Sojo and By Rotation, and she supports early-stage founders, particularly women and entrepreneurs from underrepresented backgrounds.
Katja Ruhnke is the Chair of Business Angels Deutschland and co-founder of CK Venture Capital, an investment vehicle through which she and her sister deploy their own capital into startups. Her investments include Mediaire, Fabit, Carbonwave and fairafric, and she was named Germany’s Business Angel of the Year in 2023.
Kerstin Bock is the co-founder and CEO of Openers, a German communications and startup advisory business, and an independent angel investor. Her investment experience includes backing companies such as Levy Health, Ordinary Seafood and The Climate Choice, both personally and through angel-investment programmes.
Laura Modiano works with the startup ecosystem across EMEA at OpenAI and is an independent early-stage angel investor. She supports emerging technology companies and was personally named among the investors in AI writing startup Marker’s 2026 seed funding round.
Lea-Sophie Cramer is a German entrepreneur, angel investor and co-founder of AMORELIE, the sexual wellness e-commerce company. She backs early-stage businesses across consumer and technology sectors and was individually named as an investor in robotics startup Sitegeist’s 2026 funding round.
Lina Chong is a Partner at HV Capital and an experienced early-stage investor with a background in personal angel investing. Her investment experience includes startup Odin, alongside her work supporting technology companies through European venture capital.
Louise Herping Ellegaard is a Danish entrepreneur, founder of Clio Online and an angel investor known for her appearances on the investment television programme Løvens Hule. In 2026, she was named as the investor behind a DKK 1 million investment in mental health education business Psykoterapeuterne.
Lurdes Gramaxo is a Partner at Bynd Venture Capital, President of Investors Portugal and an experienced business angel. Recognised as Europe’s Female Angel Investor of the Year in 2020, she focuses on supporting early-stage technology and sustainability businesses across Portugal and Spain.
Maria Raga is a Venture Partner at Creandum, former CEO of Depop and an experienced angel investor. She backs early-stage consumer and technology companies and was personally named among investors in eComID and District during 2026.
Mariana Bozesan is a serial entrepreneur, impact investor and co-founder of AQAL Capital, an investment business focused on sustainable innovation. She has extensive early-stage investment experience and was recognised as Europe’s Female Angel Investor of the Year in 2019.
Mary McKenna is the co-founder and Chair of AwakenAngels, co-founder of AwakenHub and an experienced independent angel investor. With approximately 35 personal startup investments, she was recognised as Europe’s Female Angel Investor of the Year in 2023 and advocates for greater female participation in angel investing.
Melanie Gabriel is the co-Director and COO of the ETH AI Center, co-founder of Yokoy and a board member of Swiss angel investor network SICTIC. She is also an independent angel investor supporting early-stage technology businesses within Switzerland’s startup ecosystem.
Nina Dremelj is the Managing Partner of Vesna Deep Tech Venture Fund, President of Business Angels of Slovenia and an experienced angel investor. She has personally backed more than 18 early-stage startups and works to strengthen investment networks across Central and Eastern Europe.
Paola Bonomo is an experienced Italian angel investor and Vice Chair of Italian Angels for Growth, one of Italy’s established angel investment networks. Her historical investments include AdEspresso, and she was recognised as Europe’s Female Angel Investor of the Year in 2017.
Rachel Delacour is a French technology entrepreneur, co-founder and CEO of Sweep and an experienced business angel. She personally backs early-stage startups, including women-led businesses, and focuses on supporting technology entrepreneurship and sustainability-focused innovation.
Raja Skogland is a Norwegian angel investor, founder of The Visionary Company & VC and a board member of the Norwegian Business Angel Network. Her investment experience spans more than 70 startups through direct and indirect investments, with a focus on supporting early-stage founders and entrepreneurship across the Nordics.
Roberta Lucca is the co-founder of Bossa Studios, an experienced angel investor and former Venture Partner at Octopus Ventures. She has personally backed more than 20 startups, particularly in technology, gaming and creative industries.
Rupa Popat is the founder and Managing Partner of Arāya Ventures and an experienced independent angel investor with more than 30 personal startup investments. Her portfolio includes businesses such as The Lowdown, Jude and Sojo, and she was individually named among investors in Sync Savings during 2026. See her interview here.
Sarah Turner is the co-founder and CEO of Angel Academe, a UK-based angel investment network supporting technology companies with female founders. An experienced angel investor herself, she works to mobilise private capital for women-led startups and increase the representation of women in early-stage investing.
Sarah Wood is the co-founder and former CEO of Unruly, the advertising technology company, and an experienced angel investor. She supports early-stage businesses across technology and wellbeing and contributes to startup growth through investment, mentoring and board positions.
Selma Prodanovic is the founder of 1MillionStartups, an experienced business angel and startup ecosystem builder based in Austria. She has a history of personal startup investments and has supported female angel investing through initiatives including Rising Tide Europe.
Sherry Coutu is an entrepreneur, founding member of Cambridge Angels and established early-stage technology investor. With a historical portfolio of more than 50 startup investments, she has contributed to the development of the UK’s angel-investing and technology entrepreneurship ecosystem.
Simone Brummelhuis is the Founding Partner of Borski Fund, founder of The Next Women and an experienced angel investor. She supports early-stage businesses and women entrepreneurs and was recognised as Europe’s Female Angel Investor of the Year in 2021.
Sophia Bendz is a Partner at Cherry Ventures and an experienced independent angel investor who has backed numerous early-stage technology startups. She was individually named as an angel investor in Scape’s 2026 seed funding round and continues to support emerging European technology founders.
Triin Hertmann is an Estonian angel investor, President of the Estonian founders Society and former co-founder of Grünfin. She reported five new and two follow-on angel investments in 2025, including investments involving MarkeDroid, Supersimple, Knowzilla, Elnora and Yaga.
Vera Elizabeth Baker is a Partner at 4P Capital, independent angel investor and startup mentor working across European and North American investment ecosystems. She has made more than 30 personal angel investments, with an individually tracked investment in Juniper during 2024.
Verena Pausder is a German entrepreneur, angel investor and Chair of the German Startup Association. An experienced backer of early-stage technology businesses, she was personally named among the investors in construction robotics startup Sitegeist’s 2026 funding round.
Yvonne Bajela is the founder and Managing Partner of Evertrue Capital and an experienced independent angel investor. Her historical personal investments include Sojo, Jumba and LottieLabs, alongside her work backing emerging technology businesses through venture capital.

articles.title: Diseñan un parche de monitoreo que reduce su adherencia para evitar molestias al retirarse de la piel
articles.text:
El control de los signos vitales mediante sensores adheridos al cuerpo resulta indispensable en la medicina moderna, pero retirar apósitos a diario genera traumatismos sobre la piel. Cualquier persona que haya despegado una cinta sanitaria conoce la molestia punzante que causa ese tirón.
Para pacientes con tejidos sumamente vulnerables, como los recién nacidos prematuros en terapia intensiva, los adultos mayores y las personas internadas en estado crítico, esta fricción continua provoca desgarros dérmicos, irritaciones severas y heridas complejas. Frente a este desafío sanitario cotidiano, un equipo internacional desarrolló un parche adhesivo inteligente que se fija con firmeza y se retira sin dañar la piel.
Durante décadas, la ingeniería médica lidió con un dilema constante. Los sensores portátiles exigen una sujeción sólida para registrar la respiración o los latidos cardíacos sin pérdidas de señal por el movimiento. Sin embargo, las cintas tradicionales acumulan tensiones mecánicas excesivas al desprenderse, arrancando capas superficiales del tejido. Los intentos anteriores por fabricar pegamentos reversibles dependían de solventes químicos, sustancias líquidas que a menudo irritan la superficie cutánea y complican el trabajo del personal asistencial.
La solución a este obstáculo llegó mediante una investigación publicada en la revista Nature Communications, cuyos autores diseñaron una plataforma mecánica capaz de modular su fuerza de sujeción a pedido, sin recurrir a químicos ni tirones bruscos.
El desarrollo estuvo a cargo de bioingenieros de Corea del Sur y Estados Unidos, con sede en la Universidad de Ciencia y Tecnología de Pohang. La innovación se basa en los polímeros con memoria de forma, es decir, materiales inteligentes programados para recuperar una estructura geométrica predeterminada cuando reciben un estímulo térmico moderado.
Microestructuras piramidales reducen la adhesión mediante calor leve
El funcionamiento del dispositivo radica en una lámina microscópica con figuras piramidales. En reposo, estas formas permanecen totalmente aplanadas, asegurando un área de contacto amplia y una sujeción firme sobre el cuerpo.
Al momento de retirar el sensor, se aplica calor suave por encima de la temperatura de transición vítrea del polímero, esto es, el umbral físico en el cual la sustancia adquiere elasticidad y retoma su relieve original. Al activarse, las pirámides emergen en segundos, reducen drásticamente la superficie de apoyo contra el tejido y abren bolsas de aire que permiten retirar la banda sin esfuerzo alguno.
Los ensayos mecánicos comprobaron que el sistema reduce la energía de adhesión un 99%, manteniendo una estabilidad impecable durante el monitoreo continuo. Mediante correlación digital de imágenes tridimensionales, un método óptico que registra deformaciones internas bajo la superficie corporal, los investigadores verificaron que el despegue no transmite tensiones nocivas a la dermis.
“Lo que diferencia a este desarrollo de las tecnologías adhesivas existentes es que cambia activamente sus propiedades mediante la microestructura de polímeros con memoria de forma”, explicó Seok Kim, profesor de ingeniería mecánica en la Universidad de Ciencia y Tecnología de Pohang, según el comunicado de prensa.
La seguridad del paciente representó una prioridad durante los ensayos. El material fue calibrado para mantenerse inerte y firme a temperatura corporal, garantizando que los sensores no se desprendan de forma involuntaria con la rutina diaria. Cuando los profesionales necesitan retirarlo, aplican calor suave que activa la transformación en pocos minutos, sin generar molestias térmicas ni riesgos para el tejido cutáneo.
“Este trabajo es significativo porque controla las fuerzas mecánicas en la interfaz entre la piel y el dispositivo, en lugar de simplemente modificar el material adhesivo”, afirmó Jin-Tae Kim, profesor de ingeniería mecánica en la institución surcoreana, según el comunicado de prensa.
La arquitectura de kirigami facilita la adaptación a zonas curvas
El diseño sumó además un patrón inspirado en el kirigami, dicho de otro modo, la técnica tradicional de realizar incisiones precisas en una lámina para otorgarle elasticidad en múltiples direcciones. Esta red geométrica disminuye la rigidez del parche y le permite amoldarse con naturalidad a zonas de gran curvatura, como codos, muñecas o dedos, sin soltarse ante la flexión continua.
Al mismo tiempo, las aberturas microscópicas actúan como canales de ventilación que facilitan la evaporación del sudor, evitando la acumulación de humedad que suele deteriorar la piel bajo apósitos convencionales.
La utilidad clínica se comprobó al integrar el apósito con sensores inalámbricos que registran sonidos cardíacos, ritmo respiratorio y accesos de tos. El material garantizó una captación de datos tan nítida como la de las cintas comerciales, pero con la ventaja de despegarse sin dolor. De hecho, el estudio concluye que “el diseño estructural kirigami mejora aún más la adaptabilidad en superficies anatómicas con curvatura simple y doble”, demostrando su viabilidad en zonas anatómicas complejas.
“Debido a que este enfoque permite tanto una adhesión confiable como un desprendimiento suave, puede extenderse hacia una clase más amplia de tecnologías”, señaló Chang-Hee Son, profesor de la Universidad Tecnológica de Texas, según el comunicado de prensa.
Tras superar las evaluaciones preliminares en modelos biomecánicos y voluntarios sanos, los investigadores proyectan trasladar la plataforma a ensayos clínicos hospitalarios, abriendo un camino concreto para que las salas pediátricas y los centros geriátricos eliminen lesiones accidentales por vendajes de uso diario.

articles.title: Lightspeed meets revenue expectations, but stock drops on Q2 earnings | BetaKit
articles.text:
Montréal retail technology firm Lightspeed Commerce met its earnings outlook for fiscal Q2, but investors were still unimpressed.
The news: The point-of-sale and commerce tech company published its second-quarter financial results this morning, which showed that the company generated nearly $324 million USD ($454 CAD) in revenue. It posted a net loss of $4.2 million USD ($0.03 per share) in Q2—a far cry from the $32.7 million USD ($0.24 per share) it lost during the same period last year—while recording adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) of $22.7 million USD during the three-month period ending Sept. 30.
While Lightspeed’s Q2 sales represent year-over-year growth of just two percent, this figure and other comparisons to the same period last year were impacted by its April 2026 divestiture of Upserve’s US hospitality line to Skyview Equity for up to $81 million USD (a steep discount compared to the price it paid to purchase it back in 2020). Lightspeed’s stock ($LSPD) dropped nearly 15 percent on the day on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
From the source: Given that Upserve exit, Lightspeed pointed to the 15 percent year-over-year organic revenue growth it posted in fiscal Q2 as a more representative measure of the company’s health. Meanwhile, sales in Lightspeed’s two priority markets, retail in North America and hospitality in Europe, were up 17 percent. Lightspeed CFO Asha Bakshani said the firm remains focused on scaling in both and “translating that growth into sustained profitability and cash generation.”
RELATED: Lightspeed stock sinks despite narrower net loss, revenue beat in fiscal Q1
The context: Lightspeed’s stock price soared in 2021 during the early days of the pandemic, plummeted following a short-seller report, and has since struggled to regain its previous heights. Its transformation plan has the company refocusing on particular regions and verticals, divesting from non-core areas (it remains open to more such deals), and shedding staff. Last month, Lightspeed laid off employees and closed vacant positions, impacting 250 total roles; this restructuring followed other cuts earlier this year.
Final thought: Investors have not reacted favourably to the company’s latest earnings: as of publication time, Lightspeed’s stock had dropped to $13.77 CAD per share on the Toronto Stock Exchange, erasing all of its gains so far this year. That performance may be in part due to the broader rout in tech stocks; the Nasdaq is down more than 11 percent so far this month.
Feature image courtesy Lightspeed Commerce.

articles.title: Dropbox acquires Tigris Data for $350M to bolster its AI infrastructure | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Dropbox is making a big push into AI infrastructure with a $350 million acquisition of cloud technology company Tigris Data, marking what appears to be its largest acquisition to date.
Announced Thursday, the deal is expected to strengthen Dropbox’s AI infrastructure capabilities and support the development of DBX Agent Cloud, a new storage platform aimed at businesses and developers building AI models and agents.
Dropbox told TechCrunch via email that the transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026. The company also said it currently has no plans to reduce headcount as part of the acquisition. The company already cut 9% of its global workforce last month, WSJ reported.
DBX Agent Cloud will initially offer object storage as a stand-alone product, allowing businesses to purchase storage independently and use it with existing tools and applications built for Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service), which is a cloud storage service that enables businesses to store and retrieve large volumes of data.
Beyond its infrastructure ambitions, Dropbox is also bringing more AI capabilities to its core product. Users will be able to ask AI to perform supported tasks using their files, choose between different AI models, and connect their Dropbox content to third-party tools, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Muse.
The company also plans to expand DBX Agent Cloud with additional capabilities designed to help AI systems work with different types of content, including documents, images, audio, and video. Other planned additions include filesystem features that will allow AI agents to manage files and maintain continuity across tasks and sessions.
Dropbox says the updated experience has already reached more than 70,000 teams. The initial rollout is available to eligible Standard and Advanced customers in the U.S., U.K., and Australia, with broader availability planned for 2027.
Tigris Data was founded by former Uber engineers who helped develop the ride-hailing company’s storage infrastructure. The company provides cloud storage technology that helps businesses store and access data across different regions. Its platform automatically positions data closer to the users and computing resources that need it, helping reduce access times and improve performance.
Tigris Data raised $25 million in a Series A funding round last year.
While the Tigris deal appears to be Dropbox’s largest acquisition, it is not the company’s first move to expand its AI capabilities through M&A. Dropbox has previously acquired several AI-focused companies, including Reclaim.ai, Promoted.ai, and Mobius Labs.

articles.title: Missão europeia registra nova imagem do sistema de asteroides Didymos
articles.text:
A Agência Espacial Europeia (ESA, na sigla em inglês) divulgou a primeira imagem em close do asteroide Didymos, que integra um sistema binário investigado pela missão Hera. A fotografia foi registrada a aproximadamente 60 quilômetros do corpo celeste e revelou estruturas que podem ajudar cientistas a entender os efeitos de uma colisão provocada pela NASA em 2022.
A imagem foi obtida pela câmera monocromática Asteroid Framing Camera, instalada na espaçonave europeia. Embora o registro mostre claramente o asteroide maior, sua pequena lua, Dimorphos, aparece parcialmente escondida pela sombra.
Didymos tem aproximadamente 780 metros de diâmetro, enquanto Dimorphos mede cerca de 151 metros. Os dois corpos estão separados por aproximadamente um quilômetro.
O destaque da fotografia está na superfície de Didymos. Além de uma elevação central que percorre sua região equatorial, já identificada em observações anteriores, os pesquisadores encontraram diversas rochas, crateras e estruturas que parecem formar padrões de sulcos ou cristas.
“Esta é a outra face de Didymos em relação àquela que a câmera da DART mostrou pouco antes do impacto. É como olhar para um mundo completamente novo”, afirmou Patrick Michel, pesquisador principal da missão Hera e diretor de pesquisa do Centro Nacional de Pesquisa Científica da França (CNRS).
Asteroide pode ter recebido material da colisão
- Uma das hipóteses investigadas pelos cientistas é que algumas das estruturas observadas em Didymos tenham relação com o material lançado ao espaço durante a colisão da missão DART, da NASA;
- Em 26 de setembro de 2022, a espaçonave Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) atingiu intencionalmente Dimorphos. A sonda pesava aproximadamente 580 quilos e colidiu com o asteroide a uma velocidade de 6,1 quilômetros por segundo;
- O experimento tinha como objetivo verificar se uma colisão controlada poderia alterar a trajetória de um asteroide. O resultado superou as expectativas: o período orbital de Dimorphos ao redor de Didymos foi reduzido em aproximadamente 33 minutos.
Segundo Michael Kueppers, cientista da missão Hera na ESA, uma quantidade significativa de material expelido pelo impacto pode ter atravessado a distância de aproximadamente um quilômetro entre os dois asteroides.
Por isso, os pesquisadores não descartam que algumas das características encontradas na superfície de Didymos tenham origem nesse transporte de material. A equipe pretende mapear sistematicamente as estruturas dos dois corpos para identificar possíveis alterações provocadas pela colisão.
Missão Hera vai investigar os efeitos do impacto
Lançada em outubro de 2024, a Hera foi desenvolvida para investigar de perto as consequências do experimento realizado pela NASA. A espaçonave percorreu aproximadamente dois anos até alcançar a região dos asteroides, que atualmente estão a cerca de 196,8 milhões de quilômetros da Terra.
A missão pretende transformar o experimento da DART em técnica de defesa planetária mais bem compreendida e potencialmente repetível. Para isso, a sonda vai analisar as características físicas dos asteroides, a região atingida e as mudanças provocadas pela colisão.
O trabalho também deve ajudar a esclarecer por que a alteração na órbita de Dimorphos foi tão expressiva em comparação com as previsões anteriores.
A ESA informou que imagens detalhadas dos dois asteroides serão apresentadas em 25 de novembro. A expectativa é que os novos registros permitam observar com maior precisão as superfícies dos objetos e os possíveis efeitos do impacto.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: SpaceX plans to build more data center compute than Google's entire lifetime capacity in just 1.5 years — analysts say target is realistic, SpaceX to build staggering 10 gigawatts of compute in 2027 alone
articles.text:
SpaceX plans to build more data center compute than Google's entire lifetime capacity in just 1.5 years — analysts say target is realistic, SpaceX to build staggering 10 gigawatts of compute in 2027 alone
Elon Musk's venture does appear to be moving much faster than its competitors.
A scant two weeks ago, Elon Musk made yet another bold claim: he was "highly confident" that SpaceX could build 10 GW of data center capacity in 2027 alone. The grandiose statement raised a few eyebrows, but in a detailed write-up, the analysts at Semiaccurate explain how that's actually doable... if the stars align. That +10 GW figure over the existing 3 GW would mean the company had built in as much data center capacity in 1.5 years as Google did in its entire existence, according to the post. The site notes that should this forecast ring true, that would make SpaceX the fastest-building hyperscaler on the planet, far outpacing every other player.
As proof of progress, the analysts point to how quickly the Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 buildouts are progressing, estimated from aerial shots and available information. They note that Colossus 2's power generation capacity went from only 0.4 GW in January to a projected 2.4 GW by the time the year is out, at the rate that the relevant hardware is popping up. The site tallies up 9 GW of potential data center capacity across the sites it's tracking, including Colossus and Starbase facilities.
Notably, the facility includes 89 turbines capable of delivering approximately 2.5 GW, helped along by a total of 1377 Tesla battery Megapacks, all already on the campus. Due to emissions regulations, the facility will only eventually be allowed to operate roughly 1.24 GW of its own turbines.
Even with the 1.2 GW eventually coming in from the grid, there's a 300 MW shortfall to be filled by the batteries, which Semianalysis expects will top up with compute load variation and possibly external power. SpaceX has an agreement with the state of Mississippi that lets it temporarily operate the extra turbines, with a promised phase-out by July 2027.
As of September 25, Elon Musk had stated that Colossus 2 already had 550,000 GPUs working, presumably in the extant Macrohard and Macroharder facility. At the time, SpaceX was reportedly gunning to have its Gun Range and Project SPAM centers ready in short order. Judging by the photos, they appear to be progressing at a rapid pace, as there are visible facilities where there was nothing but loose dirt a few months ago — though nothing says the racks of GPUs are in there yet.
Semianalysis' team remarks that SpaceX's builds have become so fast that they kick off well before it decides how the facility will be powered, and the respective power supplies come in. We've all seen the news about the scarcity of GPUs and RAM, but for a data center, just having enough power is problem enough.
If SpaceX can keep its stream of gas turbines coming along, that's quite the achievement by itself. The analysts think that Tesla may be manufacturing mechanical and electrical equipment in modules, presumably ready to install directly from the factory, or even trucks. Heck, the aforementioned temporary turbines are mounted on truck flatbeds as "mobile" power generation, seemingly in a bid to skirt regulations.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
In the hyperscaler world, speed is the name of the game, particularly in these trying times when there are mounting suspicions that not all players will even make it to the finish line. Compute capacity being built and eventually becoming available is enticing for AI players, yes, but they're willing to pay through the nose for anything they can get their hands on right now, as current demand far outstrips supply.
Having facilities built doesn't mean that they're actually working, however, or that they're functioning at their expected rate. Zoning, permits, grid connections, power generation constraints, water supply, and public opposition are some of the few problems that have plagued builds most everywhere, none of which relate to the existence and installation of computing hardware.
Microsoft's Satya Nadella put it clearly: "You may actually have a bunch of chips sitting in inventory that I can’t plug in. In fact, that is my problem today." That's far from the only report that a significant percentage of AI accelerators are still stuck in warehouses, on hold until they can go fulfill their duties in a server rack somewhere.
Since building a datacenter involves many moving parts, even assuming that Colossus 2 wraps up as quickly as it appears to be, that doesn't necessarily mean that SpaceX will be able to replicate its success across its other sites. There is no luck involved in engineering, yes, but some factors like availability of hardware and materials, changes in legal winds, and public opposition are hard to predict, even for someone with resources as extensive as Elon Musk.
And yet, the folks at Semianalysis note that two data centers at Starbase are undergoing rapid construction, suggesting that SpaceX can indeed replicate Colossus' success. They attribute the speed to SpaceX having most of the infrastructure and power generation hardware effectively in-house, via Tesla's manufacturing ability. If that assessment holds, the firm could be bypassing supplier lead times that other hyperscalers have to contend with.
Even if SpaceX doesn't reach its "10 GW in a year" target, if the Colossus buildouts are anything to go by, the company may well be moving faster than anyone else in this space. Metrics aside, in the AI gold rush, coming first is all that's needed to win.

Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.
