articles.title: El 'Universo DC' ya tiene nueva película en marcha, aunque no es exactamente lo que los fans esperaban
articles.text:
Solo un par de semanas después del estreno de Clayface en cines, el Universo DC ya ha puesto en marcha su próxima película. La compañía liderada por James Gunn y Peter Safran no quiere que el ritmo de producciones baje, y menos aún ahora que Warner Bros., estudio al que pertenecen, se va a unir a Paramount en una de las fusiones más históricas de Hollywood. Por ello, ya ha trascendido cuál será el siguiente título de la saga.
Tal y como ha informado Deadline, DC Studios ya ha puesto en marcha una nueva película de John Constantine. Este popular personaje de los cómics, obra de Alan Moore, Steve Bissette y John Totleben, es un antihéroe que apareció por primera vez en viñetas en 1985. Se trata de un detective brujo muy cínico, astuto y estafador, aunque desea hacer algo bueno con su vida.
El regreso de Constantine a los cines con una nueva película es una noticia que los fans del Universo DC llevaban mucho tiempo esperando. Pero no exactamente así. Y es que a principios de los años 2000, el actor Keanu Reeves protagonizó una cinta que se ha convertido en un clásico de culto entre los aficionados al género. Por ello, durante años se ha pedido insistentemente una secuela. En ocasiones incluso el proyecto parecía a punto de salir adelante.
En marcha una nueva película de Constantine para el Universo DC
Con el anuncio de la próxima película de John Constantine para DC Studios, sin embargo, parece que las esperanzas de ver a Reeves retomando el personaje se desvanecen. Este filme, que está apenas en sus primeras fases de desarrollo, sería una nueva versión que llevará un guion escrito por Francis Galluppi, responsable del libreto de la próxima Evil Dead Wrath (2028).
Por el momento, DC Studios no ha querido hacer declaraciones al respecto de la nueva película de Constantine dentro de su universo cinematográfico. Por tanto, no se sabe exactamente si formará parte de la franquicia de Superman, Supergirl, los Linternas Verdes y compañía o si será una entrega independiente, de los DC Elseworlds, al estilo The Batman 2. En los próximos meses se esperan novedades al respecto.

articles.title: EA is bringing 25 classic PC games to Steam
articles.text:
Electronic Arts is launching 25 classic games on Steam, including “Anniversary Editions” of the motorcycle racer Road Rash and six Wing Commander titles. These Anniversary Editions preserve “the original look, feel and creative intent of the game” but also have quality-of-life updates to support modern systems and controls and improve performance, according to EA.
EA is bringing 25 classic PC games to Steam
Thanks to the discovery of a ‘physical media vault,’ EA was able to restore Road Rash and six Wing Commander titles for new Anniversary editions.
The seven new editions were “inspired” by the discovery of a “physical media vault” with “thousands” of Betacam, VHS, and D1 tapes and “other media assets,” EA says. As part of the digitization process, EA was able to recover master FMV sequences and reedited them to restore more than 1,500 scenes from the games. The updated Wing Commander games also officially incorporate some community-made mods.
You’ll be able to get the Road Rash and Wing Commander Anniversary editions for $9.99, and the other classic games, including Ultima and Crusader titles, will be available for $4.99. You can grab them on Steam, GOG, and the EA App.

articles.title: Why Testing Automated Driving Is Harder Than It Looks
articles.text:
Instead of waiting for rare situations to occur on public roads, engineers can create those situations virtually.
Most people assume the hardest part of automated driving is building the technology itself. After all, enabling a vehicle to recognize traffic signs, detect pedestrians, stay within its lane, and react to complex traffic situations sounds like an extraordinary engineering challenge.
It is.
But many automotive engineers would argue that the bigger challenge comes afterward. How do you prove the system works safely?
As vehicles become increasingly software-defined, validation has become one of the most important and demanding aspects of ADAS development. ADAS validation is the process of evaluating whether driver assistance functions behave reliably across relevant driving scenarios, environmental conditions, system configurations, and software versions. The challenge is no longer simply creating intelligence. It is demonstrating that intelligence performs reliably across an almost limitless variety of situations.
Imagine a new ADAS function successfully navigating a busy urban environment. The vehicle detects traffic signs, maintains safe distances, and responds appropriately to nearby vehicles and pedestrians. Does that mean the system is ready?
Not necessarily. A single test drive represents only one combination of conditions:
The next drive could look entirely different:
The real challenge is not proving a system works once. It is proving it works consistently across countless different situations.
In ADAS validation, a scenario represents a driving situation defined by elements such as road layout, traffic participants, vehicle behavior, weather, lighting, and sensor conditions. Changing just one variable creates a new scenario.
Now multiply those variables across the thousands of roads, weather conditions, traffic situations, and vehicle configurations an automated driving system may encounter. The result is what many engineers call the scenario explosion problem. There are simply too many possible combinations to evaluate using traditional physical testing alone.
Most organizations no longer struggle to create a handful of test scenarios.
The real challenge begins when those scenarios grow into thousands, hundreds of thousands, or even millions of variations.
Modern ADAS teams must answer questions such as:
As a result, validation is becoming less about individual test cases and more about managing scenario portfolios, measuring coverage, and continuously evaluating software changes.
This is where simulation moves beyond simple virtual driving and becomes part of a broader validation workflow.
Ironically, some of the most important situations to test are also the least likely to occur.
These are often called edge cases:
These events may occur infrequently in the real world, but they often represent the greatest risks to safety. Finding enough instances of these situations through road testing alone can take enormous amounts of time and effort. In many cases, engineers need a way to recreate these situations repeatedly and under controlled conditions.
Road testing remains a critical part of vehicle development. Nothing can completely replace evaluating a vehicle in the real world. However, as ADAS functionality grows, the limitations of physical testing become increasingly apparent:
The limitations of physical testing do not mean that road and proving-ground testing become less important. Instead, the opportunity lies in connecting them more closely with simulation.
One example comes from Daimler Truck, which has publicly described a validation approach that combines simulation, proving-ground testing, and public-road evaluation for advanced safety assistance systems. Read the Daimler Truck press release.
In this type of workflow, simulation can be used to explore a broader range of situations and identify relevant corner cases before selected scenarios move into controlled physical testing. The physical results can then provide another source of evidence for understanding system behavior.
This reflects an important shift in ADAS validation: virtual and physical testing are not competing approaches. Their value increases when they are connected within the same validation process.
Connecting virtual and physical validation also highlights another critical requirement: repeatability. Engineers need more than successful results. They need confidence that results can be reproduced. Consider a near-collision event encountered during testing. If the exact same situation can be recreated repeatedly, engineers can:
Repeatability transforms testing from observation into engineering. Without it, understanding system behavior becomes significantly more difficult.
This is where simulation begins to change the equation. Instead of waiting for rare situations to occur on public roads, engineers can create those situations virtually. A scenario can be repeated hundreds or thousands of times while controlling individual variables:
The emerging validation model is therefore not “virtual or physical.” It is a connected loop in which simulation helps identify what should be investigated further, while controlled physical testing provides additional evidence for evaluating system behavior.
Simulation also enables a level of automation that is impossible to achieve through physical testing alone. Modern development teams increasingly integrate virtual validation into continuous development workflows, allowing software updates to trigger automated regression campaigns against predefined scenario libraries. This helps organizations identify issues earlier, evaluate changes more consistently, and accelerate development without sacrificing confidence.
As vehicles continue to evolve, validation is becoming a data problem as much as an engineering problem. Future development workflows will increasingly combine:
The goal is not simply to run more tests. It is to create validation workflows that continuously measure coverage, identify gaps, and deliver evidence that software behaves safely as systems evolve.
In this future, success will depend not only on building intelligent vehicles, but also on building validation processes that can scale alongside them.
ADAS validation is not about demonstrating that a system works in one situation. It is about building confidence across a broad range of relevant driving scenarios, including rare edge cases that are difficult to reproduce through road testing alone.
Modern ADAS validation requires more than scenario creation. Engineering teams need to manage scenario libraries, integrate existing toolchains, connect sensor and vehicle models, automate regression testing, and scale validation across increasingly complex software releases.

articles.title: Google Cloud API Gateway Introduces Streaming Support for Real-Time and AI-Powered Applications
articles.text:
Google has announced the public preview of streaming support for API Gateway, extending its traditional request-response model to support applications requiring real-time communication. According to Google, this is particularly relevant for AI applications that provide streaming model responses, multi-step agent workflows, and interactive sessions.
The new functionality enables streaming endpoints to operate behind API Gateway while retaining existing gateway policies and security controls, thereby addressing a previous limitation:
Until now, developers building those experiences in API Gateway had to make an uncomfortable choice: put API Gateway in front of their APIs and give up streaming, or route streaming endpoints around the gateway and give up the authentication, API key enforcement, and observability that made the gateway essential in the first place.
API Gateway supports several streaming patterns, including Server-Sent Events (SSE), chunked transfer encoding and HTTP response streaming, WebSockets, and gRPC. Streaming connections can remain open for up to one hour, after which clients must establish a new connection if continued communication is required.
The new release introduces streaming support without requiring changes to existing API specifications or the use of specific APIs, extensions, or annotations. Google emphasizes that all existing API configurations and capabilities continue to work as before, including API key enforcement, JWT validation, service account authentication to backends, Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring integration, and path templating and request routing.
Another benefit of the new release is the introduction of predictable gateway hostnames. Previously, gateway hostnames included a generated hash and could only be determined after the gateway had been created. Now, they follow a deterministic format: GATEWAY_ID-PROJECT_NUMBER.REGION.gateway.dev, allowing developers to reference and configure them before creating the resource.
Google highlights the importance of streaming support for AI applications, where model responses are generated progressively rather than delivered as a single, complete response. Using the new functionality, developers will be able to stream model responses in real time, update agent progress during multi-step tasks, support tool-calling protocols and connections to remote MCP servers, and handle interactive AI applications.
API Gateway also supports model routing, providing a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint to route requests to Gemini, Claude, or OpenAI gpt-oss models based on the model field in the request payload.
Model routing plus streaming means clients get a familiar, standards-based streaming interface, while you retain centralized control over which models are reachable, by whom, and under what policy.
Commenting on Google's announcement, X user emildrops highlights two important limitations. First, "existing gateways can't be switched in place" and, second, "latency measures the whole stream, not time to first byte... so latency graphs will look broken for reasons that aren't bugs". Similarly, LinkedIn user Ehsan Elahi Zaheer points out that:
Monitoring also needs care: gateway request-latency metrics measure stream duration, not time to first byte. A single latency chart can hide very different user experiences.
During the preview period, developers must explicitly enable the new functionality by specifying the --enable-streaming command-line flag when creating a gateway.

articles.title: “AI pays off when we redesign the process, not just automate it”: Opus’ DACH lead Xenia Schmahl (Sponsored) | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Founded in 2021, AppliedAI builds Opus, the AI transformation platform that rewires how enterprises run and ties every change to the bottom line.
Many companies have tested AI, but few have scaled it across their workflows and systems. Opus closes this gap. Opus starts with how a process really runs today, and then redesigns it for AI. The result is a workflow built for the real world, which allows AI to scale in daily operations. Every run of the workflow and every decision, whether made by an AI agent or a person, is recorded.
Over time, this creates a digital twin of the organisation’s processes. Companies can always show what happened, why it happened, when, and based on which data. Before a project starts, Opus calculates what the new process will deliver, and it measures the result after go-live. Opus is now launching in the DACH region. The focus is on insurance, healthcare and other regulated industries, where strict rules make reliable and traceable AI especially valuable.
Why is 2026 the right moment for European enterprises to move AI from pilots to production, and why is DACH both a demanding and promising market?
AI models are no longer the bottleneck. When pilots fail, the reasons are usually operational: old systems are hard to connect, results are not measured, and there is no governance. These are exactly the problems we built Opus to solve. Opus takes an existing process, redesigns it for AI, and runs it in production with full governance and a complete audit trail. Today, this works reliably in regulated environments. That is why we are bringing Opus to DACH now.
DACH is a demanding market. Regulation is strict, data must stay in the region, and buyers expect governance from day one. But this is also what makes the market so promising. Banks, insurers and healthcare providers here run large, document-heavy back offices. This is exactly where reliable, well-governed AI creates the most value.
What most often prevents European companies from scaling AI beyond pilots, and how should they choose the processes and solutions most likely to deliver value?
I see three main reasons why pilots stall. First, they are built on assumptions, not on the real process, so the first exception breaks them. Second, integration and governance come too late. Third, nobody owns a clear target, and often there is no way to measure success at all.
Good starting points share a few traits. The work is high-volume and repetitive. It spans several systems and involves many documents and exceptions. And someone owns the result. But the most important criterion is the return on investment. Not every process that can use AI should use AI.
AI pays off when we redesign the process, not just automate it. That is why, at Opus, we start by mapping how a process really runs today and measuring its baseline: time, cost, quality and error rates. Opus draws on its Work Knowledge Graph, a proprietary model of over a million enterprise processes organised by industry and jurisdiction. Then we calculate the expected return of the redesigned process, ideally before anything is built or changed. Once the new workflow is live, we measure again. This way, the value is clear before the project starts and provable after it goes live.
Then start with one process, prove it on real data within weeks, and expand from there. Choosing well also means knowing where AI does not belong. If an existing system already handles a process end to end, leave it alone.
Beyond cost savings, how should companies measure the success of AI-driven automation?
Cost savings are easy to report, but they are rarely the biggest benefit. I recommend five measures:
- Capacity: Can the team handle more work without adding people?
- Quality: How accurate is each field, for each case type? Measure this on test data that was never used for training. A single “97% accurate” number hides too much.
- Exceptions: A high automation rate is not enough. A wrong result that slips through unnoticed is worse than one that is flagged.
- Cycle time: How long does a case take from start to finish? Most delays come from waiting for human review, not from the machine.
- Auditability: In regulated industries, full traceability is a result in itself.
One example from our work: with Opus, a financial regulator cut licensing reviews from weeks to minutes of structured preparation, and every step remained fully traceable.
With the EU AI Act and strict data-protection rules, how can regulated sectors such as insurance and healthcare turn compliance and governance into a competitive advantage?
Many companies see governance as a cost. I see it as the thing that lets you go live. In regulated industries, the key question is not “Can AI do this?” It is “Will this pass risk, legal and security review?”
Governance becomes an advantage when it is built in from the start. That means AI acts within clear limits, humans approve the critical steps, every action is logged, and sensitive data stays in the company’s environment. This is how we built Opus: governance is part of the foundation. Every run and every decision is recorded, and over time this builds a Digital Twin of the organisation: a living model of how the business runs and what each part of it is worth. Companies that add compliance later often cannot use AI in these processes at all.
One more point: credibility with risk teams comes from precision. Be clear about which rules apply to you, from the EU AI Act to BaFin or FINMA. And never claim more than you can prove.
As AI agents take on more complex workflows, how will the relationship between employees and AI evolve, and what role do leadership, trust, and culture play?
Nobody can say how work will look in ten years. But for the next few years, we have a clear view. AI will free up a large share of the time knowledge workers spend today on routine tasks like typing, searching and checking. We should not pretend otherwise.
The real question is what happens with that time. If companies redesign their processes now, they can create meaningful new responsibilities for these people. Employees can then focus on the work where their judgement counts and where they create real value: complex cases, difficult decisions and contact with customers.
But these new roles do not appear on their own. They must be made visible. When we map a process with Opus, we define exactly where AI does the work and where a human needs to decide. This makes the human role clear from the start, instead of leaving it to chance.
This is where leadership matters most. Leaders need to explain openly what will change, and show employees where their future role lies. Trust grows when people can see that AI works within clear limits, and when they help shape the new processes themselves. Culture follows when people experience that AI takes over routine work, not their responsibility.
Over the next three to five years, where can European businesses differentiate from the US and China in enterprise AI, and what should leaders do today to prepare?
Europe will probably not build the biggest AI models. But that is not where most value will come from. Europe’s strength is trusted, well-governed AI in regulated industries, built under its own rules and in its own languages. That is a real advantage, if leaders use it.
There are four things leaders should do now:
- Start with reality. Map how your processes really run today, including all the exceptions and workarounds. The process in the handbook is rarely the process people actually follow. With Opus Discover, AI agents interview the people doing the work and map how the process really runs, including the exceptions and workarounds.
- Define your KPIs before you start. Decide what should improve, for example cycle time, quality or capacity, and measure where you stand today. Without a baseline, you cannot prove success.
- Think in processes, not in tools. Don’t buy a new AI tool for every task. Look for a platform that can run many processes in one place, with one standard for governance.
- Plan the new roles early. Decide where people will add value once AI takes over routine work, and communicate it openly.
The winners will not be the companies with the biggest models. They will be the ones that turned AI into part of how they operate, while others were still running pilots.

articles.title: Anthropic imagine une carte d'identité pour chaque modèle d'IA
articles.text:
Anthropic a mis en ligne mardi 3 novembre un travail de recherche accompagné de son code en open source : FlashProve, un système conçu pour prouver qu’une réponse provient bien d’un modèle d’IA donné. Le laboratoire parle d’« inférence prouvable » : chaque réponse peut être rattachée cryptographiquement au modèle qui l’a produite, à la manière d’une signature au bas d’une lettre. L’entreprise prévient d’emblée qu’aucun déploiement n’est prévu, chez elle comme ailleurs.
Comment établir la carte d’identité d’un modèle ?
Le dispositif repose sur une empreinte que chaque laboratoire publierait pour chacun de ses modèles, et à laquelle n’importe quelle réponse pourrait ensuite être confrontée. Cette empreinte ne dévoile rien des poids, les réglages internes qui concentrent la valeur d’un modèle et que l’industrie garde sous clé. Les acteurs les plus fermés (OpenAI est cité en exemple) pourraient donc jouer le jeu sans ouvrir leurs coffres. Le parallèle le plus parlant vient de la messagerie : ces signatures numériques qui confirment au destinataire l’identité de l’expéditeur d’un e-mail. La vérification se veut enfin assez légère pour s’exécuter sur un simple appareil local, l’ordinateur d’un particulier compris.
Un fournisseur pourrait aujourd’hui glisser en douce un modèle moins coûteux derrière un abonnement facturé plein tarif, ou gonfler un classement en faisant plancher un modèle plus puissant que celui annoncé. FlashProve rendrait la supercherie détectable. L’été a d’ailleurs fourni un cas d’école, quand des services tiers faisaient passer les réponses de Claude pour celles de DeepSeek ou de Kimi, avant d’être confondus par Anthropic. « Comment un utilisateur peut-il vérifier ces affirmations ? » : la question posée par les chercheurs vise jusqu’aux audits de sécurité que des agents d’IA affirment avoir menés. Au moment de payer la prestation, rien ne distingue aujourd’hui le grand modèle promis d’un remplaçant au rabais.
Pourquoi personne ne compte s’en servir pour l’instant ?
Anthropic qualifie l’ensemble de « progrès intermédiaires, et non un programme de recherche achevé », et n’annonce aucun projet de mise en service, pas même pour ses propres modèles. La spécification technique et le code sont publiés sur GitHub sous licence libre ; le laboratoire dit les partager pour que d’autres équipes bâtissent dessus, concurrents compris.
La piste prolonge un chantier entamé cet été, quand l’entreprise détaillait l’étiquetage des textes générés par Claude et promettait un détecteur accessible à tous. L’étiquetage dit d’un texte qu’une IA l’a écrit ; l’empreinte de modèle monte d’un étage et désigne laquelle. Concrètement, un abonné pourrait un jour lancer la vérification depuis sa machine et confirmer que la réponse facturée au prix du dernier modèle en provient bien.

articles.title: En Japón, un hombre se encuentra con un Toshiba Libretto 50 con Windows 95 que era un ordenador portátil de lujo a su salida en 1997
articles.text:
Cuando un hombre visitó una tienda de electrónica de segunda mano en Akihabara (uno de los barrios tecnológicos más conocidos de Tokio), nunca pensó que se toparía de frente con una joya casi única. Se trataba de un Toshiba Libretto 50 con Windows 95 que estaba a la venta por unos 140 euros, pero lo más curioso es que este pequeño portátil llegó a costar más de 1.700 euros cuando salió al mercado en 1997.
Toshiba presentó el Libretto 50 el 7 de enero de aquel año, y en su momento llamó mucho la atención por sus dimensiones. Medía 21 centímetros de ancho, 11,5 de fondo y 3,4 de grosor, y pesaba unos 850 gramos que lo colocaban muy por debajo de los portátiles convencionales de aquella época que podían pesar varios kilos. Así, hablamos de un sistema Windows completo en un dispositivo que casi cabía en la palma de tu mano.
En su interior había un procesador Intel Pentium de 75 MHz, 16 MB de memoria RAM y un disco duro de 810 MB. También tenía una pantalla en color de 6,1 pulgadas con resolución de 640 × 480 píxeles, además de un pequeño teclado con 80 teclas. Y aunque estas características resultan bastante modestas actualmente, el ordenador podía ejecutar programas como Word 95, Excel 95 o Internet Explorer 3.
Tener un ordenador tan pequeño en 1997 no salía precisamente barato
El Libretto 50 se comercializó en Japón por entre 228.000 y 248.000 yenes, dependiendo de la versión elegida. Al cambio aproximado que recoge la publicación original, hablamos de unos 1.590 a 1.730 euros, una cantidad considerable para un portátil de aquella época. Eso sí, Toshiba tuvo que desarrollar un sistema de refrigeración que aprovechaba la propia placa base para disipar el calor, además de utilizar paneles de magnesio de apenas 0,7 milímetros para conseguir un equipo tan compacto.
La autonomía tampoco era especialmente elevada, ya que su batería ofrecía entre una hora y media y dos horas de funcionamiento, aunque podía llegar a las cuatro horas con una batería de mayor capacidad. Y para utilizar determinados accesorios, como una disquetera externa o conectar otros periféricos, había que recurrir a adaptadores y módulos adicionales.
Pese a su elevado precio, Toshiba decidió llevar el ordenador fuera de Japón unos meses después. En junio de 1997 anunció su comercialización internacional y, en Estados Unidos, el Libretto 50 llegó con un precio anunciado de 1.999 dólares. La compañía también fabricó una versión más rara, llamada Libretto 50M, con pantalla táctil y destinada a la aseguradora japonesa Meiji Life, aunque este último modelo no llegó a venderse al público general.

articles.title: Hackers backdoor Linux servers using trojanized CWP web server
articles.text:
A new Linux malware called CWPdoor is being distributed through a trojanized version of cwpsrv, the web server behind the Control Web Panel (CWP) management interface.
CWPdoor acts as a passive backdoor that sits dormant on the compromised system until the attacker sends a specially crafted request.
Researchers at XLab, the cybersecurity research arm of QiAnXin Technology Group, describe CWPdoor as "exceptionally stealthy" due to its passive triggering and log suppression feature.
CWP, formerly known as CentOS Web Panel, is an open-source web hosting administration solution similar to cPanel and Plesk that allows users to manage web servers and services such as email, DNS, and databases.
According to XLab, more than 340,000 CWP instances have been exposed on the public web over the past month.
The researchers discovered the CWPdoor malware on June 29 after capturing a script posing as an updater that replaced the legitimate 'cwpsrv' binary with a malicious version.
The script replaces cwpsrv versions 1.15.10 and 1.24.0, and takes several steps to hide the switch, like restoring file and directory timestamps, deleting temporary files, and wiping the command-history log.
The malware operators activate the backdoor by sending it commands to be executed, in the form of an encrypted HTTP header (X-Ngx-Integrity-Data). The request also contains headers for the timestamp (X-Ngx-Integrity-Time) and the RSA signature (X-Ngx-Integrity-Sig).
Commands and their output are encrypted using the AES-256-CBC cipher to keep them protected.
The backdoor checks whether the timestamp falls within a five-minute window and verifies the RSA signature before decrypting the command and passing it to a helper process for execution.
“Changing either the timestamp or the ciphertext independently invalidates the signature,” XLab explains.
“By binding the three fields together and enforcing a ±300-second time window, the mechanism provides replay protection and authorization control.”
The backdoor also interferes with the server’s logging module to prevent the triggering request from appearing in the access logs.
After finding the initial infection script, the researchers saw CWPdoor uploaded to VirusTotal on September 30 in an archive that included the Ebury backdoor.
What caught their attention was that the malicious cwpsrv file (cwpsrv.suspeito) in the archive had zero detections.
"This indicates that the campaign was not merely experimental: real victims already exist in the wild," the researchers say, adding that the connection between Ebury and CWPdoor remains unclear.
Ebury is a Linux backdoor and credential stealer botnet operation active since at least 2009. A report from cybersecurity company ESET in May 2024 said that the malware had infected nearly 400,000 servers since it emerged.
The researchers recommend that administrators check for the ngx_http_integrity_helper Unix socket, suspicious cwpsrv helper processes, and X-Ngx-Integrity strings in the server binary.
If a compromise is confirmed, replace the backdoored binary with a legitimate copy, upgrade to the latest version, rotate all control panel credentials, and investigate the host for additional malware.

articles.title: iOS 27.3: Diese Funktionen könnten mit dem nächsten Update aufs iPhone kommen
articles.text:
iOS 27.3: Diese Funktionen könnten mit dem nächsten Update aufs iPhone kommen
Seit Mitte September können iPhone-Besitzer:innen iOS 27 installieren. Allerdings enthält das Betriebssystem noch nicht alle Funktionen, die Apple im Sommer auf der WWDC versprochen hat. Diese reicht das Unternehmen in kleinen Schritten nach. iOS 27.2 enthält etwa ein Feature für die Nachrichten-App, das Daten direkt zu Kalendereinträgen machen kann.
Ein Feature entfernte Apple allerdings aus der finalen Version wieder: Die neu gestaltete Health-App war Teil der Beta-Version, hat es schlussendlich aber doch noch nicht aufs iPhone geschafft. In der ersten Beta zu iOS 27.3 hat Apple sie nun wieder integriert, wie 9to5Mac berichtet. Diesmal ist sie offenbar gekommen, um zu bleiben.
iOS 27.3 bringt die neue Health-App zurück
Die neu designte App bietet demnach drei zentrale Features: Der Insights-Tab liefert Informationen zu Herz-, Fitness- und Schlafdaten und schlüsselt sie auf einer “For you”-Seite passend zu euren Gewohnheiten auf. Im Longevity-Tab sollt ihr euer “Gesundheitsalter” vorfinden, das sich laut 9to5Mac aus Apple-Watch-Daten wie der geschätzten VO2Max-Leistung oder der Herzruhefrequenz zusammensetzt. Mit der dritten Funktion sollen Nutzer:innen mithilfe von iPhone und Apple Watch Werte zu Flexibilität, Kraft oder Balance selbst zu Hause messen könen.
Ein großes Update gibt es zudem für den Safari-Browser. Der bekommt eine neue, optionale Ansicht, bei der Tabs vertikal neben dem eigentlichen Inhalt erscheinen. Das dürfte vor allem auf dem großen Bildschirm des iPhone Duo und auf iPads ein Vorteil sein, weniger aber auf normalen iPhones. Alle profitieren dann aber von einem neuen, adaptiven Dark-Mode. Der soll Webseiten auf Knopfdruck im dunklen Design erscheinen lassen, auch wenn diese das gar nicht unterstützen.
Weitere Neuheiten betreffen den Standby-Modus normaler iPhones. Er lässt sich mit dem Update auch auf normalen iPhones besser an die eigenen Wünsche anpassen, indem sie ihn etwa um Wetter- oder Kalender-Compilations erweitern oder die Hintergrundfarbe wechseln.
Für das iPhone Duo kommt außerdem eine neue Bedienungshilfe: der Einhandmodus. Auf normalen iPhones sorgt er dafür, dass die obere Bildschirmhälfte per Swipe nach unten wandert, damit man bequem Bedienelemente erreichen kann. Das iPhone Duo ist allerdings schon kompakt. Deswegen funktioniert der Modus hier etwas anders. Per Swipe schiebt ihr die Inhalte vom linken auf den rechten Bildschirmbereich – oder andersherum.
Neue Siri-Funktionen leider nicht für uns
Vorerst nicht für deutsche iPhones vorgesehen sind neue Siri-AI-Funktionen. Im Stile eines KI-Agenten kann Siri für Nutzer:innen künftig Aktionen in Apps ausführen. So ist es möglich, den Versand einer iMessage mithilfe der Sprachassistenz zu timen, oder Fotos per Sprachbefehl in der Fotos-App zu bearbeiten. Außerdem kann Siri Tab-Gruppen in Safari oder Playlists in Apple Music erstellen.
Die Beta zu iOS 27.3 legt außerdem den Grundstein für die kontroverse “Audio Intelligence”-Funktion auf der Apple Watch. Dabei kann Siri über den Tag hinweg aufgenommene Unterhaltungen zusammenfassen oder auf Wunsch ein Transkript der vergangenen 15 Sekunden in einer Unterhaltung erstellen.
Dass alle Features in der fertigen Version von iOS 27.3 landen, ist nicht gesagt. Apple kann sie jederzeit wieder aus den nachfolgenden Versionen entfernen. Wann genau das Update erscheint, bleibt vorerst offen. Apple will die neue Health-App aber noch 2026 aufs iPhone bringen. Zunächst wird das Unternehmen einige Folge-Betas veröffentlichen, inklusive der öffentlichen Beta, die neugierige Nutzer:innen installieren können.

articles.title: L'IA menace désormais les cartouches de jeux Nintendo Switch et Switch 2
articles.text:
L’intelligence artificielle n’en finit plus de bousculer le marché des composants. Après la mémoire de nos PC, ses besoins pourraient avoir une conséquence inattendue : fragiliser la production des cartouches Nintendo. Un fournisseur historique préfère désormais miser sur des puces plus rentables. Faut-il craindre une hausse des prix des jeux Switch et Switch 2 ?
Quel rapport entre les serveurs qui font tourner les IA et les petites cartouches que l’on glisse dans une Nintendo Switch ? Les deux dépendent, à des degrés différents, d’une industrie de la mémoire sous pression. Et quand les fabricants doivent choisir ce qui sort de leurs usines, les produits les moins rentables risquent de passer au second plan. C’est précisément le tournant annoncé par Macronix, un important fournisseur taïwanais de puces utilisées dans les cartouches Nintendo.
Pourquoi les cartouches Nintendo deviennent moins intéressantes à fabriquer
Dans son bilan du troisième trimestre, Macronix explique vouloir se retirer progressivement de la production de mémoire ROM, celle qui permet notamment de stocker les données des jeux sur cartouche. Cette activité a reculé de 39 % sur un an et ne représente plus que 5 % de ses ventes. Le groupe privilégie d’autres types de puces mémoire, pour lesquels la demande et les marges sont meilleures.
L’explication tient aussi aux capacités de fabrication : les lignes de production ne peuvent pas être agrandies du jour au lendemain. Macronix évoque une capacité de 25 000 galettes de silicium de 12 pouces par mois, ainsi que de lourds investissements dont les effets ne se feront pas sentir immédiatement. Dans ce contexte, consacrer de la place à des composants peu rentables devient moins séduisant.
Les jeux Switch et Switch 2 vont-ils coûter plus cher ?
Pas nécessairement, et surtout pas du jour au lendemain. Le retrait progressif d’un fournisseur ne signifie ni l’arrêt des cartouches ni une pénurie déjà constatée. Nintendo a d’ailleurs réaffirmé son intention de continuer à proposer des jeux physiques. En revanche, moins de capacités disponibles et moins de fournisseurs potentiels pourraient compliquer les négociations et peser sur les coûts de production à terme.
Il faut aussi distinguer les deux générations de consoles. La chaîne d’approvisionnement des cartouches Switch 2 n’est pas nécessairement identique à celle de la première Switch : d’autres acteurs, notamment ROHM, sont évoqués pour certaines mémoires. Il serait donc prématuré d’affirmer que toutes les cartouches Switch 2 sont directement touchées par l’annonce de Macronix. À ce stade, le risque industriel est réel, mais son ampleur pour Nintendo reste à établir.
- Montée en gamme du design et des finitions
- Écran 7,9" (20 cm) LCD convaincant
- Performances et qualité d'image en nette hausse
Pour les joueurs, la question est simple : cette évolution finira-t-elle par se retrouver sur le prix des jeux en boîte ? Rien ne permet encore d’annoncer une hausse générale provoquée par ce retrait. Les éditeurs peuvent modifier leurs choix de supports, absorber une partie des coûts ou les répercuter, selon les cas. Et le marché du jeu numérique change aussi l’équation : d’après l’analyste David Gibson, le numérique représentait 61,5 % du chiffre d’affaires logiciel de Nintendo au deuxième trimestre calendaire 2026. Un indicateur économique, à ne pas confondre avec la proportion de jeux vendus à l’unité en téléchargement.
À terme, quel avenir pour les jeux Nintendo en cartouche ?
Le sujet dépasse le simple prix d’une puce. Sur Switch 2, les « cartes clés de jeu » (Game-Key Cards) illustrent déjà une autre manière de vendre du physique : la boîte contient une carte, mais celle-ci ne renferme pas le jeu complet et impose de le télécharger. Ce n’est pas la même chose qu’une cartouche qui embarque directement les données du jeu, notamment pour les joueurs attachés à la conservation de leurs achats.
Cela ne veut pas dire que les cartouches traditionnelles sont condamnées. Nintendo affirme vouloir maintenir le support physique, et la réorientation de Macronix ne suffit pas à prédire une disparition des jeux complets sur cartouche. Mais elle rappelle une réalité : la fabrication de ces supports dépend d’arbitrages industriels sur lesquels les joueurs et les éditeurs n’ont pas toujours la main.
Pour l’instant, aucune pénurie générale de cartouches Nintendo n’est établie. Reste une question de fond : si fabriquer des jeux physiques devient moins intéressant économiquement, combien de temps les éditeurs continueront-ils de privilégier des cartouches contenant réellement leurs jeux ?

articles.title: Estos son los dos mejores iPhone en oferta que puedes comprar ahora mismo
articles.text:
El otro día un amigo me dijo que quería comprar un iPhone. Como suele ser habitual, todo el mundo que se quiere comprar uno, tampoco quiere gastar mucho y cuando le digo los precios del iPhone 18, se asustan y me preguntan por otra recomendación. Para mi amigo y para los centenares de personas que se encuentran en la misma situación, deben saber que hay opciones de iPhone en oferta, de modelos anteriores, que son una magnífica elección para el 90 por ciento de las personas.
Teniendo en cuenta la ligera innovación de los iPhone en los últimos años, recurrir a un modelo de hace uno, dos o incluso tres años atrás, es una decisión inteligente. Aquí te dejamos dos opciones que yo recomendaría a cualquier persona. Además, si quiere ya meterse de lleno en el ecosistema de Apple, hay unos AirPods en oferta bastante interesantes.
El iPhone que recomendaría al que no se quiere gastar mucho
Si echamos la vista atrás y miramos los últimos lanzamientos de Apple, uno de los mejores teléfonos es el iPhone 15. Buena cámara, buena pantalla, autonomía aceptable, y te aseguras actualizaciones de software durante muchos años. Lo mejor además es que estos iPhone en oferta tienen un precio muy asequible, lo mismo que te cuesta hoy en día un Android de gama media alta. En PcComponentes lo tienes por sólo 689 euros dentro de las ofertas de Black Friday.
¿Pero qué pasa con todas esas personas que quieren algo más? Pues que el iPhone 17, el teléfono del año pasado, es prácticamente idéntico al iPhone 18 actual sólo que cuesta unos 400 euros menos. En PcComponentes también tienes el iPhone 17, con 256 GB de capacidad, y por sólo mil euros.
Además, tienes que saber que comprar en PcComponentes también te asegura toda la garantías de Apple por lo que si tienes cualquier problema, puedes acudir tanto a PcComponentes como a la propia Apple.
Los mejores auriculares de Apple, por sólo 135 euros
Cuando se ven tantos AirPods por ahí, es por algo. Son posiblemente los mejores auriculares que hay dentro de ese rango de precio. El perfecto complemento para tu iPhone y que ahora tiene un precio mucho más bajo. Los AirPods 5, con cancelación activa de ruido y carga con puerto USB-C, pueden ser tuyos por sólo 135 euros.
Tiene una autonomía de hasta 20 horas, traducción en tiempo real, audio espacial y sonido envolvente y resistencia IP57 por lo que puedes practicar deporte con ellos sin temor a que el sudor los estropee.
Estos han sido sólo algunas ofertas interesantes pero prepárate porque los próximos días, con motivo del Black Friday, vas a ver como PcComponentes derriba por completo los precios de miles de productos. Adelanta los regalos de Navidad y disfruta de la mejor tecnología al mejor precio.

articles.title: Uzoma Dozie wants banks to rethink SME lending with AI
articles.text:
Speaking on the sidelines of AFIS 2026 in Luanda, Angola, Uzoma Dozie, the former Diamond Bank chief and Sparkle MFB CEO, argues that African banking is stuck in a collateral trap, explains why digital banks must move beyond one-to-one payments, and details how AI can reduce the cost of SME lending. GODFREY GEORGE reports.
Across Nigeria’s banking industry, small enterprises and mass-affluent individuals account for a substantial share of the deposit base that funds commercial balance sheets. Yet, when those same small businesses apply for credit, they receive less than 1% of total bank lending.
For Uzoma Dozie, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Sparkle Microfinance Bank, this disparity captures why capital is failing to support the real economy.
Speaking to TechCabal at the Africa Financial Industry Summit (AFIS) in Luanda, where the central theme was “Making Capital Count”, the veteran banker argued that conventional lenders are held back by an outdated obsession with physical collateral, locking out the very businesses driving national employment and gross domestic product.
“Capital tends to flow towards areas of certainty, even though every investment carries some level of risk,” Dozie said. “What drives capital, particularly from a banking perspective, is trust. Take big businesses and large corporations: their accounts are audited and verified by professionals, so banks can lend based on information they trust.”
“But when you move down to small businesses and individuals, you are looking at the person. You may understand that they have a business, but you do not have sufficient information about that business. The bank either decides not to lend or lends at a price that reflects the perceived risk.”
To break this impasse, Dozie argues that the definition of collateral must be completely overhauled through transactional data.
“Every small business generates data. Every transaction is data,” Dozie said. “If we see data as information that can generate insights, we can use it to make credit decisions. For me, that is part of making capital count: changing our mindset about what constitutes collateral for small businesses and scaling lending by examining cash flows and business data. In some cases, this could even be less risky than traditional collateral-based lending.”
Moving beyond buzzwords
Dozie, who led Diamond Bank before its merger with Access Bank, rejects the industry’s rush to adopt superficial digital labels.
To him, technology in banking is not a recent novelty but a continuation of second-generation banking reforms that introduced automated teller machines (ATMs), Internet portals, and mobile banking applications to improve customer convenience.
Licenced as a microfinance bank, Sparkle, he noted, was designed to apply those lessons to segments that traditional retail banking fails to serve efficiently.
“When I hear people talk about wanting to become a digital bank, I think we have created names and buzzwords without really looking beneath the surface,” Dozie observed.
“The difference between our service model and traditional personal banking is that we do not have people involved in every customer interaction. We do not rely on account officers to deliver our services. You cannot bank millions of Nigerians using a purely human-touch model. There is a limit to the consistency, repeatability, and operational efficiency you can achieve that way.”
Rather than competing directly for the unbanked mass market or chasing standard retail transactions, Sparkle targets mass-affluent individuals and small enterprises whose economic activities intersect with the broader population.
“An affluent individual in Nigeria probably has four or five people they pay, including people who run small businesses,” Dozie explained. “On the small-business side, it was never just about providing a bank account. A bank account is a given because every business needs one. What was important to us was providing business support services.
“We built these services to capture business data. Once we capture that data, we can use it to generate intelligence about the business, make better decisions, and help the business access credit or even connect with people interested in investing in it.”
Rethinking financial inclusion
Dozie also challenged the way the financial sector evaluates financial inclusion, cautioning that tallying the number of registered bank accounts can create a misleading impression of progress.
In an economy where an estimated 100 million people live below the poverty line, an account without an economic foundation remains largely ornamental.
“If we do not solve the problems of identity and social inclusion, financial inclusion will not happen,” Dozie said. “A bank account is useful for making and receiving payments, as well as storing money. But if you have 100 million people living below the poverty line, financial inclusion cannot simply be about opening bank accounts for them.”
Meaningful inclusion, Dozie argued, requires structural integration where government social support—ranging from healthcare and insurance to emergency relief and education—is channelled directly through formal banking rails, giving citizens a clear reason to use an account.
At the enterprise level, inclusion hinges on simplifying operational cash flows. Small businesses must pay staff, manage inventory, and disburse wages, while households must pay domestic staff like security guards and gardeners.
This operational reality has shaped Sparkle’s transaction focus. While many digital banks concentrate on individual, peer-to-peer (one-to-one) transfers, Sparkle has prioritised collective and multi-party flows: one-to-many payments, payroll schedules, and batch transfers.
“Anyone can facilitate one-to-one transactions,” Dozie noted. “But one-to-many, collective payments, and many-to-one transactions are areas where Sparkle specialises. If you look at what we offer, you will see that it is quite different from what other players are doing.”
Conversational services and cheaper credit
On artificial intelligence, Dozie dismissed the notion that the technology is merely speculative, pointing to practical deployments across Sparkle’s marketing, customer engagement, and credit operations.
At the interface level, conversational AI allows users to communicate in their preferred format and check account balances directly, stripping out administrative costs that previously required separate software tools or customer service staff.
For commercial borrowers, machine learning algorithms analyse internal cash flows, matching payment patterns against market dynamics to build a more accurate financial profile than traditional paper statements permit.
“Internally, AI allows us to use customers’ cash flows to identify insights and correlations between their payments, their markets, and their business activities,” Dozie said. “We can then use that information to make better credit decisions. This helps us reduce the cost of lending and potentially offer credit at lower interest rates than would ordinarily be possible through traditional lending models.”
Dozie added that this analytical capability is also available to merchants, providing them with insights into their operational performance and customer behaviour.
“They give us access to their data, and we use it to provide insights that help them make better decisions,” Dozie said. “At the same time, we use that information to make better decisions about how we serve them and grow alongside their businesses. For us, it is not just a buzzword. We are only scratching the surface.”

articles.title: Leapwork Play Reaches GA with Governance for Playwright Tests
articles.text:
Leapwork made Play generally available on September 30, 2026 for teams managing Playwright test suites. The service adds requirement traceability and approval workflows around standard Playwright code, which teams can run in their existing continuous integration (CI) pipelines or through Leapwork's hosted execution service.
In its announcement, Leapwork says Play imports existing Playwright suites without changes. Engineers can connect Jira and Git repositories, along with product documentation, to build a knowledge base that supplies context for generated tests. They can also record a browser journey and turn the recording into a test.
Leapwork says Play monitors connected repositories for pushes that change application behaviour or the interface, then recommends corresponding test updates. Separately, its product page describes self-healing that fixes broken test steps instead of failing a run. The sources do not explain whether teams can require approval before a locator repair is accepted or how such repairs are recorded in the audit history.
For teams that need to review test changes, Play links each test to its originating requirement, ticket or document. Leapwork says the service retains authoring history and approvals alongside full execution logs, which teams can export as evidence. The service also reports flaky tests and coverage across applications or teams.
Role-based permissions and approval workflows control who can create and run tests. Leapwork includes the full governance, security and audit capabilities in enterprise packages, but the announcement does not specify which individual controls are available in the free tier.
Donovan Brady, vice-president of developer relations at Leapwork, described the management problem in the announcement: "What slows an enterprise team down now is proving where a test came from and managing thousands of them across dozens of teams once they exist."
Teams can also operate Play through an AI coding assistant using a server for the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Leapwork's product page names Claude Code, Codex and Cursor as clients and describes its hosted execution as Chromium-based. Leapwork says its hosted service runs suites in parallel, including environment and test data management.
Open-source Playwright already provides failure diagnostics through its Trace Viewer, including action details, network requests and screenshots. Those facilities help engineers investigate individual runs; Play's additional scope is central management of test provenance and approvals across teams.

articles.title: Garmin Forerunner 70 com 5 ATM cai 38% com cupom no Mercado Livre • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Garmin Forerunner 70 com 5 ATM cai 38% com cupom no Mercado Livre
Garmin Forerunner 70 resiste à água e possui bateria que dura até 28 dias; smartwatch para treinos recebe desconto com cupom no mês da Black Friday
O Garmin Forerunner 70 está saindo por R$ 1.599 no Pix com cupom DESCONTOSESPECIAIS no Mercado Livre. O smartwatch com resistência a até 5 ATM, bateria de longa duração e suporte a atividades esportivas, recebe desconto de 38% sobre o preço original de R$ 2.599 durante o Black November 2026.
O Garmin Forerunner 70 possui um corpo de 43 mm resistente a até 5 ATM, oferecendo proteção a condições extremas e permitindo seu uso em esportes aquáticos, segundo a fabricante. Os apenas 512 MB de espaço interno são dedicados ao SO e não permitem salvar músicas ou instalar apps localmente.
Os sensores especializados do smarwatch cobrem diversas atividades físicas diferentes, como caminhada, corrida e ciclismo, e o modo Garmin Couch traça planos de treino personalizados. Ele também possui medidores do sono, saúde da mulher e oxigenação do sangue, e monitora o consumo de calorias, álcool e cafeína.
Este acessório também pode ser de grande ajuda em situações de risco: no caso de uma emergência médica, ele pode disparar mensagens para contatos pré-determinados, informando a localização exata do usuário para serviços de resgate e pessoas próximas, mas apenas se estiver pareado a um celular.
A tela AMOLED de 1,2″ do Forerunner 70 reproduz imagens com cores bem definidas e brilho forte. O vidro Gorilla Glass 3 protege-a contra pancadas e arranhões.
Sua bateria resiste a até 13 dias de uso no modo smartwatch (5 dias com Always-On ligado), até 28 dias no modo de economia, e até 16 horas com navegação ativa e todos os recursos disponíveis (até 23 horas apenas com o GPS ligado), segundo a fabricante.
O Garmin Forerunner 70 (R$ 1.599 no Pix com cupom DESCONTOSESPECIAIS) suporta iPhone e Android e possui conectividade Bluetooth e GPS multibanda, que determina a posição exata do usuário em tempo real.
Durante todo o mês de novembro (Black November), o Mercado Livre e concorrentes oferecem diversos cupons e ofertas como essa, em antecipação para a Black Friday 2026, em 27 de novembro.
Acompanhe os Achados do TB no Telegram ou WhatsApp e não perca nenhuma promoção.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: Instagram brings Edits to desktop to take on CapCut | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Instagram announced on Thursday that it’s bringing Edits, its short-form video editing app, to desktop on Mac. The desktop version is designed for more complex video-editing projects that benefit from a larger screen, mouse, and keyboard, the company says.
The move puts Edits in more direct competition with ByteDance’s CapCut, the video-editing app Meta sought to challenge when it launched Edits last year. CapCut, which is a massively popular tool for creators, has been available on desktop for Windows and Mac since 2021.
Instagram notes that the desktop app includes licensed and royalty-free music, sound and video effects, and automatic captions in multiple languages. Audio and text styles that creators saved on the mobile app sync over to the desktop app, and users can customize keyboard shortcuts or import them from other editing software.
It also features a full multi-track timeline, keyframes for transitions, audio waveforms for accurate cuts, and more. Additionally, creators can import their own font files.
“A lot of creators have described the same moment to us: a project gets too big for your phone,” Brett Westervelt, head of Edits, said in a blog post. “You’ve got a dozen clips going, you’re trying to land a cut on the exact beat, and your thumb covers the part of the timeline you need to see. Your work is growing, and your tools should grow with it. We’re expanding Edits to take on your most ambitious projects on desktop.”
Creators can publish from the desktop editor directly to Instagram with native features like tagging and location built in. The company says this gets rid of the need for creators to edit on desktop, download the file, move it to mobile, and then make more edits before posting it.
Edits will also support horizontal and vertical video formats, with watermark-free exports in 4K resolution for sharing across platforms or personal use, Instagram says.
The company plans to ship weekly updates to improve the desktop editor, noting that it’s currently working to make it possible for creators to edit one project across both desktop and mobile seamlessly.
Instagram also said it’s going to continue to grow the mobile Edits app for the more than 50 million creators who use it.

articles.title: Claude AI can plug directly into your bank account
articles.text:
Anthropic has a new pitch for managing your personal finances: let Claude do it instead, with a new Personal Finance feature that connects it to your bank and card accounts via the Plaid bank bridging platform. You can ask the chatbot “where did my money go this month,” for example, and it’ll create an overview with a breakdown of spending by category, including rent and utilities, shopping, and food. Claude can also answer broader questions around what bills are left before your next payday, if you can afford big purchases like holiday trips, and how much money you could be saving each month.
Claude AI can plug directly into your bank account
With access to your bank account via Plaid, Anthropic’s chatbot will try to explain where your money is going and what you can afford.
Its access is read-only, and with Plaid facilitating the connection, Claude doesn’t see your banking passwords and your bank doesn’t have to deal with unvetted AI bots crawling around your accounts.
Claude can’t move, manage, or invest your money, according to Anthropic, and it “isn’t designed to give investment advice.”, but it can see the bank’s name, account names, account type, the last four digits of the number associated with it, your balances and credit limits, and up to two years’ worth of your transaction history.
If you choose to give it access to all that, Claude can explain financial terms you don’t understand and answer questions about your balances and transactions.
Personal Finance in Claude is rolling out in beta this week to Claude Pro, Max, and Ultra plan subscribers in the US. Anthropic’s announcement follows OpenAI introducing a similar feature for ChatGPT in May, which also plugs into your bank accounts through Plaid. Allowing AI to have oversight into your finances might ring some alarm bells, but according to the sign-off in Anthropic’s press release, it’s just the beginning:
“Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust. We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it.”

articles.title: Why Integrated Gate Drive Regulation Matters For High Reliability Space GaN Designs
articles.text:
Eliminating the need for a separate bias regulator dedicated to the gate driver for a more streamlined power architecture.
As Gallium Nitride (GaN) technology becomes increasingly prevalent in space power systems, designers are leveraging its inherent capabilities to deliver higher efficiency, faster switching speeds, and greater power density. These advantages help designers support the growing demands of modern satellite platforms.
While GaN devices are central to many modern power architectures, achieving their full efficiency and switching performance depends on the gate driver that controls them. Infineon HiRel’s new, rad hard single-channel gate driver for GaN delivers the precise drive conditions that GaN devices require. Designed specifically for extreme environment applications, the device incorporates an integrated low dropout regulator (LDO). The LDO simplifies gate-drive implementation while providing a tightly regulated voltage optimized for GaN operation, while also reducing the total bill of materials (BOM).
The switching advantages of GaN stem from device characteristics such as low gate charge, reduced output capacitance, and fast transition times. These attributes enable lower switching losses and support operation at higher frequencies than traditional silicon MOSFET (Si) technologies.
Designers must provide stable and controlled gate-drive voltages to achieve optimal switching behavior. Even relatively small variations in gate voltage can affect switching losses, power-stage efficiency, electromagnetic interference (EMI), device stress, and long-term reliability. GaN devices have extremely high slew rates (dv/dt) when switching. As a result, maintaining a stable and well-controlled gate-drive voltage is critical for predictable system performance across operating conditions.
Traditionally, designers generate the gate-drive supply rail using external regulators, bias circuits, or dedicated auxiliary power supplies. While effective, these approaches add components, consume board area, and create additional design considerations related to regulation accuracy, startup behavior, and power sequencing. In space systems, every additional component increases design complexity. It can also drive up qualification and testing costs, add weight, and extend development timelines. Infineon HiRel’s new RIC70115 gate driver simplifies this architecture with many integrated features, such as an integrated LDO that generates a tightly regulated 4.8 V gate-drive rail from input voltages ranging from 4.75 V to 15 V.
By regulating the gate-drive supply internally, the RIC70115 helps ensure that GaN transistors receive a consistent drive voltage, even as upstream supply rails vary during normal operations. This approach aligns directly with recommendations outlined in the application note, which emphasizes the importance of maintaining tightly controlled gate-drive conditions to support efficient and reliable GaN HEMT operation in space environments. Even better is that no additional external components are needed to deliver this regulated drive voltage, helping customers meet their SWaP-C needs. For space programs operating under tight development timelines, this reduction in design complexity can support faster qualification efforts and lower implementation risk.
Space power systems present unique challenges beyond those encountered in terrestrial applications. Every additional component introduces potential reliability considerations, increases PCB area requirements, and compromises qualification and system-level verification efforts.
The integrated LDO within the RIC70115 eliminates the need for a separate bias regulator dedicated to the gate driver. This results in a more streamlined power architecture that supports the industry’s ongoing pursuit of reduced size, weight, and power (SWaP) advantages. By consolidating gate-drive regulation within the controller itself, designers can reduce component count without sacrificing the precision required for high-performance GaN operation.
As designers transition from Si to GaN, solutions that simplify implementation without sacrificing performance stand out.
The RIC70115 does just that. With high-speed gate driving and integrated voltage regulation, the device helps optimize GaN operation. Rather than developing and validating a separate regulated gate-drive supply, designers can rely on the device to provide a controlled and consistent bias environment directly within the gate-driver architecture. The integrated approach helps reduce design complexity while enabling the efficiency, switching speed, and power density advantages that drive GaN adoption in next-generation satellite power systems.
Evaluate RIC70115 with Infineon HiRel’s companion evaluation board, the RIC70115EVAL1. Prepopulated with two RIC70115 gate driver ICs and two IG1NT052N10R GaN HEMTs in a half-bridge configuration, the evaluation board highlights RIC70115’s ability to operate in both high- and low-side configurations.
When paired with the right gate driver, GaN can enable a more power-dense spacecraft power architecture. Through its integrated LDO, the RIC70115 helps designers reduce complexity, streamline development, and take full advantage of GaN’s efficiency and performance benefits. Take the next step in next-generation space exploration: download the RIC70115 datasheet and the application note to learn more.
