articles.title: Swift n’est plus : après 22 ans de service, le télescope spatial de la NASA s’est écrasé sur Terre
articles.text:
Le télescope spatial Swift a achevé son voyage ce 4 novembre en se désintégrant dans l’atmosphère. Une fin discrète pour un engin qui a passé sa vie à traquer les explosions les plus puissantes de l’Univers.
Swift perdait de l’altitude depuis des années. Dépourvu de moteur, il a été freiné peu à peu par les infimes traces d’air présentes à son altitude, de quoi accélérer progressivement sa chute. Et le sauvetage orchestré par la NASA et la start-up Katalyst n’a pas abouti : le vaisseau LINK, qui devait remonter le télescope de 1 450 kilogrammes sur une orbite plus haute, a subi plusieurs pannes majeures. Swift se dirigeait donc vers une fin certaine, et elle a finalement eu lieu.
Swift est rentré dans l’atmosphère au-dessus de l’Indonésie
Le télescope est entré dans l’atmosphère ce mercredi à 13h39 en France. Il se trouvait alors au-dessus du nord de l’île de Sumatra, en Indonésie, a fait savoir la Space Force américaine. Sa chute est restée, a priori, sans conséquence.
Car la NASA s’attendait logiquement à ce que la majeure partie de l’engin brûle en traversant les couches de l’atmosphère. Elle estimait à une chance sur 2 100 que des morceaux survivants blessent quelqu’un. L’agence précise toutefois que certains éléments ont pu résister à la rentrée.
Ce scénario n’a d’ailleurs rien d’exceptionnel. Selon une étude citée par Space.com, au moins trois gros objets, satellites hors service ou étages de fusée, retombent en moyenne chaque jour sur Terre. Un rythme appelé à s’accélérer avec le déploiement des méga-constellations de satellites et qui pourrait, à terme, effectivement poser problème.
Un bilan crucial pour la compréhension du cosmos
Lancé en novembre 2004, le télescope Swift a réalisé des observations jusqu’au 20 octobre dernier. Au fil des années, il a observé plus de 2 000 sursauts gamma et 1 400 supernovae, ces étoiles qui explosent en fin de vie. Il s’est aussi intéressé aux trous noirs qui dévorent la matière, aux éruptions de rayons X de certaines étoiles, ainsi qu’aux comètes et aux astéroïdes de notre Système solaire.
La NASA espère désormais s’inspirer de la mission de sauvetage qui, malgré son échec, a permis de belles avancées, pour prolonger la vie d’autres télescopes. À commencer par l’emblématique Hubble. Ce 29 octobre, l’agence spatiale a ainsi lancé un appel aux entreprises privées pour remonter l’engin sur une autre orbite. Autrement, il subira exactement le même destin que Swift au début des années 30.

articles.title: 18 Millionen Domains und ein Wertverfall: Was von der .de-Goldgräberzeit übrig ist
articles.text:
Im Internet ist fast alles beliebig oft verfügbar. Nur die Adresse nicht: Jede Domain gibt es bloß ein einziges Mal. Für shopping.des wurden 2008 fast zwei Millionen Euro gezahlt, für kredit.de fast 900.000 Euro. Der Handel mit solchen Namen zeigt, dass digitale Adressen ein knappes und mitunter kostspieliges Gut sind – und das seit nunmehr vier Jahrzehnten: Am 5. November wird die deutsche Länderkennung .de 40 Jahre alt.
Die Verwaltung übernahm 1986 zunächst das US-amerikanische Forschungsnetzwerk CSNET. 1988 ging sie an die Universität Dortmund – zu diesem Zeitpunkt waren gerade einmal sechs .de-Domains registriert. Mit der Verbreitung des Internets wuchsen die Anforderungen. 1993 entstand der Interessenverbund IV-DENIC, am 17. Dezember 1996 gründeten 37 Internet-Service-Provider die DENIC eG als genossenschaftlich organisierte Registrierungsstelle.
Heute zählt .de mehr als 18 Millionen registrierte Domains und gehört damit zu den größten Länderendungen weltweit. Die technische Infrastruktur bewältigt nach Angaben der DENIC rund 3,5 Milliarden Nameservice-Anfragen täglich. Sie sorgt dafür, dass Internetadressen weltweit erreichbar sind. „Aus den frühen, überschaubaren Netzstrukturen ist eine leistungsfähige digitale Infrastruktur geworden“, sagt DENIC-Vorstand Tom Keller zum Jubiläum.
Digitales Gold: Hunderttausende Euro für Top-Adressen
Nach den akademischen Anfangszeiten entdeckten auch Geschäftemacher die Internetdomains. Dass Internetadressen als digitale Immobilien gehandelt werden, zeigt der florierende Zweitmarkt. Zwar kostet eine Neuregistrierung einer .de-Domain meist nur wenige Euro im Jahr, doch für kurze, einprägsame Alltagsbegriffe werden weiterhin hohe Summen gezahlt.
Wie wertvoll begehrte Begriffe unter .de nach wie vor sind, belegen die Zahlen der Domainpreisdatenbank: So wechselte zuletzt die Adresse ferienhaus.de über den Kölner Marktplatz Sedo für 357.000 Euro den Besitzer – der teuerste öffentlich dokumentierte Verkauf einer deutschen Domain im Jahr 2025. An die schwindelerregenden Rekordwerte aus den Boomjahren 2007 und 2008 reicht das heutige Preisniveau allerdings nicht mehr heran. Der Markt hat sich im Vergleich zur damaligen Hochphase spürbar abgekühlt.
Geopolitische Kuriosität: Der Hype um .si
Wie stark die Abkürzungen am Ende einer Webadresse die Spekulationen befeuern können, zeigte jüngst eine Posse um die slowenische Länderendung .si. Nachdem US-Präsident Donald Trump gefordert hatte, Künstliche Intelligenz (KI beziehungsweise AI) in „Super Intelligence“ (SI) umzubenennen, stürmten Domain-Händler und Tech-Unternehmen plötzlich das slowenische Register. Binnen kürzester Zeit explodierten die Registrierungszahlen für Adressen mit der Endung des kleinen EU-Landes – pikanterweise die Heimat von Trumps Ehefrau Melania. Der Fall verdeutlichte schlaglichtartig, dass Top-Level-Domains selbst im Zeitalter von Apps und Social Media nichts von ihrer Wucht verloren haben.
Neue Welle von Endungen: Von .agent bis .taylorswift
Trotz der ungebrochenen Anziehungskraft bewährter Adressen wächst die Vielfalt im Namensraum. Pünktlich zum runden Geburtstag von .de kündigt sich ein neuer globaler Vergabeschub an. Wie der Branchenverband Eco mitteilte, hat die weltweite Internet-Verwaltung ICANN soeben die Bewerbungsliste für eine neue Runde generischer Endungen (gTLDs) vorgelegt. Insgesamt gingen 1.615 Bewerbungen von 481 Antragstellern ein, darunter 333 direkte Markenbewerbungen.
Der Trend spiegelt aktuelle technologische und kulturelle Entwicklungen wider: Neben Adressen aus dem KI-Umfeld wie .agent oder .api sowie Tech-Marken wie .openai und .chatgpt bewerben sich Interessenten auch um prominente Namen wie .taylorswift. Sport- und Finanzbegriffe wie .olympic, .euro und .bitcoin stehen ebenfalls auf der Liste. Ob all diese Endungen tatsächlich an den Start gehen, entscheidet sich in den kommenden Prüfverfahren.
„Verbundenheit mit Deutschland“
Zum runden Geburtstag der deutschen Länderkennung blickt die Branche geschlossen mit Stolz auf die heimische Erfolgsgeschichte: „Vierzig Jahre .de sind eine echte Erfolgsgeschichte“, sagt Thomas Rickert, Director Names & Numbers beim Verband der Internetwirtschaft Eco. Der Namensraum des Internets werde zunehmend auch zu einem wirtschaftlichen Wettbewerbsfaktor. Und auch DENIC-Vorständin Barbara Stolz zeigt sich überzeugt, dass die Traditionskennung das verlässliche Fundament der deutschen Netzwelt bleibt: „.de steht wie kaum eine andere Länderkennung für die Verbundenheit mit Deutschland.“
Apps, KI-Assistenten und der Bedeutungsverlust der Adresszeile
Gleichzeitig wächst unter Experten die Skepsis, ob klassische Domainadressen ihre einstige Dominanz dauerhaft behaupten können. Längst tippen nur noch die wenigsten Internetnutzer eine vollständige Webadresse per Hand in die Browserzeile ein. Auf Smartphones dominieren App-Ökosysteme, in denen Internetadressen unsichtbar im Hintergrund bleiben.
Zudem leiten KI-gestützte Suchsysteme und Chatbots eine fundamentale Trendwende ein: Anstatt wie klassische Suchmaschinen auf eine Liste verlinkter Webseiten zu verweisen, fassen moderne Sprachmodelle und KI-Agenten die gesuchten Informationen direkt zusammen. Wer im Netz gefunden oder gekauft werden will, muss nicht mehr zwingend über eine einprägsame Domain verfügen, sondern vielmehr in den Trainingsdaten und Datenquellen der KI-Modelle optimal auffindbar sein.

articles.title: More Kenyans borrow through M-PESA as overdraft revenue climbs 86%
articles.text:
Safaricom, Kenya’s largest telecommunications operator, generated KES 4.9 billion ($38 million) from Fuliza, its M-PESA overdraft service that lets customers complete transactions when they lack enough money in their wallets.
On Thursday, Safaricom said at its investor briefing held in Nairobi that Fuliza’s revenue rose 86% in the six months to September 2026, with the number of borrowers nearly doubling to 17.2 million. The service, operated by Safaricom in partnership with NCBA Bank and Kenya Commercial Bank (KCB), became the company’s largest mobile lending business by revenue, even as the average amount borrowed fell 24.6%.
The figures point to growing reliance on short-term credit as a revenue source for M-PESA. Lending is growing much faster than payments revenue. However, smaller loan sizes and declining repayment ratios raise questions about borrower behaviour and the business’s economics.
Fuliza disbursed KES 1.16 trillion ($8.97 billion) during the period, up 84% from the previous year. Its customer base also grew 88.9% to 17.2 million.
Revenue rose at almost the same pace as customer growth. The average amount borrowed, though, declined 24.6% to KES 192 ($1.49), from KES 254.60 ($1.97).
The numbers suggest Fuliza is reaching more customers through smaller advances. Safaricom has not disclosed how much of the growth came from customers borrowing more frequently, new borrowers entering the service, or changes in credit limits.
Fuliza’s growth contrasts with Safaricom’s other mobile lending products, which it operates with banking partners.
KCB M-PESA, a savings and loan service offered with Kenya Commercial Bank (KCB), generated KES 500 million ($3.9 million) in revenue, up 11.9%, even as its active customer base fell 7% to 4.2 million.
M-Shwari, Safaricom’s savings and microloan service with NCBA Bank, recorded revenue growth of 7.7% to KES 1 billion ($7.8 million), while active customers fell 5.8% to 7.4 million.
As Safaricom looks to expand M-PESA beyond payments into credit, savings, insurance and merchant services, its investor presentation shows credit revenue grew 54.4% to KES 7 billion ($54.3 million) in the half-year, compared with 13.6% growth in overall M-PESA revenue to KES 100.07 billion ($775.7 million).
Fuliza accounted for roughly 71% of revenue from the six lending products, making it the portfolio’s main source of earnings.
The repayment figures offer another dimension to the growth. Fuliza’s repayments reached KES 1.15 trillion ($8.94 billion), equivalent to 99.6% of disbursements, down from 102.4% a year earlier. KCB M-PESA’s ratio also fell to 96.7% from 99.5%, while M-Shwari’s declined to 105.3% from 108%.
“Behavioural scoring and multiple funding partners are helping us extend responsible credit, personalise access and manage portfolio risk more effectively for customers and businesses across Kenya,” Safaricom CEO Peter Ndegwa said.
The figures show Fuliza’s growth, but not the full picture of the risk behind it. The repayment-to-disbursement ratio fell to 99.6% from 102.4%, though the comparison does not show how much of the loans issued during the period remain unpaid. Repayments recorded in the six months may include money owed from earlier lending periods.
Safaricom did not disclose Fuliza’s non-performing loan ratio in either report. The disclosures also do not show how credit risk is split between Safaricom and its banking partners.

articles.title: Trucos para reducir el consumo de electricidad del aire acondicionado
articles.text:
Un solo grado de diferencia en el termostato puede elevar el gasto energético hasta en un 10%, tanto al bajar la temperatura en verano como al subirla en invierno. Así lo advierten la Organización de Consumidores y Usuarios (OCU) de España y la petrolera Repsol, que coinciden en que una configuración adecuada del aire acondicionado permite reducir de forma significativa el consumo eléctrico sin sacrificar el confort durante los meses de temperaturas extremas.
La temperatura del termostato marca la diferencia en la factura
Según la OCU, en verano conviene mantener el equipo entre 24℃ y 26℃ (75℉ y 78℉), un rango que genera un ambiente confortable y evita contrastes bruscos con el exterior. La diferencia entre la temperatura interior y la exterior no debería superar los 12℃ (22℉), límite que previene molestias físicas asociadas a cambios térmicos abruptos.
En invierno, la recomendación se ubica entre 20℃ y 22℃ (68℉ y 71℉), suficiente para contrarrestar el frío sin forzar al equipo a un sobrecalentamiento innecesario. Durante la noche, el rango sugerido baja a 15℃-17℃ (59℉-63℉), lo que además de favorecer el descanso reduce el gasto energético en las horas de sueño.
Mantener la temperatura estable evita sobreesfuerzos del equipo
Encender y apagar el aparato de forma repetida obliga al sistema a trabajar más para alcanzar nuevamente la temperatura deseada. Por eso, tanto la OCU como Repsol recomiendan mantener una configuración estable en lugar de alternar constantemente el encendido y el apagado, una práctica que favorece la eficiencia y prolonga la vida útil del equipo.
Los modelos con tecnología inverter optimizan el rendimiento al ajustar la potencia de manera progresiva. A esto se suman los sistemas inteligentes o smart, que permiten controlar el aparato desde el teléfono móvil y evitar que funcione sin necesidad.
El modo ECO y el mantenimiento regular reducen el gasto
La limpieza frecuente de los filtros y la verificación de que la unidad exterior no esté bloqueada evitan que el sistema trabaje en exceso y disminuyen el riesgo de averías. El uso del modo ECO puede reducir el consumo hasta en un 30%, mientras que la función deshumidificador mejora la sensación térmica sin necesidad de bajar la temperatura, lo que aporta eficiencia adicional.
Anticiparse a las jornadas de calor y encender el aire acondicionado antes de que la temperatura interna suba en exceso permite una climatización más eficiente, ya que el equipo no debe realizar un esfuerzo adicional para enfriar un ambiente ya caldeado.
La orientación del flujo de aire influye en el rendimiento
La dirección en la que se distribuye el aire también incide en la eficiencia del sistema. En verano se recomienda dirigir el flujo hacia arriba, de modo que el aire frío descienda de manera natural por su mayor densidad. En invierno, en cambio, conviene orientarlo hacia abajo para aprovechar el ascenso natural del aire caliente.
Tapar las entradas o salidas de aire, así como bloquear la unidad exterior, obliga al sistema a trabajar más y aumenta el consumo eléctrico de forma directa. Por esa razón, mantener estos espacios despejados resulta clave para un funcionamiento óptimo del equipo.
Apagar el equipo por completo evita gastos innecesarios
Dejar el aire acondicionado en modo stand by durante periodos prolongados incrementa el consumo, aunque el aparato no esté en funcionamiento activo. La recomendación es apagarlo y desconectarlo por completo cuando no se vaya a utilizar durante un tiempo extendido.
Si se detecta una disminución en el rendimiento del equipo, tanto la OCU como Repsol aconsejan contactar a un profesional para su revisión, con el fin de evitar que un desperfecto menor derive en un problema mayor o en un consumo eléctrico más elevado del habitual.

articles.title: Valve support wins praise after restoring games a Steam user deleted during depressive episodes
articles.text:
In context: Steam has long let players permanently remove games from their accounts. One user ended up using that option far more than they wanted to as a result of years of depressive and manic episodes. Plenty of the games they deleted were ones they'd played and loved, so they eventually asked Steam Support if any could be brought back. Less than 14 hours later, an agent replied to say the games had been restored. 
 
 
The user, who goes by 3lizardintrenchcoat on Reddit, shared the support ticket on r/Steam in late November 2025. In it, they admitted the request felt "insane and over the top" before asking whether some of the paid games they had deleted over the years could be brought back.
They also offered an easier fallback in case that wasn't possible. All they wanted was a list of every game they'd ever played on the account, free ones included. As they pointed out, Steam's purchase history only shows games that are still active and that were paid for, so it couldn't fill in the gaps on its own.
An agent named Lucy replied early the next morning, confirming a restore to the user's library. If anything still seemed to be missing, she offered to send over the full list of previously owned games, too.
The story got a second life this week after the Waste.gg account posted a screenshot of the exchange on X. That post described it as a restore of the user's "entire game library" and has since crossed 2.2 million views. Strictly speaking, though, the reply only mentions "your game" in the singular, so exactly how many titles came back hasn't been confirmed.
 – Waste.gg (@skinwaste) November 3, 2026
Valve's support team has racked up a few of these moments lately. Back in June, it sent a new dad a free Steam Deck OLED carrying case after his newborn threw up on the original. He had only asked whether he could buy a new one. Gestures like that arguably carry a bit more weight coming from a store that, since 2024, reminds buyers at checkout that a purchase only gets them a license.
Even so, Steam's "permanent" removal tool has never been quite as final as its name suggests. Anyone who remembers a removed game can search for it through Steam Support, choose "It's not in my library," and restore the old license in a couple of clicks. But Steam doesn't provide players with a list of the games they've removed. That's the exact gap this user ran into before support stepped in.

articles.title: The EU-Startups Podcast | Interview with Károly Ludvigh, CEO and co-founder of ABZ Innovation | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Key points:
- Why existing agricultural drones on the market fell short on reliability, and why ABZ decided to build its own hardware from the ground up
- How technology is transforming the day-to-day work of farmers, even in a sector that looks traditional from the outside
- Building for customers who prioritise reliability over exciting technology, and the engineering lessons that come with it
- How the war in Ukraine has reshaped Europe’s drone industry: manufacturing capacity, investment, and the shift toward local production
- ABZ’s stance on dual-use and defence applications versus staying focused on agricultural and civilian industrial use cases
- Scaling across 40+ countries with divergent UAV regulations, and a look at what drones may routinely do in agriculture within five to ten years
In this episode, we sit down with Károly Ludvigh, CEO and co-founder of ABZ Innovation, one of Europe’s leading manufacturers of heavy-duty agricultural and industrial drones.
Headquartered in Hungary, ABZ Innovation designs and builds drones for spraying, spreading, cleaning, and specialized industrial applications – combining high-payload hardware, modular architecture, and a European full-stack autonomy platform to turn drone technology into a practical automation tool for complex environments.
With operations in more than 40 countries and a newly opened manufacturing facility in Szentendre that stands among Europe’s largest civilian drone factories, ABZ sits at the heart of the continent’s fast-growing drone and AgTech ecosystem.
Károly’s path to building one of Europe’s most ambitious drone companies is anything but conventional. From his years in tech journalism to building drone systems as a hobbyist in a basement over a decade ago, his journey reflects a philosophy that runs through everything ABZ does: simplicity and reliability over hype.
When the company set out to offer drone-based crop spraying, it discovered that the products available on the market simply couldn’t deliver the dependability a sustainable business required – so ABZ built its own drones from the ground up.
We explore what it takes to build technology for customers who need reliability above everything else, how farmers – often seen as working in a traditional sector – are embracing dramatic technological change, and how the war in Ukraine has reshaped Europe’s drone industry, from manufacturing capacity to investment appetite and the push to build more technology locally.
Károly also shares his perspective on dual-use and defence applications, Europe’s quest for genuine technological sovereignty in drones, and what it takes to scale drone technology across more than 40 markets with wildly different regulatory environments.

articles.title: The Agent Smith Dilemma: Governing Agentic Identities
articles.text:
For the past few years, North Korean operatives, posing as remote IT workers, systematically infiltrated hundreds of Western enterprise networks. They passed technical interviews, cleared background checks using stolen identities, and sat comfortably inside corporate trust boundaries with legitimate credentials. They drew salaries, funneled funds back to Pyongyang, and routinely exfiltrated sensitive data on their way out. Major firms, including prominent cybersecurity vendors, have publicly admitted to falling for the scheme. (As an aside, listen to Nicole Perlroth’s Podcast “To Catch a Thief” for a fascinating deep dive)
The scheme worked because enterprises grant trust once. HR verifies a person at hiring, IT creates an account, a laptop is provisioned. The user is then authorized. Nothing in the security stack was built to answer the one question that mattered: Is the entity driving this session who we think it is?
Now enter the AI agent era.
Inside the enterprise, the volume of non-human identities executing sensitive tasks is expanding exponentially. Organizations are rapidly onboarding thousands of AI agents into critical workflows, complete with administrative service accounts and API keys. Enterprises now extend the same trust model to AI agents, with less scrutiny.
What Trust Models Should AI Agents Have?
Every autonomous AI agent deployed across your enterprise today is a new proxy identity operating inside your perimeter. It holds credentials, accesses sensitive databases, and chains tools together at machine speed. Crucially, it almost always executes under an inherited human permission set. When an LLM-powered agent acts on behalf of an authorized employee, every system log records a routine authorized action by that human.
But few agents are built maliciously. The true exposure is that the instructions driving an agent can be hijacked after trust has been granted. An AI agent can be compromised mid session through selective prompt injection, hidden instructions, or a poisoned external tool.
In The Matrix, Agent Smith’s real threat was his ability to step into any character’s shell, inherit their presence, and replicate instantly across the system. The modern AI agent is the enterprise’s Agent Smith. It steps into an employee’s user account, inherits their exact privileges, and multiplies across the ecosystem—executing tasks as a trusted proxy.
Agentic Attacks Have Started
Placing a covert human operative inside a company requires effort: a real person to pass the interview, maintain cover, and do enough daily work to avoid suspicion. AI agents eliminate that ceiling. The cost of scaling an AI-orchestrated intrusion campaign is limited only by the price of tokens.
Compounding the problem is that we cannot predict what AI agents will do. The companies building frontier LLMs openly acknowledge that their systems frequently take unexpected actions outside established guardrails, admitting that creating a perfect list of behavioral rules is an impossible task.
Across the cybersecurity ecosystem, threat intelligence groups are already documenting an unprecedented shift from AI-assisted scripting to fully operationalized agentic attacks. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) recently documented a financially motivated intrusion where attackers deployed a multi-agent framework directly inside a victim’s cloud environment. In under six hours, the agents planned and executed a credential-harvesting campaign that compromised thousands of enterprise secrets. Because the agents ran inside the victim’s own cloud, all malicious traffic originated from legitimate internal IP addresses—perfectly demonstrating the trusted-proxy vulnerability.
My Agent “Did It”
When an agent goes off-script, it exposes a glaring governance question: Who is actually responsible? Is it the frontier AI vendor who trained the model? The developer who wired up the API? Or the business user who entered the prompt?
Most enterprise governance frameworks hold the human user responsible. But holding a person legally and operationally accountable for the decisions of an unpredictable software agent may strain a reasonable idea of fairness. Yet, “my agent did it” may not be an acceptable defense in a board room or a court of law.
Worst of all, we are managing these non-human identities with tools built for human timelines. Identity and Access Management (IAM) grew up around human actions: hire, provision, periodically review, and offboard. An AI agent, by contrast, spins up in milliseconds, executes thousands of queries an hour, spawns sub-agents, reaches through uninventoried API connectors, and disappears long before any access control review takes place. When an agent acts maliciously, most security teams cannot answer three basic questions: Who authorized this agent? Which human is accountable for its output? How do we revoke its access mid-execution?
Solving the Identity Proxy Crisis
The discipline required to solve this may be informed by the hard lessons of identity impersonation.
- Demand Provenance via an AIBOM: Before an agent is granted access, security teams must verify its code lineage, system prompt integrity, and underlying permissions. Just as a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) inventories code libraries, an AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM) extends that discipline to models, agent skills, and data connectors. You cannot govern an artifact you cannot identify. Provenance also has to hold at runtime. In August, researchers documented a malicious MCP server that passed install-time review, then directed connected agents to collect SSH keys and cloud credentials after its third call.
- Enforce Workload Identity: Stop letting agents inherit long-lived human credentials. Agents require their own distinct, short-lived tokens that are tightly scoped to specific tasks, ensuring that if an agent is hijacked, the blast radius is contained. Each token should be bound to a named human sponsor, which answers the governance question before an incident does.
- Implement the “Rule of Two”: Under Meta’s Agents Rule of Two, an agent should combine no more than two of three properties: processing untrusted input, accessing sensitive data, and changing systems or communicating externally. When a task needs all three, a deterministic broker outside the model holds the action for human sign-off. Database drops and financial transfers belong in that category. Outbound traffic, including DNS, should be denied by default.
- Machine-Speed Revocation & Kill Switches: An identity that acts in milliseconds cannot be controlled by human-speed SIEM alerts. Security teams need automated circuit breakers (i.e. kill switches) capable of severing an agent’s execution path mid-session the moment it violates a hard budget or behavioral limit.
Governing non-human, agentic identity is no longer an edge-case. It is an emerging and growing attack surface. Enterprise security teams need to treat autonomous agents with the same scrutiny and continuous monitoring applied to human “identities”.

articles.title: What’s in Budget 2026 for Canadian tech? | BetaKit
articles.text:
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s second federal budget will be tabled on Thursday at around 4 pm EST. His government’s first budget was largely well-received by the tech and business ecosystem, and today’s is expected to continue focusing on shoring up Canada’s economy so it’s more resilient to outside shocks.
One insider told BetaKit that “everything’s a priority, so nothing’s a priority” as innovation policy advocates anticipate Budget 2026.
Beyond the finance minister’s assertion that this budget will be “about entrepreneurs,” the government has signalled very little about new measures for the innovation sector. However, there are a handful of files the industry is expecting movement on. A proposed capital gains rollover is one, as is hundreds of millions of dollars in new funding for the space sector. The government will also likely provide an updated immigration plan.
Sean Mullin, a senior fellow at the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs & Public Policy who recently served as a special advisor to the prime minister on economic affairs, said the recently dropped national security strategy, which put tech front and centre, could offer some clues. Along with frontier AI, it lists critical minerals, defence, energy, transportation, pharmaceuticals, biotech, food security, and financial systems as priority sectors Canada needs to build on. The recent Canada-EU Summit also set up several infrastructure projects, including an undersea data cable connecting Canada and Europe.
As one policy insider told BetaKit, “everything’s a priority, so nothing’s a priority.” It remains to be seen which sectors will see their wishes reflected, and which matters of national interest get the biggest financial boost.
Taxes
The ask: Business and tech groups want tax changes that will make Canada a more competitive place to invest.
The Council of Canadian Innovators, the Canadian Venture Capital & Private Equity Association (CVCA), the National Angel Capital Organization (NACO), and other investor groups launched a campaign asking the feds to create a tax incentive similar to the US Qualified Small Business Stock regime, and to create a capital gains tax deferral when proceeds are reinvested in another Canadian company. Build Canada went a step further, suggesting a corporate tax change that only taxed profits, not reinvested earnings.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB) is asking the feds to cut the small-business rate from nine to six percent and to extend the preferred tax rate for small businesses to a company’s first $700,000 of income, rather than $500,000.
What the feds have said: On Monday, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne asserted this budget would be “about entrepreneurs,” and teased that small business tax troubles would be a target.
On the investor side, CVCA CEO Benjamin Bergen said he was “cautiously optimistic” about progress on his organization’s proposed tax initiative, while NACO CEO Claudio Rojas told BetaKit that the government is showing promising signals about wanting to take action.
Aerospace and defence
The ask: Canadian defence tech firms want clearer and faster-moving procurement rules. Aspiring neoprime Dominion Dynamics asked the feds to lower the threshold for contracts awarded through the Defence Investment Agency to $25 million, and to create “agile procurement models” for software and other advanced defence tech. The Canadian Strategic Mission Corporation, while advocating for funding toward its own nuclear micro-reactors, asked for increased investment in dual-use technologies.
Similar procurement asks came from the spacetech sector. Satellite company Kepler Communications wants the government to apply the defence Build-Partner-Buy framework to the space sector, and more clarity on how to be selected as a strategic partner. A coalition of space companies, including Maritime Launch Services and Reaction Dynamics, was bolder, calling for a new national space industrial strategy and for the feds to commit to being the first customers for domestic space companies.
What the feds have said: Multiple sources told BetaKit they expect more movement on the spacetech front than net-new commitments for defence. In particular, sources are anticipating hundreds of millions toward space launch efforts.
The federal government has committed more than $200 million through defence envelopes to companies building sovereign launch capacity—something Canada still does not have. The Department of Defence signed a $20-million deal with NordSpace to access its Newfoundland spaceport over the next 10 years.
Artificial intelligence
The ask: The tech sector wants AI infrastructure built in Canada. CCI recommended that the feds build a “sovereign industrial base” of Canadian firms by providing domestic compute capacity, better access to high-quality data, and procurement rules that prioritize buying Canadian. Similarly, the Canadian Shield Institute called for a “strategic sovereign compute entity” that Canadian companies can tap for computing power.
Meanwhile, other groups are focused on adoption. Accountant group CPA Canada asked for more responsible AI adoption and stronger governance, while CPA Canada suggested an AI and digital investment tax credit to encourage small businesses to integrate the technology.
What the feds have said: Many of these asks (more domestic AI infrastructure, adoption, responsible governance) were alluded to in the federal AI strategy released in June, so it’s unclear how much more Canadians should expect on the AI front from the budget.
The feds are also already spending on computing power and infrastructure. The government released its $2.4-billion Sovereign AI Compute Strategy in 2024; under Prime Minister Mark Carney, the government has topped up the strategy and deployed millions through the AI Compute Access Fund. A condition of Cohere’s $1.6-billion investment from the feds was that the company invest at least $1.7 billion in new computing infrastructure (meaning data centres) in Canada by 2030.
Quantum computing and deep tech
The ask: Canada’s quantum computing industry wants more funding to support building a full-scale quantum computer. Industry group Quantum Industry Canada wants more funding for its operations, as well as a renewed national quantum strategy. Member company Photonic, which is part of the federal Canadian Quantum Champions Program (CQCP), wants the feds to continue supporting the program. Meanwhile, Zero Point Cryogenics argues that Canada’s entire quantum supply chain—including itself, which makes cryogenic freezer tech—should be included in this program.
Other deep tech sectors argue that their sectors need more federal attention. Canada’s Semiconductor Council wants a national semiconductor and photonics strategy, including funding commitments. Nuclear fusion company General Fusion wants (unsurprisingly) a national fusion energy strategy.
What the feds have said: The government already committed more than $330 million to the quantum industry in last year’s budget. Beyond deploying funds through the CQCP, it hasn’t signalled that much else is in the works.
AI and digital innovation minister Evan Solomon said in May that Canada wouldn’t pursue a national semiconductor strategy, and that some elements would be covered in the since-released AI strategy. However, the feds also announced that Ottawa’s federal semiconductor facility would be opened up for private investment, and no announcements have been made yet.
FinTech
The ask: The FinTech sector wants long-awaited measures that would boost competition in the financial sector to finally come into effect.
Industry group Fintechs Canada, FinTech company Neo Financial, and EQ Bank asked for the feds to follow through on (and, in some cases, speed up delivery of) an open banking system. Fintechs Canada and EQ Bank also asked for an accelerated rollout of Real-Time Rail (RTR); Payments Canada, the organization responsible for delivering it, wants the government’s continued support for the launch.
Wealthsimple wants the feds to implement a ban on investment and registered account transfer fees that was announced last year. On crypto, the Canadian Web3 Council and Shakepay recommended the government loosen its language around a ban on stablecoin interest and yields.
What the feds have said: Last year’s budget saw the feds commit to a “competitive and innovative” financial system and to push open banking, RTR, and stablecoins forward. All that is left is finalized regulations on open banking and stablecoins, as well as specific RTR go-live dates.
On stablecoin yields, the government’s draft regulations for stablecoins have actually carved out somewhat of an exception for stablecoin yields when rewards are paid out based on transaction activity.
Wealthsimple got some movement toward its goal when the feds took the first steps to ban account transfer fees at federally regulated banks on Wednesday, CEO Michael Katchen said.
Immigration and talent
The ask: The business sector wants an immigration plan that brings in skilled workers, as well as measures to upskill existing talent for new advances in tech.
Following the Liberals’ immigration clampdown, CFIB and other business groups want to give provinces more control over immigration levels, as they say some sectors are struggling to find enough skilled talent. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce suggested not a net increase or decrease, but an approach tailored to different regions.
Tech has some specific asks to grow the number of startup founders in Canada. CCI wants a more competitive Start-Up Visa Program (which was put on pause last December) that offers temporary residency first with a pathway to permanence tied to business performance. CVCA supports that ask, particularly through an Entrepreneur Pilot that prioritizes high-growth venture sectors.
What the feds have said: The feds are expected to release an immigration plan for the next three years in the budget. What’s unclear, according to Bloomberg, is whether this plan will show a marked increase in numbers or keep things the way they are.
Feature image courtesy François-Philippe Champagne via LinkedIn.

articles.title: ElevenLabs now lets users publish AI-generated music directly on SoundCloud | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Audio AI company ElevenLabs on Thursday said users will be able to publish AI-generated music created using its ElevenMusic platform directly on SoundCloud.
ElevenLabs is also offering SoundCloud Artist Pro users three months of ElevenMusic Pro, which lets you generate up to 1,000 songs, split songs’ stem files 500 times, and five custom styles or vocals per month.
The company first released a music-generation model in 2025, and followed it up in April 2026 with a consumer app that lets you generate songs using prompts. Then a month later, it released a new music model that could switch genres mid-track and handle more complex vocals. ElevenLabs said that users have so far created over 25 million tracks using its models.
SoundCloud has also been giving AI tools to artists, though it’s taking a different approach. Last month, it partnered with AI music tooling company Moises to let artists export and import songs to and from SoundCloud. The company also has integrations with other platforms like Google Flow Music and the music remix platform, Hook.
“SoundCloud has always been a place where artists experiment, push boundaries, and turn creative ideas into something bigger. By becoming the first platform to bring ElevenMusic creations directly to fans beyond its own ecosystem, we’re opening up new possibilities for artists to experiment, share their work, and build an audience,” SoundCloud CEO Eliah Seton said in a statement.
ElevenLabs also has a partnership with Spotify in which authors can use its audio models to generate narrations for their audiobooks and publish them on the music streaming service. While Spotify has signed partnerships with labels for products that let people use AI for remixing tracks, it has not yet announced any model partners like ElevenLabs.
Overall, though, music streaming platforms today seem more inclined toward labeling and helping users filter out AI-generated music, especially as the tech slowly grows popular with musicians. Deezer, for example, is introducing a toggle that lets you filter out AI music completely, while Bandcamp has put a blanket ban on AI-generated tracks. Spotify and YouTube have taken a more cautious approach to labeling tracks.

articles.title: The UK's AI strategy is missing one crucial piece: compute
articles.text:
The UK's AI strategy is missing one crucial piece: compute
The UK needs compute sovereignty, not just AI partnerships, to build competitive companies
Britain is starting to treat AI as a matter of national security as well as economic growth. Last week at the UN General Assembly, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced a new AI partnership between the UK and US, designed to protect critical national infrastructure from sea lanes to airspace.
It is an important development, particularly as AI moves from chatbots and productivity tools into defense and other systems where reliability really matters. But underneath it sits a rather basic question that receives far less attention: where will the computing power come from?
AI and Financial Inclusion Strategist at io.net.
We have become accustomed to talking about AI in terms of models. Britain has strong universities, a healthy startup ecosystem and a growing collection of companies building products around the technology.
Yet their work all depends on the same thing: reliable access to compute. Models have to be trained somewhere, inference has to happen somewhere and the GPUs doing that work have to be available when companies need them.
Why smaller companies are squeezed out
The largest cloud providers are committing enormous amounts of money to AI infrastructure, and the biggest AI companies are securing GPU capacity years ahead. From a commercial perspective, this makes sense. A hyperscaler wants predictable demand, and a large AI company wants to know that the computing power it needs will be there when its next training run begins. The problem comes further down the market, where a growing number of companies are competing for whatever capacity is left.
And it is not only companies. An Oxford University study found that just 32 countries host specialized AI data centers at all, with US and Chinese firms operating more than 90% of them. American tech giants run 87 major AI hubs worldwide, while European companies run just six. Entire nations are effectively standing in the same queue as the startups, renting computing power on someone else's terms.
For a British AI company that has raised a few million pounds and needs 500 GPUs for eight weeks, the economics look very different from those of a company capable of signing a multibillion-pound infrastructure deal. It does not need to own a data center. It does not necessarily want to make a five-year commitment. It needs access to compute for a particular project, at a particular moment, and it needs to know what that access will cost.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
At the moment, that is exactly what it struggles to get. Rental prices for Nvidia's latest chips rose by nearly half in just two months earlier this year, and CoreWeave, one of the largest specialist providers, raised prices and stretched its minimum contracts from one year to three. Andreessen Horowitz has described one of its startups signing a contract for GPUs, only to be told at the last minute it would have to wait another three months because a bigger customer had offered three times the price.
The appetite is clear: when the government's Sovereign AI Fund opened up compute for startups, it received over 200 applications requesting more than 67 million GPU hours in just three months. Yet much of the market is still poorly designed for that kind of customer.
The paradox of scarce and idle capacity
There is an odd paradox developing in AI infrastructure. We hear constantly about a shortage of GPUs, yet much of the capacity companies already pay for sits unused. One analysis of around 23,000 cloud clusters found average GPU utilization of 5%, meaning organizations are paying for roughly 20 times more capacity than their workloads actually use.
Worried about being caught short, companies buy for their busiest possible day, lock in capacity before they know exactly what they will use it for and hold on to it in case they need it later, so for much of the time, expensive hardware simply sits idle. The result is a market where capacity can be scarce for one company while sitting idle somewhere else.
So on one side there are companies searching desperately for compute, and on the other, capacity that is mostly going unused. Connecting the two seems an obvious step. Bringing more of the GPU capacity spread across data centers, infrastructure providers and enterprise environments into a common marketplace would give British AI companies another way to get the computing power they need, particularly when they are too small to negotiate directly with the largest providers or do not want to lock themselves into a single cloud.
It also goes to the heart of the sovereignty question Burnham keeps returning to. Plenty of computing power already sits on British soil, spread across university clusters, company server rooms, regional data centers and specialist providers, but in pieces too small to matter on their own.
Pooled together, that capacity would give British companies a source of compute under UK jurisdiction, rather than one dependent on the expansion plans of a few American cloud giants. Because it is spread across the country rather than concentrated in a handful of sites, it would carry the benefits of AI well beyond London and the South East, exactly the kind of regional growth Burnham built his reputation on.
What government and policy should do
Britain wants to create AI companies capable of competing globally. Those companies need researchers, capital and customers, but they also need somewhere to run their workloads. If access to compute becomes dependent on the size of a company's balance sheet or its relationship with a handful of cloud providers, Britain risks creating an AI economy where the infrastructure is effectively reserved for the largest players.
There is a role for the government here. It has committed over £2 billion to public compute, including expanding the AI Research Resource twentyfold by 2030, and that investment is welcome. But much of it is going into a small number of national supercomputers, while demand from startups already far outstrips what is on offer.
That points to a simpler idea. Alongside building new supercomputers, the government should invest in making the most of the compute that already exists. New facilities take years to plan, connect to the grid and fill with chips, and each one adds capacity a single site at a time. The technology to link GPUs from many different locations into one usable network already exists, and it can put idle capacity to work without waiting for a single new building to go up.
Public funding could back that kind of pooling directly, for example by buying time on it for British startups. Government procurement could also give smaller AI companies a route into compute without requiring them to make the sort of infrastructure commitments expected of much larger businesses.
If companies can move workloads between providers without rebuilding their entire technology stack, they have more choice, and providers have to compete harder on price and service. That is good for the companies buying compute and ultimately good for the UK economy.
AI policy has spent a lot of time asking what Britain should build. The more immediate question may be whether British companies will be able to get enough compute to build it. That is the problem worth solving.

articles.title: Anthropic loosens game restrictions
articles.text:
Anthropic loosens Claude's game cloning ban — AI will now offer to build original games in the requested genre
The developers must balance Claude's capabilities with the need to avoid 'pirating' games.
The explosion of cloning and reverse-engineering games with AI has forced Anthropic to completely block its AI tools from executing these tasks. However, this has also negatively impacted game developers, who have started complaining that they can no longer use the tool for their own legitimate purposes. The Anthropic team has updated the rule so that Claude will now offer to build an original game in the same genre when asked to copy an existing one, according to an X post by technical staff member Addy Osmani.
"Last week some of you ran into Claude Code pushing back on game projects it should have just built. We'd added a short rule to the Opus 5.5 prompt to steer Claude away from recreating specific existing games, but it was also kicking in when you referenced one just to describe the mechanics you wanted," Osmani wrote. "We've updated that rule in 2.1.317. You can name a game to describe what you want, and Claude should now build an original game in that genre. If you ask for a copy of the original, it'll offer to build something similar instead."
Game decompiling used to be difficult task — often taking teams of dedicated and skilled volunteers months, if not years, to complete. The availability of AI tools has made this process so much faster and easier, although that doesn’t automatically mean that the decompiled version comes out clean. But what’s worse is that some bad actors have been using the technology to reverse engineer game demos from small and indie developers and blackmailing them by threatening to release an AI-completed version of their game — holding the developers’ games hostage and asking for ransom so that their work is not spoiled or destroyed.
Anthropic engineers are now trying to find a balance between preventing its tools from being used to copy games and earning the ire of software giants, publishers, and game developers while also ensuring that its paying customers can continue to use Claude for their own games.
Osmani also said on his post, "We want Claude to be as helpful as possible when you're building something original, but also to protect your work if someone else tries to copy it."
Frontier AI is becoming increasingly powerful, allowing programmers and developers to get things done more quickly and efficiently. But its unprecedented capability is also leading to unintended consequences, such as the ability to create rough clones of expensive software, such as Adobe Creative Suite and Microsoft Office.

articles.title: ‘Total repudiation’: The blue wave is about to hit AI
articles.text:
On Tuesday night, Democrats made history as they took control of the House and the Senate, and a blue wave swept through traditionally red and swing states — with the nation’s first Black woman governor elected in Georgia, the country’s first Native American woman governor elected in New Mexico, and a Maine Senator ceding to a Democrat after 30 years in office. In these and other campaigns, one theme kept coming up: holding AI companies accountable to the American people. Now, the AI industry is left considering the prospect of regulation, data center construction slowdowns, and more.
‘Total repudiation’: The blue wave is about to hit AI
AI companies have a new threat: a wave of Democrats who campaigned against them.
‘Total repudiation’: The blue wave is about to hit AI
AI companies have a new threat: a wave of Democrats who campaigned against them.
Publicly, most major AI company CEOs have remained silent. OpenAI and Anthropic did not provide comments to The Verge; Elon Musk’s call on X to vote “red” for the midterms — the SpaceX CEO had spent close to $450 million backing Republican campaigns for the election — vanished after results poured in.
Privately, CEOs have discussed significant compute capacity constraints for their companies after Tuesday’s results, particularly OpenAI, per The Wall Street Journal. Meta’s platforms president, Dina Powell McCormick, says many are considering moving data center construction abroad. AI executives are reportedly privately nervous about the results but may also be able to blame them for not delivering as much revenue to investors. Many of the incoming leaders have promised to drag CEOs to testify. On X, a popular post by former X product lead Nikita Bier warned that “This is going to be like the Nuremberg Trials but for AI researchers.” (On Tuesday night, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman did post about how “people should always be in control of the future,” but he spent other parts of the evening talking about RAM.)
Tuesday’s results were a “total repudiation” of the AI field, says Wes McEnany, the former Deputy Labor Policy Director of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, & Pensions, who now works with the nonprofit Future of Life Institute. He said that AI touches “every aspect of people’s lives,” whether they’re applying for jobs, using social media, or even paying electricity bills while living near a data center, and that they’re tired of not having “any agency in that conversation.”
The bipartisan backlash against data center construction is the most tangible manifestation of that backlash. It’s going to be unquestionably more difficult to build them across the country, after 43 out of 44 local data center moratoria on Tuesday’s ballots passed, sending a clear message to AI companies. In Texas, the fastest-growing data center buildout area and a key battleground state, governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she plans to “issue a moratorium — a ban — on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans.” Similar promises have been made in a handful of other key states.
“Data centers were clearly on the ballot,” said Guru Sethupathy, GM of AI governance at Optro.
In recent months, there’s been an increasing number of protests and collective bipartisan action to battle data centers being built in a wide range of states. Residents are concerned about noise pollution, electricity bill rate hikes, and more. When NBC News polled voters on Tuesday, 76 percent opposed data centers in their communities.
“The data center backlash is one of the most bipartisan political issues I’ve ever seen,” Shaunna Thomas, co-founder and director of the Guardrails Alliance, a Super PAC pushing for AI regulation.
“Data centers are an entry point to looking at this broader corporate accountability lens of, ‘My bill is going up, why?’” said Kyle Jacobs-Morse, deputy executive director at The Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit tech industry watchdog. “People found that it was big tech companies that were the culprit.” He added that particularly in the gubernatorial races in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio, Democratic campaigns prioritized potential local issues stemming from data centers, including “spillover costs” for local residents, communities, and state governments.
“I do think we’ll hear more questions about who benefits from and who pays for AI, especially as it pertains to infrastructure, but what I’m more curious about is what changes we can expect around regulation,” said François Ajenstat, CEO and founder of Golden Analytics.
Experts say the midterm results have likely ended Trump and congressional Republicans’ repeated attempts to bar state-level AI restrictions. Thomas considers the idea “completely dead,” while McEnany said “any member who votes to wipe out state AI laws is going to be looking for a job in the next [election].” Jacobs-Morse expects to generally see more “tech accountability bills.”
OpenAI recently began calling its data centers “compute campuses,” and President Trump in September attempted to change the name of AI as a technology to “super intelligence.” But midterm results suggest that a significant portion of American voters aren’t buying the rebranding efforts.
“I don’t think it was working, and I think the prospect of it working is extremely low after the election,” Thomas said.
“The Trump idiosyncrasies around some of this stuff… they did not play well at the ballot box,” Jacobs-Morse said.
But some in and around the tech industry are taking the news more positively than others. One X user wrote that “we’re *maybe* back to being a rational, steady hand as a country and can really lead,” while others wrote that the recent results could be good for preventing an AI bubble burst. Katie Barr, CEO of Glen Echo Group and a partner at Orchestra, said she wouldn’t “over-read” the results as an overwhelming tech rejection but rather a reckoning on “affordability, jobs, safety, and whether people have a say in what’s happening in their communities and their lives.”
Analysts at Yorkville Ives & Co. wrote in a note that though tech investors should prepare for “major hurdles for AI and tech legislation” and a slowdown of the planned construction of up to 1,000 data centers across the country, there could be a “slight positive” in that it could help avoid a bubble and slow capital fundraising flooding the market.
There will also likely be a reckoning on AI safety. Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) was reelected after campaigning for AI safety policy, and in a victory speech Tuesday by Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Ossoff said, “The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.” Some AI safety legislation is already being considered, like the bill to “ban superintelligence” introduced in September by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas).
President Trump has dismissed the idea of a safety crisis in AI as a “hoax,” writing on social media that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.” After the midterms, however, Republican lawmakers will need to decide whether to fall in line or negotiate with Democrats on safety-focused policy measures. Either way, Adam Kovacevich, founder and CEO of Chamber of Progress, a pro-tech industry advocacy group, said he expects AI safety legislation to continue to happen in blue states.
“There’s a lot of open questions about where democrats go next on tech policy. Do we revert to the Biden era war on tech, the Obama era tech honeymoon, or something in between?” Kovacevich said.

articles.title: Nicolas Cage rompe su silencio por el fichaje de Ryan Gosling como nuevo 'Ghost Rider' de Marvel
articles.text:
Marvel ya prepara su próxima gran película de Ghost Rider con Ryan Gosling como protagonista. El actor de La La Land y Barbie se pondrá en la piel del Motorista Fantasma para una entrega que llegará en 2028, después de Avengers: Secret Wars, con la intención de abrir camino a una nueva era marvelita. Pero si de alguien queríamos saber su opinión, ese era Nicolas Cage.
Aunque este mismo año hemos podido verle en Marvel en el papel de Ben Reilly /Spider-Noir, en realidad Nicolas Cage interpretó a Ghost Rider en dos películas estrenadas en 2007 y 2012. Por ello, muchos de los fans de La Casa de las Ideas ya asocian irremediablemente su rostro al del Johnny Blaze. Ahora, el intérprete ha revelado al fin qué piensa sobre este nuevo reboot.
"Ryan va a darle su toque personal y tengo muchas ganas de verla. Ryan sabe lo que pienso de él como actor. Hemos tenido conversaciones muy agradables y seguimos en contacto. Me alegré por él, le deseé mucha suerte en sus aventuras y estoy deseando ver la película", asegura en una entrevista concedida a The Hollywood Reporter. En definitiva, Nicolas Cage ha dado su bendición a Ryan Gosling como Ghost Rider.
Qué sabemos de Ghost Rider
De Ghost Rider se sabe es que fue el propio Ryan Gosling, muy fan de sus cómics, quien les presentó la idea a los ejecutivos de Marvel. El filme estará dirigido por Shawn Levy, cineasta responsable de Deadpool y Lobezno. Y es que actor y director ya saben lo que es trabajar juntos, pues están desarrollando actualmente Star Wars: Starfighter, la nueva película de la franquicia galáctica.
También tenemos la fecha de estreno. Ghost Rider se estrenará en cines el 28 de julio de 2028. Esto quiere decir que llegará después de la película de X-Men, que se estrena en mayo de ese mismo año y será la primera entrega de la nueva era de Marvel después de cerrar el multiverso con Avengers: Secret Wars. Lo cierto es que, con la compañía desarrollando abiertamente toda una Saga Mutante, se desconoce exactamente cómo encajará el filme del Motorista Fantasma en esos planes.

articles.title: Building a Culture for a Kubernetes-Based Platform in a Bank
articles.text:
In a banking environment, open source can earn trust by running real workloads, as Marcy Paramonova and Stéphane Cusin explained in their talk Building Cloud Native Culture in a Bank at KubeCon & CloudNativeCon Europe. Deploying Kubernetes was the easy part; the hard part was culture: community of practice, shared knowledge, rituals, ownership. Teams try things, keep what works, and improve bottom-up.
Open source was not an obvious choice in their banking environment, Cusin mentioned. They received questions about support and accountability. Instead of trying to convince people with theory, they started running real workloads. Over time, trust was built by operating the platform day after day:
Open source stopped being seen as a risk. It became the foundation.
They treated their first version of Kubernetes like a project. "We delivered it, we got a good adoption", Cusin said. But the operation was incredibly hard. Not because the technology was broken, but because they hadn’t built the culture around it yet:
Nobody knew who to call, responsibilities were blurry, and teams were consuming the platform without really contributing to it. Every incident felt like a fire drill.
They realized deploying Kubernetes was the easy part. The hard part was building the culture with a community of practice around it. The shared knowledge, the rituals, the ownership model, Cusin explained:
Without that culture, no platform survives its own success.
They invite people to experiment, for instance by having a yearly competition where everybody can submit their ideas and the one that wins, actually gets implemented. Many of their improvements came from the bottom up, Paramonova argued.
They used open source as a compass, something that helped them orientate a subject, Cusin explained:
When Kubernetes appeared, we recognized it immediately. Strong Kubernetes, transparent governance, and real production users. The compass pointed; we followed. And now we are watching OpenStack the same way.
A compass doesn’t force you in one direction. It helps you recognize the right opportunity when it arrives, Cusin said.
They tried things, and some of them didn’t work. They kept the ones that did. The act of trying, of deliberately designing how teams interact, creates the culture we have today, Cusin said. Structure first, the culture follows.
Every organization is different; every regulated environment has its own constraints, Paramonova said. You need a compass during your journey. It’s something that will guide you when everything else is uncertain. For us, it was open source, she concluded.
InfoQ interviewed Marcy Paramonova and Stéphane Cusin after their talk.
InfoQ: How did you gain trust from your development teams?
Stéphane Cusin: Over time, trust emerged from a combination of transparency and reliability. When developers see that the platform consistently helps them deliver applications safely and efficiently, adoption follows naturally.
Marcy Paramonova: Trust was not something we could establish by presenting a roadmap or writing good documentation, though both matter. It came from running things. From being present when something broke. From being honest about what was not yet ready.
Cusin: Today, our culture is centered around ownership, automation, transparency, and continuous improvement. Teams are empowered to move quickly, but they do so within a framework of shared standards and platform capabilities. The result is not only greater efficiency, but also greater consistency, reliability, and visibility across the organization.
InfoQ: How did Kubernetes transform how your organization builds software?
Cusin: Kubernetes gave us a common platform and a common operating model. In the first version of our platform, we gave teams flexibility. We exposed many Kubernetes capabilities directly and allowed teams to customize their deployment model extensively. In practice, that often resulted in different patterns emerging across teams.
One of the lessons we learned as platform engineers is that developers do not come to a platform looking for more infrastructure choices. They come to a platform to deliver software.
In our current platform, Kubernetes is no longer the product. Kubernetes is the implementation detail. The product is a simple, secure, and standardized software delivery experience.
We provide opinionated deployment patterns, standardized Helm charts, and common platform capabilities. As a result, when an engineer moves from one team to another, the deployment experience is largely the same. They do not need to relearn how applications are packaged, deployed, monitored, or operated.
Paramonova: The transformation I experienced most directly was organizational. Kubernetes gave teams a common language. It created shared abstractions that made collaboration across different parts of engineering much more natural.
Before, a lot of knowledge was siloed by team or by technology stack. Kubernetes did not erase those silos overnight, but it gave everyone a shared foundation to build on. That changed conversations, and changed what was possible.
