articles.title: Physical AI Pushes The Limits Of Hardware
articles.text:
Autonomous machines promise to transform industries, but memory bottlenecks, power constraints, specialized architectures, and safety requirements are forcing chip designers to rethink the entire system.
Key Takeaways:
The race is on to develop physical AI fit for widespread use, but building these sensor-powered systems will require engineering teams to address a variety of technical challenges concurrently and continuously.
Analysts predict significant market growth for physical AI, with the promise that autonomous systems will fundamentally reshape industries spanning transportation, manufacturing, medicine, energy, and more. PwC’s Strategy& projects that the global physical AI market could reach approximately €430 billion by 2030, reflecting the potential commercial impact of autonomous systems across multiple industries.
“Physical AI systems are expanding beyond automotive to robotics and drones, and the bottlenecks for development of these applications cover the entire system,” said Licinio Sousa, senior director of Interface IP for Automotive and Physical AI at Synopsys. “AI is expanding from the data center to the edge, and with machines such as robots, drones, and vehicles, all driven by the need for autonomy, privacy, personalization, faster response, and less reliance on the cloud.”
The list of technical challenges that need to be addressed is long and intertwined. Memory capacity and bandwidth need to be increased, latency and power consumption need to be decreased, product lifespans need to be stretched, and safety needs to be verified. And if that isn’t hard enough, addressing any one of these can create problems elsewhere.
Specialized architectures
Solving these system-wide bottlenecks requires highly specialized hardware and software that are optimized for specific use cases.
“We need to start talking about optimized, more tailored compute that you build for the specific workload, and this is where physical AI gets more interesting,” said Michal Siwinski, executive vice president and chief product and marketing officer, and general manager for Security Solutions at Arteris. “That workload needs to be highly optimized for the hardware. We’re basically going back to ASICs in the traditional sense of what ASICs were supposed to be — very application-specific, extremely optimized, versus more generic. Some of that is already starting. It will be interesting to see how the more nimble systems evolve for very specific applications between the software and the hardware and the workload, and keep evolving because the models are moving way faster.”
Autonomous robotics systems share some of the same technology found in self-driving vehicles, particularly in perception and control, but each physical AI use case adds unique challenges.
“Robotics is not a new AI stack,” Vasanthan Karunanithy, staff systems architect for Automotive at Micron Technology, said at the recent JEDEC Automotive Forum. “From an ADAS system, the robot inherits real-time perception, path planning, and motion control. From an intelligent cabinet, robotics inherits natural language understanding, contextual reasoning, and personal interaction. In embodied intelligence, the bigger challenge is running these two workloads together and then exchanging information at the end. So that is the commonality between these two segments. But there is also a difference that tells the scale of the channel. An autonomous vehicle operates in a relatively structured road environment and draws power from a larger source — the vehicle battery. But when you look at robots, they operate in an unstructured 3D environment. [A robot] also needs to maintain multiple degrees of freedom. It has to manipulate objects and maintain balance, and it has to understand the commands in the instructions. It has to do all this with a limited power source compared to automotive.”
Those distinctions vary considerably across applications. Autonomous vehicles operate within established transportation infrastructure, but they must respond to unpredictable road conditions. Mobile and humanoid robots, in contrast, may need to navigate less structured environments, coordinate manipulation and balance, and operate within much more restrictive power budgets. Meanwhile, industrial robots may operate in controlled environments with fixed electrical power. These differences make it hard to optimize a single architecture for every form of physical AI.
Fig. 1: Robotic system. Source: Synopsys.
Designers must build system architecture with these requirements in mind from the start.
“As workloads and models evolve, we are already seeing purpose-built silicon designed to meet the specific needs of each class of machine,” Sousa said. “Our customers continue to address the need for advanced VLA (vision-language-action) models. In the hardware world, this translates to more intensive compute and AI engines. At the same time, the spectrum of use cases makes it harder for a single monolithic architecture, leading to a transition to chiplets where compute, AI, memory, and I/Os can be scaled using a UCIe interface based on specific use cases.”
Chiplets offer one potential path to scalable physical AI platforms, particularly when heterogeneous compute, memory, and I/O requirements justify advanced packaging. However, they also can ratchet up costs and complexity due to customized packaging, thermal management, and die-to-die communication. Monolithic SoCs may be preferable for smaller, highly integrated systems where power, size, and cost are constrained.
Those constraints apply to both hardware and software. “The sensors are going to be much more focused on use cases, and you need to make sure that you have good use cases, and it’s customized, and you need to have a software layer on top of it as well,” said Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI & Solido at Siemens EDA. “I always joke that everything involved in the real world is analog and we are trying to abstract it to digital, so one of the most important things is redundancy. Sensors have gotten pretty good. We can sense in terms of visual, thermal, pressure, anything. We have gotten good in terms of radar and everything else. What’s more important is making sure that the sensors can operate in the environment, and that environment needs to be captured in a way that it doesn’t make it doesn’t really degrade, or you have redundancy built in.”
Still, the effectiveness of redundancy can vary, depending on whether components can fail independently and whether the system can identify and respond to faults. Adding sensors alone doesn’t guarantee reliable operation, especially when environmental conditions can affect multiple sensors at once.
Tailoring the compute architecture to the workload or use case introduces tradeoffs, as well. “There is the question of how close the intelligence needs to be to the actual origination of where the sensing is happening, and there’s a push-pull,” said Yasmine King, corporate vice president and head of Automotive at Analog Devices. “If you have intelligence distributed throughout a system, that makes it more complicated to update. Centralizing allows one point of over-the-air updates, easy to patch and fix, but it can create latency issues when you need to react quickly to this data. In a vehicle, if a pedestrian runs out in front of your car, you need to be able to respond extremely quickly. So where you locate your intelligence is based on what sensory information you’re trying to gather, and how quickly you need to respond.”
Fig. 2 Analog Devices’ Yasmine King speaks at Reuters Automotive 2026 Oct. 27, 2026. Source: Semiconductor Engineering
The placement of intelligence is an architectural decision involving more than compute performance. It requires balancing response time, communication bandwidth, power consumption, updateability, as well as coordination of distributed components. Centralized compute may simplify management, while local processing can reduce communication delays and preserve essential functionality when connectivity is interrupted.
Physical AI’s memory wall
Memory capacity, bandwidth, latency, and energy consumption stand out as key chokepoints for physical AI, alongside potential supply constraints for some memory technologies. The challenge is designing a memory subsystem capable of feeding increasingly demanding AI workloads within tight power and thermal limits, not just adding a sufficient number of memory components.
“The billions of associated model parameters also need to be stored and transported across storage, memory, and processing elements,” Sousa said. “Today, this is referred to as the memory wall. As memory footprint continues to grow, DRAM needs an ultra-fast interface, such as LPDDR6, to no longer be a bottleneck to processing.”
Performance also depends on access patterns, latency, data reuse, cache capacity, memory-controller efficiency, and the energy required to move data. Increasing raw bandwidth may provide limited benefit if workloads are constrained by other parts of the memory hierarchy.
Workload-specific system design can help offset some memory burdens. “Coming up with right-sized memory, right-sized compute and redundancy, everything that needs to fit into your thermal and power envelope is going to be very key,” said Balasubramanian. “The most important thing is that size matters. You don’t need a 100-gallon tank in your Prius. You need a 10-gallon tank. That’s the analogy I use in terms of memory. You can manage it in a way that you don’t need a huge DRAM, but you have a pretty good cache and an SRAM built in. It can always store critical requirements in DRAM, but you can move everything else to flash or SRAM when needed. The memory path, in terms of cache coherency from DRAM to SRAM, to the actual compute, and to making the actual physical AI, is going to be very key.”
The trade-offs between these memory technologies are significant. On-chip SRAM and caches can provide fast access to frequently used data, but their capacity is limited by silicon area and cost. External DRAM offers greater capacity, while flash provides nonvolatile storage for models, software, and other information that doesn’t need to remain in active memory.
Moving information among these tiers can reduce some capacity requirements, but it adds transfer overhead and latency. Cache coherency, meanwhile, focuses on keeping copies of data consistent across caches and memory, rather than simply moving information between storage technologies, but that adds more overhead. So engineers must consider the working set, data locality, and access frequency when determining how much memory belongs at each level.
Automotive memory innovations will likely loom large in how the issue is addressed for physical AI.
“It’s very closely coupled to our automotive range at the moment, and we see the majority of requirements from the robotics side coming directly from the automotive side,” said Rob Fisher, senior director of product management at Imagination Technologies. “A lot of automotive players will now present their chips as automotive and robotics platforms, so the 4-, 6-, and 8-bit support are really going to benefit memory bandwidth and memory footprint of embedded edge-type applications. It’s less of a concern in data centers, but the impact is different. You can probably have a bigger model in a data center by using a smaller bit width on your words. In an automotive application and a robotics application, you’ll probably take the other side of that benefit, which is a smaller memory footprint. You’ll constrain your model to do exactly what you need it to do, and then you’ll reduce the amount of memory and bandwidth you have available to contain it.”
Lower-precision representations can reduce model storage and memory bandwidth requirements, making them particularly attractive for embedded AI. But the benefits depend on whether the accelerator efficiently supports the chosen numerical format and whether quantization preserves the application’s required accuracy. Formats such as 6-bit representations can also introduce packing or implementation overhead, limiting the gains achievable on hardware not designed for them.
Flash storage also plays a critical role in managing memory for autonomous systems.
“DRAM is constrained in capacity, power, and availability,” Sousa said. “Faster storage bandwidth shortens load time, so the same DRAM budget can support larger models. These systems run continuously on batteries and often without active cooling, so every data transfer costs power and adds delay, making it necessary for each component — mechanical, electronic, and software — to limit power consumption and improve efficiency. Interfaces such as MIPI, UFS, LPDDR, PCIe, etc., have techniques built in to ensure fast transmission of bursty data and then transitioning to long low-power idle modes.”
Faster non-volatile storage can shorten model-loading delays and, when paired with appropriate model partitioning or weight-streaming techniques, allow systems with limited DRAM to execute workloads whose total model footprint exceeds available active memory. However, storage bandwidth alone does not increase the amount of data that can be kept in DRAM at any point in time.
The interfaces used to move that data also differ in their power-management mechanisms and operating characteristics. Their efficiency depends on the particular specification, implementation, transfer patterns, and opportunities to enter low-power states.
Physical AI’s memory demands could eventually justify new memory technologies or variants of existing ones, provided the market becomes large enough to support the investment.
“Memory is a critical technology, and it’s going to be needed in all the physical AI that’s out there,” said Steven Woo, fellow and distinguished inventor at Rambus. “What’s different about these markets is some of them are going to just leverage the memories that are out there, but it’s possible some of them could become so big in terms of market sizes that they may warrant their own type of memory or some variant of an existing memory. We saw that with HBM, for example. People were using other kinds of memories, and suddenly the market got big. And if you go back before LPDDR, phones were just using binned, carefully selected DDR parts that just happened to be low power. The market got big enough, and people said, ‘Well, let’s just make a special part.’ Physical AI has the potential to become a big enough market on its own, so that if the requirements vary enough, there could be another kind of memory.”
Whether such specialization occurs will depend on the scale and consistency of demand. Unlike data centers, physical AI spans applications with widely differing requirements for cost, capacity, endurance, bandwidth, temperature, and energy efficiency. That diversity may favor adaptations of existing memory technologies in some markets and purpose-built solutions in others.
Validating the edge cases
Ensuring a system behaves safely, including under rare and unexpected conditions, is another major challenge. Solving the validation problem is especially important as physical AI developers target integration into heavy machinery, medical devices, and other safety-critical technologies.
“The validation loop that we need to bring physical AI into before we get into any production is paramount, and I would say is the most important thing we need to do,” said Siemens’ Balasubramanian. “What happens if there is a huge power cut or there’s an earthquake, and your fiber optic cable is cut from the outside world, or there’s a power cut? How do you manage that kind of a scenario on the edge? Having some kind of compute, some kind of memory, and some kind of intelligence close to the sensor is going to be very key, and the way people do that is by coming up with what they determine is the most important thing given use-case needs. In an industrial environment, when do I need to stop the assembly line? When do I need to know that I need to phone back or start the siren or anything else? Those are some of the things that need to be handled within a given sensor.”
These scenarios illustrate why safety-critical functions cannot always depend on continuous cloud connectivity or centralized decision-making. Local processing may be necessary to recognize faults, trigger protective actions, or place equipment into a defined safe state when communications or power systems fail.
But verification and validation address different parts of the problem. Verification establishes whether a design satisfies specified requirements, while validation examines whether the system behaves appropriately in its intended operating environment. Safety assurance may additionally require hazard analysis, fault-injection testing, evaluation of common-cause failures, and evidence of compliance with applicable standards.
Systems must therefore be designed to establish and verify trust throughout the relevant hardware and software stack, with assurance requirements matched to each use case.
“When we’re designing something for a wheelchair, we have specific needs, like any physical AI application,” said Owen Kent, co-founder of assistive robotics startup ATDev. “You have to be able to really put this hardware through the wringer in your quality management system and your third-party electromagnetic compatibility testing. Whatever hardware you use, whether it’s custom or not, you have to be able to verify safety.”
For developers, that means evaluating whether components function correctly in normal operation, as well as how the complete system responds to degraded sensors, communication failures, unexpected inputs, and other foreseeable hazards. Passing component-level tests is necessary in many applications, but it does not by itself establish system-level safety.
Conclusion
Physical AI’s practical limits extend across the entire path from sensing to action. Designers must match models and hardware to the task, move data within available energy and thermal budgets, and validate how machines behave when conditions or connections change. Increasing compute capacity only helps when the rest of the system can support it.
“Start with standards-based, low-power and proven interfaces along the whole path, from sensor to processor to actuator,” said Balasubramanian. “They give designers predictable behavior, ecosystem interoperability, and silicon-proven building blocks.”
A relevant example is the MIPI Camera Security Framework, which combines the Camera Service Extensions (CSE) 2.0 specification with complementary security specifications. CSE 2.0 supports data-integrity protection and optional encryption of CSI-2 camera data, while the broader framework addresses authentication of imaging-system components and secure-session establishment.
“It provides end-to-end security for camera data, covering integrity, authentication, and confidentiality from the image sensor to the SoC,” he said. “It also gives designers flexible options to minimize compute and traffic overhead, power, and latency, so security can be matched to the application rather than designed for the worst case.”
The distinction matters because confidentiality is optional, and the level of protection depends on the security services and configurations implemented. The broader framework lets developers balance protection against processing overhead, power consumption, and latency, rather than applying identical protections to every data stream.
It’s not enough to make autonomous machines more capable. They also must be dependable within real-world constraints. For physical AI, the architecture choices that conserve memory, power, and bandwidth must also support predictable behavior, resilience, and the safety assurance that widespread deployment demands.

articles.title: TikTok launched a dedicated TikTok Shop app
articles.text:
TikTok has released a standalone app for TikTok Shop in a few countries, as spotted by social media consultant Matt Navarra. According to its App Store listing, the TikTok Shop app offers:
TikTok launched a dedicated TikTok Shop app
The new TikTok Shop app is now available in a few countries, but not the US.
- Personalized picks inspired by your interests
- LIVE streams & short videos to see products in action
- App-only deals, free shipping offers & exclusive first-order benefits that make every order feel worth it
- Secure payments for safe checkout
- Easy order tracking & 24/7 support from purchase to delivery
But it appears the app, which is also available on Android, hasn’t launched widely yet. Navarra says it’s currently listed in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, and the Philippines, and not in the UK or US App Store. (I’m personally not seeing it on the US App Store on my iPhone.) Still, the fact that the dedicated app exists at all could signal that TikTok is planning to make an even bigger push into online shopping.
TikTok didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

articles.title: 'I think the best soundtrack of any game is one that inspires and elevates the core ideas of the gameplay' — Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 composer says he's 'honored' to have composed 'a score of this scale' for multiplayer, which is typically 'an afterthought'
articles.text:
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 composer says multiplayer music is usually 'an afterthought' and 'cobbled together' from existing campaign music — 'This is the first time we've specifically composed a score of this scale for multiplayer'
Jason Graves says any game soundtrack should "elevate" the "core ideas of the gameplay"
- Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 composer Jason Graves says Modern Warfare multiplayer music is usually "an afterthought"
- He says it's typically "cobbled together" from "existing campaign music," and he did the same thing for Modern Warfare 2
- Graves adds that "the best soundtrack of any game is one that inspires and elevates the core ideas of the gameplay"
According to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 composer Jason Graves, this is the first time a Modern Warfare multiplayer mode has received a full score, as they are typically "an afterthought."
"As far as I know, this is the first time we've specifically composed a score of this scale for multiplayer for Modern Warfare," Graves revealed in an interview with TechRadar Gaming. "It's the first time the multiplayer gameplay itself has received so much love and attention. Normally, it's usually a bit of an afterthought, cobbled together from existing music from the campaign, maybe getting some original lobby music."
Graves, who has worked on numerous video game projects, including Dead Space, said that was what he did for Modern Warfare 2 in 2022, but for Modern Warfare 4, "we have discrete tracks for lobbies, countdowns, streaks, and after-action reports amongst other things."
The composer mentioned how multiplayer has a "completely different vibe from the campaign," and made sure to capture the "forward momentum and pure adrenaline," but believes first-person shooter (FPS) games don't have a "specific list of characteristics" versus a fantasy role-playing game (RPG) in terms of music.
"A lot of my job is simply motivation and excitement, either before, during, or after a multiplayer match," he said. "So I'm here to get you pumped up and ready for action, motivate you towards the finish line, and slap you on the back with a big swaggering beat when you complete your objective."
When discussing his intentions for composing a soundtrack and what defines Modern Warfare in particular, Graves explained that music should always enhance the gameplay.
"There's definitely an incredible history that lives in the Modern Warfare soundtracks," Graves said, "And I'm honored to have contributed my small part to two of them. I think the best soundtrack of any game is one that inspires and elevates the core ideas of the gameplay.

articles.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
articles.text:
Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs.
Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities.
Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem.
Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents 🔗
Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance.
In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering.
Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training.
Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools.
These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications.
Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill.
Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗
Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation.
PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model.
Explore the Onshape importer guide.
Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗
Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation.
David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes.
Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection.
Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries.
Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗
Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator.
The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error.
The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing.
Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene (ovstage), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments.
Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets 🔗
With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin, developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows.
Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments.
For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment.
Find assets in SimReady Central Library, and learn how to contribute.
Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale 🔗
A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene.
When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns.
Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling.
With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements.
Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve.
Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing 🔗
In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit.
Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab, Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable.
Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments.
The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors.
Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab.
Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset 🔗
Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task.
Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot.
Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial.
Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗
Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view.
Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views.
DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics (ovphysx), scene updates (ovstage), rendering (ovrtx) and the user interface (ovui). He also used Astra with SimReady (simready-foundation) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together.
Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗
Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street.
Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions.
Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗
Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene.
To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones.
Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement.
Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example, then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data.
Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗
Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements.
Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control.
Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗
Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible.
The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering (ovrtx), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections.
Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill.
Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗
A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio.
The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect.
Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.

articles.title: La Nasa n'a pas pu le sauver : le télescope Swift s'est désintégré dans l'atmosphère (vidéo)
articles.text:
C’était son dernier plongeon. Ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026, le télescope Swift de la Nasa est retombé sur Terre, mettant fin à près de 22 ans de mission. Selon l’US Space Force, l’observatoire est rentré dans l’atmosphère à 13h39 (heure de Paris). Il s’est enflammé dans le ciel, « au-dessus de la région de Sumatra du Nord, en Indonésie », détaille l’agence spatiale dans un communiqué.
Cette désintégration, qui a donné lieu à un spectaculaire bolide (une grosse étoile filante), a pu être filmée depuis la surface de la Terre.
L’Aerospace Corporation, un centre de recherche qui travaille pour l’armée américaine et suit les rentrées atmosphériques des satellites, a publié de son côté une carte sur X montrant l’endroit où Swift est retombé.
Swift se désintègre après une tentative de sauvetage ratée
Officiellement, la mission de Swift était déjà terminée depuis quelques jours. Sa dernière observation du ciel a eu lieu le 20 octobre, alors que le télescope évoluait à 275 km au-dessus de la surface terrestre. À cette altitude, Swift ne parvenait plus à compenser le freinage de l’atmosphère et s’est mis en mode sans échec. Trois jours plus tard, la Nasa a expliqué avoir « fermé les yeux » de Swift, en coupant ses instruments.
Quelques mois plus tôt, la Nasa avait tenté de sauver Swift à l’aide de LINK, un remorqueur de l’entreprise américaine Katalyst Space. Lancé le 3 juillet, l’engin n’a pas pu remplir sa mission, et la Nasa a renoncé au sauvetage. LINK devait essayer de placer Swift sur une orbite plus adaptée, à 600 km de la surface de la Terre, mais des problèmes techniques l’ont empêché de mener à bien cette mission (LINK s’étant mis à tourner de façon incontrôlée).
« La Nasa s’attendait à ce que la majeure partie du vaisseau se consume lors de son passage dans l’atmosphère, mais certains composants pourraient avoir survécu à la rentrée », précise la publication de blog de l’agence spatiale.
Le satellite pesait environ 1 450 kg. Avant sa chute, la Nasa estimait à environ 1 sur 2 100 le risque qu’une personne soit touchée par un débris. Comme l’orbite de Swift était peu inclinée, les fragments éventuels ne pouvaient retomber qu’entre 20,6 degrés de latitude sud et 20,6 degrés de latitude nord.
Une mission de la Nasa prévue pour 2 ans, qui en a duré près de 22
Swift a largement dépassé les attentes de la Nasa. À l’origine, il avait été envoyé dans l’espace en 2004 pour une mission principale de 2 ans. Il devait étudier les sursauts gamma, les explosions les plus puissantes connues dans l’Univers.
L’observatoire a finalement servi pendant plus de 2 décennies, comme « outil polyvalent pour explorer l’Univers », résume la Nasa. Swift a ainsi permis d’étudier des galaxies alimentées par des trous noirs supermassifs, des supernovae, ou les comètes et astéroïdes de notre système solaire.

articles.title: PhysicsWallah, Lenskart, Nykaa post stellar profits
articles.text:
PhysicsWallah, Lenskart, Nykaa post stellar profits
PhysicsWallah posted a record quarterly top-line and doubled its net profit in Q2FY27. Lenskart’s net profit too rose over two-fold year on year. Nykaa’s profit grew three times, and revenue rose 28% YoY.
Dear Reader,
The earnings season is in full swing.
PhysicsWallah, Lenskart and Nykaa were among the major Indian companies that reported their Q2FY27 results yesterday.
Expanding scale and cost efficiencies helped PhysicsWallah post a record quarterly top-line and double its net profit. Lenskart’s net profit too rose over two-fold year on year.
Nykaa’s profit grew three times to Rs 101 crore and revenue rose 28% YoY to Rs 3,006 crore. The beauty and fashion retailer has also acquired an 82% stake in cosmetics brand Simply Nam. The acquisition is expected to help Nykaa expand its premium makeup portfolio.
Meanwhile, Nasdaq-listed SaaS company Freshworks posted a net profit of $18.3 million in the third quarter of 2026, compared with a loss of $4.7 million in the year-ago period. Revenue rose 14% year on year to $245.4 million.
In an important step towards Atmanirbhar Bharat, the Cabinet has approved a Rs 2,814-crore scheme to promote processing of critical minerals such as lithium and nickel and reduce import dependence.
In other news, Razorpay has secured Sebi’s approval for its proposed IPO of Rs 5,000-6,000 crore, according to sources. The fintech firm is targeting a valuation of around $5 billion through the public offering.
Lastly, the Democrats have taken control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives in the US midterm elections, with Indian Americans also making a mark.
In today’s newsletter:
- Lenskart’s profit doubles, revenue grows 36% in Q2
- PhysicsWallah posts Rs 1,242 Cr top-line; net profit doubles
Here’s your trivia for today: What was the first item ever sold on eBay? (Scroll down for the answer)
Retail
Lenskart’s profit doubles, revenue grows 36% in Q2
Omnichannel eyewear retailer Lenskart’s net profit more than doubled in the second quarter of FY27, while revenue rose 36% year on year. The growth was driven by higher eyewear volumes, premiumisation of products, and stronger demand in India and overseas.
The company reported a net profit of Rs 227 crore in Q2FY27 compared to Rs 102 crore in the year-ago period, a growth of 123%. Revenue was Rs 2,845 crore, a YoY growth of 36%.
Key takeaways:
- India revenue grew 35.3% year on year to Rs 1,668 crore, supported by a 26.5% growth in eyewear volumes and rising demand for premium lenses. Same-store sales growth reached 20.8%, compared with 14.8% a year ago. International revenue grew by 29.5%.
- The company added 143 stores in India, including 94 in Tier II+ markets. It also entered 61 new cities. Its India network now spans 2,868 stores across 665 cities.
- Lenskart maintained its consolidated product margin at 70%, compared with 69.2% a year ago, despite continued rupee depreciation. In-house frame manufacturing grew 71.7% YoY, while lens manufacturing increased 52.2%, helping offset currency pressures and strengthen control over product quality and costs.

PhysicsWallah posts Rs 1,242 Cr top-line; net profit doubles
The second quarter of the 2027 financial year marked a pivotal turn for PhysicsWallah, as expanding scale and cost efficiencies together yielded a record quarterly top-line and a two-fold growth in net profit. The edtech firm achieved its highest-ever quarterly revenue, driven by expanding student enrolments and enhanced course realisations.
Key takeaways:
- Consolidated revenue from operations reached Rs 1,242.26 crore, up 18.2% YoY. Total income, which includes other non-operating receipts, grew 21.5% YoY to Rs 1,334.64 crore.
- Consolidated profit after tax doubled to Rs 142.29 crore in the second quarter, rising 104.1% YoY from Rs 69.72 crore. The net profit in Q2FY27 comes after a loss of Rs 87.04 crore in Q1FY27.
- “We delivered record revenue and a sharp improvement in profitability, while our learner base kept widening across K-12, vernacular and new categories. Our focus remains on scaling affordable, tech-led education with disciplined capital allocation,” said Founder and Chief Executive Officer Alakh Pandey.
News & updates
- Startup momentum: Indian startups with a valuation of over $500 million rose to 51 in 2026, from 47 in 2025, despite a lower number of AI companies. Their combined value is about Rs 3.3 lakh crore, with an average valuation of Rs 6,400 crore, according to the 2026 ASK Private Wealth Hurun India Gazelle Index report.
- Canva restructuring: Graphic design platform Canva is undertaking a major workforce restructuring affecting 1,271 employees, or 22% of its workforce, as it adapts to rapid technological change. In a note to employees, CEO Melanie Perkins described this as the hardest moment in Canva’s 13-year history.
- Accounts hack: Nearly 30 Indian investors who trade US shares through Stockal Securities have reported unauthorised access to their accounts, alleging that their blue-chip holdings, worth millions of dollars in total, were sold off without their consent and replaced with shares in a little-known company that subsequently lost almost 60% of its value.

articles.title: Closing the Identity Gap at the Service Desk
articles.text:
Organizations have invested heavily in securing employee logins. Multi-factor authentication (MFA), conditional access policies and other identity controls make it harder for attackers to gain unauthorized access. But these protections can be undermined if the process for recovering access isn't held to the same standard.
When an employee needs to regain access to their account, it’s often the service desk that provides the password reset or account recovery. Yet identity verification commonly still relies on knowledge-based questions, such as an employee's manager's name or department.
This creates a gap in identity security where a weaker route into an account can bypass stronger login security. And as social engineering attacks become more convincing, that gap is becoming increasingly dangerous.
Why Knowledge-Based Verification Can No Longer Be Trusted
Attackers can gather a surprising amount of information before making a call. LinkedIn profiles, company websites, social media and leaked data can reveal everything from job titles and colleagues to office locations and personal details.
Armed with this information, an attacker can answer verification questions correctly and appear to be a legitimate employee.
This becomes particularly dangerous when passing these checks is enough to authorize a password reset or recover an account. An attacker could gain access to that account without ever needing to compromise the employee's original credentials.
The risks of knowledge-based authentication are well established. NIST's digital identity guidelines no longer recognize security questions as an acceptable authentication method. Against the threat landscape in 2026, knowing information about someone is not proof of their identity.
Secure your Active Directory passwords with Specops Password Policy
Verizon’s Data Breach Investigation Report found stolen credentials are involved in 44.7% of breaches. 
Effortlessly secure Active Directory with compliant password policies, blocking 4+ billion compromised passwords, boosting security, and slashing support hassles!
AI and Social Engineering Make the Gap More Dangerous
Cybercriminal groups such as Scattered Spider have made the service desk a preferred target. Rather than trying to bypass MFA directly, attackers impersonate employees and convince service desk agents to reset passwords or register new MFA devices. A convincing phone call can be enough to gain access to an account.
Generative AI is making these attacks harder to detect and easier to scale. Attackers can use AI to create believable stories, generate natural-sounding conversations and even impersonate employees' voices. This makes it increasingly difficult for service desk agents to distinguish legitimate callers from attackers.
A 2025 Gartner survey found that 62% of organizations had experienced a deepfake attack involving social engineering or automated processes in the previous year.
Meanwhile, Verizon's 2026 DBIR found that social engineering through texts and voice calls had a 40% higher success rate than traditional email phishing.
Service desk agents can no longer rely on how convincing someone sounds. Identity verification needs to be based on secure, consistent checks rather than an agent's ability to recognize an impersonation attempt.
It's Not Just a Security Problem
Access recovery also comes at a cost. Account lockouts create service desk tickets which interrupt employees' work and put pressure on overworked IT teams. When someone loses access outside office hours, even a routine reset can mean hours of downtime.
There is a monetary cost as well; a single help desk password reset costs around $70. Multiply that by hundreds or thousands of requests, and the expense quickly adds up.
Secure self-service recovery can help employees regain access without contacting the service desk, while streamlined identity verification helps agents handle requests that still need support. With the right processes in place, organizations can reduce the workload without weakening security.
Closing the Gap: What Secure Service Desk Verification Looks Like
It’s unrealistic to expect service desk agents to become experts at spotting AI-enabled social engineering attempts. Training is still crucial, and agents should feel confident in refusing requests or escalating when something doesn’t sound right.
Alongside that, they need a reliable way to verify identities before making sensitive account changes. Verification should be a required step, not a judgment call based on how convincing someone sounds.
Solutions like Specops Secure Service Desk help organizations put this into practice through a straightforward four-step process:
- An employee contacts the service desk: An employee, ‘John Doe’, calls because he can't access his account. The agent starts a recovery request through Specops Secure Service Desk.
- The agent locates the account: Using John's details, the agent finds his account and initiates the verification process.
- Identity verification takes place: Specops Secure Service Desk supports a range of verification methods, including email, SMS, and third-party authenticators like Duo, so organizations can choose an appropriate method for the request whether the caller has access to a smartphone or not.
- The agent proceeds once verification succeeds: Only after John has successfully verified his identity can the agent carry out the requested action, such as resetting his password.
The goal is to make secure identity verification a consistent part of service desk workflows, without adding unnecessary friction for agents or employees.
Make Account Recovery as Secure as Login
Strong login security means little if attackers can bypass it with a convincing call to the service desk. Password resets and account recovery need verification that's just as robust as the authentication controls they protect.
By replacing knowledge-based questions with consistent, secure verification, organizations can reduce the risk of impersonation without making life harder for employees or service desk agents.

articles.title: Le bouclier ultime d'Apple aurait cédé : un iPhone 18 Pro piraté malgré le mode Isolement
articles.text:
Une animation de jeune fille qui danse aurait-elle remis en cause les promesses de protection sans faille du mode Isolement proposé sur iPhone ? C’est en tout cas ce que laisse penser une vidéo publiée par le groupe de hackers Calif.
Un CV de chat, une jeune fille qui danse et un iPhone 18 Pro piraté malgré le mode Isolement
Le groupe de hackers Calif affirme être parvenu à jailbreaker un iPhone 18 Pro dont le mode Isolement était activé. Il s’agit d’un exploit, étant donné que le mode Isolement permet justement de protéger les utilisateurs contre les piratages, notamment en bloquant les pièces jointes des messages et en limitant certaines technologies web. L’entreprise à la pomme décrit elle-même le mode Isolement comme une « protection extrême » contre les tentatives de piratage.
Mais il semble que ce mode de protection d’Apple ne soit pas infaillible. Dans une vidéo publiée sur X par le groupe de hackers Calif, nous pouvons voir une personne ouvrir un article du média américain Techcrunch intitulé « Apple affirme qu’aucun utilisateur ayant activé le mode Isolement n’a été piraté à l’aide d’un logiciel espion ». Il s’agit bien entendu d’une petite provocation. La personne quitte ensuite cette page et accepte via AirDrop un document PDF qui n’est autre que le CV d’un chat. En réalité, ce CV renfermerait un virus. Dès lors, aussitôt ouvert, une animation de jeune fille qui danse, ainsi que le logo « C » (Calif), se mettent à parcourir frénétiquement l’écran de l’iPhone 18 Pro.
 Lockdown Mode helps, until it doesn't. pic.twitter.com/1UyxPHQUAe
— Calif (@calif_io) November 3, 2026
Par la suite, le membre du groupe Calif a installé la mise à jour iOS 27.2, ce qui implique un redémarrage total de l’appareil, mais rien n’y fait : une fois le téléphone rallumé, la jeune fille qui danse et le logo « C » se remettent à parcourir frénétiquement l’écran du téléphone. À noter que le groupe de hackers montre dans sa vidéo que le mode Isolement est bien activé sur le téléphone.
Comment sont-ils parvenus à contourner le mode Isolement ?
Autant dire que nous ne savons pas comment Calif est parvenu à jailbreaker un iPhone 18 Pro dont le mode Isolement était activé. Le groupe n’a fourni aucune information complémentaire ni précisé les étapes qui ont permis ce piratage. Nous ne savons d’ailleurs pas si ce mode opératoire est aussi possible lorsque iOS 27.2 est déjà installé sur le téléphone.
Dans tous les cas, il semble qu’un iPhone 18 Pro en mode Isolement ait bel et bien été jailbreaké. Rappelons au passage que le groupe est aussi parvenu à pirater un iPhone Duo le jour de sa sortie. Les appareils Apple présentent clairement de solides défenses face aux tentatives de piratage, mais ils ne semblent pas non plus infaillibles.

articles.title: Boost Mobile slashes prices on pre-paid mobile plans and refurbished smartphones - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Boost Mobile has introduced new offers for prepaid SIM plans and refurbished devices that can save customers thousands of dollars per year at a time when cost-of-living pressures and rising interest rates are impacting everyday Australians.
Boost Mobile, which offers full access to the Telstra prepaid mobile network, has pulled the trigger early on its Black Friday offerings and will give Australians the opportunity to review their household expenses and find savings on their mobile plans which run from 28 days and longer expiry options up to a year.
“Australians are always looking for smart ways to save, and your mobile plan is one of the easiest places to start,” said Bobby Geldens, CEO, Boost Mobile Australia.
“It only takes a few minutes to check what you’re paying, what you’re getting and whether you’re actually getting good value.
“This Black Friday sales season is a great opportunity to set yourself up heading into the new year.”
Until November 30 Boost Mobile is offering a $39 prepaid SIM plan for just $12 – that’s a saving of 69 per cent.
This is available for new activations and includes 80GB of data on the first three recharges.
Boost Mobile is also offering up to 15% off selected refurbished devices, along with 10% off storewide until November 30, via the online Boost Mobile Refurb Shop.
An iPhone 15 Pro Max is now available for $875.50.

A Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra is also available from $723.60.

articles.title: Marruecos destina otros 11 millones de euros para seguir estudiando la viabilidad de construir un túnel bajo el Estrecho de Gibraltar
articles.text:
Marruecos planea destinar más de 120 millones de dirhams, unos 11 millones de euros, en 2027 para estudios sobre el túnel submarino que pretende conectar con España, un proyecto que se lleva gestando durante décadas y que no ha sido hasta estos últimos años cuando se han comenzado a lanzar las primeras piedras. Eso sí, el dinero no se destinará a la construcción, sino que financiará una nueva evaluación sobre siesta idea de hace 40 años puede realmente construirse.
Por qué importa. La cifra muestra que Rabat mantiene su parte de un proyecto que durante mucho tiempo ha dependido de que ambos países avancen al mismo ritmo. España ya está financiando sus propias actualizaciones técnicas, y cualquier decisión de construir requeriría un nuevo acuerdo bilateral con Marruecos, como ya recordó el Gobierno español en 2023, tal y como comparte el medio Europa Sur.
Los detalles. La asignación aparece en los documentos del proyecto de presupuestos para 2027 del Ministerio de Equipamiento y Agua de Marruecos, según cuenta La Razón. Pertenece a la SNED, la empresa estatal marroquí encargada de los estudios, y forma parte de un programa de trabajo conjunto con su homóloga española, Secegsa. El plan consistirá en revisar los estudios de ingeniería anteriores, actualizar el sistema de gestión ambiental, explorar físicamente las estructuras subterráneas, y encargar nuevos estudios geoestratégicos, jurídicos y económicos.
Dentro de este plan también consta promover el proyecto, pues el programa todavía necesita la aprobación de la 44.ª sesión del Comité Gubernamental Conjunto, así que el gasto aún no está cerrado.
Presupuestos hasta ahora. En los documentos presupuestarios de Marruecos también se incluye una subvención de 30 millones de dirhams para el Ministerio de Equipamiento y Agua en 2027, y posteriormente 7 millones de dirhams al año en 2028 y 2029 para operaciones de campo y apoyo, según comparte La Razón. El límite de la subvención anual de la SNED también se ha elevado a 15 millones de dirhams. En agosto de este año, la empresa informó de que había comenzado a preparar un estudio exploratorio del túnel y había iniciado mediciones sísmicas y tectónicas a ambos lados del Estrecho.
Lo que los estudios deben resolver. El Gobierno de España reconocía en 2025 que las campañas geológicas anteriores arrojaron resultados limitados debido a la tecnología disponible en ese momento, tal y como cuentan desde Cádiz Directo. La idea ahora es ir cerrando poco a poco esa brecha con estudios geológicos en torno al Umbral de Camarinal, uno de los obstáculos más importantes del proyecto. Hay 553.187 euros reservados precisamente para construir un modelo geológico tridimensional de la zona supervisado por el Consejo Superior de Investigaciones Científicas (CSIC).
Dentro de esta serie de estudios también participan los sismómetros de fondo oceánico, conocidos como OBS, los cuales registran la actividad sísmica en el lecho marino. Además, el pasado mes de octubre, la Universidad de Salamanca se adjudicó un contrato de 123.607 euros para analizar muestras de sondeos marinos, según cuentan desde Cádiz Directo.
La parte española. Secegsa está actualizando su diseño preliminar de 2007 con el apoyo de la empresa pública de ingeniería Ineco, tal y como cuentan desde Europa Sur. Un cambio notable es que ahora se propone que la terminal norte esté situada cerca de Vejer, lo que significa que se deben estudiar nuevas conexiones ferroviarias con las redes española y europea. Ineco contrató además al especialista alemán en túneles Herrenknecht para evaluar si la excavación es viable.
Un largo camino hasta ahora. Ambos países acordaron en 1979 estudiar un enlace permanente, y las dos empresas estatales se crearon en 1981. Tras un periodo más tranquilo, los trabajos se relanzaron en abril de 2023 en la 43.ª reunión del Comité Gubernamental Conjunto. España ha aportado 2,3 millones de euros en fondos de recuperación europeos para sus propias actualizaciones, según Europa Sur. Los estudios previos hacían referencia a la construcción de un túnel ferroviario bajo el lecho marino, frente a un puente.

articles.title: Shigeru Miyamoto (73 años), sobre la inteligencia artificial generativa: “Si la IA llegara a encargarse de todo, siempre habrá un papel para nosotros”
articles.text:
Shigeru Miyamoto cree que, aunque la inteligencia artificial tome más funciones, los creadores tienen algo que ofrecer. “Si la IA llegara a encargarse de todo, siempre habrá un papel para nosotros”, ha dicho el diseñador de Nintendo. Para ello, hace referencia a cómo se concibe una obra y cómo se desarrolla.
El creador de Mario y The Legend of Zelda ha comentado este tema en una comparecencia relacionada con la concesión de la Orden de la Cultura de Japón. Cuando le han preguntado sobre la IA generativa y el desarrollo de videojuegos, ha hecho referencia a los cambios tecnológicos que ha vivido su generación.
La evolución de las herramientas
Por ejemplo, recuerda cómo pasaron de las máquinas de escribir a los procesadores de texto. En aquella época, las herramientas estaban en constante evolución. Cree que el avance de los ordenadores les ha ayudado a entender mejor la capacidad de los diseñadores. En este sentido, considera que la IA generativa puede suponer un cambio similar.
Ha explicado que hay un aspecto que es el de la estructura global. Es decir, cómo se concibe algo. Y otro que es el de rellenar los huecos o de pulir detalles. Estos pueden ser trabajos agradables. Pero existe el riesgo de confusión entre la satisfacción de hacer el trabajo y el hecho de tener una obra de calidad.
La intención del creador
Por ello cree que cuanto más deleguen en la inteligencia artificial, más oportunidades de reflexionar sobre lo que realmente importa de su obra tendrán los creadores. También ve aquí un potencial beneficio de la herramienta, que es que te hace repensar qué es lo que tú aportas.
Además, también recuerda que los diseños de copia y pega raramente sobreviven. Lo que les falta es la intención personal. Aquí sigue siendo el creador el que tiene la intención y el ordenador es una herramienta para realizar el trabajo.

articles.title: Sequoia Capital raises around €8.9 billion in new funds and closes London office; most local partners opt to stay in Europe | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Sequoia Capital, one of Silicon Valley’s oldest and most prominent venture capital firms, has closed its London office as part of a broader restructuring.
In an announcement titled “The Sequoia of Tomorrow”, the firm outlined several sweeping changes and confirmed that it has raised €8.89 billion ($10 billion) in new funds. The biggest announcement is that it no longer sees the need for a physical European presence. While the firm is exiting Europe, three of its four London-based partners have decided to remain in Europe rather than relocate to California.
“We are closing our London office, which means several people will be leaving Sequoia. This is not about the team – they are excellent. We simply don’t see the need for a local presence. We believe that Europe will continue to produce outlier founders and companies, and that we can continue to provide world class support from our home base in the Bay Area,” the firm said.
Despite being offered the opportunity to move to San Francisco, three of Sequoia’s four London-based partners – Luciana Lixandru, Julien Bek, and George Robson – have opted to remain in Europe. Anas Biad is the only London-based partner who has confirmed he will relocate to the United States and remain with Sequoia.
Lixandru joined Sequoia in 2020 as its first European partner and has backed companies such as Trade Republic, Pennylane, and Rillet. “My conviction on Europe hasn’t moved, and neither am I; when given the opportunity to move to San Francisco, I chose to stay here and focus on this wonderful, imperfect ecosystem. Europe is where my family is, and where I want to build,” she wrote on LinkedIn.
She further confirmed that she will remain a Sequoia partner, continue serving on portfolio company boards, and also invest personally in the next generation of European founders.
Bek, who spent a decade investing in European founders through Sequoia, backing companies including Revolut, Miro, Attio, and Dust, added that he is already thinking about what the next decade in European venture could look like.
“My heart is in Europe, and I’ve decided to stay here. I’ll continue supporting the founders I work with and serving on my boards,” he said.
The closure of Sequoia’s London office follows a similar move by fellow US VC giant Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), which shuttered its London office in early 2025, less than two years after opening its first international outpost in the UK.
After roughly 20 years of expansion, during which it built multiple businesses across geographies, Sequoia says it is now pulling back to focus on what it does best: high-conviction, highly selective venture capital investing.
As part of this restructuring, the firm has decided to simplify the structure of the Sequoia Capital Fund, sunset its batch accelerator Arc and Scouts programmes, and streamline both its operational and investing teams. It is also eliminating the distinction between its Early and Growth stages, consolidating into one team under a single mission. The firm is also doing away with its Monday partner meeting cycle.
“Founders operate 24/7, and so do we. Founders shouldn’t have to adhere to our process – we will do our best to adhere to yours,” the firm added.
European founders have already weathered a16z’s exit and now need to prepare for a phase where Sequoia may be hard to reach, especially without a local partner to back them. While the firm has insisted it can keep backing European companies from its Bay Area base, the attention will be on the UK partners who decided to stay, and the European tech ecosystem will watch their next move closely.

articles.title: Una campaña atribuida a Rusia infectó iPhone y Android desactualizados con solo abrir un sitio web
articles.text:
Hackers vinculados al servicio de inteligencia exterior de Rusia usaron fallas ya corregidas de iPhone y Android para infectar teléfonos de quienes visitaban ciertos sitios web, sin que la víctima tocara nada. La empresa francesa de seguridad Sekoia publicó el hallazgo.
Sekoia atribuyó la campaña, con confianza “moderada a alta”, al grupo APT29, también conocido como Midnight Blizzard o Cozy Bear. La firma lo describe como un grupo de origen ruso, atribuido de forma amplia al Servicio de Inteligencia Exterior de Rusia (SVR). Detectó la actividad a mediados de octubre.
El ataque empezaba cuando un usuario abría uno de los sitios afectados. Un código JavaScript inyectado en la página identificaba el modelo del teléfono y la versión del navegador. Con esos datos, un servidor de los atacantes enviaba la cadena de explotación adecuada para iPhone o para Android, según describió Sekoia.
Las cadenas de explotación son secuencias de fallas de seguridad encadenadas que permiten tomar control de un aparato. Funcionan “sin interacción del usuario”: no hace falta pulsar un enlace ni descargar un archivo. Los atacantes buscaban robar cookies del navegador, que pueden servir para reutilizar sesiones abiertas, y en algunos casos contraseñas de WiFi o datos completos del equipo.
Tres vías de entrada y tres cadenas de ataque
Sekoia identificó tres formas de llegar a las víctimas. La primera fue inyectar el código en sitios legítimos comprometidos. La segunda, crear dominios falsos que copiaban sitios conocidos. La tercera, vulnerar un servicio ucraniano de análisis de tráfico web que utilizan miles de sitios, según informó Ars Technica.
Entre los sitios imitados estaba america250.org, de la iniciativa por los 250 años de la independencia de Estados Unidos, y el del hotel Raffles London at The OWO, cercano al Ministerio de Defensa británico y a la residencia del primer ministro. Ars Technica señaló que el presidente de Ucrania, Volodímir Zelenski, se alojó allí el 14 de octubre.
La primera cadena apuntaba a iPhone con iOS 16.7 y robaba cookies de Safari. La segunda, contra iOS 18.5, usaba un conjunto de herramientas llamado DarkSword y extraía mensajes de texto, iMessage, bases de datos de WhatsApp y Telegram, contraseñas del llavero de iCloud, ubicación y fotos. Sekoia sospecha que DarkSword fue creado por un proveedor comercial de vigilancia.
La tercera cadena atacaba a Android con versiones de Chrome de la 139 a la 145, salvo la 143, por motivos que Sekoia no pudo explicar. Robaba cookies, datos de inicio de sesión, historial y contraseñas de WiFi guardadas.
Los teléfonos actualizados no eran vulnerables
Todas las fallas usadas ya habían sido corregidas por Apple y Google antes de que empezara la campaña. Según Sekoia, ninguna es una falla desconocida para los fabricantes y ninguna funciona contra dispositivos totalmente actualizados. “Un usuario con un sistema operativo al día está a salvo de estos ataques”, afirmó la firma.
Los programas maliciosos tampoco se instalaban de forma permanente en el teléfono. Reiniciarlo detenía la actividad hasta que el usuario volviera a visitar un sitio comprometido, según BleepingComputer. Eso no devuelve los datos que ya se hubieran copiado antes del reinicio.
Sekoia relacionó la campaña con el grupo ruso por las coincidencias técnicas, los patrones de operación, la infraestructura y el perfil de los objetivos, que incluían sitios vinculados a la guerra contra Ucrania. Ars Technica añadió que hay similitudes con un ataque anterior atribuido a APT29.
La empresa no precisó cuántos dispositivos fueron infectados. Sekoia informó que coordina con los equipos nacionales de respuesta a incidentes informáticos de los países afectados para identificar a las víctimas y evaluar cómo desactivar la infraestructura de los atacantes.

articles.title: OpenAI president says AI could make death a choice, predicts major medical breakthroughs within 18 months
articles.text:
Big quote: We're still waiting for AI to cure cancer, not to mention the many other things we were promised it would bring. But OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman is boldly confident that the technology will one day cure all that ails us – to the point that death could even become a choice.
Speaking at WSJ Tech, Brockman said the huge medical advancements we're still waiting for AI to enable will happen in the next year to year and a half.
"Having cures for diseases is something that's become also a trope in this field, but I think that you're gonna see real delivery and real significant strides and impacts on biology, health, and curing of diseases over the next 12 months, 18 months," he said.
"I think that we all suffer, that the question of even just thinking about death becoming a choice. All of this is possible."
Being OpenAI's president means Brockman is always going to laud AI as potentially allowing us to live forever, while the promise of huge breakthroughs in the next 12 to 18 months has been around since ChatGPT launched.
 – Fireside Alpha (@firesidealpha) November 5, 2026
But Brockman isn't alone when it comes to faith in AI's future medical applications. Last month, Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar claimed that many AI researchers are so sure the technology will cure cancer one day that they've taken up smoking. He referred to this as a "kind of this mass psychosis social delusion."
Others in the tech industry share similar beliefs. Futurist Peter Diamandis said last year that the key to living much longer is to not die "from something stupid" before 2030, after which point a combination of technologies, with AI the driving force, will help us achieve "longevity escape velocity."
Bryan Johnson, the biohacker millionaire famed for trying to fight off aging, said AI is one of the technologies that could ensure no condition is presumed incurable.
Then there's Elon Musk. He said this year that longevity or semi-immortality is an extremely solvable problem because the body ages in sync. He said nobody has an old left arm and a young right arm, so we are programmed to die, but we could change that programming to live longer.
 – Fireside Alpha (@firesidealpha) November 1, 2026
Curing diseases like cancer and making death an option, however, still feels like the stuff of fantasy. But perhaps these sorts of promises will distract people complaining about "compute campuses," or data centers, as they are and always shall be called.

articles.title: Zyxel Switch Hacks Blamed on Patched Flaw Actually Exploited a Zero-Day
articles.text:
A recently patched vulnerability in Zyxel GS1900 series switches was exploited in the wild as a zero-day to hack almost 1,000 devices, cybersecurity firm Binarly reports.
The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-107441 (CVSS score of 8.8) and is described as an out-of-bounds write issue in the CGI program of the Zyxel GS1900 series switch firmware.
According to Zyxel, an unauthenticated attacker could exploit the security defect via crafted HTTP requests to achieve OS command execution.
The vulnerability impacts 10 GS1900 switch models. Zyxel rolled out fixes for it on October 23 and published an advisory on November 3.
On the same day, Binarly warned that attackers had exploited CVE-2026-107441 in attacks previously attributed to a Chinese hacking group.
The previous report came from GreyNoise, which warned on September 21 that the hackers exploited CVE-2026-7273, a Zyxel bug patched in June, to compromise roughly 1,000 devices in August.
GreyNoise linked the attacks to Red Heron, a Chinese threat actor that Acronis caught targeting Gitea instances in a large-scale hacking campaign, and CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to its KEV catalog.
Now, Binarly says that the attackers did not target CVE-2026-7273. They deployed variants of the Jitterly and Sixzut malware analyzed by Acronis, but their exploit targeted a previously unknown vulnerability.
“Because the threat actor was exploiting a different vulnerability, and the patch for CVE-2026-7273 remained ineffective, this had no effect on protecting devices from being exploited by this threat actor,” the cybersecurity firm notes.
Binarly notified Zyxel of the findings on September 29, and the vendor confirmed the new vulnerability, now tracked as CVE-2026-107441, two weeks later.
“Cases such as this highlight the urgency for a more reliable way of checking vulnerabilities in software. Advisories and version numbers certainly help, but they cannot be blindly trusted. We truly believe the definitive way to assess whether software components contain vulnerabilities is by looking at their binary code,” the company notes.
