articles.title: CoolIT, PurposeMed among companies honoured at Start Alberta Tech Awards | BetaKit
articles.text:
Two of the Calgary tech ecosystem’s most high-profile exits, CoolIT Systems and PurposeMed, received accolades on Wednesday night as they landed among the companies honoured at the Start Alberta Tech Awards.
“You can build a real company in Alberta without burning through capital.”
Start Alberta is an Alberta-focused database on startups and funding that is operated by The A100, a community of tech and innovation leaders, founders, and investors founded in 2010 and serving Western Canada. Now in its ninth year, the Start Alberta Tech Awards celebrate “outstanding achievements” in Alberta’s tech sector.
“These award honourees are building technology that meets real needs for people around the world,” Tamara Woolgar, the executive director with The A100, said in a press release. “Together, they show what’s possible when we build in Alberta.”
Held at Calgary’s National Music Centre, recipients were honoured across 10 categories. CoolIT Systems took home the Deal of the Year award for its $4.75-billion USD ($6.6 billion CAD) exit to Ecolab. Announced last March and closed in July, the exit secured by the advanced liquid cooling company is the largest disclosed acquisition price for an Alberta-based company in history.
CoolIT’s win was mirrored by another historic exit in the Calgary scene this year: PurposeMed. The company behind telehealth startups Freddie, Frida, and Foria took home the Anchor of the Year award, honouring a “flagship company that supports the foundation upon which others build in Alberta.” PurposeMed and Freddie were recently acquired by dating platform Grindr in another high-value acquisition, netting $250 million USD.
RELATED: Platform Calgary unveils 10 most promising startups ahead of Calgary Innovation Week
“You can build a real company in Alberta without burning through capital,” said PurposeMed co-founder and CEO, Pete MacLeod, in a statement. “I’d love to see more founders realize you can do big things and keep talent here.”
Helcim, the Calgary-based FinTech and payment processing platform, took home Scaleup of the Year for more than doubling its team since 2021. Last August, the company closed a $53-million CAD Series C round at a valuation of $250 million with more than $150 million in annual recurring revenue.
The remaining list of winners and award categories include:
- Most Promising Founder: Cheng (Jack) Su, EnerNode AI. EnerNode uses AI to manage oil and gas operations. Founded in 2026, it has already seen industry adoption in Western Canada, and was selected for the Plug and Play Canada and NVIDIA Inception programs.
- Investor of the Year: Graphite Ventures. Graphite Ventures boasts teams in Calgary and Edmonton, leading early investment in companies like PataBid, WaitWell, Black Owl, ResolvMD, and Ontopical. It was also selected to manage the University of Alberta Innovation Fund.
- A100 One to Watch: NiaHealth. Edmonton-based NiaHealth is a medtech company offering blood testing, medical consultations, and personalized health metrics. It has raised more than $8 million since founding in 2023.
- VCAA Rod Charko Service Award: Jade Alberts. Longtime Calgary ecosystem builder Jade Alberts received the award for his decade of work with Peer Guidance, a fractional support network for founders, as well as hosting Founders’ Coffee, a weekly meetup for entrepreneurs. He has been a mentor at Innovate Calgary and has made more than 30 angel investments.
- Ecosystem Support of the Year: Kristina Milke, Sprout Fund. A general partner at Sprout Fund, Milke is a founding member of the University of Alberta’s Thresholdimpact Venture Mentoring Service and has spent more than a decade working with, investing in, and supporting Alberta founders. She also co-founded Sprout, Valhalla Private Capital, and Valhalla Angels, one of the largest angel networks in Western Canada.
- Woman in Tech: Dr. Christy Lane, Flora Fertility. Lane is the co-founder and co-CEO of Flora Fertility, a fertility insurance startup. The company closed a $5-million USD seed round in April, and is now expanding into Canada. Flora Fertility is Lane’s third venture, after Vivametrica, which she exited in 2020.
- Leader of the Year: Dr. Caley Shukalek, PurposeMed. Shukalek was chief medical officer of PurposeMed. Under his leadership, Freddie expanded to all 50 US states, and expanded HIV care in Canada.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.

articles.title: Aina's smart ring has a screen, a joystick, and a mic so you can talk to AI agents | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Hardware startup Aina released a smart ring today that features a screen, a joystick, and a mic so that you can talk to your agents and take notes. The $399 ring has a speaker so you can take calls using it as well.
The startup, which raised $5.5 million in July, is positioning the ring as a controller of sorts for both AI and non-AI apps.
The company previously made Mirage, a three-key controller that let you invoke buttons based on the app on your Mac’s screen. For instance, if you were on a Google Meet call, you could map keys to camera on/off, mic mute/unmute, or to leave the meeting.
Aina has baked in lessons from that device to create the new ring, which it’s simply calling “AI ring.” Using its mic, you can take notes, send a prompt to agents, set reminders, and dictate notes on your Mac using Wispr Flow or the startup’s own dictation engine.
Now, there are already smart rings in the market that do similar things, like the Pebble Index 01, Sandbar Stream, Oasis, and Natura, which is probably why Aina has added more controls and functionality to stand out. Its ring comes with a speaker so that you can take calls, and there is a screen, which lets you see notifications from your phone or which apps you are controlling.
For navigation, there is a joystick, and it also supports gestures, so that it can trigger different actions based on what’s on your Mac or phone’s screen. The ring also lets you control music or even smart home devices like Apple TV.
I have used the ring for a few days, and it feels like a smartwatch in a ring format, with more controls. I can get notifications and reply to them. It surfaces my meetings; I can call Uber if I want to get a ride home.
It’s easier to use Apple TV’s remote itself, but the Aina ring proved useful the couple times I couldn’t find the remote. Granted, a lot of the software and features are still being fleshed out, so it’s hard to figure out where such a device ring might sit in my daily usage, but it is squarely aimed at folks who are surrounded by digital devices and AI applications.
“Phones and laptop screens were designed for an age of browsing where you think about opening apps. For interacting with proactive agents, we need a better interface, and that is what we had in mind while designing Aina,” Apoorv Shankar, Aina’s founder, told TechCrunch over a call.
Companies are trying to cater to programmers and AI enthusiasts with specialized hardware that could help them harness different agents. This includes OpenAI’s experimental keyboard and Rabbit trying to position itself as a controller. The hope with such hardware is that enough people will have multiple agents running to invest in specific gadgets to keep tabs on them.
Aina’s ring goes on preorder starting Thursday at early-bird pricing of $399, and the company plans to start shipping the device in January 2027. Once the early-bird period ends, the ring will cost $499.

articles.title: Lançamento da Artemis 2 provocou interferência em sinais de GPS
articles.text:
O lançamento da missão Artemis 2, da NASA, provocou alterações gigantescas na ionosfera terrestre, camada eletricamente carregada da atmosfera. O fenômeno foi tão intenso que chegou a interferir na precisão de sistemas de GPS, segundo estudo conduzido por pesquisadores da Universidade Nacional Cheng Kung (Taiwan).
Publicado nesta quarta (4), o levantamento identificou duas grandes regiões de perturbação atmosférica provocadas pela passagem do foguete Space Launch System (SLS). As estruturas se estenderam por aproximadamente cinco mil quilômetros, atravessando o continente americano de leste a oeste.
Os pesquisadores analisaram dados de redes de receptores GPS terrestres de alta precisão, utilizadas por instituições científicas dos Estados Unidos para acompanhar movimentos das placas tectônicas e investigar fenômenos relacionados a terremotos.
A partir do tempo que os sinais de satélite levam para chegar às estações, os cientistas conseguiram identificar alterações na concentração de elétrons da ionosfera durante a passagem do foguete.
O resultado chamou a atenção: as perturbações provocadas pela Artemis 2 foram mais intensas do que as observadas em outros lançamentos de foguetes até então. Segundo o estudo, chegaram a ser até dez vezes mais fortes do que aquelas registradas após voos de teste da Starship, da SpaceX.
Como o foguete abriu ‘buracos’ na atmosfera?
- A ionosfera é uma região da atmosfera terrestre que começa a aproximadamente 50 quilômetros de altitude e se estende por centenas de quilômetros. Ela recebe esse nome porque contém partículas eletricamente carregadas, incluindo elétrons livres e íons;
- Essas partículas influenciam a propagação de sinais de rádio que atravessam a região, incluindo aqueles utilizados pelos sistemas de navegação por satélite;
- Quando um foguete atravessa a atmosfera em velocidades supersônicas, produz ondas de choque que podem provocar alterações na distribuição dessas partículas. O resultado é uma espécie de buraco temporário na ionosfera, caracterizado pela redução da concentração de elétrons em determinadas regiões;
- No caso da Artemis 2, os pesquisadores identificaram duas dessas estruturas. A primeira foi provocada pela passagem do estágio central do SLS, com aproximadamente 65 metros de comprimento;
- A segunda surgiu após duas ignições dos motores do estágio superior do foguete, responsáveis por impulsionar a cápsula Orion para fora da gravidade terrestre em direção à Lua;
- Essas queimas ocorreram a aproximadamente 185 quilômetros de altitude, mais de uma hora depois da decolagem. Apesar da potência do estágio central, foram justamente as manobras do estágio superior que provocaram as perturbações mais expressivas.
Alterações podem afetar carros autônomos e drones
As mudanças na ionosfera não ficaram restritas a observações científicas. Os pesquisadores identificaram alterações na densidade de elétrons que poderiam resultar em erros de posicionamento de vários metros nos sistemas GPS.
Isso acontece porque os receptores precisam calcular a distância até diferentes satélites para determinar sua localização. Quando os sinais atravessam uma região da ionosfera com concentração alterada de elétrons, podem sofrer mudanças no tempo de propagação, comprometendo a precisão das medições.
Charles Lin, professor de ciências da Terra da Universidade Nacional Cheng Kung e um dos autores do estudo, alertou que erros de apenas alguns metros podem representar riscos para tecnologias que dependem de posicionamento preciso. “Um erro de posicionamento de alguns metros é suficiente para fazer um carro autônomo mudar de faixa”, explicou o pesquisador à Space.com.
Segundo Lin, os efeitos também podem atingir a localização de drones e outras tecnologias de navegação automatizada.
O cientista acrescentou que, embora lançamentos de foguetes já sejam conhecidos por provocar esse tipo de perturbação, os efeitos das manobras orbitais realizadas durante uma missão interplanetária ainda não haviam sido observados dessa maneira.
Com o aumento das viagens espaciais em direção à Lua e a Marte, os pesquisadores esperam que esses fenômenos se tornem cada vez mais relevantes para o monitoramento da chamada meteorologia espacial.
O estudo foi disponibilizado como pré-publicação na revista científica Geophysical Research Letters.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Nintendo says it’s not planning another Switch 2 price hike
articles.text:
Nintendo president Shuntaro Furukawa said during the company’s latest earnings call that it’s “not considering additional changes” to the Switch 2’s price, Reuters reports. The Switch 2 got a $50 price hike earlier this year, bringing its starting price up to $499. Nintendo said in Thursday’s earnings report that Switch 2 sales have dropped 37.4 percent year-over-year.
Nintendo says it’s not planning another Switch 2 price hike
Nintendo’s president says it will have ‘sufficient’ RAM as shortages drive up console prices.
According to Reuters, Furukawa also gave an update on the RAM shortage, saying, “There has been no major change to the memory situation and Nintendo is in a position to secure sufficient quantities.”
Earlier this week, one of Nintendo’s Switch 2 cartridge suppliers announced it plans to stop making ROM memory to focus on memory for data centers instead. Demand from AI data centers is driving the ongoing RAM shortages that’s leading to a wave of tech price increases. Microsoft has raised Xbox Series X / S prices multiple times now, increasing the Series S’s starting price from $299 to $499. The PS5 has also been hit with price hikes, taking its starting price up to $649.

articles.title: Flutterwave wants to keep more money in its ecosystem
articles.text:
In 2017, Flutterwave was a company of about 50 people that had convinced Uber, the world’s largest ride-hailing company, to trust its payments infrastructure to process transactions across African markets. The company was small enough for employees to understand what other teams were doing and step in when needed.
“I had just learned about a payment company that was looking to do amazing things on the continent,” Kanyinsola Ajibade, investor relations lead, who joined Flutterwave that year, told TechCabal in an interview.
Flutterwave’s story began in 2016, when its co-founder, Olugbenga “GB” Agboola, encountered a problem while working in financial services. After stints at PayPal, GTBank, a tier-one Nigerian bank, and South Africa’s Standard Bank, Agboola was frustrated by how difficult it was for businesses to move money across African markets.
“If I want to send money to Ghana, does money have to move from Lagos to New York, and from New York to Ghana?” he told McKinsey in 2022. “It didn’t make sense to me. If you get on a plane from Lagos to Ghana, you get there faster than doing a money transfer.”
The problem wasn’t that Africa lacked payment systems, but that those systems didn’t work seamlessly together. Businesses expanding across borders had to navigate different banks, payment methods, and settlement arrangements, making it harder to collect payments and move money between markets.
For a merchant in Johannesburg selling to a customer in Nigeria, cross-border payments meant relying on a SWIFT transfer and waiting for confirmation before releasing the goods. SWIFT messages could take up to 48 hours as they passed through correspondent banks, frustrating instant trade. Agboola wanted to make those transactions faster and easier.
“Those were the driving forces behind Flutterwave: How do we become like a butterfly that can create a ripple effect in the ecosystem and still be tiny, yet we can make waves? Hence the name Flutterwave, ” he told McKinsey in 2022.
Meanwhile, Iyin Aboyeji, a co-founder of Andela, a global tech talent network, faced the same problem while trying to support African developers and their businesses and had the same conclusion: without payments infrastructure, promising businesses would struggle to grow their revenue.
“A lot of our talents were desirous of building products, but when I would look at the ideas they came up with, it was very clear to me that if we didn’t have payments, many of those products could not scale revenue as fast,” Aboyeji, Flutterwave’s first chief executive officer, told TechCabal in an interview.
Their ambition became Flutterwave, a payments technology company Agboola founded while at Access Bank, a tier-one Nigerian bank, with Aboyeji and Adeleke Adekoya, then Access Bank’s head of digital banking. The idea was to connect merchants to banks, card networks such as Visa and Mastercard, and other payment providers through a single Application Programming Interface (API)—a tool that lets different apps and computer systems talk to each other—allowing businesses to collect and disburse money without building separate integrations for every market.
A decade later, Flutterwave says it has processed over $50 billion in transactions, serves more than two million businesses, and has expanded beyond payment processing into remittances, consumer payments, and banking. Aboyeji has left the company, and Flutterwave is now pursuing a wider financial-infrastructure strategy while working towards profitability and a potential public listing.
The infrastructure problem
In 2016, Nigeria’s electronic payment infrastructure processed ₦65.16 trillion ($257.04 billion at ₦253.50/$) and included bank cards, ATMs, and the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System Instant Payment service. But those rails did not mean businesses could easily accept payments online, manage failed transactions, or expand into other African markets.
Interswitch, founded in 2002, had built Webpay, the default payment processor for businesses by 2015. But merchants faced integration costs of ₦150,000 ($3,068.74 at ₦195.52/$); it did not work on mobile phones, and some startups reported transaction failure rates as high as 90%.
Paystack, founded in 2015 and publicly launched in January 2016, emerged from this gap. It approached the problem by making online payments easier for Nigerian businesses to integrate and manage. Flutterwave addressed a related but broader opportunity: connecting payment systems across countries, banks, and payment methods so businesses could accept and settle funds across multiple markets.
“When we started, Africa’s payment landscape was completely fragmented. The hardest part was building an infrastructure from scratch that could securely handle transactions across totally different markets,” Agboola told TechCabal in an email response.
Flutterwave wanted to build infrastructure that connected the different payment methods, banks, and financial systems businesses needed to reach customers across Africa. Its JavaScript API would give merchants and payment service providers a common integration through which they could accept cards, bank transfers, and local alternatives across multiple markets, rather than build each connection separately.
The proposition was that businesses should not have to understand the underlying complexity of African payments to sell to customers in different countries.
But Flutterwave still had to earn trust, and that meant proving it could move money fast and securely. That prompted the team to travel to San Francisco for a deal of a lifetime, at the time.
“Onboarding a global giant like Uber early on also helped build further trust with prospective customers. When other businesses saw that Uber trusted us to process their payments, it made choosing Flutterwave a much easier decision,” Agboola said.
It wasn’t only Uber that gave the fintech credibility. Access Bank’s PayWithCapture, a QR-code payment product launched in 2015. Both needed technical infrastructure that connected their products to the payment systems customers used.
For Uber, Flutterwave worked with Access Bank to develop a solution for local payment processing. With PayWithCapture, it had an opportunity to help a bank extend a product it had already launched but lacked the technical capacity to scale.
“Pay with Capture was a very pivotal moment, as first-time clients, as well as processing for Uber,” Aboyeji said. “Pay with Capture was a digital banking proposition that didn’t have the capability or technical talent to build without OTT.”
These early relationships helped Flutterwave demonstrate that banks and businesses could use its technical infrastructure to make their existing products work. They also offered a route into a market where a new payments company needed more than a working API: Access Bank provided a connection to the banking system, while Uber offered a practical test of whether that arrangement could solve a global merchant’s local payments problem.
Building trust
Flutterwave could build an API, but software alone could not make money move across Africa. Banks held funds, licenced institutions performed regulated functions, and settlement depended on commercial and technical arrangements that varied across markets. Before it could offer businesses a simpler payments experience, the company had to persuade financial institutions to work with a young technology provider and trust it with critical parts of their operations.
“In payment processing, you need banking relationships because banks are licenced to hold funds, are licenced to acquire,” Temiloluwa Adesina, Flutterwave’s deputy chief product officer for retail, told TechCabal.
Beyond convincing banks or regulators, Flutterwave had to prove that it could make the entire ecosystem safer and more efficient. “The biggest lesson for us was that tech alone doesn’t scale on this continent; deep trust and regulatory partnerships do,” Agboola said.
Its bet may not have paid off without an early relationship with Access Bank, where Agboola worked when Flutterwave started. Access Bank became the fintech’s banking partner, and late Herbert Wigwe, the founding Group CEO of Access Holding Plc, helped the fintech pitch technology companies in its early days.
“He was the sure reference with Silicon Valley investors and gave us business that helped us grow to become Africa’s most valuable startup,” Aboyeji said in a 2024 tribute to Wigwe.
Aboyeji told TechCabal in 2022 that Access Bank wanted to invest in Flutterwave in the early days, but couldn’t due to Nigerian banking regulations that prohibited banks from getting involved in non-banking activities.
The relationship illustrates an important feature of payments infrastructure: a new provider may simplify a merchant experience, but its service still relies on institutions that supply the underlying regulated and settlement functions.
“We were a young African company asking global brands and established local banks to rely on our technology,” Agboola said.
Product experiments and the cost of adapting
Four years after Flutterwave started, the world shut down, forcing businesses to move online.
Globally, the World Bank found that more than 40% of adults in low- and middle-income economies who made merchant payments digitally during the pandemic had done so for the first time. In India, more than 80 million adults made their first digital merchant payment after the start of the pandemic. Electronic payments rose by 49.58% in Nigeria.
The shift created an opening for payment companies, including Flutterwave, Remita, an electronic payment platform, and fintech OPay, to move closer to the businesses whose transactions they processed.
Flutterwave launched Flutterwave Store in 2020 to help merchants create online shopfronts, display products, and accept payments while physical shops faced restrictions. It operated in 15 African countries and connected merchants to third-party logistics providers, including Sendy, a logistics and delivery platform, in Kenya and Sendbox, a logistics company, in Nigeria. Flutterwave said 20,000 businesses joined in its first 11 months.
“We wanted to be able to help people, small businesses, to … accept payments,” Ajibade said.
The product reflected the company’s view that helping a business sell online could create more opportunities for payment activity. It also moved Flutterwave closer to the business’s daily operations than limiting its role to the moment a customer paid. Building to fit into the problem is one of Flutterwave’s core theses.
“We are customer-obsessed, close to the ground with our customers, speaking to them,” Adesina said.
Within the company, ideation starts from market understanding: where it is going, and what the customer needs. Its broader product history reflects a company trying to find the middle ground between problem identification and sustainable demand.
Rave, later known as Flutterwave for Business, gave developers and businesses access to payment APIs. Barter offered consumers virtual dollar cards at a time when foreign-exchange restrictions and card-payment difficulties made international spending harder. Send App extended the company into cross-border remittances, while Swap was introduced to help businesses and consumers access foreign exchange.
Adesina, who started at Flutterwave helping merchants understand its APIs, describes the company’s product development process as built around understanding customer needs, studying adjacent industries, building quickly, and testing whether a solution has a sufficiently strong market.
“Once ideation happens, you need to move fast, and you need to build quickly,” he said. “We move fast in terms of bringing it to life and then validating our business in the market itself.”
That approach helps the company identify new revenue opportunities, but it also means not every product will survive when customer behaviour, operating costs, or market conditions change.
Barter was discontinued in March 2024 after years of service disruptions and card rejections. Disha, a creator-storefront platform the company acquired in 2021, paused operations indefinitely in March 2024, requiring more than 100,000 creators to move their profiles and content elsewhere.
“When you are a startup, you focus on speed and product-market fit,” Agboola said. “But when you become the infrastructure that thousands of global businesses rely on to survive, your priorities change.”
Capital financed the expansion
Capital was difficult to secure in Flutterwave’s early years because Interswitch was already an established player in Nigeria’s electronic payments industry, and investors questioned whether another company could compete.
Aboyeji recently said the founders pitched hundreds of investors. Flutterwave raised a $230,000 seed round in August 2016, before it joined Y Combinator’s Summer 2016 cohort.
“Paystack referred us to YC,” Aboyeji told TechCabal. Paystack was the first Nigerian company to join the YC accelerator program.
Initially, Flutterwave had to prove that it could solve the fragmentation of African payments and that the market was large enough to support the business. As the company evolved from addressing payment fragmentation to building a broader financial infrastructure, investor confidence also grew.
“Over time, one major thing that has helped us is building on investor confidence,” said Ajibade.
Flutterwave became one of Africa’s fintech unicorns after raising $170 million in a Series C round in March 2021, and it is currently worth more than $3 billion and has raised over $500 million.
Early capital helped Flutterwave build its payment infrastructure, acquire customers and establish itself in its first markets. But as the company proved that its model could work, expansion introduced new costs: entering additional countries required investment in local infrastructure, regulatory licences and the teams needed to operate in those markets.
Its subsequent funding rounds supported that expansion while allowing it to develop and deploy new products. The $35 million Series B in 2020 and $170 million Series C in 2021 came as Flutterwave sought to extend its reach across Africa and demonstrate that its payment infrastructure could be replicated across different markets. By the $250 million Series D in 2022, the company was explicitly allocating capital towards customer acquisition, expansion, complementary products and acquisitions.
As Flutterwave matured, capital also became a means to acquire capabilities rather than developing every technology in-house. Its January 2026 acquisition of open-banking startup Mono brought financial-data access, identity verification and account-to-account payment technology into its ecosystem. Ripple’s investment in the company’s June 2026 Series E round was tied to integrating Ripple’s stablecoin and payments infrastructure into its network.
Over the decade, Flutterwave has also had to prove that it can survive currency fluctuations on the continent. For instance, in Nigeria, the naira has fallen from ₦253.50/$ in 2016 to over ₦1,300/$ in 2026.
“When you are in the African markets, you learn that you have to be resilient,” Ajibade said. “You have to be able to build a strategy for macro changes that you might get into. I want to credit that to our finance and operations team, who were able to build core structures to help protect the business.”
Regulation and corporate governance
Flutterwave’s expansion has brought it into increasingly complex regulatory environments, while also exposing questions about whether its internal management and governance had matured alongside its ambitions.
In April 2022, an investigation by Rest of World, the US nonprofit tech publication, documented allegations from former employees involving bullying, sexual harassment, administrative failures, and disputes over employee stock options. The reporting also raised questions about potential conflicts of interest involving shares that departing employees sold to Berrywood Capital, an investment vehicle reportedly associated with Agboola.
Flutterwave disputed several allegations, describing them as false or previously addressed, and said it had introduced policies and investigated complaints.
The episode raised doubts about a company whose commercial value depended on trust: merchants relied on it to process payments, banks depended on its technology and controls, and investors had committed capital to a business expected to operate across multiple financial systems. These allegations forced the company to become stricter with corporate governance.
“Governance naturally evolves as a company grows,” Flutterwave said in an email response to TechCabal.
Regulatory challenges soon exposed another dimension of the problem. In July 2022, Kenya’s central bank said Flutterwave was not authorised to provide payment services in the country and directed regulated financial institutions to stop dealing with it.
Separately, Kenya’s Assets Recovery Agency froze funds in accounts linked to the company while investigating allegations of money laundering and fraud, which Flutterwave denied. The agency subsequently withdrew its forfeiture case, and a court ordered the release of the frozen funds in 2024.
In September 2025, the Bank of Ghana suspended Flutterwave’s remittance partnerships for one month over breaches of its inward-remittance guidelines, although the company said its other services in Ghana remained operational.
These episodes underscored the difficulty of expanding a financial-services business across jurisdictions where licensing, settlement, and remittance rules differ.
The company told TechCabal that there is no single approach to building a global financial-services business because regulation and financial infrastructure remain local.
For a payments business, regulatory disputes are more than legal expenses. Regulatory restrictions can complicate banking relationships, settlement arrangements, and the ability to serve merchants in a market. Flutterwave is exploring acquisitions to close some of these gaps. It is preparing to acquire an undisclosed bank in East Africa, with Kenya, Ghana, Rwanda, Tanzania, South Africa, and Egypt strategically important.
“Every country has its own regulatory framework, licensing requirements, financial infrastructure, and policy priorities,” Flutterwave said. “One of our biggest lessons has been that to build globally, you also have to be deeply local.”
Flutterwave says it holds more than 50 licences globally, and has made changes to its leadership and compliance functions as it has grown.
“As we establish and grow businesses in different countries, we have to build structures that meet local corporate governance and regulatory requirements,… while maintaining strong group standards and global best practices,” the company said.
Flutterwave’s growth also exposed it to the fraud risk of building a payments business at scale. In October 2023, about ₦19 billion ($14.27 million) was reportedly transferred to approximately 6,000 account holders across 35 financial institutions from Flutterwave.
In April 2024, TechCabal reported another incident in which insiders estimated that ₦11 billion ($8.26 million) had been diverted, although Flutterwave said no customer funds had been lost or compromised. Fraud cases are not strange to financial institutions; banks lost ₦5.25 billion ($3.94 million) in Q3 2025.
The company says it monitors transactions through a 24-hour fraud desk and works with financial institutions and law enforcement to investigate suspicious activity. In 2024, Flutterwave partnered with Nigeria’s Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) to establish a cybercrime research centre. A year later, it said its security measures included encryption, tokenisation and multi-factor authentication to protect customers against fraud.
The long walk to profitability
Flutterwave’s scale has not translated into profits.
The company says it has processed over $50 billion across one billion transactions, but transaction value is not the same as revenue, and revenue is not the same as profit. Payment processors earn a fraction of the value they process, while carrying the costs of technology, customer support, compliance, fraud prevention, local operations, and relationships with financial institutions.
Agboola identified profitability and operational efficiency as priorities in 2025, ahead of a potential public listing. In July 2026, he told The Africa Report that Flutterwave was working towards profitability and would consider going public after achieving that milestone.
Now, the company’s strategy increasingly involves moving closer to the underlying financial infrastructure. In 2022, Flutterwave received a switching and processing licence from the Central Bank of Nigeria, allowing it to perform functions in the payments value chain that previously depended on other licenced institutions.
Its January acquisition of open banking startup Mono brought a Nigerian microfinance banking licence into its ecosystem, creating a route to hold deposits and develop banking services within the scope of that licence.
Controlling more of the transaction lifecycle could reduce dependence on third parties, improve settlement and create new income sources. Agboola told TechCabal in April that the company’s new phase would keep funds on its platform, improving margins.
A banking business gives Flutterwave access to deposits and interest income, while transaction data helps it assess the needs and repayment capacity of small businesses seeking working capital, invoice discounting or trade finance.
Its recent partnerships around stablecoins and blockchain-based settlement point to a similar interest in finding new ways to move value across financial systems that remain difficult to connect. Flutterwave’s mission remains connecting Africa to the world through payments, but the practical meaning of that ambition has widened considerably.
“In 2016, we set out with the mission to solve payment fragmentation across Africa,” Agboola said. “Flutterwave is much larger than a payment gateway now; we are building the continent’s financial infrastructure…. The mission hasn't changed; we are still connecting Africa to the world, but our capacity to drive global commerce has scaled.”

articles.title: altM raises $10.3M in Series A funding led by Rainmatter, Mela Ventures
articles.text:
altM raises $10.3M in Series A funding led by Rainmatter, Mela Ventures
Bengaluru-based altM will use the funds to expand its manufacturing capacity, strengthen research and development, support customer qualification programmes, and grow its engineering and commercial teams.
Specialty chemicals startup altM has raised $10.3 million in a Series A funding round, with Rainmatter by Zerodha and Mela Ventures joining as new investors. Existing backers Omnivore, Theia Ventures, Aureolis Ventures and Spectrum Impact also participated in the round, along with strategic angel investors.
The Bengaluru-based company said it will use the funds to expand its manufacturing capacity, strengthen research and development, support customer qualification programmes, and grow its engineering and commercial teams. The investment will help altM transition from pilot-scale production to commercial manufacturing.
Founded in 2022 by Apoorv Garg and Yugal Raj Jain, altM uses lignocellulosic biomass, including sugarcane bagasse and rice straw, to produce industrial chemicals. Its processes use the cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin components of biomass to derive multiple products from a single feedstock.
The startup caters to industries such as beauty and personal care, textiles, construction, packaging and consumer goods, with a focus on developing bio-based alternatives to fossil-derived raw materials.
"We are pleased to partner with altM as they move into commercial-scale production. Re-wiring foundational supply chains away from fossil-derived inputs is one of the most critical challenges facing modern manufacturing today," said Abhinav Negi, Lead - Climate & DeepTech, Rainmatter by Zerodha.
"Solving DeepTech problems involves research and understanding interplay of multiple areas. altM is tackling one of the hardest problems in industrial chemistry which is creating new age materials that can match the performance of fossil-derived inputs while fundamentally changing where their carbon comes from," said Krishnakumar N, Managing Partner, Mela Ventures.
Since raising a $3.5 million seed round in 2023, altM has built an integrated research and pilot manufacturing facility in Bengaluru, bringing laboratory research, demonstration manufacturing and pilot production under one roof. The company said it has expanded its laboratory footprint nearly fivefold in less than two years, commissioned a demonstration manufacturing facility, and taken six molecules to demonstration scale. Of these, three have been selected for pilot plant production.
The products being prepared for commercialisation include a lignin-derived SPF booster for suncare, a cellulose-based rheology modifier, and bio-derived ferulic acid for cosmetics and personal care formulations.
"Industrial manufacturing has relied on fossil carbon for more than a century. We are building a new source of industrial carbon from agricultural residue," said Apoorv Garg, Co-founder and CEO of altM. "Our focus is on developing materials and manufacturing processes that allow customers to adopt these materials at the performance, cost, quality, and scale required for industrial applications."
"We've believed in altM from early on, and what makes us double down on our confidence is the team's ability to turn ambitious science into something real and commercially scalable. Going from the lab to reliable manufacturing and, ultimately, customers is a difficult journey. altM has shown a rare ability to make that transition," said Abhilash Sethi, Partner at Omnivore.

articles.title: GhostMap Android flaw lets malicious app trigger persistent boot loop
articles.text:
Attackers can force Android devices into a continuous boot loop using a specially crafted app that requires no permissions and only needs to be installed.
To cause the persistent denial-of-service (DoS), the app triggers a vulnerability that researchers dubbed 'GhostMap' that makes Android map a file into an unallocated memory region. The affected process crashes when it attempts to read from that region.
Romanian cybersecurity company Bitdefender discovered the flaw while analyzing an Android banking trojan that kept crashing its emulators when it tried to read an application resource.
The researchers demonstrated the vulnerability by creating an app that contains no executable code, requests no permissions on installation, and does not need to be launched on the device.
According to the company, Google has been aware of GhostMap since August but closed the issue without releasing a patch, classifying it as "not reproducible."
Making phones unusable
In a report today, Bitdefender explains that GhostMap stems from two Android libraries that interpret ZIP compression methods differently. This allows a malformed APK (Android package file) to bypass size checks and be mapped beyond the file’s actual contents.
"Reading such an entry causes a SIGBUS (a signal sent by the CPU to stop a process that accesses an invalid memory space) in whichever process touches the file," the researchers say.
To demonstrate the crash-loop effect, Bitdefender created an app containing a resource that the core Android service ‘system_server’ automatically attempts to read after installation.
The read triggers the flaw and restarts the process, causing it to read the same resource and crash again in an endless loop.
During the tests, the researchers used a Pixel 10 device running Android 17 with the August 5 security patch. The device started the crash string about one second after installing the app, the loop repeating for 110 times in normal boot mode and 72 times in safe mode.
Bitdefender warns that the boot loop also prevents users from accessing Safe Mode, which would normally provide a way to troubleshoot the problem and restore the device.
Stopping the crashes is possible in two ways: a factory reset, which erases all locally stored data, and by deleting the malformed file via ADB.
However, using ADB requires the debugging option to already be active on the device. Additionally, restoring via ADB requires the scripts to act before the system crashes.
Google’s response
Bitdefender reported the issue to Google on August 20, but received a “Won’t Fix (Not Reproducible)” reply, with the issue being out of scope.
The researchers submitted an extended version on August 25, believing Google misclassified the original report. The tech giant still deemed it out of scope for a security update, though it reserved it for consideration in a future update.
BleepingComputer has reached out to Google asking about the fix status for GhostMap, but we are still waiting for a reply.
Bitdefender says the only chance to block the attack is during installation, noting that third-party security tools may help detect a possible threat and display a warning, but do not have permission to block installation.

articles.title: The AI boom is coming for Switch cartridges, as a key chip supplier quits making ROM
articles.text:
The big picture: Memory makers have spent most of this year steering their factories toward AI data centers, a shift that is reportedly impacting the chips inside Nintendo Switch game cartridges. Taiwanese chipmaker Macronix is one of the main suppliers of the ROM in those cards. It's now winding down that business to make more flash memory instead. That said, Nintendo likely won't run short of cartridges anytime soon. 
 
 
MST Financial analyst David Gibson posted about the change on X after digging through the company's latest quarterly report. Macronix won't develop any new ROM products from here on. The latest quarter is also the last in which Macronix will report ROM sales separately. Those sales made up just 5% of revenue, down from 26% a year earlier.
Meanwhile, the rest of Macronix's business has never made more money. The company booked NT$10.95 billion (about $338 million) in net profit last quarter on a 70.5% gross margin. A year earlier, that margin sat at just 13.5%.
Nearly all of Macronix's revenue now comes from NAND and NOR flash, which split the company's sales almost evenly. NOR has been especially hard to come by. TrendForce estimates a single AI server needs three to five times more of it than a regular server. That's part of why NOR contract prices roughly doubled in the first half of this year.
Chairman Miin Wu said during the company's earnings call that data center customers are "chasing us for more capacity." So none of Macronix's planned NT$37.8 billion (about $1.2 billion) in new spending is going toward ROM. Micron made a similar call late last year when it shut down its Crucial consumer brand to free up supply for AI customers.
For Nintendo, the fallout looks manageable for now, since Rohm group companies also make ROM for its game cards. Gibson himself thinks physical cards will stick around for a while yet.
It's also unclear how much of this reaches the Switch 2. Gibson's thread says Macronix's chips sit in cards for both consoles. But Nintendo Life has since pulled the Switch 2 from its own headline over conflicting reports.
Still, Gibson expects the move to nudge more games toward digital, including Game-Key Cards that hold only a download license rather than the game itself. Downloads already account for around 60% of Nintendo's software sales. Even so, a Nintendo executive said just last month there are "no plans to ditch physical" on the Switch 2.
The memory crunch is already squeezing Nintendo on another front, too. The company reported today that Switch 2 sales fell 41% year over year to 2.67 million units last quarter. That came after it raised the console's price in the US, Canada, and Japan as memory costs climbed.

articles.title: Groenlandia inaugura un nuevo aeropuerto en una ciudad remota entre icebergs para ser la “Ibiza del hielo”
articles.text:
Las ambiciones expansionistas de Donald Trump han hecho que Groenlandia se pasase meses acaparando titulares. Se ha hablado de su relación con Dinamarca y el pulso independentista de la isla, su riqueza minera en tierras raras e incluso de su valor geoestratégico en la pugna por controlar el Ártico. La isla también es noticia a menudo por su pérdida masiva de hielo, acelerada por el cambio climático. Sin embargo, Groenlandia protagoniza otro fenómeno del que se habla mucho menos: su turistificación, que se nota sobre todo en la expansión de su red de aeropuertos.
Tras la inauguración de tres aeródromos en un tiempo récord, ya hay quien habla con cierta sorna de una “Ibiza sobre hielo”.
Vuelo con destino Ilulissat. Tras meses acaparando titulares por la fijación de Donald Trump en convertirla “en parte” de EEUU y el pacto de seguridad con Washington y Copenhague, Groenlandia vuelve a ser noticia. Aunque por una razón bastante distinta. Hace unos días la isla inauguró un nuevo aeropuerto con vuelos internacionales que, de entrada, mejorará la comunicación de la isla con Dinamarca e Islandia.
La terminal se sitúa en Ilulissat, la tercera urbe más poblada de Groenlandia (5.100 vecinos), y se estrenó la semana pasada con un vuelo con destino Copenhague que duró 4,5 horas y transportó a 169 pasajeros, incluidos cargos públicos.
¿Un aeropuerto para 5.100 personas? No. Y esa es la clave. Ilulissat no es solo la tercera ciudad más populosa de Groenlandia, aunque eso equivalga a tener poco más de 5.000 habitantes, cerca del 10% de los 56.000 que se estima que viven en el conjunto de la isla. La localidad es también uno de los puntos más atractivos y visitados de Groenlandia. De hecho, se la conoce como la “Ciudad de los Icebergs”.
Aunque su nombre quizás no sea muy conocido en los circuitos turísticos internacionales y a menudo quede eclipsado por el de la capital groenlandesa (Nuuk), Ilulissat ofrece una oferta interesante para los amantes de los paisajes helados y la aventura: paseos en trineos tirados por perros, visitas al fiordo de hielo de Ilulissat (Patrimonio de la Humanidad de la UNESCO), excursiones en barco para ver icebergs, avistamientos de ballenas y (si acudes en la época adecuada del año) actividades para disfrutar de la aurora boreal.
Según Trap Greenland, antes de 2019 Ilulissat registraba 31.103 pernoctaciones de viajeros, incluidos los groenlandeses. La web también habla de miles de cruceristas.
Bonito sí, accesible no. El problema (al menos hasta ahora) es que Ilulissat era tan atractivo como inaccesible. Si querías llegar a la ciudad, ubicada en la costa occidental de Groenlandia, tenías básicamente dos opciones: pagar por un crucero o buscar la forma de llegar vía aérea. Si optabas por esto último, podías volar hasta uno de los aeropuertos principales de Groenlandia, como el internacional de Nuuk, y subirte allí a una aeronave con destino Ilulissat.
La alternativa era volar directamente a bordo de un pequeño avión desde Islandia. Según precisa la agencia Associated Press, no hay conexiones por carretera que conecten Ilulissat con otras ciudades importantes de la isla, lo que no resulta extraño si tenemos en cuenta que casi el 80% de la superficie terrestre de Groenlandia está cubierta por hielo.
Las condiciones son tan complicadas que durante décadas la principal puerta de acceso a la isla ártica desde el extranjero fueron las antiguas bases aéreas militares de Estados Unidos situadas en Kangerlussuaq y Narsarsuaq.
Más allá de Ilulissat. Si la nueva terminal de Groenlandia ha despertado tanto interés no es solo por la inauguración en sí. Lo realmente interesante es el contexto. El nuevo aeropuerto de Ilulissat es la tercera infraestructura de ese tipo que la isla ha estrenado en un tiempo récord.
El avance más importante llegó hace justo dos años, a finales de 2024, con la inauguración de una terminal en Nuuk pensada para conexiones internacionales. Incluso se hablaba de ofrecer vuelos en verano con EEUU. El pasado abril el Gobierno regional fue un paso más allá y estrenó otra infraestructura en Qaqortoq que facilita el acceso al sur.
¿Una ‘Ibiza sobre hielo’? La expresión no es nuestra. La usaba con ironía hace poco The Guardian en una pieza en la que repasaba precisamente la apertura de aeropuertos en la isla y su aparente apuesta por el sector turístico, algo que no ocultan las autoridades isleñas. Durante el vuelo inaugural entre Ilulissat y Copenhague, el propio primer ministro de la región, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, reconocía que “si Groenlandia quiere ser independiente necesita una base sólida, tanto económica como industrial y empresarial”.
¿Y la respuesta es el turismo? Desde luego es un motor económico valioso en un contexto complejo para la industria pesquera de la isla. Por supuesto, no todo son oportunidades. En Groenlandia ya hay quienes ven con escepticismo (o un enfoque crítico) la apuesta por un sector que, advierten, no siempre tiene en cuenta a los empresarios locales.
La realidad es que, a día de hoy, Groenlandia está lejos aún de ser un destino de masas. En 2025 recibió ‘solo’ 180.000 visitantes, si bien se trata de una cifra récord que mejora en un 8% el balance de 2024. También hay que valorarla teniendo en cuenta la población de la isla, de apenas 56.000 personas. En 2024 el sector representó el 4,9% del PIB.

articles.title: Exclusive: RadianX promises solar-powered devices that never need charging | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Batteries have transformed electronics, giving us powerful phones, tablets, e-readers, and smart watches. But eventually, every battery runs flat.
Maybe not for long. One startup, RadianX, envisions a world in which portable and edge devices can cut the cord for good without running out of power. The key is a better breed of solar panels.
RadianX has developed a new type of solar material from a family known as perovskites. The material is just as good as existing solar panels outdoors, but twice as good at harvesting light indoors.
“We can harvest any kind of photon, whether it’s an outdoor or indoor photon, and keep the device running longer — or running forever,” Josh Douglas, co-founder and COO, told TechCrunch.
The indoor efficiency of RadianX’s tech could be the key to unlocking what the company calls “edge energy.” Think an e-reader that never needs charging or an IoT sensor that never needs a battery swap. But as with any new category, unexpected uses could emerge, including long-runtime robots or wearables that have been held back by limited battery power.
To fund a commercial-volume production line, RadianX recently raised $5 million in a seed round led by SOSV and Twynam, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. Other investors included One Small Planet, Sachsen Ventures, Avila VC, California Innovation Fund, quantumEDGE, Riceberg Ventures, and Alumni Ventures. Alongside the seed money, Pacific Union Technology Precision Manufacturing is pitching in $4 million of non-dilutive investment to build a dedicated production line for the startup.
It’s not an entirely new idea — solar-powered calculators have been around for decades — but it’s one that has been overlooked more recently because the power demands of modern devices have outstripped traditional solar panels’ capacity.
“It’s power density,” Vivian Qu, co-founder and CEO of RadianX, told TechCrunch. “The reason why perovskites have been so interesting is the high power density”
Perovskites are also not a new idea, though the class of materials has struggled to gain a foothold. They’re still more expensive than typical silicon-based solar panels, and they’re not quite as durable, though they’ve made strides in recent years.
But they make up for those shortcomings in power delivery — RadianX’s 1.2 meter by 0.6 meter panel, for example, harvests light with 22.33% efficiency, which the company said is the best on record.
For RadianX, durability is also less of a concern. The company has been able to hit a key industry standard for durability, and by targeting indoor devices, the company’s panels are subject to less wear-and-tear. The panels, which can be as thin as 0.7 millimeters, can be sized to fit.
To wring more power out of the panels, RadianX is also developing power electronics tailored to perovskites. Most existing electronics are tuned for silicon panels, but “silicon has a very different light-soaking characteristic,” she said.
Unlike many other solar companies, RadianX isn’t planning to sell bare panels. “RadianX is trying to package all of this and sell this to device makers as something they don’t need to worry about,” Qu said.
Ultimately, Qu and Douglas hope their power packages will land in everything from e-readers to factory sensors — and maybe a few places they haven’t dreamt of yet.

articles.title: The FAA is finally ditching floppy disks
articles.text:
It’s the year 2026 and the Federal Aviation Administration is still running critical pieces of American airspace on 3.5-inch magnetic floppy disks.
The FAA is finally ditching floppy disks
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wants credit for dragging America’s air traffic control out of the 1980s, but retiring 3.5-inch floppies won’t fix a broken system running on overworked controllers and private-sector hype.
But those technology artifacts could be headed for the dustbin after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced an effort to ditch floppy disks in favor of a new digital system.
Duffy announced Thursday that the FAA is rolling out the Enterprise – Information Display System (E-IDS) to replace four legacy setups across more than 400 air traffic control facilities. E-IDS aggregates real-time weather alerts, equipment outages, restricted airspace changes, and pilot reports onto a modern digital dashboard, replacing manual workflows and archaic physical storage media.
Upgrades have already kicked off at five sites — including control hubs in Atlantic City, Nashville, Rochester, Atlanta, and Salt Lake City — with a targeted rollout across 435 facilities by the end of 2028.
“Good news America: floppy disks are out, 21st century tech is in,” Duffy said in a release.
Duffy, a former reality TV star and Fox Business host, has been using floppy disks as a scapegoat for the air travel disruptions that have plagued the country for years now. He waves them around during speeches or TV interviews, while highlighting that the FAA still uses “copper wires and floppy disks” as a symbol of government obsolescence.
Indeed, our air traffic control system is deeply out of date, especially when held up alongside the more modern approaches of other nations. A Government Accountability Office report from September 2024 found that 90 percent of the nation’s critical air traffic control infrastructure was due or past due for a “technology refresh.” Nearly half of the 138 systems surveyed were “considered unsustainable” or “potentially unsustainable” due to shortfalls in funding, insufficient maintenance expertise, or even a lack of spare parts.
But E-IDS is not an overnight breakthrough cooked up in a single executive sprint; it’s an existing FAA contract that has spent years working through procurement, safety validation, testing, and vendor timelines. The initial contract for E-IDS was awarded to Leidos, a defense contractor headquartered in Reston, Virginia, by the FAA back in August 2020, during the first Trump administration.
The scope of the problem was understood, even back then. But since then, it has gotten much worse. The FAA has faced backlash in recent years over ground stops, close calls on runways (including one involving President Donald Trump), chronic burnout among air traffic controllers, and high-profile software meltdowns, like the 2023 NOTAM outage. Duffy is clearly trying the frame the system’s problems around relics like the floppy disk, as if obsolete tech is the only reason for the disruptions.
But as we’ve noted before, it’s a much bigger problem than just the systems themselves. Replacing an information system with digital panels is relatively low-hanging fruit compared to the systemic crises plaguing American aviation, such as a crippling deficit of thousands of certified professional controllers. Duffy has been lobbying Congress for an additional $30 billion, on top of the $12.5 billion “down payment” he got in 2025, for his ATC modernization plan.
Under Duffy, the USDOT has made a big deal about recruiting gamers, specifically, to take on these roles. And the administration is also relying on its tech oligarch allies, including Elon Musk and Peter Thiel, to help them clean up the mess — even if they happen to make it worse in the process.

Menaces envoyées par mail, décollage d’un Rafale : ce que l’on sait de la vague d’alertes à la bombe qui frappe les vols européens
articles.text:
La menace se répand comme une traînée de poudre chez les compagnies aériennes européennes.
Ce jeudi 5 novembre 2026, un Airbus A320 d’Aer Lingus qui reliait Dublin à Rome a dû quitter sa route au-dessus de la France pour rejoindre la base aérienne d’Évreux, dans l’Eure, à la suite d’une alerte à la bombe.
C’est l’un des 14 vols au moins concernés ce jour-là, selon le décompte de Libération, après une dizaine mardi et un appareil de Wizz Air lundi. Jeudi à la mi-journée, aucune inspection dont le résultat a été rendu public n’avait permis de trouver un explosif.
Un Rafale et un Mirage 2000 ont escorté l’avion jusqu’à Évreux
Matignon a annoncé le déroutement vers 9h30, et l’armée de l’Air et de l’Espace a indiqué à l’AFP avoir fait décoller ses avions de permanence pour intercepter l’A320. Un Rafale serait parti de Saint-Dizier, en Haute-Marne, avant d’être rejoint par un Mirage 2000. L’appareil a atterri à Évreux vers 10h avec 151 passagers et 6 membres d’équipage, mis à l’abri pendant l’intervention des démineurs.
6 autres pays au moins ont été touchés dans la matinée. En Bulgarie, 3 avions se sont posés en urgence à Sofia ou à Plovdiv, et le ministère des Transports a indiqué que leur inspection n’avait révélé aucun engin explosif. 4 vols à destination de Prague ont aussi été menacés, tout comme un avion parti de Varsovie vers Bruxelles.
En Italie, un vol Finnair venu d’Helsinki a été accompagné par des avions de chasse jusqu’à Rome-Fiumicino, tandis qu’un appareil de Wizz Air reliant Milan à Varsovie a été redirigé vers Vienne. 2 vols à destination de Milan Malpensa et un autre à destination de Bucarest ont également été visés.
Des mails à Prague et à Sofia
Le mode de transmission des alertes n’est connu que pour une partie des vols. À Prague, un représentant de l’aéroport a expliqué à CNN que les menaces contre les 4 avions de jeudi étaient arrivées via un mail anonyme, dont la police tchèque a jugé la crédibilité faible tout en déclenchant les mesures de sécurité prévues. Le même canal avait déjà été utilisé mardi en Bulgarie, où des alertes ont été envoyées au ministère de l’Intérieur selon la police des frontières, et à Rome, d’après un responsable de l’aéroport de Fiumicino cité par l’agence AP.
Pour la plupart des avions visés jeudi, dont celui d’Aer Lingus, aucune précision n’a été donnée à ce stade sur la manière dont l’alerte a été transmise.

articles.title: J’ai testé le Roborock F25 Steam : sa vapeur fait fondre les taches… et son autonomie
articles.text:
C’est tout de même bien mieux une maison propre. C’est encore mieux sans avoir systématiquement recours à un détergent. À cet effet, le Roborock F25 Steam promet de nettoyer votre maison de fond en comble, d’un bord de plinthe à l’autre, avec de la vapeur pour une efficacité accrue. Alors, que vaut-il ? À un peu moins de 600 euros, chaque carreau de carrelage a intérêt à être comme neuf.
- Puissance d'aspiration efficace
- Vapeur radicale contre les taches tenaces
- Très bonne maniabilité et roues motrices
- Nettoyage du bord des plinthes
- Entretien facile
- Tarif élevé
- Autonomie sacrifiée en mode vapeur
- Peut laisser quelques traces sur sols brillants
- Consommation d'eau élevée en mode vapeur
Si certains aspirateurs laveurs se contentent de nettoyer le sol à l’eau froide ou chaude, d’autres proposent un mode vapeur permettant de décrasser le carrelage ou le parquet en profondeur. C’est justement ce que propose le Roborock F25 Steam qui vient compléter la gamme lancée l’an dernier par le constructeur.
Lancé durant l’été 2026, ce nouveau venu dans la gamme, commercialisé au prix conseillé de 589 €, utilise la vapeur pour décoller les taches incrustées. Les 180 °C annoncés correspondent à la température mesurée à la sortie du chauffage interne, et non au contact du sol. Les 180° se retrouvent par ailleurs dans sa conception, lui permettant d’être positionné à plat, pour passer sous certains meubles. Reste à le distinguer du F25 Ultra, qui propose lui aussi de la vapeur. Le Steam se passe du lavage des sols à l’eau chaude et de l’application, mais annonce une aspiration plus forte et une meilleure autonomie en mode Éco. Un nouvel appareil est-il justifié ? La réponse dans notre test.
Design et ergonomie
Côté esthétique, le Roborock F25 Steam reprend la silhouette de la gamme F25, avec son réservoir d’eau propre placé très bas, son plastique mat et ses réservoirs translucides. La qualité de fabrication est solide, l’appareil ne grince pas et ne semble pas faiblir. Seul regret, la partie supérieure du réservoir d’eau propre est très sensible aux traces de doigts et à la poussière.
Avec 5,6 kilos sur la balance, ce n’est pas un poids-plume. Cependant, son centre de gravité très bas et l’entraînement du rouleau vers l’avant le rendent simple à manipuler. L’appareil propose des roues motrices, facilitant son utilisation.
Autre atout de cet appareil, son inclinaison à 180°, lui permettant de se coucher totalement. L’idéal pour nettoyer sous les meubles pas trop bas comme un lit, un meuble TV ou une étagère sur pieds. Toutefois, il ne passera pas sous tous les meubles, bien loin de là.
Sur la partie avant, une LED bleue, surtout utile dans les zones sombres, permet de faciliter le ramassage des poussières en tout genre, parfois difficilement visibles.
L’aspirateur se pilote avec trois boutons sur le manche, avec un écran sur le bloc moteur, qui affiche le niveau de batterie, l’état de la vapeur, mais surtout, le mode sélectionné. Il n’y a pas d’application. On s’évite ainsi un compte à créer, une connexion, et un double pilotage d’un aspirateur à main avec un smartphone.
La station reste compacte, elle nettoie automatiquement le rouleau à la vapeur et à l’eau chaude, avant de le sécher. Le bac à eau sale intègre, comme à l’accoutumée, un séparateur amovible pour les plus gros éléments, afin de les séparer du reste. Il est vivement recommandé de le rincer après chaque utilisation.
Performances de lavage
À première vue, les différences avec le F25 Ultra précédemment testé ne sont pas nombreuses. Pourtant, le F25 Steam apporte bel et bien des prestations légèrement différentes. La puissance d’aspiration est sur ce modèle de 25 000 Pa, lui permettant de collecter l’immense majorité des saletés et poussières au sol.
La vapeur fonctionne correctement et permet d’éliminer les taches au sol, même les taches de gras. Elle est également efficace sur les taches de café, permettant de tout ramollir sur son passage. Cependant, elle est loin d’être indispensable partout. Les autres modes de lavage suffisent généralement pour un nettoyage quotidien. Le rouleau, auquel Roborock attribue une force d’appui de 33 N, vient à bout des taches peu incrustées sans avoir à repasser à trois reprises.
Il aspire globalement tout ce qui se trouve sur son passage, des miettes à la poussière, aux croquettes du chat à côté de la gamelle, mais également les liquides renversés.
Sur les côtés, la promesse de Roborock est d’arriver à moins de 1 mm des plinthes. Si cette valeur est difficile à mesurer, nous avons pu constater un nettoyage efficace des bords, collectant une immense majorité des poussières et saletés qui y sont présentes. Le résultat est satisfaisant, bien que pas parfait non plus, comme sur l’immense majorité des concurrents de cette gamme.
Deux bémols sont à ajouter toutefois. Le F25 Steam ramasse efficacement les déchets en marche avant, mais se montre nettement moins convaincant en marche arrière. Aussi, en mode vapeur, on peut observer quelques traces sur un carrelage brillant. Un passage en mode « Éponge » permet toutefois de régler le problème rapidement, mais impose un changement de mode.
Autonomie
C’est le talon d’Achille de l’appareil, et il faut le savoir avant d’acheter. Les 80 minutes annoncées ne valent qu’en mode Éco, dans les conditions les plus favorables. En mode Auto, l’aspirateur a tenu autour de 50 minutes, ce qui permet de nettoyer une maison de 90 mètres carrés sans aucun problème. Toutefois, si la vapeur est l’argument majeur de ce F25 Steam, elle vaporise également l’autonomie de l’appareil. Avec ce mode, la batterie de 4600 mAh du F25 Steam se réduit à peau de chagrin pour n’offrir que 21 minutes d’autonomie.
Notons de surcroît que la vapeur consomme aussi beaucoup plus d’eau que les autres modes. Le réservoir d’un litre suffit largement pour un nettoyage classique, mais en vapeur continue sur une grande surface, j’ai dû le remplir pour finir une pièce.
La recharge complète prend environ quatre heures sur la station. Petite subtilité à connaître : l’auto-nettoyage interrompt la charge, et il refuse de démarrer si la batterie est quasiment vide. Mieux vaut donc s’arrêter vers 10 à 20 %, seuil que l’assistant vocal signale, pour garder de quoi lancer le cycle de nettoyage.
Comment entretenir mon F25 Steam ?
Une fois reposé sur sa base, un appui sur le bouton dédié lance un cycle très complet. Rinçage du circuit, traitement du rouleau à la vapeur et à l’eau chaude, rotation dans les deux sens, essorage et finalement, séchage à l’air chaud à 95 °C.
Un capteur dédié, habilement nommé DirTect, prolonge le lavage du rouleau tant que l’eau ressort trouble. Concernant le séchage, un mode rapide de 5 minutes est proposé, mais il est bruyant. Un mode silencieux de 30 minutes, certes plus long, mais également nettement plus discret, est également disponible.
Il est toutefois indispensable de vider le bac à eau sale après chaque session de nettoyage. De préférence, une fois que l’appareil a terminé son cycle de nettoyage automatique, afin d’éviter les odeurs désagréables.
Parmi les autres opérations d’entretien à faire manuellement, un nettoyage hebdomadaire du filtre semble opportun, et un passage de la brosse dans le conduit d’aspiration de temps en temps ne fait jamais de mal. Côté détergent, Roborock propose ses propres produits, à verser dans le réservoir dédié uniquement. Le détergent n’est toutefois pas indispensable pour le nettoyage quotidien : l’appareil peut aussi fonctionner avec de l’eau du robinet seule.
Roborock F25 Steam : l’avis de Clubic
Le Roborock F25 Steam est un aspirateur laveur qui ne manque pas d'arguments pour séduire. Avec ses 25 000 Pa de puissance d'aspiration, son rouleau efficace et sa vapeur à 180 °C, il vient à bout des saletés du quotidien comme des taches les plus tenaces. Sa maniabilité, malgré ses 5,6 kg, son nettoyage précis le long des plinthes et son système d'auto-nettoyage complet renforcent cette bonne impression.
Mais tout n'est pas parfait. Si la vapeur constitue son principal argument commercial, elle exploite aussi grandement la batterie, faisant chuter l'autonomie à moins de 25 minutes assurément. Ainsi, il est difficile d'envisager un ménage complet de votre maison à la vapeur en une seule fois. La consommation d'eau augmente également de manière importante. Heureusement, le mode Auto offre 50 minutes d'autonomie, et se montre très convenable pour l'entretien quotidien.
Au final, le F25 Steam remplit très bien sa mission et se révèle agréable à utiliser au quotidien. C'est un très bon aspirateur laveur, mais dont la vapeur mérite d'être utilisée avec parcimonie.
- Puissance d'aspiration efficace
- Vapeur radicale contre les taches tenaces
- Très bonne maniabilité et roues motrices
- Nettoyage du bord des plinthes
- Entretien facile
- Tarif élevé
- Autonomie sacrifiée en mode vapeur
- Peut laisser quelques traces sur sols brillants
- Consommation d'eau élevée en mode vapeur
