articles.title: Zu perfekt zum Reinbeißen? Warum uns KI-Essensbilder weniger Appetit machen
articles.text:
Zu perfekt zum Reinbeißen: Studie zeigt, warum KI-Essensbilder weniger Appetit machen
Burger, Döner, Croissants, Fleischspieße und auch den beliebten Matcha Latte trifft es. Wer sich in Restaurants, Cafés oder an Imbissständen etwas bestellen will, wirft gerne mal einen Blick auf die Speisekarte oder die Menütafel draußen, um eine Idee davon zu bekommen, wie das Gericht oder das Getränk wohl aussehen. Das sorgt bei manchen momentan allerdings eher für Unmut als für Appetit.
Der Grund dafür: Einige Gastronomien gestalten ihre Karten oder Menüs mittlerweile mithilfe von Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI). Auch bei der nahenden Weihnachtsmarktsaison dürften entsprechende Abbildungen von Glühwein und Co. öfter zu sehen sein. Zeit für die Frage: Verdirbt uns die KI den Appetit?
„Einheitsbrei“ vs. günstige Alternative?
Hier scheinen sich viele Nutzer auf Plattformen wie Instagram einig zu sein: KI-generierte Essensbilder wirken auf sie unnatürlich oder wie „Einheitsbrei“. Einige berichten sogar davon, dass die Darstellungen bei ihnen Ekel auslösen, etwa weil die Texturen sie an Löcher oder Insektenwaben erinnern. Andere wiederum verteidigen die Gastronomen. Für kleine Betriebe sei ein professionelles Grafikdesign oft nicht mehr bezahlbar, heißt es in einem Kommentar. Dann sei es verständlich, für Werbung auf KI zurückzugreifen.
Der Deutsche Hotellerie- und Gastronomieverband (Dehoga) teilt mit, aus Sicht der Betriebe sprächen neben der Kosten auch Zeit, Verfügbarkeit und Tempo dafür, KI zu nutzen. Eine Wochenkarte, die sich jeden Montag ändere, sei etwa mit klassischer Fotografie nicht zu bebildern. Belastbare Zahlen, wie verbreitet KI-Karten in Deutschland seien, gebe es nicht.
Nachfrage bei einem Lángos-Stand in Berlin, der für seine Speisekarte auf die Technologie zurückgegriffen hat. Er nutze sie, weil es einfacher und viel schneller sei, damit das Menü zu entwerfen, sagt ein Mitarbeiter. Einigen falle das KI-Design auf, allerdings weder positiv noch negativ.
Pannen bei KI-Essensbildern auf Lieferando
Für spöttische Reaktionen hingegen sorgten kürzlich KI-generierte Fotos auf der Bestellplattform Lieferando (Just Eat Takeaway). Online machten einige Motive die Runde, die von der Produktbeschreibung teils stark abwichen, etwa ein Bild eines Chickenburgers mit Buns aus Reis statt aus Brot. Das Unternehmen schreibt auf Anfrage, ein Test mit KI-erstellten Bildern habe in einigen Fällen nicht auf Anhieb geklappt.
„Wir entschuldigen uns für ungenaue Bilder, arbeiten an deren Entfernung und haben die Verwendung des Tools ausgesetzt. Grundsätzlich ist die neue Technologie für unsere Partner sehr hilfreich, ihre Fehlerquote gering und wir werden sie weiter verfeinern“. Man teste Technologien wie KI zur Verbesserung des Bestellprozesses und zur Unterstützung der Restaurants. Produktbilder sollten Gerichte „ansprechend darstellen“.
Studie: Wie realistisch und appetitlich wirken KI-Essensbilder?
Doch werden KI-generierte Essensbilder so ansprechend wahrgenommen wie reales Essen? Damit beschäftigt sich auch die Forschung. Der Psychologe und Postdoktorand Alexander Diel von der LVR-Universitätsklinik Essen, Universität Duisburg-Essen, hat mit einem internationalen Team dazu eine Studie im Fachmagazin Nature veröffentlicht. Die Wissenschaftler ließen 87 Personen an einem Online-Test teilnehmen.
Diesen wurden 60 Bildpaare gezeigt, die aus einem echten Foto und einem KI-Foto desselben Essens bestanden – etwa eine Kugel Vanilleeis oder Weintrauben. Ohne jeweils zu wissen, ob es sich um reale oder KI-generierte Bilder handelt, sollten die Teilnehmer auf einer Skala bewerten: Wie echt wirkt die Abbildung? Wie groß ist die Bereitschaft, das gezeigte Lebensmittel zu essen? Wie gesund und für wie kalorienreich wird es eingeschätzt?
Das Ergebnis: Die KI-generierten Bilder wurden im Schnitt als weniger realistisch bewertet – und lösten etwas weniger Appetit aus als die echten Fotos. Bei der Einschätzung zum Kaloriengehalt und zur Gesundheit schnitten sie gleich ab.
Forscher: KI-Bilder sehen möglicherweise zu perfekt aus
Sehe das abgebildete Essen unrealistischer aus, wirke es vielleicht auch weniger appetitlich, erläutert Diel das Ergebnis. Eine Erklärung dafür könne sein, dass das Bild „zu perfekt“ aussehe, die Oberflächen zu glatt oder zu symmetrisch ausfielen oder andere optische Fehler aufträten, vermutet er. Generell wisse man aus vorangegangenen Studien, dass Menschen sensibel gegenüber Essen eingestellt seien.
„Wir als Menschen möchten evolutionär bedingt neues Essen ausprobieren, weil es uns potenziell wieder neue Nährstoffe bringen kann. Aber neues Essen kann auch schädlich sein oder uns vergiften. Deshalb sind Menschen besonders vorsichtig gegenüber Essen, das sie nicht kennen oder das anders aussieht.“
Was bedeutet das nun für KI-generierte Speisekarten? Diel sagt: „Als Ableitung aus meiner Forschung würde ich sagen: KI-generierte Bilder von Essen werden nicht zuverlässig so wahrgenommen wie reales Essen. Sie haben das Potenzial, noch realistischer zu sein, aber es ist ganz und gar keine Garantie. Wenn sie vor allem große Fehler oder Anomalien enthalten, wirken sie oft abstoßend auf Personen.“
Ein weiterer Punkt sei, dass KI-Bilder nicht das tatsächliche Gericht eines Restaurants, sondern ein beliebiges Gericht zeigten, das aus Trainingsdaten der verschiedenen Modelle abgeleitet wird. Das wiederum könne Frust bei Kunden auslösen, wenn die Abbildung nicht der Realität entspricht. Auch die Dehoga weist darauf hin, Authentizität sei „der Kern des gastronomischen Versprechens“.

articles.title: Oxford’s FluoRok raises €26.64 million to scale fluorochemical production without hazardous hydrogen fluoride | EU-Startups
articles.text:
FluoRok, an Oxford-based chemical manufacturing startup that has developed a patented process to produce fluorochemicals without using highly hazardous hydrogen fluoride (HF), has secured a €26.64 million ($30 million) Series A financing round.
The round was led by Orano Ventures Fund/Supernova Invest, with participation from investor Bidra Innovation Ventures. Existing backers Oxford Science Enterprises, BGF, GGF, Volta Energy Technologies, and the University of Oxford also participated in the round.
“We back companies whose technologies support a sovereign, sustainable industrial transition. FluoRok has already shown its process works at pilot scale, and taking hydrogen fluoride out of fluorochemical production tackles a safety and supply problem the whole industry shares. We are pleased to join a strong group of investors supporting the team as it moves to industrial scale,” said Florian de Beauchaine, Investment Manager, Orano Venture Fund/Supernova Invest.
FluoRok says its Series A funding round exceeded its original target and included several angel investors, smaller partners such as EverQuest Capital Partners, CPI Enterprises, and WS Investment, as well as approximately €1.15 million ($1.3 million) in grant funding from Innovate UK through its Investor Partnerships programme.
Founded in 2022, FluoRok is a University of Oxford spin-out developing a patented manufacturing platform that bypasses the conventional HF-based process used to produce fluorochemicals entirely. Conventional fluorochemical production has relied on a 250-year-old process that depends on HF, one of the most hazardous chemicals in industrial use, and high-purity fluorspar predominantly sourced from China, creating safety, supply, and cost risks.
FluoRok bypasses this process by relying on mechanical activation combined with base chemistry to unlock fluorine from lower-grade mineral sources and even fluoride-containing industrial waste streams, under controllable conditions. The process runs on off-the-shelf industrial equipment, which makes it faster and easier to scale.
The company targets critical end markets including pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and lithium-ion battery manufacturing, sectors where fluorochemicals are indispensable but supply remains heavily concentrated and hazard-prone.
Dr. Gabriele Pupo, founder and CEO, FluoRok, said, ”We are thrilled to welcome new investors on our journey to fundamentally change how the world makes fluorochemicals, with safer chemistry and better economics.”
“Closing another oversubscribed round, backed by both new and existing investors from around the world, is a testament to the strength of our technology, the incredible commercial traction and the speed of execution of the FluoRok team. This funding will ensure FluoRok can swiftly move from start-up to scale-up and take a further step towards becoming a large-scale industrial manufacturer,” he added.
FluoRok says it has completed pilot qualifications and established strong commercial traction with key customers, with products being validated by more than ten partners across eight countries and three continents.
The Series A funding round builds on the €12.43 million ($14 million) secured in previous rounds and more than €11.54 million ($13 million) in UK and European public funding to date. It plans to use the new capital to transition from startup to industrial scale, including building demonstrator facilities for its reagents and battery electrolyte salts, expanding its team, and deepening its commercial partnerships.
The company also plans to scale its platform for next-generation battery products such as LiFSI and FEC, and for a waste-to-value stream that transforms fluorinated polymer waste, over 25,000 tonnes of which is incinerated annually in Europe alone, into high-value chemical intermediates.

articles.title: Bambu Lab releases the H3C printer to take 3D printing to an all-new level - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Bambu Lab has unveiled its first third-generation 3D printer – the H3C – which is capable of multi-material printing to take the category to an all-new level and produce prints we could have only dreamed about just a few short years ago.
The H3C has new Swaptek architecture, which includes nine print tools, each with its own filament path and heating.
A material switch can now be achieved in as little as six seconds which speeds up print time and reduces waste.
To achieve multi-material printing it required a machine that can handle such a capability.
And that’s how Bambu Lab conceived the idea for the H3C.
The company brought all its engineering experience to the table to come up with a machine that could handle more than one material and overcome the limitations experienced with older models.
As a result the new H3C has three new major parts – the Swaptek to handle the tool changes, FlexFeed Extruder to deal with flexible materials, and the AMS 3H, which can store and dry and feed the material to the printer.
When they work together it makes bringing nine materials together as effortless as it is to reach for one.
Each of the nine print tools has its own filament path and its own heating so the filament stays loaded and ready to go.
This means it’s ready to go in an instant and can be preheated ahead of the switch.
This means there’s no need to retract one material to feed the next, resulting in faster more efficient printing.
Swaptek also introduces capabilities like mixing colours and mixing nozzle sizes within a single print.
The FlexFeed Extruder makes printing with soft TPU easier than ever before.
The issue with softer filament was that it would bend and buckle before it reaches the nozzle so regular extruders had to slow down to remain stable and reliable.
But FlexFeed can handle both 1.75 and 2.85 mm filament and switch them on the fly.
The larger 2.85 mm TPU can now stay rigid under pressure, melt in greater volume, and push through with more force.
The result is being able to print at up to three times the flow rate of a regular printer.
This softer TPU is used to print comfortable wearables like shoes which is now easier to print than ever before with the H3C.
AMS 3H integrated filament management system is fully enclosed and has been designed to work seamlessly with Swaptek.
Each spool sits in a sealed airtight chamber to protect it from moisture and filament feeds into the print tool automatically.
Alongside the multi-material system is a motion platform built from scratch.
The toolhead and X-axis assembly are 40 per cent lighter, which means they can operate smoother and faster.
Prints can be finished, on average, more than 10 per cent faster than on the previous models without reducing any detail.
The new Bambu Lab H3C is available now and is priced at $3,999.
Stay tuned to Tech Guide for a full review of the Bambu Lab H3C in the coming weeks.

articles.title: The Wizard of Open Weights: Chris Alexiuk Makes AI Easy With Open Models
articles.text:
Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it.
“We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers.
Alexiuk’s preferred “rooftop” is YouTube, where he’s built a following teaching curious thousands how to build, fine-tune, evaluate and ship production LLM applications and agents.
“I think the people who will most help us understand how to build and apply AI likely haven’t even heard of it yet,” he said. “Trying to get knowledge and information out to as many people as humanly possible is what continues to drive me.”
Bringing NVIDIA Nemotron to Developers Everywhere
Having spent years teaching developers to build with open models, Alexiuk has concluded that transparency isn’t a feature of good AI; it’s the precondition for it.
“Fully open source AI is necessary for the democratization of intelligence,” he said. “You should have access to the weights, the data that went into it, the training recipes, everything.”
That’s why, on his LinkedIn profile, Alexiuk styles himself “No. 1 Nemotron Fan,” referring to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of open source, multimodal models built for long-running, self-evolving and specialized AI agents.
“I think Nemotron is the most important project that exists,” said Alexiuk, who also uses the pseudonym “Joe Nemotron” across social media. “I’m a firm believer that openness is a very important thing to undertake, so I’m going to be the No. 1 fan of whoever is doing that the best. And that is Nemotron.”
It’s this matter-of-fact directness and affable approachability that makes Alexiuk’s teaching style so appealing. On the social media platform X, he goes by the handle “llm_wizard.” His avatar: a laughing cartoon caricature sporting a slouchy sorcerer’s hat and brandishing a magic wand.
It’s no surprise, then, that Alexiuk likens Nemotron to a magical library — its users fellow wizards in search of knowledge that can move mountains.
“You’re a wizard in search of prepared spells, and Nemotron has a spell for everything,” he said. “Just choose the one you need.”
In non-wizard terms?
“There’s a category of model that’s going to be close to the kind of work you want to accomplish,” Alexiuk said, explaining that Nemotron supports that whole ecosystem of AI users: from individual developers using a model like Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for repetitive, high-frequency execution work to a company deploying Nemotron Ultra for long-running autonomous agents, deep research and enterprise tasks.
“I think that openness helps more people understand AI and hopefully leads to more people doing really ingenious things with these tools at the limit,” Alexiuk said. “If a tool is amplifying skill, it’s amplifying human expression.”
From Birding to Model-Building
Alexiuk first became fascinated with machine learning in a computational physics class at Trent University in Ontario, Canada.
“After that, I learned about TensorFlow and that you could build image classifiers that ran on your GPU,” he recalled. As an initial one-off project, Alexiuk built a classifier that would alert him whenever his friend’s distinctive pet bird, a Yellow-Faced Gray Budgerigar, appeared in frame on his webcam during shared video game sessions.
“Because we were playing video games, I wasn’t focused on my friend’s webcam, but I didn’t want to miss seeing the bird when it appeared,” Alexiuk said. “And then my whole life changed, because in that instance I realized it’s crazy what you could do with technology.”
Since then, he’s been embedding himself in the open source AI community.
“To imagine within the span of a few years going from freaking out because I could know my friend’s bird was in the camera frame to being able to make any website in a matter of minutes with a model that’s running on my laptop — I cannot wait to see what’s next,” Alexiuk said. “It’s never been more accessible to get into and learn about AI.”
And if another LLM wizard arises to challenge him for the title of No. 1 Nemotron Fan?
“It would be the greatest day of my life to be surpassed by an even bigger fan of Nemotron, who had heard about Nemotron through the work I was doing,” Alexiuk said. “That would be a capstone to my career that I can only dream of.”
Hear more from Alexiuk by following the NVIDIA Nemotron Labs Livestreams series on YouTube.

articles.text:
Wazzup. ☀️️
Yellow Card, the stablecoin infrastructure company and one of the sector’s most-funded startups, launched in Africa in 2019, before expanding into other emerging markets. Now, it is taking that focus to Brazil. What’s taking it all the way to South America? Business, apparently.
Yesterday, Yellow Card announced that it had acquired GoMoney, a Brazilian crypto payments company, giving it direct operations in Latin America’s largest cryptocurrency market. The deal lets Yellow Card customers pay in Brazilian reais and settle transactions using stablecoins. Having built its business across Africa, Yellow Card is now taking that experience across the Atlantic.

capital markets
China inquiry prompted OPay to halt US IPO
OPay made it to Wall Street, rang the opening bell, and was ready to start trading. But its big moment ended before a single share changed hands.
What happened? On October 30, the Nigeria-focused fintech was preparing to list on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) after pricing 16 million shares at $19 each. The offering would have raised $304 million and valued OPay at over $4 billion. But hours after setting the price, the company called off the listing, citing an inquiry from an unnamed foreign regulator.
Bloomberg reported on Wednesday that the inquiry came from a Chinese regulator, citing people familiar with the matter.
Explain like I’m new here. OPay, founded by Chinese businessman Zhou Yahui, operates one of Nigeria’s largest digital payments platforms, serving more than 50 million customers who use it to transfer money, pay bills, and access financial services. The company also operates in other emerging markets, but has no business operations or revenue in China. Yet, its founder’s Chinese connection has now become a complication in its ambition to go public in the US.
OPay has not disclosed what the Chinese regulator is investigating. But it maintains that the inquiry does not reflect problems with its financial performance or operations and expects the matter to be resolved.
Zoom out: OPay’s listing would have been a major moment for Africa’s fintech industry, giving international investors access to one of its largest digital payments businesses. But its experience shows that growing a successful business in Africa is one thing; navigating the regulatory demands of international capital markets is another.

regulation
Kenya’s Treasury wants banks to make loans cheaper
If you’ve been reading TC Daily for a while, you’d know that a cat-and-mouse game has been playing out in Kenya. The Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) wants to get the economy moving by cutting interest rates to encourage commercial banks to make loans cheaper. The banks have responded, but not quite as much as the regulator would like.
What’s new? Kenya’s Treasury Cabinet Secretary, John Mbadi, has joined the conversation, urging banks to lower their lending rates and extend more credit to businesses, farmers, and manufacturers.
Explain like I’m new here. Since June 2024, the CBK has reduced its benchmark interest rate from 13% to 8.75% to make loans cheaper, encouraging businesses to borrow, expand operations, and create jobs. But while banks have reduced their rates, the average lending rate remained at 14.4% in September 2026; borrowers haven’t enjoyed the full benefit of the central bank’s cuts.
There’s some progress, though. Private sector lending has recovered, growing 10.6% in September, compared with a 2.9% contraction in January 2025. The government also said it is borrowing less from banks, leaving lenders with more money to finance businesses.
Zoom out: Kenya is trying to revive economic activity from both ends. Beyond encouraging cheaper loans, the government has approved payments for verified outstanding bills of KES 50 million ($385,000) or less owed to suppliers, some of whom have waited years to get paid.
The banks have been given room to lend, and the government is promising to pay what it owes. Whether Kenyan businesses finally get some breathing room depends on how quickly both promises turn into cash in hand for business owners who urgently need it.
companies
Africa’s new credit rating agency courts 15 countries ahead of 2027 debut
When you apply for a loan, a lender wants to know whether you can repay. Governments face the same scrutiny when they borrow billions from investors. The difference is that instead of checking payslips and bank statements, investors rely on credit rating agencies to assess a country’s ability to repay its debts. Africa wants another agency doing the grading.
What happened? The Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA) is in discussions with 15 African countries and expects to publish its first sovereign credit ratings by March 2027. The agency is backed by an African Union initiative and led by interim CEO Sifiso Falala. At launch, the AfCRA said its researchers were preparing to assess five countries first, including Togo, Kenya, Seychelles, Burundi, and Mauritius.
Explain like I’m new here: The agency officially launched in Mauritius on October 7. When countries want to raise money through international bonds, investors need to know how risky the investment is. Three agencies have dominated this business, including S&P Global Ratings and Moody’s, both headquartered in the US, and Fitch Ratings, headquartered in New York and London.
They assess a country’s economy, government finances, debt levels, and ability to repay, and their ratings influence how much interest investors demand. These agencies have been criticised for relying heavily on external data that do not always reflect local realities. The African Union (AU) endorsed the idea of creating AfCRA in 2018, and the African Peer Review Mechanism developed its institutional framework. It is finally moving towards operations.
Why Africa wants another scorecard: According to the AU, 23 of its 55 member states have no sovereign rating from the three major international agencies. Countries such as Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan and Sierra Leone have been among those without ratings in recent assessments—making it harder to attract investors in international capital markets.
Africa’s external debt-service payments also climbed from $61 billion in 2010 to $163 billion in 2024. AfCRA hopes better-informed assessments can help investors understand the continent’s risks and potentially improve access to financing.
There are other players, including Nigeria’s Agusto & Co, Côte d’Ivoire’s Bloomfield and South Africa’s Sovereign Africa Ratings, that already operate in this space. The difference is AfCRA’s proposed continent-wide sovereign rating mandate.
AfCRA wants to raise $15 million from African investors in exchange for a two-thirds stake. However, there is a credibility question. AfCRA plans to use an issuer-pays model, where governments pay to be rated, but it questions whether paying clients can influence government grades.
It said independent committees and separation between commercial operations and rating decisions will protect its assessments. Its first ratings are expected by March 2027, probably drawn from the countries that agree to be assessed.
startups
Helium Health gets $2.5 million Google grant for AI maternal care
Helium Health, a Nigerian healthtech, wants to tackle a problem plaguing Nigerian women: maternal mortality.
The startup has secured a $2.5 million grant from Google.org, Google’s philanthropic arm, to deploy AI-powered tools that identify pregnancy risks and help connect women to appropriate care. It hopes to reach 1.9 million pregnant women over three years, starting in Lagos before expanding to Delta, Kano, and Oyo.
Explain like I’m new here: Nigeria already has several initiatives tackling maternal deaths. In November 2024, the Federal Government launched the Maternal Mortality Reduction Innovation Initiative (MAMII), targeting 172 high-burden local government areas across 33 states.
It combines community identification of pregnant women, referrals, free maternal services, emergency transport, and better-equipped health facilities. By October 2026, more than 32,000 women and 1,700 newborns had benefited from emergency obstetric and neonatal care, while the national emergency medical service had transported nearly 79,000 beneficiaries to appropriate care.
What is AI expected to do? AI could help Helium’s community health workers process patient information, flag potential complications and prioritise women who need urgent attention. It has been tested outside Nigeria.
Kenya’s Jacaranda Health runs PROMPTS, an SMS-based maternal health service that uses AI to assess messages from pregnant women, flag danger signs, and prioritise urgent cases for human follow-up. By mid-2025, the platform had reached more than 3.3 million mothers, and its AI triage system, TRIM-AI, was about 17% more accurate at identifying high-risk messages in preliminary tests.
Why this matters: The grant arrives as Nigerian healthtech funding has become harder to secure. Funding into the sector fell from nearly $55 million in 2023 to $18 million in 2024 and just $3 million in 2025, according to TechCabal Insights. In addition to the grant, Google’s $2.5 million comes with access to Google engineers and AI product experts.
Yet, AI cannot replace a functioning health centre, trained medical staff, ambulances, or emergency obstetric care. An algorithm can flag a dangerous pregnancy, but it cannot deliver a baby or perform an emergency C-section. Resources still need to be in place for Helium Health’s technology to translate into better outcomes for mothers.

articles.title: Google's Quick Share can now back up your Android photos to a Windows PC automatically
articles.text:
In a nutshell: While there are plenty of free and paid-for cloud backup services for your phone's media, an option to automatically back up photos and videos to a PC with ease would be a welcome one. Now, Google has revealed its version of a tool that performs this function for Android users.
The addition appears in Google's November system services release notes, under Google Play services version 26.43, dated November 2. The company confirms that Quick Share is gaining automatic photo and video backups from Android to Windows.
Quick Share already lets users wirelessly move files between Android devices and Windows PCs. Automating the process should make it more useful for anyone who wants a local copy of their camera roll without remembering to transfer everything manually.
The setup is expected to involve using the Quick Share Windows app, a nearby Android phone, and the same Google account signed in on both devices. Google still hasn't published detailed instructions, so we don't know the exact process just yet.
Reports also point to a shared Wi-Fi network, daily camera roll backups, and a "Back up now" option for starting transfers manually. The feature will likely appeal to those who don't want to rely on cloud backups or have eaten through Google's 15GB of free storage, which is shared across Photos, Gmail, and Drive.
Samsung owners might not get the feature when it first rolls out. Android Authority's earlier examinations of unreleased app code suggested that Samsung phones would be excluded, with a later discovery pointing to Samsung PCs being left out, too. Google's release notes don't mention either restriction, but the automatic backup option could initially be limited to Pixel devices.
The update marks the latest expansion of Quick Share's capabilities. There was the arrival of AirDrop interoperability on the Pixel 10 family, followed by Samsung bringing the functionality to its Galaxy S26 series earlier this year.
As is usually the case with Google Play services updates, availability is rolling out gradually. Having the latest version installed doesn't necessarily mean the backup option will appear immediately, and users should also keep Quick Share for Windows updated. Google hasn't provided a date for when everyone with eligible hardware will receive it.

articles.title: Google revela solución para el fallo de los Pixel Watch que drena su batería
articles.text:
Si en las últimas semanas notaste que la batería de tu Pixel Watch se agota con una rapidez inusual, no se trata de un problema aislado. Google confirmó la existencia de una falla que reduce drásticamente la autonomía del dispositivo y anunció que ya desplegó una solución para los equipos afectados.
El alcance del problema abarca varias generaciones
El inconveniente no se limita a un modelo específico. Los reportes de usuarios señalan que cualquier Pixel Watch desde la segunda generación en adelante presentó esta reducción en la duración de la batería. Si bien no se trata de una falla de alcance masivo, resulta significativa para quienes la experimentan: algunos casos documentados en Reddit mostraron una autonomía máxima de 12 horas, cuando previamente el reloj podía superar las 48 horas con la función de pantalla siempre encendida desactivada.
Hasta el momento, Google no reveló públicamente el origen técnico del problema. Las primeras sospechas apuntaron a una actualización reciente de Wear OS, aunque la compañía no confirmó ni descartó esa hipótesis.
Un dato que refuerza las dudas sobre el origen real de la falla es que la solución anunciada no llega a través de una actualización del sistema operativo, sino mediante las aplicaciones instaladas en el reloj, lo que hace pensar que el inconveniente podría originarse en la Play Store o en alguna de las apps que Google preinstala en sus dispositivos.
El procedimiento para resolver el drenaje de batería
La compañía con sede en Mountain View confirmó al medio especializado 9to5Google que ya desplegó una actualización destinada a corregir el problema en las unidades alcanzadas. Según explicó la empresa, la falla se presentó en un número limitado de unidades.
Para aplicar la corrección, los usuarios deben ingresar a la Play Store del reloj, acceder a la sección “Administrar apps” y seleccionar la opción “Actualizar todas”. Una vez completado este proceso, la duración de la batería debería normalizarse en los equipos afectados.
El despliegue continuará en los próximos días
Google indicó que la solución llegará de manera progresiva a todos los usuarios afectados en los días siguientes. Esto implica que, en caso de que un usuario todavía no perciba mejoras en la autonomía de su Pixel Watch tras actualizar las aplicaciones, es probable que deba esperar un poco más hasta que el fix termine de distribuirse por completo.
Otro cambio afectará a los modelos con conectividad LTE
Este no es el único ajuste que Google aplicará sobre su línea de relojes inteligentes. La compañía también anunció que eliminará, a partir del 12 de diciembre, la función “Señal de seguridad” en los Pixel Watch 2 y Pixel Watch 3 con LTE.
Este servicio permitía utilizar herramientas de emergencia, como el SOS y la detección de caídas, sin necesidad de contratar un plan de datos móvil adicional, ya que estaba vinculado al plan Google Health Premium. La función estuvo disponible únicamente en Estados Unidos, Canadá, Reino Unido y Alemania.
El proceso de baja del servicio comenzará con notificaciones por correo electrónico y mensajes push, y los usuarios dispondrán de 30 días desde ese aviso para seguir utilizando la función antes de su cese definitivo. Una vez eliminada, las funciones de emergencia continuarán operativas siempre que el reloj esté conectado a WiFi, emparejado por Bluetooth con un teléfono cercano o vinculado a una línea móvil activa. Por ese motivo, Google recomienda a los usuarios activar una eSIM en el dispositivo o contratar un plan de datos independiente con un operador.

articles.title: El PP quiere modificar la ley en Cantabria para que el PSIR pueda ser solo inmobiliario y permita construir vivienda
articles.text:
Toda cerradura tiene su llave, y el urbanismo cántabro ahora mismo posee en su llavero una ganzua de cuatro letras: PSIR. Con ella, el Gobierno regional podría convertir suelo rústico en urbanizable sin pasar por el plan del ayuntamiento (siempre que el proyecto sirva a un “interés regional”). Esta condición ha servido desde casi siempre: si había casas, debían acompañar a un equipamiento público. Según elDiario.es, Podemos denuncia que el PP quiere borrar de un plumazo este contrapeso.
Qué es un PSIR. Son las siglas de Proyecto Singular de Interés Regional, una figura creada en 2001. El Gobierno declara el interés regional, una comisión técnica (la CROTU) da el visto bueno provisional y el Consejo de Gobierno el definitivo. Sirvió para polígonos, algún que otro hospital o la rehabilitación de la Universidad Pontificia de Comillas. Irónicamente, de los cinco PSIR ejecutados, cuatro son polígonos.
Tres reglas en 25 años. La primera ley, la de 2001 exigía al menos un 40% de vivienda protegida cuando había casas. La de 2022 sumó al Parlamento al trámite y elevó ese requisito al 100% si el proyecto era de vivienda protegida. En 2025, la Ley de Simplificación Administrativa, con el respaldo de Vox, permitió incluir vivienda privada “de forma complementaria” en los PSIR con grandes equipamientos. Según Podemos, la nueva enmienda que el PP registró el 17 de septiembre borra dicha expresión: un PSIR podría ser solo de viviendas (otra regularía las juntas de compensación y permitiría empezar a construir).
Nombres propios. Bosques de Santander, el magno proyecto urbanísito de unos 70.000 metros, prevé 7.850 viviendas (4.710 libres y 3.140 protegidas) en Santander, Bezana y Camargo, promovidas por Real de Piasca. Al norte de la S-20, a la altura de Corbán, otro megaproyecto urbanístico (casi 20.000 metros cuadrados) será La Ciudad de la Justicia. Según Cantabria Económica, esto entró a petición del Gobierno y aporta la parte de "interés público". Y claro, los vecinos de Rucandial se han organizado para frenarlo. Son más de treinta familias que podrían perder su casa. Podemos admite que las enmiendas, registradas apenas dos semanas antes de su presentación, no mencionan el proyecto.
Qué dice cada parte. Pablo Gómez, portavoz de Medio Ambiente de Podemos, reconoce que la supuesta “Ciudad de la Justicia” (todavía no me acostumbro al nombre) puede ser necesaria, pero sostiene que eso no hace que cualquier operación residencial vinculada a ella sirva al interés general. Considera “especialmente grave” tocar la ordenación territorial a través de una ley de vivienda y pide al Gobierno que explique qué se precisa para cambiarlo.
Lo que está claro es que no hay más explicaciones. El Ejecutivo defiende el modelo (María José Sáenz de Buruaga, la presidenta, prometió vivienda protegida “sin precedentes”) y el consejero Roberto Media apela a construir más junto a la iniciativa privada. Sin más. El desenlace dependerá del Parlamento: el PP tiene 15 de los 35 escaños, por debajo de la mayoría de 18, y en 2025 se apoyó en Vox. La enmienda sigue en trámite, de hecho.
El contraste valenciano. Esta misma semana, el PP valenciano registró enmiendas a la Ley del Suelo de la Generalitat para destinar a vivienda protegida parcelas privadas vacías reservadas a equipamientos, según La Vanguardia. Es otro mecanismo y otra región, pero con la misma salvaguarda que aquí está en discusión: esas viviendas quedarían protegidas de forma permanente, sin poder pasar nunca a libres.
Comprando. Esta enmienda no cambia nada a día de hoy, y su efecto futuro admite dos lecturas. Ahora mismo, la vivienda usada cuesta 2.423 euros el metro cuadrado de media en Cantabria, un 14,2 % más que hace un año y, en Santander, en torno a 3.300, unos 264.000 euros por un piso de 80 metros, según mis cuentas. Bosques de Santander, el proyecto que ha prendido el debate, no arrancaría hasta 2029 y reservaría 1.140 viviendas protegidas en su primera fase, frente a las 13.000 personas inscritas en la capital para optar a 282 pisos protegidos en construcción.
El Gobierno sostiene que, con más viviendas, la ídem se abarata. Sin embargo, los críticos temen que lo que se levante sean las típicas colmenas de segundas residencias o viviendas de lujo. Entretanto, la fila ante la puerta para tener piso/casa sigue creciendo (y las llaves siempre están del mismo lado).

articles.title: Russia-Linked Hackers Hit iOS, Android Devices With Exploit Chains via Watering Holes
articles.text:
Russian state-sponsored threat actor Midnight Blizzard is believed to have targeted iOS and Android users in Europe and the US with zero-click exploits targeting n-day vulnerabilities, cybersecurity firm Sekoia reports.
Also known as APT29, Cozy Bear, The Dukes, Nobelium, and Yttrium, and believed to be sponsored by the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), Midnight Blizzard is known for targeting government organizations, diplomats, IT services providers, and NGOs for intelligence gathering.
The attacks uncovered by Sekoia, mounted as part of a large-scale watering hole campaign, involved compromised or cloned high-profile websites of organizations in the US, Ukraine, the Czech Republic, and Bulgaria.
Midnight Blizzard injected malicious JavaScript code in the websites of a Ukrainian gas production company, a major industry trade association, and a far-right European political party, and modified legitimate files on the site of a Bulgarian military-related website.
The code was designed to fingerprint visitors, harvesting browser and device configuration data and sending it in JSON format before the exploit is delivered.
In an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) setup, the APT registered two lookalike domains that acted as reverse proxies for high-profile sites, injecting malicious code into copies of america250.org, the site of the 250th anniversary of American independence, and the website of the Raffles London at The OWO hotel near sensitive UK government institutions.
“By doing this watering hole impersonation of the Raffles London at The OWO, the intrusion set may have sought to target diplomatic delegations and high-profile guests through targeted spear-phishing campaigns. Recent open-source reporting, for example, indicates that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stayed at Raffles London during a visit on 14 October,” Sekoia notes.
The hackers also targeted Ukrainian web analytics service Plerdy in a supply chain attack, adding their malicious code to the tracker file. This exposed hundreds of websites to the exploit kit for one week, including army, special forces, and military equipment (ballistic, UAV) sites.
Sekoia identified three exploit chains (two targeting iOS and one targeting Android) used across the campaign. All three target previously patched vulnerabilities, and the iOS chains rely heavily on the DarkSword exploit kit that was uncovered earlier this year.
The first reimplements the initial remote code execution (RCE) code from DarkSword for arbitrary read/write access, and then exploits CVE-2024-27834 to bypass Apple’s Pointer Authentication Codes (PAC) protection and execute code that steals cookies outside of Safari.
CVE-2024-27834 was patched in May 2024 in iOS 17.5 and iPadOS 17.5, iOS 16.7.8 and iPadOS 16.7.8, macOS Sonoma 14.5, Safari 17.5, tvOS 17.5, watchOS 10.5. On Wednesday, CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog, telling federal agencies to patch it within two weeks.
The second chain relies solely on DarkSword for initial access, code execution, and privilege escalation. The final payload was designed to fully harvest the device: messages, emails, voicemails, credentials, tokens, contacts, calls, calendar entries, browser cookies and history, photos, and iCloud Drive content.
Midnight Blizzard’s last exploit chain targets Android users via CVE-2026-3910, a Chrome vulnerability patched in March as a zero-day, and CVE-2025-27038, a Qualcomm bug patched with Android’s August 2025 security update.
The final payload, AndroSnitch, targets data stored in Chrome, including cookies, account information, passwords, browser history, and Wi-Fi passwords. It is similar to AndroSnatch, a Chrome cookie stealer Google TAG observed in Midnight Blizzard attacks mounted between 2023 and 2024.
“The adoption of packaged n-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation. Over the long term, we assess that the proliferation and reuse of CSV [Commercial Surveillance Vendor] exploits among state-sponsored intrusion sets will likely become more frequent,” Sekoia notes.

articles.title: Stop Letting Your Hard Work Stay Invisible At Review Time
articles.text:
This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!
Hard work rarely speaks for itself.
When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).
That plan stalled my career for about five years.
I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.
So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”
Honestly, it never occurred to me.
I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).
Today, I would take a different approach.
Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.
Now is a great time to start the conversation.
Hard work is invisible by default
Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.
Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.
A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.
Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.
Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)
The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.
Just ask
Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.
If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”
A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)
When the answer is “no”
Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.
Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.
Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.
Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.
—Brian
I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened
Don’t try this at home: To better understand the risk AI slop poses to scientific publishing today, IEEE Spectrum contributor Benjamin Skuse put IEEE’s research integrity checks to the test by submitting two entirely AI-generated papers. “Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up…”

Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill
Policy change doesn’t just come down to paid lobbyists—lawmakers want to hear from working experts, too. One engineer shares what he learned from his first two visits to Capitol Hill.

Could community colleges help fill the coming talent shortage in the U.S. semiconductor industry? Alternatives to four-year university degrees are a promising option for the technicians who will be needed to run new fabs.

articles.title: Box taps Nvidia’s Nemotron for new agent-first content retrieval system | TechCrunch
articles.text:
At its developer conference on Thursday, Box showed off a new feature that will build Nvidia’s Nemotron embedding system into the core of its product.
Called Box Content Retrieval, the new feature allows agents to answer queries far more effectively by relying on the embedded metadata created by Nemotron.
Box says the upshot for users is faster, more accurate, and less expensive queries. Nvidia’s VP of generative AI software, Kari Briski, told TechCrunch that she expects queries to be answered four times faster, with 20% fewer errors and 90% fewer tokens used.
The system will be available to all of Box’s Enterprise Advance customers, rolling out early next year.
“This dramatically boosts both the relevance of our search technology for agents,” Box CEO Aaron Levie said. “Instead of an agent having to kind of read through each document, we can send back chunks from the documents that are most relevant to the user’s query or whatever the task is that the agent is doing.”
The feature is an implementation of Nvidia’s Nemotron Embed project, which offers open-weight embedding models to improve automated retrieval systems. Major labs have often overlooked such models, which use LLMs to pre-process data so it can be better used by agents. The sector has been a focus for Nvidia’s open source model project, with its recent Nemotron release in July topping the RTEB benchmark, which measures retrieval quality.
The system will be most useful when paired with active agents, Box says, giving the example of lawyers, who will ostensibly be able to find relevant clauses and precedents more easily under the new system. Because Nemotron’s embeddings go beyond simple keywords to map underlying concepts, a search tool can surface related legal themes even when different wording or language is used.
While the Nemotron models are freely available, the system also relies heavily on Box’s pre-existing metadata and permission controls, which will make it challenging to recreate from scratch. “We’re probably packing in five different technologies into one simple API,” Levie told TechCrunch.

articles.title: Grimes is going to star in an AI movie that’s coming to theaters
articles.text:
The AI-generated sci-fi film Gods Don’t Give Gifts has added a bit of star power: Pop star Grimes is going to appear in the movie. Billed as “the first AI film to come to theatres,” Gods Don’t Give Gifts is a notable test case for the commercial potential of AI films, and it releases on December 4th. Grimes — who will be lending both her likeness and vocal performance to the movie, which you can see in the clip above — potentially gives the project some legitimacy.
Grimes is going to star in an AI movie that’s coming to theaters
The sci-fi anthology, titled Gods Don’t Give Gifts, releases in December.
AI studio Fable, which is producing the film, claimed in a press release that “casting the likeness of an actor with their spoken vocal performance will become more common with animated films using AI: audiences will see actors, athletes, musicians giving vocal performances with their likeness in films.” Gods Don’t Give Gifts is being directed by Jack London, better known under the online handle Gossip Goblin.
Gods Don’t Give Gifts is an anthology that’s set in a future “where bodies are disposable and consciousness has been commoditized” and depicts what happens when “four interconnected stories collide with the horrifying consequences of humanity’s attempt to transcend the flesh.” Those themes seem to fit pretty snugly with Grimes’ interests, as she has explored themes of transhumanism and artificial intelligence in the past. It’s also not the only AI project she’s working on, with an AI-themed album called Psy Opera in the works.
Here’s the trailer for Gods Don’t Give Gifts:
While there has been plenty of hype around the potential for AI in Hollywood, there’s yet to be a project that shows that the technology is actually a vital storytelling tool. Previous examples, like two different takes on The Odyssey — including one made with Elon Musk’s Grok — have left plenty to be desired.

articles.title: Chasse aux mines : la France dévoile sa solution pour déployer rapidement ses drones en haute mer
articles.text:
La Marine nationale dispose déjà de drones de surface capables de repérer des mines marines. Problème, il leur manque un navire pour les emmener loin des côtes.
Début août 2026, la Direction générale de l’armement (DGA) avait annoncé la commande de 12 drones supplémentaires et l’affrètement de navires pour les porter, sans préciser lesquels. Elle a présenté sa solution le 5 novembre, en marge du salon Euronaval, avec deux plateformes civiles baptisées « Protée », fournies par les Chantiers de l’Atlantique et Les Abeilles International et affrétées pour 10 ans au maximum.
Une nouvelle avancée pour le programme SLAM-F (système de lutte anti-mines du futur), lancé en 2020 pour remplacer tous les moyens de guerre des mines de la Marine.
Des navires de guerre qui se font attendre
Les Protée doivent permettre de mettre en œuvre plus rapidement les drones au large, notamment pour soutenir les forces stratégiques, mais ils ne seront qu’une étape.
Dans un billet publié le 5 novembre, le ministère des Armées rappelle en effet que d’autres navires sont prévus. La DGA prépare l’acquisition de bâtiments de guerre des mines (BGDM) qui permettront « d’aller loin et partout, tant en métropole qu’en projection ».
Reste que ces bâtiments se font attendre. Le rapport annexé au projet d’actualisation de la loi de programmation militaire prévoit leur acquisition « dès 2032 », et 4 exemplaires au lieu de 6 à l’horizon 2035.
D’ici là, la Marine doit réduire sa flotte de chasseurs de mines, de 8 navires fin 2024 à 2 fin 2030. Les Protée et leurs drones devront assurer la relève en attendant les BGDM.
Des navires civils pour embarquer les drones de la Marine
D’après les éléments fournis par la DGA, chaque Protée mesurera 80 mètres pour 4 000 tonnes de déplacement. Un équipage civil conduira le navire, tandis qu’un détachement de la Marine se chargera des opérations.
Pour répondre aux besoins de la Marine, ce navire civil pourra recevoir, sous forme de modules, un poste de commandement, deux drones de surface, deux drones sous-marins, des moyens de neutralisation des mines ou une équipe de plongeurs démineurs.
L’intérêt des drones tient d’abord à la distance qu’ils mettent entre les équipages et le danger. Ils descendent aussi plus bas que les chasseurs de mines, jusqu’à 300 mètres de profondeur contre 100 mètres. Leurs sonars sont épaulés par des algorithmes qui aident l’opérateur à trier les échos, mais la décision de neutraliser une mine « reste toujours humaine », précise le ministère dans son billet.
D’autres drones, commandés à Thales et Exail, sont par ailleurs attendus à partir du premier semestre 2028.
